A sender fixes deliverability. It doesn't fix a list of wrong job titles, and sending more of the same list to more mailboxes just gets you rejected faster. Fix who's on the list, then let Smartlead push it.
Your problem sits upstream

You don't have a sending problem yet, because you don't have anyone to send to. Buying a mailbox rotation before you have a list is paying to scale an empty pipe. Start with who, and the how gets easy.

Smartlead has become the sending infrastructure a large slice of the agency world runs on. Unlimited mailboxes, unlimited warm-up, one inbox for every reply. The two questions worth answering before you pay are whether sending is the thing that's broken for you, and what the invoice looks like once the add-ons land.

The conflict of interest, before anything else: we build Gojiberry, and we don't sell a cold email platform. Every other page ranking for this search is written by a company that sells one, and none of them says so at the top. That shapes what we're able to tell you, so here's the shape. Smartlead sends better than we will, and this review says exactly that.
Table of contents
Here's what sits behind every figure below, including the one test we haven't run.

We worked from the published product on 8 August 2026. That means every tier and every add-on read straight off Smartlead's own pricing page on that date, the self-serve product opened and clicked through, the three pages currently outranking this one read line by line, and the public review corpus on G2, Capterra and Trustpilot pulled the same day. The scenarios we price below are the ones our readers live in: three salespeople at one company, and a five-client agency.

One thing you won't find here is a scorecard of measured deliverability rates. We haven't run a controlled inbox-placement test across identical lists on four platforms, and an invented percentage would be worth less than this sentence admitting it. When we run that test, the numbers land on this page. We pay for every plan ourselves, no vendor read a word of this before publication, and Gojiberry is our own product.

Smartlead is cold email infrastructure. You bring the list and the offer, it handles everything between hitting send and reading the reply: sequences, mailbox rotation, warm-up, deliverability plumbing and a shared inbox that collects answers from every account you've connected.

The defining choice is that neither mailboxes nor warm-up are metered, at any price point, including the $39 entry plan. Most competitors meter one or both, so the sales team that wants twelve sending domains pays the same as the one running two. Pricing moves on contacts and monthly send volume instead of on seats or inboxes.

In a typical stack it replaces the sequencer and the warm-up tool, and on the higher tiers it can absorb the client-reporting layer as well. It doesn't replace your CRM, and it doesn't replace whatever you use to decide who belongs in a campaign.

This is the part most reviews blur, so here it is flat. Smartlead is an excellent purchase for one profile and a poor one for another, and the dividing line is whether you already know who you're writing to.
Good fit
Poor fit

You build a campaign as a chain of email steps with delays between them, and Smartlead adds sub-sequences on top: a branch that fires when a lead behaves a certain way, so a reply of "not now" can drop someone into a slower nurture chain instead of ending the thread. Spintax and variable blocks let each mailbox send a slightly different version of the same message, which is how you keep twenty accounts from looking like one robot.

Every connected mailbox can sit in the warm-up network, exchanging traffic with other accounts so it builds a history before it touches a stranger. Sender rotation then spreads a campaign across all of them, so no single address carries the daily load. Neither feature carries a cap or a surcharge, and that's the single strongest argument for the product.

The master inbox pulls replies from every connected account into one screen, and an AI pass tags each one as interested, out of office, referral or unsubscribe. It works well enough that the tagging is worth trusting for triage, less well for anything you'd act on without reading. On a five-client setup it's the difference between one person handling replies and three.

SmartProspect is the lead database bolted into the platform, so you can search for contacts and push them straight into a campaign without leaving the tab. The filters are the classic set: role, sector, company size, geography. What you can't filter on is whether the company did anything recently, and that gap is the whole reason this article ends where it does. If you'd rather clean a list you already own, our free email verifier will tell you what's still deliverable before you pay to send to it.

SmartDialer adds calling inside the platform, billed from credits starting around $9 a month. It's a reasonable convenience for a team that already calls the same accounts it emails, and it isn't a reason to choose Smartlead over anything else. Treat it as a line item you might switch on later.

SmartAgents handle the writing and the replying: drafting variants, answering common objections, keeping a thread alive without a human touching it. They're competent at the mechanical parts of a conversation. They still work from whatever list you point them at, so an agent with a bad list is a faster way to reach the wrong people.

Separate workspaces let an agency keep each client's campaigns, mailboxes and stats apart, and white label puts the agency's own brand on the dashboard the client logs into. White label is billed for each client workspace rather than once for the account, which is the detail that reshapes the agency math later in this article.
Here's the published grid, read off Smartlead's pricing page on 8 August 2026. The annual column is what you pay per month when you commit for a year, a discount of 17 percent.

Verified prospect emails follow the tiers as well: 2,000 on Basic, 30,000 on Pro, 50,000 on Unlimited Smart and 170,000 on Unlimited Prime. Unlimited Prime also carries three SmartServers with OAuth and at least three client workspaces. Nothing meters the mailboxes or the warm-up here, which is worth repeating because it's the reason the $39 plan works as a real plan and not as bait.
Ultra Premium warm-up sits behind the two Unlimited tiers, so the strongest version of the feature Smartlead sells itself on isn't available on the two plans a small team would pick.
Run the math for a team of three

Three salespeople, annual Pro, nine new mailboxes across three domains. That's $78.30 for the plan, plus $40.50 for the mailboxes at $4.50 each, plus roughly $3.25 a month once you spread the three domains at $13 a year across twelve months. The total is about $122 a month, close to $1,465 for the year. Add the entry tier of inbox placement testing and you're at roughly $171 a month.

Now the agency. Five clients, annual Pro, twenty-five mailboxes. That's $78.30 for the plan, $145 of white label at $29 per client workspace, $112.50 of mailboxes, and $49 of placement testing. The total is about $385 a month against a $78.30 advertised price, near five times the sticker. Nothing here is hidden and nothing here is unfair. It's not the number on the pricing page, and it's the number you'll be paying. If that arithmetic is the reason you're reading, we also keep a list of Smartlead alternatives with their own pricing broken out.

Deliverability is the promise Smartlead is sold on, and the machinery behind it is real. Warm-up runs on every mailbox at no extra cost, rotation spreads volume so no single address spikes, and SmartDelivery will run placement tests that tell you which providers are filtering you before your prospects do.

Two caveats matter more than the marketing suggests. The Ultra Premium warm-up tier is reserved for Unlimited Smart and Unlimited Prime, so a Basic or Pro subscriber gets the standard version. And placement testing is a separate subscription that starts at $49 and climbs to $599, which puts the diagnostic tool out of reach for exactly the small teams most likely to break something.

There's also a recurring complaint in the public review corpus about warm-up pausing without any notification, which is the kind of silence that costs a campaign a week. It shows up often enough to plan around: check the pool yourself rather than assuming it's running.

None of this changes the arithmetic that governs everything else. Google has held bulk senders to a spam complaint rate below 0.3 percent since February 2024, and complaint rate is driven by relevance, not by infrastructure. You can warm every mailbox you own and still cross that line by writing to people who never wanted to hear from you. Sending well and sending to the right people are separate problems, and only one of them is solved by a sender.
Here are the three public scores, all collected on 8 August 2026.
G2: 4.6 out of 5
Around 309 reviews. This is the largest and most product-focused sample of the three, and the one to weight most heavily.
Trustpilot: 3.2 out of 5
128 reviews, read from the listing's public structured data. A full point and a half below G2 on the same product.
Capterra: 4.3 out of 5
Seven reviews. That sample is too small to carry any weight, and we're only listing it so you know we looked.
This is where every page currently ranking above us goes stale. Each of them builds its argument on the gap between the two scores, and each of them quotes a Trustpilot number from a different month.

Forty-odd extra reviews arrived in a few weeks and the score fell. That's a live signal, and it's the sort of thing that gets buried when a page written in May is still the top result in August. Read it carefully before you conclude anything: a falling average during a spike in volume usually means the newest cohort is unhappier than the old one, and it can also mean the product reached a much larger, less patient audience.

The honest explanation isn't that one score is fake. It's that the two sites collect from different people. G2 attracts the operator who runs the tool every day and reviews the product: the sequence builder, the inbox, the warm-up. Trustpilot attracts the person who went looking for somewhere to complain, usually after a support ticket or a billing dispute, and that person reviews the company.

Both scores are true about different things. If you want to know whether the software works, read G2. If you want to know what happens when something goes wrong at eleven at night before a client campaign launches, read Trustpilot. A competitor page noticed this and buried it in an FAQ answer, which is a strange place to put the most useful sentence on the page.

One gap we'll name rather than paper over: G2 publishes sentiment labels with a frequency count next to each, and those counts are the most precise thing available on support quality. They can't be pulled reliably by machine, so ours will be counted by hand and added here rather than estimated now.
Three limits. Calling them defects would be unfair, because they're the edges of what the product set out to be.

Start with a number a rival published and then walked past. Testing Smartlead's built-in prospecting against their own ideal customer profile, they pulled 413 contacts with a usable email address, of which exactly one matched the job title they were targeting. The rest were unrelated functions. They noted it in a single sentence and moved on to the next feature.

That one line is the whole review. The sending worked. The list didn't. And you can't fix a targeting problem by adding mailboxes, because every mailbox you add sends the same wrong list to more people.

So here's the concession no competitor writing about Smartlead can make. If what you need is a cold email platform, buy one. Gojiberry isn't a cold email platform and won't pretend to be. We sit in front of the sending, not in place of it.

Gojiberry is an AI-powered multichannel prospecting platform. It tracks more than 30 buying-intent signals across socials and the web, surfaces the leads who are in-market right now, and triggers personalized outreach across channels. Pricing is $99 a month on Pro, with 2 AI agents and up to 1,800 prospects contacted per month, then Custom for teams of five and up.

This matters more the longer a list sits still. B2B contact data decays at roughly 2.1 percent a month, about 22.5 percent a year, so the file you bought in January is meaningfully wrong by autumn. Signals move in the opposite direction: they're generated by the change that broke your data in the first place.

Smartlead sends brilliantly. Gojiberry decides who is worth sending to, from more than 30 buying signals, and writes the first message.

A note on the price column before you read it. We only publish figures we checked ourselves on the vendor's own page, and the date those figures were checked. Smartlead and Gojiberry were both checked on 8 August 2026. Instantly, Lemlist and Saleshandy were not re-checked for this article, so their rows describe how each one bills rather than quoting a number that might already be three months old. That's precisely the mistake this whole page exists to avoid repeating.
Two of those match-ups have their own pages here: Smartlead versus Lemlist if personalization is what you're weighing, and Smartlead versus Instantly if the choice is between two volume senders.

For an agency whose channel is email, yes, without hedging. Uncapped mailboxes and warm-up at every price point, a master inbox that makes multi-client reply handling survivable, white label, sub-sequences and a dialer if you want one. Budget for the real number rather than the sticker, which for five clients is closer to $385 a month than $78.30, and it still holds up against anything in the category. Nothing in this review argues otherwise.

For a three-person sales team without a list, the answer changes, and it isn't about the money. You'd be buying a strong solution to a problem you don't have yet. Your bottleneck is that nobody knows which forty companies deserve a message this month, and a rotation of nine mailboxes makes that worse by sending the guesswork faster. Fix the list, then buy the sender. If you're weighing the whole category rather than this one product, our roundup of Smartlead alternatives lays the options side by side.
Why we built this instead of another sender

Before Gojiberry there was Coco.ai. Roman spent his days prospecting on socials, and the part that worked was never the tooling. It was catching someone in the week they'd changed jobs, or the fortnight after a funding round, when the message landed as timing rather than as an interruption. He was doing that search by hand, one profile at a time, and it didn't scale past one person.

Coco.ai turned into the place we learned what a signal was worth and how quickly it goes cold. We had already bought the senders. Every one of them asked the same question at setup, which is who do you want to write to, and not one of them helped answer it. So we built the part that was missing.

That's also why this review concedes the cold email case so early. Two products can occupy different halves of the same motion, and pretending otherwise would have made for a worse article and a worse stack.

No. There's a trial, and paid plans start at $39 a month on Basic, or $32.50 a month on annual billing, checked 8 August 2026. That entry plan covers 2,000 contacts and 6,000 emails a month, with no cap on mailboxes or on warm-up, which makes it a real plan and not a trial in disguise.

Take five clients on annual Pro with twenty-five mailboxes. The plan is $78.30, white label adds $145 because it's billed at $29 per client workspace, the mailboxes add $112.50, and entry-level placement testing adds $49. That's roughly $385 a month. The advertised figure for the same setup is $78.30, so plan for close to five times the sticker.

No. Smartlead is an email platform, and there's no social step you can insert into a sequence. Teams that want both usually run a second tool alongside it and accept two subscriptions. If you're heading that way, read our HeyReach review before you pick one.

They're close enough that the answer comes down to how you're structured rather than to features. Smartlead's edge is the agency layer: client workspaces, white label and per-client reporting. Instantly's is a simpler product surface for a single team. Both bill on volume rather than seats, and neither one supplies buying signals, so the gap this article describes applies to both.

SmartProspect will hand you contacts filtered by job title, industry, headcount and geography. Whether that counts as finding leads depends on your standards. One published test against a defined customer profile returned 413 usable contacts with a single one at the right job title, so treat the output as raw material and not as a finished list.

Because the two audiences aren't the same. G2 collects from daily operators judging the software and sits at 4.6 across roughly 309 reviews. Trustpilot collects from people who went looking for a place to raise a support or billing problem and sits at 3.2 across 128 reviews, both checked 8 August 2026. Read G2 for whether the product works and Trustpilot for what happens when it doesn't.

Unlimited in volume, yes, on every tier and at no extra charge. There's a tier distinction worth knowing: Ultra Premium warm-up is reserved for Unlimited Smart and Unlimited Prime, so Basic and Pro subscribers run the standard version. Users also report the warm-up pausing without notification, so check the pool yourself instead of assuming.

That's the intended pairing. Gojiberry watches more than 30 buying signals, surfaces the accounts that moved this week and writes the first message against the signal. Smartlead carries the delivery. The two don't compete for the same job, and a team running both is buying the two halves of one motion rather than the same half twice. Mindflow saw a 31 percent lift in reply rate after switching outbound to an intent trigger.
Tell Gojiberry who you sell to and it starts finding prospects who are already looking. Keep Smartlead for the sending, we handle the who.

Clay plans and prices, as of August 2026
Annual billing takes about 10% off, on both paid plans.
Every plan comes with unlimited seats, so the size of your team doesn't change what the subscription costs.

Enterprise doesn't get a listed price. Contract data aggregated by Vendr puts the median Clay Enterprise deal at around $30,400 a year, with reported contracts running from roughly $12,000 to $154,000.

Free caps tables at 200 rows and excludes phone number enrichment. Launch raises that ceiling to 50,000 rows per table. Enterprise adds custom allocations, unlimited rows and imports, SSO, role-based access control and a dedicated growth strategist, on an annual commitment. Both paid plans open with a 14-day trial.
Clay publishes its prices, so you've already seen the numbers. What you came for is what those numbers cover, and that's the part the pricing page hands back to you.

There's a second problem. Clay rebuilt its lineup on March 11, 2026, and a good share of what you'll read elsewhere still describes Starter, Explorer and Pro, none of which a new customer can buy today. This page gives you the current grid, how the two meters work, and what the invoice looks like once the extras are counted.
Gojiberry finds your prospects for you
Clay gives you the parts to build a prospecting system. Gojiberry ships the finished one, for 99 dollars a month.
Table of contents

Seven things moved on March 11, 2026, and they're the reason older comparison pages read so differently from Clay's own site today. Everything below is reported by third parties rather than announced line by line on the pricing page.
Most of that went the buyer's way. If you land on a page describing Clay as a credit trap that charges you for nothing, check the date on it. It's describing a model that stopped existing in March.
Two meters run at the same time, and they don't measure the same thing. Data Credits pay outside providers. Actions pay Clay.

Clay says around 90 percent of its customers never reach their Actions limit. In practice, Data Credits are the meter that runs dry, and the Actions column mostly tells you how much room you have to keep rerunning a table you're still debugging.
The headline price is two subscriptions added together, and Clay lets you see the split. On annual billing you're buying a year of each meter up front.
Two numbers here look the same and don't mean the same thing
The Actions half of Growth costs $185 a month. Launch, as a whole plan, also costs $185 a month. One is a slice of the bigger plan, the other is the smaller plan.
If a spreadsheet or a sales rep ever hands you the figure on its own, ask which of the two it is before you budget around it.

Both meters scale on their own. When your tables run fine and the credits run out in week three, you raise the credit side and leave the Actions side where it is. That's the useful part of the split, and it's why nobody's real invoice matches the pricing page.

It also means two companies on the same plan can pay double one another. One team enriches 800 rows a month and stays inside the allocation. The other runs a five-column waterfall across 4,000 rows and tops up twice before the month ends. Same plan name, same logo on the invoice, and two totals that don't look anything alike.
Gojiberry watches more than 30 buying signals, checks each account against your ICP, and hands you the ones worth contacting. No tables, no credits, no workflow to debug.
The subscription is the only part a pricing page shows you. Five other line items decide what a Clay stack costs you over a year, and four of them are billed by somebody else.

We're not going to hand you a single annual figure for a five-person team. The total we had drafted rested on a $99 seat price that we couldn't confirm anywhere on the vendor's own plan comparison page when we checked in August 2026, and a headline number we can't verify is worth less than this sentence. The calculator below runs the same arithmetic on figures you control instead.
Pick a plan, add the seats and tools you'd be paying for alongside it, and you'll get an annual figure for the whole stack rather than for the subscription on its own.

Both paid plans open with a 14-day trial, which is enough to build one table and watch what it consumes. If it's the product judgment you want rather than the numbers, our full Clay review covers what it does well and where it frustrates people.

Clay is excellent for a specific team. That team has somebody whose job includes building workflows, and a data problem that no single provider solves, so it's worth combining several sources inside one piece of logic.

The results Clay publishes about its own customers back that up. Intercom grew outbound-sourced pipeline by 140 percent with it. That kind of number doesn't come out of a tool you log into twice a week.

Then there's the shape of the product. Clay is a workflow builder rather than a finished one. Somebody has to design the tables, configure the enrichment columns, debug the lookups that come back empty and watch the credit burn while all of that happens. In a company of 2 to 10 people, that somebody is usually the founder.

Price isn't what decides this one. Whether $167 a month is expensive depends on what it replaces, and the build hours have to come out of somebody's week either way. Work out whose week that is before you pick a tier. If the answer is nobody's, the best Clay alternatives are grouped by how much building each one asks of you.

These two aren't interchangeable, and pretending otherwise would cost you money. Clay does things we don't do at all: CRM enrichment at scale, and waterfalls that chain provider after provider on a single field until one of them resolves it. If your fill rate is the problem, Clay fixes it and we won't.

The difference worth weighing is parts against a finished product. Clay hands you the components and the logic, and you're the one assembling them. We hand you accounts that are moving right now, with the first message already written, and a thinner record than a seven-column Clay table produces.

Launch is $185 a month, or $167 a month on annual billing. Growth is $495 a month, or $446 on annual billing. Free stays at $0 with 100 Data Credits and 500 Actions, and Enterprise is quoted on an annual commitment. Annual billing takes about 10% off either paid plan.

No. Every plan includes unlimited seats, so adding a third or a tenth person to the workspace doesn't change the subscription price. What moves your bill is consumption: the Data Credits your enrichments buy, and the Actions your workflows spend running. A ten-person workspace and a two-person workspace pay the same subscription.

Data Credits do, up to twice your monthly allocation, according to third-party reporting. Actions don't roll over at all and reset each month. So a quiet month banks you some credit headroom, and it banks you no platform capacity.

No, and it isn't sold as that. You get 100 Data Credits and 500 Actions a month, tables cap at 200 rows, and phone number enrichment is excluded. That's enough to see how a table and a waterfall behave, and a hundred credits go in a few dozen records.

They were retired on March 11, 2026. Starter was $149, Explorer was $349, Pro was $800, and Launch at $185 and Growth at $495 replaced all three. Existing customers kept their old pricing, and the window to move between legacy tiers closed on April 10, 2026. If a page still quotes those three, it's out of date.

No. Lookups that return nothing stopped consuming credits in the March 2026 update. Reporting at the time put the old behavior at 20 to 30 percent of a heavy user's monthly allocation, so this is the single biggest change in the buyer's favor.

Not for every workflow, and yes for most of the social ones at any serious volume. Sales Navigator Core is listed at $119.99 per month, or $1,079.88 per year and per license, on the plan comparison page we checked in August 2026. Count it as a separate line when you budget, because somebody else bills it.

Reviewers on G2 and Reddit put the first production workflow at 20 to 40 hours. That covers designing the table, ordering the providers in a waterfall, writing the conditional logic and testing on a small batch before you point it at your whole list. It gets much faster after the first one.
Tell Gojiberry who you sell to and it starts finding companies showing buying signals. 99 dollars a month, no annual contract, no workflow to build.

Apollo plans as of August 2026

Apollo publishes its prices and makes a selling point of doing so, which means you've already seen the four tiers above. What the pricing page doesn't tell you is what one credit buys once you start clicking.
So this page has the current grid, the credit cost of every action Apollo charges for, and the arithmetic of what a team of three or five can do with a month's allowance.
Gojiberry finds your prospects for you
Apollo gives you a database to search. Gojiberry watches more than 30 buying signals and tells you which accounts are worth contacting right now, for $99 a month.
Table of contents
A credit is the unit Apollo bills you in, and one leaves your balance the moment you reveal something. The catch is that reveals aren't priced the same.

Two things follow. Every seat gets its own allowance, so a five-person team on Basic opens each month with 12,500 of them rather than 2,500. That's a real point in Apollo's favor, and several comparison pages get it wrong by describing one pool shared across the account for a year.
The second one decides your budget if you're calling. A mobile costs eight times what an email address costs. A team running email barely watches the meter. A team that dials watches it move all day.
Divide the month's allowance by the price of what you're after and each plan turns into a number of contacts. Here are both extremes, with the whole month spent on one type of reveal.

Real usage lands somewhere between those two columns. The dialer is where the arithmetic turns against you. At 2 credits a minute, a rep who spends two hours a day on the phone burns 240 credits a day, or 4,800 a month. That's past the whole Professional allowance on call minutes alone, before a single contact has been revealed.

Then there's a ceiling almost nobody quotes. Free and Basic cap you at 250 emails a day, and Basic gives you one mailbox per user. Unlimited sending, along with unlimited Google and Microsoft mailboxes, starts at Professional. If volume email is the plan, that daily cap bites well before your credit balance does.
Apollo charges the same credit whether the contact fits your ICP or not, and eight of them for a phone number. Gojiberry works out who is worth contacting first, then hands you the list.
Two add-ons sit outside the plans, and the good news comes first. Both are billed per team rather than per seat, so on a team of five they're one line on the invoice instead of five.
Inbound, $149 a month per team

It identifies companies visiting your website, up to 50,000 a month globally, plus up to 10,000 individual contacts a month in the US only. It tracks 100 domains and enriches 5,000 form submissions a month.
Advanced Dialer, $149 a month per team
It adds international dialing, a parallel dialer, a power dialer and local presence. If your reps call outside the US, this is the line where that lives.

Two conditions are worth knowing before you budget for either one. You have to be on a paid plan before you can add them, so neither is a way to stretch the free tier. And Apollo describes both as introductory pricing that may change.
None of what follows is published on the pricing page. These four points are reported by third parties, so read them as a reason to check your own paperwork before you sign anything.
A tier list doesn't tell you which one you need. What you're doing next month does. Four situations, and where each one lands.
You want to test the data quality before you send anything

Free, with one warning. 100 credits is 100 email addresses or 12 phone numbers, and you're held to 2 sequences, 250 emails a day and a 25-record selection limit in the Chrome extension. It's enough for a sample and too thin for a pilot.
You're running email at low volume with the CRM connected

Basic, at $59 a month, $49 if you pay yearly. That's where unlimited sequences, CRM integrations, waterfall enrichment and 6 intent topics start. Keep the 250-a-day cap and the single mailbox in view.
You're running volume, several mailboxes and US phone outreach

Professional, at $99 monthly, $79 on the annual plan. It's the first tier with unlimited sends, unlimited Google and Microsoft mailboxes, the US dialer, 4,000 minutes of call recording, automated workflows and analytics.
You're calling internationally, or you need SSO and custom reports

Organization, at $149 monthly, $119 annually, with its 3-seat minimum and annual commitment. It adds 12 intent topics, 8,000 recording minutes, customizable reports, advanced security, SSO and the option to plug in your own LLM API key.
That's the invoice side of the decision. If you want the product judgement that goes with it, our full Apollo review covers what the tool is like to live in day to day.
Gojiberry costs $99 a month for the team
Not per seat. No credits to count, and no phone reveal to pay for before you know who you're calling. Tell Gojiberry who you sell to and it starts finding companies showing buying signals.

Start with what Apollo does well, because it's a lot. A small team doing email at volume gets a contact database and a sequencer on one invoice, with no five-figure commitment and no sales call to see a price. Apollo displays a 4.7 out of 5 on its own pages, across more than 9,000 G2 reviews. That score is earned.

The first limit is structural. Pricing is per seat, so it climbs with every hire, while the two add-ons stay flat across the team. Hire two reps and you're paying for their data before either one has sent anything.

The second one is the one that matters at 2 to 10 people. You pay for the reveal before you know whether the contact was the right one. The credit leaves your balance the moment you click, whether the person matches your target or not, and eight of them leave for a direct dial with no more certainty attached than that.
Put a number on it. A five-person team on Professional with annual billing pays $4,740 a year. Gojiberry costs $1,188 for the whole team, flat, with the same five people on it.
If it's the seat math rather than the product that sent you looking, we keep the best Apollo alternatives in a separate piece.

One thing the table can't show. Apollo does things Gojiberry doesn't, in particular the searchable contact database, the dialer and CRM enrichment. If your motion leans on any of those three, that's a solid reason to stay where you are.

The difference worth weighing is the direction of the work. Apollo hands you a search engine and leaves you to guess what to search for. Gojiberry starts from the signal and works back to the company.

Apollo bills per seat. Basic is $59 monthly and $49 with annual billing, Professional is $99 or $79, and Organization is $149 or $119 with a 3-seat minimum and no monthly option. There's also a free seat at $0. Paying yearly takes around 20 percent off, and every figure here was checked in August 2026.

Eight. An email address costs one. So a number is eight times the price of the cheapest reveal. Spend a Professional allowance of 4,000 credits entirely on dialing data and it works out to 500 phone numbers a month, against 4,000 email addresses if you spend it the other way.

No, and this is the point most comparison pages get wrong. Credits are granted per seat and per month, upfront, so a five-person team on Basic opens each month with 12,500 credits because every seat carries its own 2,500. Apollo's own pricing page doesn't describe an annual pool shared across the account.

It's enough to see whether the data holds up on your market. 100 credits buys 100 email addresses or 12 phone numbers, and you're limited to 2 sequences, 250 emails a day and a 25-record selection limit in the extension. As a trial it does the job. As a month of prospecting it runs out in an afternoon.

250 a day on Free and on Basic, with a single mailbox per user on Basic. Unlimited sending, plus unlimited Google and Microsoft mailboxes, starts at Professional. If your plan is volume email, that daily cap decides your tier long before the credit balance does.

Apollo's pricing page describes credits as granted per seat and per month, upfront, and it publishes no rollover policy there. So treat the month as the unit, and check your own agreement before you count on carrying anything into the next one. We'd rather say that than repeat a figure we can't source.

Basic, at $59 a month or $49 with annual billing. It's the first paid tier, and it's where CRM integrations, unlimited sequences, waterfall enrichment and 6 intent topics appear. The free plan doesn't include them, so $49 is the floor if the CRM has to be connected.

Third-party reports describe contracts that auto-renew, with written notice due 30 days before the renewal date. The same reports put payments as non-refundable, and say a downgrade takes effect immediately with nothing back for the remainder of the term. None of that sits on the pricing page, so read your own agreement.

We have all had those weeks · days spent chasing leads that go nowhere. This is where AI for sales prospecting flips the script. It is not here to replace you; it gives you superpowers, moving you from guessing to knowing.

Think of it like a high-powered flashlight in a dark room full of potential customers: it instantly lights up the people already looking for a solution like yours. Here is a practical playbook for making it work · without the common mistakes.
A specialized-tool stack or Gojiberry?
3 quick questions to see which tool actually fits your real outbound needs.
Free . No signup . 60 seconds

Manual slog · 200 calls to a "hot" list that turns out cold · is exactly why AI-driven prospecting is now essential. By sifting data from your CRM, socials and web activity, it uncovers high-quality leads traditional methods miss. It is a shift from spray-and-pray to a laser-focused strategy that respects your time.
Never dump messy CRM data into a new AI tool and expect miracles. AI needs clean, accurate information · garbage in, garbage out.

Forget gut feelings. AI scores analyze thousands of data points · company size, tech stack, recent funding, online behavior · so your time goes to genuine-fit prospects. Companies adopting AI-driven prospecting see an average 25% lift in conversion rates, with top performers hitting 40%, while cutting manual prospecting time by around 30%.

What if you knew a prospect was getting ready to buy before they reached out? AI tracks subtle signals across the web · a decision-maker engaging with a competitor post on socials, a company posting a job listing your product fits. Gojiberry specializes in flagging these moments, turning cold outreach into a warm, perfectly timed conversation.
The set-and-forget trap
Never let AI run fully on autopilot without a human in the loop. You are the strategist; AI is your fast, data-crunching intern. Review its suggestions and guide its focus.
Ignoring data hygiene
Congratulating a CEO on a five-year-old promotion happens when the AI runs on stale data. Clean your CRM before plugging in a tool.
Audit your CRM
Are contact details current? Are job titles still accurate?
De-dupe and standardize
Remove conflicting entries and set a consistent format for names, companies and fields.

This is the foundation · get it wrong and nothing else matters. "Tech companies in North America" is a wish list, not an ICP. Get specific on firmographics (industry, size, revenue, geography), technographics (their current stack), and pain points. Best move: interview your 10 happiest customers, learn why they chose you, and use their exact language to build a hyper-accurate ICP.

With a clear ICP, connect a clean data source and let a platform like Gojiberry scan the market for lookalike prospects that fit your criteria. Instead of digging through databases by hand, you get a curated list of high-potential accounts, many you would have missed.

Good fit is not enough · timing is everything. A good tool constantly monitors for trigger events: a new funding round, a decision-maker starting a new job, or someone at a target account engaging with a competitor post on socials. These signals are your cue to reach out with something immediately relevant.

Use AI to assist, not replace. Let it draft based on the prospect profile and the signals you found, then refine it, inject your personality, and make sure it resonates. That is how you personalize at scale without sounding like a machine.
Gojiberry combines lead identification, intent tracking and enrichment in one connected workflow, so warm, in-market leads land in your CRM or Slack.

The market is saturated. A flashy features list means little · what matters is how well a tool fits your workflow, how easily reps adopt it, and whether it solves the problem you actually have today. The main categories:
Lead-scoring platforms
Rank leads by likelihood to convert · great for prioritizing a large, messy database.
Personalization engines
Pull data from socials, news and announcements to craft hyper-relevant outreach.
All-in-one solutions
Platforms like Gojiberry combine lead identification, intent tracking and outreach in one connected workflow.
First question
Are you overwhelmed with leads, or struggling to find new accounts at all? Pick the tool that fixes your real bottleneck.

Run a small pilot with one or two reps for a month before rolling out. In one survey of 1,000+ sales pros, 45% use AI weekly · 81% reported shorter deal cycles and 80% higher win rates. The top challenges were data quality and CRM integration, which is exactly why you ask those questions upfront.

Start targeting prospects who are actually ready to buy. Gojiberry is your AI copilot for B2B prospecting, surfacing high-intent leads from signals across the web and socials. Free trial, no credit card required.

Treating the AI like a magic wand. Set-it-and-forget-it with messy data sends you on wild goose chases. AI is powerful but not a replacement for your brain · guide it, clean your data, and use your intuition to vet its suggestions. It is a partnership, not a replacement.

Yes. AI does the heavy lifting of finding the reason to reach out · a new product launch, a decision-maker posting about a challenge on socials · so instead of a generic check-in you can lead with genuine relevance. The AI provides context; you provide empathy and connection.

Pull 20 ICP contacts from your CRM and manually check them. Are titles correct? Are they still at the company? If more than 3 or 4 are out of date, you have a hygiene problem. Spend a weekend cleaning up before investing in any tool · it pays for itself.

For most teams, starting with an all-in-one like Gojiberry is smarter: it streamlines the workflow, keeps data in one place and reduces the learning curve. Add specialized tools later if you find a specific gap, but start with a simple, integrated solution.

How many emails do you want to send a day?
emails per day
To send 1,000 emails a day safely you need around 25 inboxes across 9 domains, and 2 to 3 weeks of warm-up before you send anything.
We count 40 emails a day per inbox and three inboxes per domain. And that's before you write a word or find anyone worth writing to 😅
Table of contents

An email outreach automation tool runs a sequence in your place. You load a list, write a first email and two or three follow-ups, connect your sending inboxes, and the tool spaces the sends across the week, stops the sequence the moment someone replies, and drops every reply into one inbox.

Most of them do three more things around that: they warm your inboxes, rotate the sending across them so no single address carries the whole volume, and verify addresses before you touch them. That covers the mechanics. If you want help with the words themselves, our email subject line generator gives you openers to test.
This is the line that decides your bill, and most comparisons skip it. Four of the ten tools below hand you a contact database. The other six expect you to arrive with a list.

Gojiberry, Apollo, Snov.io and Amplemarket include the data. Instantly, Smartlead, Woodpecker, GMass, Saleshandy and Lemlist sell you the sending, and the contacts arrive from somewhere else: a second subscription, a credit pack, an export you built by hand.

What that changes in practice: Instantly Growth costs $47 a month, and Instantly Credits, the lead database, costs its own subscription on top. Two lines, not one. Saleshandy prices its Lead Finder as a separate product from its outreach plan. Woodpecker and Lemlist bundle a small credit allowance and sell you more when you finish it. So when you compare $39 against $99, you are often comparing half a setup against a whole one.

It also changes your week. A sender with no data waits for you every Monday. Somebody has to open Sales Navigator, build the segment, export it, verify it and upload it before anything sends. That hour belongs in the price too.

How to read this table. Every figure comes from the vendor's own pricing page, checked on 30 August 2026. The entry price column shows the cheapest paid plan on monthly billing, with the annual equivalent next to it, because half the confusion on this query comes from pages that quote annual rates without saying so. Apollo and Amplemarket meter per user. Everyone else meters volume.

We opened all ten pricing pages ourselves on 30 August 2026 and wrote down the monthly rate, the annual rate and the unit the meter runs on. We took nothing from another comparison post, because the figures circulating on this query disagree by 20 to 30 percent, and the reason is almost always an annual price quoted as if it were monthly.

We judged three things: whether the tool hands you contacts or waits for you to bring them, what one working setup costs at a real volume rather than at the entry tier, and what each tool does that its neighbours do not. We pay for the tools we write about. No vendor read a word of this before publication.

What we did not do: run ten parallel campaigns on an identical list and score the reply rates. We have not run that test, and an invented percentage would be worth less than this sentence admitting it. So you will find no benchmark we cannot source and no score out of ten. Gojiberry is our own product, it gets the same two paragraphs as everyone else, and we state its volume limit in plain terms further down.

Brings you contacts. Gojiberry reads your website, works out what you sell and who you sell it to, then watches for accounts showing buying signals and adds lookalikes of the people who already convert. It scores each prospect, writes the copy, contacts them across email and social, and drafts your replies in one inbox. Copywriting, sequencing, signal tracking and lead finding sit inside the same subscription.

Price. Pro is $99 a month, billed monthly: two agents prospecting around the clock, up to 1,800 prospects contacted a month, email waterfall enrichment across 15 or more data providers, smart scoring, Copilot mode, and CRM, API and MCP integrations. The Custom plan adds senders across every channel for teams of five and up. A free plan lets you start without a card. Read the 13 intent signals we watch if you want the mechanics.

Does not bring you contacts on the sending plan. Instantly splits its product in two: Outreach handles the inboxes, warm-up and campaigns, and Instantly Credits sells you the lead database as its own subscription. The sending side is the strongest argument here, because every tier includes unlimited email accounts and unlimited warm-up, so the meter runs on emails and contacts rather than on people. A team of twenty pays the same as a team of five.

Price. Outreach Growth is $47 a month on monthly billing, or $37.60 a month on annual, with 5,000 emails and 1,000 contacts. Hypergrowth is $97 a month, Light Speed $358, and Enterprise runs on a quote. Annual billing takes roughly 20 percent off. Add Credits and the real invoice starts nearer $94. If you want the field around it, we mapped the best Instantly alternatives separately.

Does not bring you contacts. Smartlead sells sending infrastructure at agency scale and nothing pretends otherwise. Unlimited mailboxes and warm-up on every tier, rotation across all of them, one master inbox for the replies, and white-label client portals so each client logs into something that looks like yours. That last piece is the reason agencies pick it over Instantly, and it costs $29 a month per client workspace.

Price. Base is $39 a month on monthly billing with 2,000 leads and 6,000 sends, Pro is $94, Unlimited Smart is $174 and Unlimited Prime is $379. Annual billing takes about 17 percent off every tier. The head to head with its closest rival sits in Smartlead vs Instantly.

Brings you a small credit allowance. Woodpecker includes Lead Finder credits in the bundle and sells more when you finish them, so it sits between the two camps. What separates it from everything else here is the meter: you pay for contacted prospects, not for seats or mailboxes. One prospect who receives a five-step sequence counts once, and the counter resets every month. Unlimited email accounts and unlimited team members come with it.

Price. The entry plan is $35 a month on monthly billing for 500 contacted prospects, dropping to around $24 a month on annual. Above that the meter scales with your volume rather than jumping between named tiers. Several add-ons sit outside the base price: LinkedIn outreach per connected account, extra warm-up slots, the integrations and API pack, and an agency panel billed per active client. Below a few hundred prospects a month this is one of the cheapest tools in the category. Above that, the arithmetic turns against it.

Does not bring you contacts. GMass is a Chrome extension that turns Gmail into a mail merge tool. Your campaigns send from your real Gmail address, your list comes from a Google Sheet, and the whole thing lives inside an interface you already know. Nothing else on this page has a setup time measured in minutes. The top tier adds MultiSend, which rotates sending across several Gmail accounts.

Price. GMass raised its prices on 1 January 2026. Standard is $29.95 a month on monthly billing, or $20.75 a month on annual. Premium is $39.95 monthly and $29.08 annual. Professional is $59.95 monthly and $49.92 annual. Team plans start at $175 a month for five users. The ceiling is not the software: Gmail caps you at 500 sends a day on a personal account and 2,000 on Workspace, whatever you pay GMass.

Brings you contacts, and leads with them. Apollo is a database with sequencing attached rather than a sender with data attached, and the order matters. You search a contact pool of more than 200 million records, filter, reveal and push straight into a sequence. A dialer with call recording arrives at the Professional tier. The catch is the credit system: revealing a verified email costs one credit, a phone number costs eight, and credits do not roll over.

Price. A free tier exists and covers evaluation. Basic is $59 per user per month on monthly billing, or $49 on annual. Professional is $99 monthly and $79 annual. Organization is $149 monthly and $119 annual with a three-seat minimum, which puts its real entry near $357 a month. Annual billing takes roughly 20 percent off, and every seat pays full price. The full breakdown sits in our Apollo pricing guide.

Sells the contacts as a separate subscription. Saleshandy's Lead Finder is its own product with its own price, and the outreach plans include only a small starting credit grant. What you get for the low sticker is a competent email-first sender: unlimited connected mailboxes on every tier, sender rotation, warm-up, verification and inbox placement testing during live campaigns rather than only during warm-up.

Price. Outreach Starter is $36 a month on monthly billing, or $25 a month on annual, with 2,000 active prospects. Pro is $99 monthly and $69 annual. Scale is $199 monthly and $139 annual. Annual billing takes around 30 percent off, which is the steepest discount on this page and the reason its headline figure looks lower than Smartlead's. Budget the Lead Finder as a second line if you plan to prospect inside the tool.

Brings you contacts, and verifies them. Snov.io bundles the finder, the verifier and the sender on one credit balance, which suits a founder who would rather manage one subscription than three. Every paid plan carries unlimited seats and unlimited sender accounts, so a five-person team pays what a solo founder pays. Two quotas run at once though: credits for finding and verifying, recipients for sending.

Price. Starter is $39 a month on monthly billing with 1,000 credits and 5,000 recipients. Pro starts at $99 a month for 5,000 credits and climbs with the credit pack you pick. Annual billing takes roughly 25 percent off. A free Trial plan renews 50 credits every 30 days, which is enough to see the interface. LinkedIn automation sits outside every plan at $69 a month per connected account.

Sells the contacts as credits. Lemlist gives you access to a lead database and meters it, so heavy prospecting means buying more. The product itself sells personalisation: custom images with the prospect's logo in them, video thumbnails, and LinkedIn, calls and SMS in the same sequence as the email. Nobody else on this list matches the personalisation assets.

Price. Lemlist reshuffled its plans during 2026. The Email plan is now $69 a month per workspace on monthly billing, or $55 annual, with unlimited users and a 50,000 email monthly cap. Multichannel is $109 per user per month, or $87 annual, with unlimited sends. Enterprise runs on a quote from five seats. Watch the switch: the moment you need LinkedIn, the billing flips from one workspace price to a price per person, and a three-person team goes from $69 to $327 a month.

Brings you contacts. Amplemarket is the closest thing here to what Gojiberry does, and the most expensive: a database of more than 200 million contacts, buying signals, AI agents that research and draft, multichannel sequencing and deliverability tooling in one contract. Teams that buy it usually cancel three or four other subscriptions on the same day.

Price. The Startup plan is $600 a month on an annual term and includes two users, which works out at $300 per seat. Growth includes four users and Elite includes ten, both on a quote. Amplemarket publishes no monthly billing option, so the smallest commitment you can make is $7,200 for a year. That price puts it outside the reach of most teams reading this page, which is worth saying plainly rather than burying.
Every page on this query prices the tools one by one. Nobody adds up a working setup. Here are three, at published prices, for one person doing real outbound.

Two things fall out of that. The middle row is what most teams end up with, and it costs roughly twice the row above it, because the sender and the database are two products with two invoices. And the second seat changes everything: Apollo bills per user, so two people on Professional is $198 a month on monthly billing while the Instantly line stays flat.
What none of these three lines include

The mailboxes themselves. The calculator at the top of this page told you how many inboxes your volume needs. Every one of them is a Google Workspace or Microsoft 365 seat you pay for separately, at roughly $6 to $7 a month each, plus a few dollars a year per domain.
At 1,000 emails a day that is 25 inboxes and 9 domains, so add $150 to $175 a month to whichever row you picked, before the software.
Your sequencer is only as good as your list
Gojiberry reads your website, finds the accounts showing buying signals, writes to them across email and social, and drafts your replies.
You have seen the ten and you have seen the real cost. Here is where we sit in it.

Gojiberry runs the whole sequence of decisions, in order. It reads your website and works out what you sell and who buys it. It watches for the signal: a job change, a funding round, a hire, an interaction with a competitor. It picks the accounts that match your ICP and scores them, so you see the strong ones first. It writes the message with the signal that triggered it. It sends across email and social. Then it drafts your reply when someone answers, and puts every conversation in one inbox.

Pro costs $99 a month and contacts up to 1,800 prospects a month with two agents running around the clock. Email waterfall enrichment pulls addresses from 15 or more data providers. The Custom plan adds senders across every channel for teams of five and up.

The honest limit is volume, not capability. 1,800 prospects a month is not agency-scale infrastructure, and if you push 100,000 emails a month you want Smartlead, not us. We are built for a founder or a sales team of two to ten, where the ceiling is the hour nobody has on Monday morning rather than the sending.
Gojiberry is backed by Y Combinator, used by more than 2,000 teams, rated 4.8, and made and hosted in the EU.

Two agents prospecting for you from 99 dollars
Up to 1,800 prospects contacted a month, each one with the signal that triggered it. No card to start.

Start with the arithmetic from the calculator at the top. Keep one inbox under 40 sends a day, put no more than three inboxes on a domain, and 1,000 emails a day means around 25 inboxes across 9 domains. There is no configuration that gets you around that, and no plan you can buy that changes it.
Then five steps, in this order.
Read any pricing page on this list and you will find deliverability presented as a feature you buy. Some of it is. Here is the honest split.
What a platform controls
Authentication, sending pace, rotation across inboxes, warm-up, list verification and the unsubscribe mechanism.
What it cannot control
Complaints from people you wrote to, stale data, a domain you already burned, and the receiving provider's final filtering decision.
Where the line falls
The tool handles the mechanics. Whether people want your email decides the rest, and no vendor can sell you that.

One number worth knowing if you scale: Google applies extra requirements to anyone sending 5,000 or more messages a day to Gmail accounts. SPF and DKIM, a DMARC record, valid forward and reverse DNS, TLS, one-click unsubscribe, and spam complaints kept below 0.30 percent in Postmaster Tools. Those are Google's own published email sender guidelines, and they apply whatever software you send with.

People ask about this rule on every cold email query and nobody answers it. It splits where your result comes from: 30 percent from the list, 30 percent from the offer, 50 percent from the timing and the relevance of writing to that person now. Some versions swap the middle two.

Treat it as a rule of thumb rather than research. We have seen no study behind those numbers and we are not going to pretend otherwise. What survives the arithmetic is the part that matters: better targeting beats better wording every time, and the hours you spend rewriting a subject line for a list of the wrong people return nothing.

So spend your effort in that order. Get the list right, get the offer right, then write. When you reach the writing, our cold email templates give you twelve openers built around a specific trigger rather than a first name variable.
Three checks, in this order, before you put a card down.
Three moments, and they are not negotiable.

A real reply. The second a human writes back with a real sentence, the sequence stops and you answer. Every tool here does the stopping. You do the answering. Our follow-up email generator covers the touches before that point, not after it.

An objection. Somebody tells you they already use a competitor, or that the timing is wrong. Nothing automated has enough context to answer that well, and the attempt reads as automated to the person on the other end.
Anything about price. The moment money enters the thread, a person takes the keyboard. That is the conversation you ran the whole campaign to get.

Four pieces, in order. Buy separate sending domains and create your inboxes on them. Warm every inbox for two to three weeks. Build a list and verify it. Then connect the inboxes to a sequencer, write a first email and two or three follow-ups, and let the tool space the sends and stop on reply.
The order matters more than the tool. People usually buy the sequencer first and discover the domain and list work afterwards, which costs them a fortnight.

It depends on whether you arrive with a list. If you have the contacts and want volume, Instantly at $47 a month or Smartlead at $39 give you unlimited inboxes and no per-seat fee. If you want the database in the same subscription, Apollo at $59 per user or Snov.io at $39 cover both.
If the problem is that nobody on your team has time to build the list every week, that is where Gojiberry sits, at $99 a month flat with up to 1,800 prospects contacted.
Yes, and plenty of teams do. Every sender on this page accepts a CSV, so an export from Sales Navigator, a conference list or your own CRM works fine. Verify it before you send.

The cost moves rather than disappearing though. You save the data subscription and you spend the hours instead, every week, and the quality of the list becomes whatever the person building it had time for that Monday.
Around 40 a day from one inbox, once that inbox has warmed for two to three weeks. Past that, providers start throttling you and your reputation drops before your reply rate does.

So the volume you want decides your infrastructure, not your plan. 1,000 a day means roughly 25 inboxes across 9 domains. The calculator at the top of this page does the arithmetic for whatever number you have in mind.
Not because they are automated. They land in spam because the domain is new and unwarmed, the authentication is missing, the list bounces, or too many people mark the message as unwanted.
Fix the first three yourself with SPF, DKIM, DMARC, warm-up and verification. The fourth is not a technical problem: it means you wrote to people who had no reason to hear from you.
No. Instantly, Smartlead, Woodpecker, Saleshandy, Snov.io and Lemlist all include warm-up in the subscription, and Instantly and Smartlead put no limit on how many inboxes you warm.
Standalone warm-up tools made sense when senders charged extra for it. In 2026 you are usually paying twice for the same thing.

Four on this page do both: Gojiberry, Apollo, Snov.io and Amplemarket. The difference between them is what triggers the outreach. Apollo and Snov.io give you a database to search, so you still decide who and when. Gojiberry and Amplemarket watch for a signal and bring you the account with the reason attached.
The price gap is large. Amplemarket starts at $600 a month on an annual term for two users. Gojiberry Pro is $99 a month, billed monthly.

Gojiberry finds who to write to, writes it, sends it and prepares the reply. You show up for the meeting.

It's built for people who want outbound to be cheap and fast to set up. Freelancers, founders doing their own prospecting, small sales teams where email is the main channel. On that job it's one of the better buys at the price.

This review keeps circling a different question. Sending more email is a solved problem in 2026. Working out which twenty people on a list of two thousand deserve a message isn't solved, and no sending tool decides it for you.

Yes, if you need a cold email tool and you already know who you're emailing. It's easy to learn, the sequence builder does what you'd expect, and $34 a month on annual billing buys a lot for the money. For a two to ten person team where email carries the pipeline, it holds up.

It's a weaker call if your problem sits upstream. When you're unsure which accounts to contact, a better sending engine doesn't move the number you care about. That gap is where most of this review lives.

I ran the seven-day trial on my own domains, connected two mailboxes, built a three-step sequence with follow-ups, and pulled a small list out of Lead Finder to see what the data looked like. Every price in this article comes from the Saleshandy pricing page and was checked on September 3, 2026, add-ons included. We pay for the tools we write about, and no vendor read a word of this before publication.

What you won't find here is a scorecard of measured reply rates or inbox placement. I haven't run a controlled send across several platforms on one identical list, and a made-up percentage would be worth less than this sentence admitting it. When we run that test, the numbers land on this page. One disclosure to get out of the way: Gojiberry is our own product, and our client results sit in full on the case study hub.

Saleshandy is a cold email and outreach platform. The core of it is the sequence engine: you connect as many mailboxes as you like on any plan, rotate sends across them, and run multi-step follow-ups that stop the moment someone replies.

Around that sit the pieces most teams would otherwise buy separately. Lead Finder is now included on every plan, with 1,500 to 8,000 credits a month depending on the tier, drawing on a database of 852 million contacts. One credit reveals a verified work email and six reveal a mobile number. Warm-up, email verification, a unified inbox for replies and CRM integrations come with the subscription.
There's a calling add-on and a light CRM view, and a sequence can hold manual tasks and call steps next to the email ones. Email is still the center of gravity, and everything else orbits it.
Two limits, and they're different in kind. The first is a scope choice you can live with. The second decides whether the tool solves your problem at all.

Saleshandy will drop calls and manual tasks into a sequence, and there's a dialer add-on at $23 to $55 a month. What it won't do is run a genuine multichannel motion across the social channels where a lot of B2B conversations now start. If email is your channel, fine. If you want a prospect touched in three places over two weeks, you'll be stitching tools together and paying twice.

There's also a ceiling on the send-more strategy. Google holds bulk senders to a spam complaint rate under 0.3%, and the quickest route across that line is a well-written email sent to people who never asked for it. Volume without targeting has a price, and it lands on your domain reputation rather than your invoice.
Lead Finder hands you an email address that resolves. Whether the person behind it is in the market this quarter is a separate question, and the database can't answer it.

B2B contact data decays at roughly 2.1% a month, close to 22% across a year, so a list you built in January is meaningfully wrong by summer. Verification catches the bounces. It won't tell you that a company just opened a role you sell into, or swapped out a tool in its stack.

That's the split. Saleshandy helps you contact prospects. Gojiberry works on which prospects deserve contacting in the first place, by watching signals across socials and the web and surfacing the accounts that moved this week. Mindflow lifted its outbound reply rate 31% by triggering on the signal instead of the list, and the write-up is here.
Find prospects showing real buying signals before you reach out.
Three published plans plus a custom Enterprise tier. Annual billing knocks roughly 30% off the monthly rate, and the figures below were taken from the pricing page on September 3, 2026.

For what's in the box, that reads fair. Starter gives you 2,000 active prospects, 6,000 emails a month and 1,500 lead credits, which is enough to find out whether outbound works for you at all. Pro is where most teams settle, at 30,000 active prospects, 100,000 emails and 4,000 credits a month.
What a team of three pays

The subscription isn't the whole bill. Mailboxes are an add-on at $2.99 to $3.99 each per month and domains cost $14 a year, so a three-person team on annual Pro with twelve mailboxes and three domains lands near $115 a month against a $76 sticker. Still inexpensive for this category. Budget from the setup you'll be running rather than the banner price.
People compare the two because both end with an email in somebody's inbox. They start from opposite ends of the same motion.

Saleshandy is about reaching prospects. It gives you the database, the sequence engine and the deliverability plumbing, then leaves the targeting call to you. That's a reasonable division of labor when you know your market cold.

Gojiberry starts a step earlier. It watches for the moments that make an account worth writing to, a hiring signal, a tool change, a funding round, and hands you the account with the reason attached. Same channel, different question answered.

Job moves are the clearest case. Median US job tenure runs 3.9 years, and about 22% of employees have been in post under a year. On any list you own, a slice of your buyers changed seats and nobody sent you a memo.
of Wispra's weekly demos now come from intent signals rather than list-based outbound.

network growth at Baur Software by scaling outreach that still read as personal.

Lemlist costs more and does more with it. The personalization work and the multichannel steps are further along, so it earns the premium when your messages carry images, custom pages or several channels. Saleshandy is the simpler and cheaper tool, and for plain email sequences the gap narrows fast. Our full take sits in the Lemlist review.

Both are strong at the same job, and choosing between them comes down to workflow rather than capability. Instantly's inbox management has its fans, while Saleshandy bundles more contact data into the base plan. Neither one tells you who to write to. There's a longer breakdown in the Instantly review.

LOOK ELSEWHERE IF

So: worth it, inside a boundary. As a sending tool for a small team, Saleshandy is one of the best value options on the market this year. As an answer to who should be receiving those emails, it isn't one, and no amount of extra sending capacity turns it into one.
Why we built Gojiberry

Before Gojiberry there was Coco.ai, and Roman spent his days prospecting on socials for it. He'd check who had changed jobs, who was hiring, who had just posted about a problem we solved, then write to those people by hand. The messages that worked weren't better written, they were better timed.

Doing that manually caps out around thirty accounts a week, and it dies the moment you're busy closing. So we built the watching part into software and kept the writing human. Coco.ai was the training ground, and everything we got wrong there is why the signal comes with a reason attached instead of a score.

Starter is $34 a month billed yearly, or $41 month to month. Pro is $76 annual or $99 monthly, and Scale is $149 annual or $189 monthly. Enterprise is quoted on your volume. Mailboxes, extra credits, the dialer and inbox placement testing sit outside those figures, all checked September 3, 2026.

Yes. It's the strongest thing the product does. Small teams running straightforward outbound get unlimited mailboxes, sender rotation, warm-up and follow-ups without a per-seat bill. If you need something to load into that sequence, we keep a set of cold email templates that still get replies.

It does. Lead Finder comes with every plan and covers 852 million contacts and 42 million companies, filtered by title, seniority, industry, headcount, location and tech stack. You spend 1 credit per verified email and 6 per mobile number, and unverified results cost nothing. Monthly allowances run 1,500 on Starter, 4,000 on Pro and 8,000 on Scale.

Not in a meaningful sense. The filters include hiring signals and firmographics, which help you describe a segment, and that's contact data rather than intent. Intent is behavioral: a company adding roles you sell into, changing a tool, raising money, publishing something that reveals a problem. Gojiberry tracks more than 30 of those signals and surfaces the account while the moment is still live.

Depends what's broken. Lemlist if you want deeper personalization and multichannel sequences and you'll pay for them. Instantly if you want a comparable sender with a different interface. Gojiberry if the sending already works and the targeting doesn't, since we pick the accounts and the timing before anything gets written.

No permanent free tier. There's a seven-day trial with no card required, capped at 100 sent emails, 2,000 prospects and 50 lead credits. That's enough to judge the interface and the data quality, and not enough to judge deliverability.

That's the pairing that makes sense. We decide which accounts moved and why, Saleshandy carries the delivery at volume. Wispra now sources 60% of its weekly demos from signals rather than a static list, and there's a full set of client results if you want the detail.

HeyReach solves one problem with unusual precision: running a lot of sender accounts from a single dashboard without losing track of who said what to whom. The only question worth answering on this page is whether that's your problem.
Table of contents

Three things went into this page. We read the pricing grid on the vendor's own site on August 10, 2026 and took every number from there, because comparison articles still quote plan names HeyReach has retired and discounts that expired. We went through the plan grid tier by tier, counting what each one includes in senders, credits and branding rights. And we read the public review corpus rather than cherry-picking from it, then summarized the recurring complaints in our own words further down.

One thing you won't find here: a scorecard of measured acceptance rates across sender accounts. We haven't run a controlled test on an identical list, and an invented percentage would be worth less than this sentence admitting it. When we run it, the numbers land on this page. Gojiberry is our own product and it gets one section, near the end, where we say what it replaces and what it doesn't. We pay for the tools we write about, no vendor read a word of this before publication, and our customer results are published case by case.

HeyReach is a cloud platform for running outreach across several LinkedIn sender accounts at once. It launched in 2023 out of an agency problem: when you run outbound for eight clients, each with three sender profiles, you spend your morning logging in and out of twenty-four accounts and answering replies in twenty-four separate inboxes.

The architecture matters more than the feature list. Campaigns execute on HeyReach's servers instead of your browser, so nothing pauses when you shut your laptop. Each sender gets a dedicated residential proxy on the entry plan, and that keeps a team of five from looking like five people sharing one connection. And a single campaign can draw from several senders at once, rotating the sending between them instead of stacking it on one profile.

In a stack, it replaces the per-seat automation extension and the spreadsheet you were using to track which account touched which prospect. It doesn't replace your data source. It was never designed to.
Good choice if
Bad choice if

Is HeyReach your tool?
