An icebreaker is the first line someone reads before they decide whether you're worth two more seconds. Get it wrong and the rest of your message never gets read at all. The generator above writes one for you, whether it's a cold message on socials, a first email, a discovery call, or the Monday standup.
It's free, there's no sign-up, and nothing you type leaves your browser. Below the tool you'll find 50 openers we use ourselves, sorted by moment, with the reason each one works.
A great first line still needs the right person on the other end. Gojiberry finds the ones already looking.
Table of contents

An icebreaker generator takes a bit of context, who you're talking to and where, and hands back an opening line you can use straight away. The good ones don't invent a personality for you, they give you a shape to pour your own detail into. That distinction matters more than it sounds. A line like "hope you're doing well" is technically an opener and it does nothing. A line that names something specific about the person buys you the next sentence.

Most of the tools ranking for this search were built for meeting facilitators. Ours started somewhere else, in a sales team that was tired of sending openers nobody answered. So it covers both jobs, and it doesn't pretend they're the same job.

The first job is warming a room. Eight people join a call, half have their cameras off, and someone has to make the first thirty seconds bearable. Here the icebreaker is a group question, it's low stakes, and the only real failure mode is being boring or making someone uncomfortable.

The second job is earning attention from a stranger. You're one of forty messages in an inbox that day. Here the icebreaker isn't small talk, it's evidence that you did some homework. The stakes are completely different, and so is the writing. A question that works beautifully in a standup will get you deleted in a cold email, because it costs the reader effort and gives them nothing back.

Pick the moment first. The tool writes differently for a cold message than it does for a Monday standup, and that choice changes everything downstream. Then pick a tone. Direct works when the person is senior and busy, warm works when there's already a loose connection, and playful works when your market is small enough that being memorable beats being safe.

The one field that decides whether this is useful is the second one. "What you noticed" is where your homework goes. Write the real thing: she's hiring two SDRs, they shipped four integrations last quarter, he wrote a post arguing that intent data doesn't work. If you leave it empty, you'll get a generic line, and a generic line is worse than no line because it signals effort you didn't make. For a team meeting, put the topic there instead, like the sprint or the reorg.
Hit generate and you'll get three versions. Take the one that sounds like you'd say it out loud. Regenerate as many times as you want, there's no limit and no credit counter.

These aren't theoretical. The openers below come from campaigns we run and campaigns our customers run. Mindflow rebuilt their outbound around intent signals and moved their reply rate up 31 percent, and the first line was a big part of that.
Read the Mindflow case study

Five moments, ten openers each. Steal them, but swap in your own detail, because the detail is the whole point. The line underneath each one explains why it works, so you can build your own instead of running out after ten.

Reply rates have been falling for years. Instantly's benchmark analysis puts the average cold email reply rate at 3.43 percent in 2026, down from around 8.5 percent in 2019. The inbox got crowded, filters got smarter, and a lot of that crowding is low-effort AI output. Which means the bar for a first line went up at exactly the moment it got easier to generate one.

Depth is what still moves the number. An analysis of 11 million emails by Hunter found that real personalization lifts reply rates by 52 percent, and that small, tightly targeted campaigns beat broad blasts by a factor of 2.76. Merge tags don't count as depth. Everyone has a first name.
Four things separate the openers that work from the ones that don't.

There's a fifth thing that isn't about the sentence at all. Keep the whole message short. Woodpecker's data on more than 20 million cold emails points the same way as everyone else's: under 80 words does better than anything longer. A brilliant opener attached to a 200 word message is still a 200 word message.
These four show up in roughly half the cold messages we receive. They're not offensive, they're just invisible, which is worse.
"I hope this email finds you well"
It finds them nothing. This costs you the one line where you had their attention, and it tells them a template is coming.
"I came across your profile and was impressed"
Impressed by what? Without the specific, this is the written version of eye contact with no words.
"Congrats on the new role!"
Fine on its own. Useless when the next sentence pivots to a demo, because it exposes the compliment as a hinge.
"Quick question for you"
It's never quick and it's rarely a question. Readers have learned this, and the pattern now triggers suspicion.

There's one more that deserves its own sentence, because AI made it common. The opener that describes what the company does back to the company. "As a leader in workflow automation, you're no doubt focused on efficiency." They know what they do. Telling them proves only that a model read their homepage.
Finding the person who's  in-market this week is the hard part. Gojiberry tracks over 30 buying-intent signals across socials and the web, then hands you the leads worth writing to.

Every generator on this page, ours included, solves the same narrow problem: the blank page. You've got a name, you've got a fact, you want a sentence. That's a real problem and it's now a solved one.

What no generator knows is whether this week is the right week to write at all. The same opener, the same person, the same product, sent in March instead of June, is the difference between a reply and silence. Timing isn't a writing problem, so no writing tool can fix it. It's an information problem.

Gojiberry is an AI-powered multichannel prospecting platform. It tracks over 30 buying-intent signals across socials and the web, surfaces the leads who are in active research right now, and triggers personalized outreach across several channels. The order matters: the signal comes first, and the first line is written from the signal. That's why the opener has something real to say.

Take a realistic small team: three people selling, roughly 400 prospects a month between them. That's about 130 each, or six a day. Written properly by hand, six good openers a day is around forty minutes of research and writing, which is fine. The problem isn't the writing at that volume, it's deciding which 400 names go on the list in the first place.

Most small teams get this backwards. They build a list of 400 from filters, then spend their energy making 400 mediocre messages sound personal. The better order is to let the signals build the list, so you're writing 400 openers to people who already did something that suggests they care. Same effort, completely different denominator.
That right column is the honest gap in every free tool, this one included. It's also, more or less, the product roadmap of every serious prospecting platform.

You're writing thirty messages a week between two customer calls and a bug you shouldn't be fixing. You don't need a better process, you need to not stare at an empty box at 9pm. Use the direct tone, paste one real detail, send the version that sounds like you.

This is who we built it for. At this size nobody has an ops person writing sequence libraries, and everyone is improvising their own openers, which means the team's messages sound like five different companies. Generating from the same tool with the same tone setting fixes that in a week, for free.

Pick the meeting or remote setting and you'll get group questions instead of sales openers. The trick with these isn't the question, it's the timebox. Say the limit out loud before the first person answers, otherwise ten seconds becomes four minutes.

Same settings, different room. If the group doesn't know each other, avoid anything that requires a work anecdote, because half the room won't have one that fits. Questions about objects and habits beat questions about achievements every time with a cold audience.
An opener is worth measuring only at the end of the chain. Here's what happened for four teams that changed what they wrote by first changing who they wrote to.
Mindflow

Wispra
60% of their weekly demos now come from intent signals. Read it

Over 100 meetings after moving from email blasts to intent-based outreach. Read it
Baur Software
Network doubled by scaling authentic outreach rather than volume. Read it

The pattern across all four is the same and it's slightly deflating if you love writing: the opener improved because the list improved. When the person on the other end just posted about the exact problem you solve, the first line writes itself. When they didn't, no amount of wordcraft saves it. All four stories are on the case study hub.
Why we ended up building this

Before Gojiberry there was Coco.ai. Roman spent his days prospecting on socials, and he was doing by hand exactly what this page describes: reading posts, spotting the people who'd just said something that suggested a need, and writing a first line from it. It worked. It also ate his week.

Coco.ai became the place we learned what a buying signal looks like, and how quickly a good one goes cold. The generator you used at the top of this page is the small, free version of that idea. The rest of it, the part that watches for the signal in the first place, is what we spent the last two years building.
The icebreaker is one line. These handle the rest of the message, and they're all free with no sign-up.

Yes, completely. No sign-up, no credit card, no credit counter, no limit on how many times you hit generate. The tool runs entirely in your browser, so nothing you type is sent to a server or stored anywhere.

Four things. It names something the reader can verify in five seconds, the detail is recent rather than dug out of an archive, it can be answered in a single line, and it connects to the reason you're writing. Miss the last one and the opener reads as a hinge, which is worse than having no opener at all.

One sentence, two at most. The whole message matters more than the opener in isolation, and the data is consistent on this point: cold emails under 80 words outperform longer ones. If your icebreaker is eating 30 of those words, it's too expensive.

Yes, and the generator has two settings for exactly that, team meeting and remote team. Just don't mix the two families. A group question that works in a standup will get you deleted in a cold email, because it asks the reader for effort and gives them nothing in return.

They get more replies than a blank page or a template, and fewer than a line written from a real, recent signal. Personalization depth is what moves the number, not the fact that a model wrote the sentence. Mindflow rebuilt their outbound around live intent signals and lifted their reply rate by 31 percent, and you can read how they did it.

You can, and for a single message it's a fine choice. The difference is consistency and speed at volume. This tool gives you three structured options in one click without a prompt, which matters when a small team wants everyone's openers to sound like the same company. Neither option solves the real bottleneck, which is knowing who to write to this week.

The subject line earns the open, the icebreaker earns the read. They should never say the same thing. If your subject line already spends your best detail, the first line of the email has nothing left to prove and the reader feels the drop immediately.
A perfect first line to the wrong person is still a cold message

You want the cheapest way into a first sequence, and the templates will teach you the shape of one. Layer intent on top once the motion works and the volume stops being the problem.
Try the cheaper route
Dripify starts at $39 a seat on annual billing, $59 month to month. Waalaxy starts at €19 a seat. Neither of those is the number most teams end up paying.

For a solo founder watching every euro, Waalaxy wins. For anyone who wants campaigns running with the laptop shut, Dripify wins, and it's the better pick for most people who land on this page. Below: both price grids, the safety difference, and the three-rep math that settles it.
Gojiberry finds the accounts worth writing to
Both of these tools automate how you send. Gojiberry decides who you send to, from more than 30 buying signals.
Table of contents

Both tools do the same job at different levels of commitment. They push a list you already have through a sequence of connection requests, messages and follow-ups. The split that matters isn't feature depth, it's where the software runs.

Dripify runs on the vendor's machines, so you close your laptop and the campaign keeps going. Waalaxy runs as a Chrome extension inside your own session, which makes your browser the engine. That one architectural choice explains most of the price gap, most of the safety argument, and most of what people write in reviews on either side.
Both pricing pages read in August 2026. Annual billing means one upfront payment on either side, and both vendors quote per user.
If you read those seven rows and neither column feels right, that's a useful result rather than a failure of the comparison. Three tools sit next door to this one.

Expandi and HeyReach figures come from their public plan pages and third-party trackers rather than our own account, so confirm the current rate before you budget. We put HeyReach and Waalaxy side by side here.
How we compared these two

We read both pricing pages on the same afternoon in August 2026, priced every tier at one, three and five seats, and took the public ratings from G2 and Capterra rather than the badges each vendor picks for its own site. We ran the plan quotas against the invitation ceiling the platform enforces, because capacity you can't legally spend isn't capacity.

One thing you won't find here: a stopwatch on campaign setup. We haven't timed a first launch in both tools on the same list, on the same day, with the same copy, and an invented figure would be worth less than this sentence admitting it. When we run it, the number lands on this page and the badge comes back with it. We pay for the plans we test, and no vendor read a word of this before publication.

Dripify is a cloud platform for social sequences. You connect an account, import a list off a search or a CSV, then build a campaign out of profile visits, invitations, messages and follow-ups with delays between each step. Everything runs on Dripify's servers, so the campaign doesn't care whether your machine is on.

It's built for someone who already knows the target list and wants it worked through reliably. Solo founders use it that way, and so do three-person sales teams, though the per-seat bill is what eventually sends them looking around.

The tiers gate more than volume, which is the part the pricing page doesn't shout about. Basic holds you to one campaign at a time and leaves out CSV export. Pro opens unlimited campaigns and it's where most solo users land. Advanced adds team management and it's the tier agencies get pointed toward. Every plan includes 100 email finder credits a month, which covers about two days of real work.
What works
Where it costs you

Public sentiment sits in a narrow band. Dripify holds 4.5 out of 5 across 333 reviews on G2 and 4.7 across 476 on Capterra, both checked in August 2026. Praise clusters on setup being short and the interface staying out of the way. Complaints cluster on two things: what the per-seat model does to a team budget, and how thin the personalization gets once you're past the obvious variables.

Waalaxy is a Chrome extension from a French team, built so someone who has never automated anything can launch a sequence the same afternoon. You import prospects straight from a search, pick a prebuilt sequence, and it starts working through the list. The extension is the engine, which is the source of both the simplicity and the main limit.

Pro at nineteen euros gives you 300 invitations a month and 25 email finder credits. Advanced at €49 raises invitations to 800 and adds API access with Zapier, Make and n8n modules. The Business plan at €69 is the first tier with cold email sequences and multiple sender accounts, and it lifts credits to 500. The inbox is a paid add-on on every tier, including the most expensive one.

One detail changed quietly and it's worth knowing before you plan around it. The pricing page now shows three paid plans and a fourteen-day trial, with no free tier displayed, while most comparisons still describe a permanent free plan capped at 80 invitations a month. If that plan is part of your decision, check inside the app rather than trusting an article, this one included.

Review volume is where the two part company. Waalaxy sits at 4.6 out of 5 across 1,315 reviews on G2 and 4.4 across 253 on Capterra, checked on the same morning. Ease of use scores above value for money on both platforms, and the written reviews say the same thing in longer form: people like the tool and flinch at the renewal.
This is where the two stop feeling like the same product. The order of operations differs, and it shapes what your first hour looks like.

You run a search, open the extension, and push the results into a list inside Waalaxy. Then you pick a sequence from the template library, which is where the tool earns its reputation. The sequences are named for what they do, so you're choosing rather than designing. Personalization comes next, and it comes step by step: each message opens its own panel, so a three-touch sequence means moving in and out of three panels and holding the thread of your own copy in your head. Then you launch, and you leave the browser open.

You connect the account once, import from a search URL or a CSV, then open the campaign builder and drag the steps into place. Visit, invite, wait two days, message, wait three, follow up. Conditions branch the path, so the people who accept get one message and the ones who don't get another. The copy for every step sits on one screen, which sounds minor until you're editing the third touch and can still see the first. You launch, and you close the laptop.

The trade shows up on the second campaign rather than the first. Waalaxy gets you moving faster when you don't yet know what a sequence should look like. Dripify is slower to learn and faster to reuse, because a campaign you've built once is a shape you duplicate and edit rather than reassemble. If your copy is the part you're unsure about, our cold email generator writes a first draft you can paste into either builder.

What we can't give you is the number of minutes. Timing both launches on the same list, against one list, one sitting, one set of messages, is a real test that deserves real numbers, and we'd rather leave the line empty than fill it with an estimate.
Both dashboards show the same headline numbers: invitations sent, acceptance rate, replies, messages delivered. The differences are in what you can slice and what you can take with you.

Dripify reports per campaign and per team member, with conversion between steps, and the highest plan adds split-test results so you can see which of two openers is doing the work. Export is where the tier gate bites hardest. On Basic there's no CSV export at all, so your numbers stay inside the tool and your CRM stays uninformed.

Waalaxy sorts campaigns into running, paused, draft and archived, and reply detection pauses a sequence the moment someone answers, which saves you from the worst kind of automated follow-up. Handling those replies is the part that costs extra. The inbox sits outside every plan, so at €69 a month you're still looking at a separate line to answer at scale.

Neither dashboard reports the number that decides the quarter, which is whether the people in the campaign were worth contacting at the moment you contacted them. A 42% acceptance rate on the wrong 400 accounts still ends the month at zero, and no chart in either tool will tell you that's what happened.
Both connect to a CRM. What separates them is how often you have to think about it afterward.

Waalaxy syncs with more than 2,000 tools through Zapier, Make and n8n, and API access opens on the Advanced plan. Set the connection once and new leads leave on their own. Imports run the other way too, from a standard search, from Sales Navigator, or from Recruiter Lite, and CSV moves in both directions from the entry tier.

Dripify pushes through Zapier and webhooks as well, and the tier that opens them sits somewhere above Basic. Sources disagree on whether that's Pro or Advanced, and the vendor's own pages aren't consistent either. If the integration is the reason you're buying, confirm the tier on their plan comparison before you commit to a year.

The detail worth checking on a trial, in both tools, is whether a connection is configured once for the account or rebuilt for every campaign. A tool you reconfigure each Monday costs more than what's on the invoice, and the cost is paid by whoever has the least time.

Start with the part nobody controls. The platform doesn't publish its limits. What's widely observed is a ceiling around 100 invitations in a rolling seven-day window, and it moves with account age, acceptance rate, and how many requests you've left hanging.

Run that against the plans and something odd shows up. Waalaxy's Advanced tier sells 800 invitations a month, which works out near 185 a week. Dripify's quotas scale by tier toward the same place. Both let you buy more capacity than your account can legally spend, which makes the quota on a pricing page a marketing number before it's a limit.

Cloud against extension is the part people argue about, and the argument is less settled than either side pretends. A cloud tool acts from hardware you don't own, so your activity arrives from an address you don't own. An extension acts inside your session, from your own address, in a page the platform reads directly. Each one leaks a different signal, and no vendor can promise you an outcome, because the enforcement rules are private and change without notice.

What's documented is more mundane than the architecture debate. Restrictions follow volume spikes, low acceptance rates and piles of pending requests. A young account that jumps to 40 invitations a day is the textbook case, and no amount of IP rotation makes that behavior look normal.

Both tools ramp new accounts and let you cap daily activity. Dripify applies safety quotas by default. Waalaxy caps by plan, which does the same job quietly. More manual control helps when you know what you're doing and hurts when you don't, and comparison pages tend to leave that half out.

The email side has a published number, and it's worth borrowing. Google has required bulk senders to keep spam complaints under 0.3% since February 2024, and the threshold is written down in Google's own sender guidelines. Nothing on the social side is that explicit. The logic carries anyway: contact enough people who didn't want to hear from you and the platform makes the decision for you.
Gojiberry watches more than 30 buying signals across socials and the web, checks each account against your ICP, and sends you the ones worth writing to.
Both vendors quote per user. That single sentence decides everything below.

Dripify publishes three tiers plus an enterprise quote. Basic is $39 a seat on annual billing and $59 if you pay by the month, and it holds you to one campaign at a time. Pro is $59 yearly and $79 monthly, and that's where unlimited campaigns start. Advanced is $79 annual and $99 monthly, and it adds team management and the A/B testing. The trial runs seven days and asks for no card.

Waalaxy publishes Pro at €19, Advanced at €49 and Business at €69, all per seat each month, with 50% off for paying a year up front and 20% off for a quarter. Cold email starts on Business. The trial runs fourteen days. The inbox add-on is billed separately whatever tier you're on.
Totals are the published per-user rate multiplied by seats. Sales Navigator sits on top at roughly $99 a seat, and most teams running either tool are already paying it.

The agency line is the one to read twice, because we'd rather lose the click than sell you a compromise. Neither tool is built for five client accounts. Both bill per seat, both put five separate inboxes in front of you, and the platforms built for that shape bundle sender accounts under one subscription instead. If that's your situation, price a per-sender tool at your real account count and skip the rest of this comparison.
Run the math for a team of three

Three reps on Dripify Pro: $2,124 a year, and building the list is still someone's Monday. Three reps on Waalaxy Business: €1,242 a year paid up front, and building the list is still someone's Monday. Gojiberry is $99 a month for the workspace, so a third hire doesn't change the invoice. What changes is who builds the list.

There's a second number nobody puts on a pricing page. B2B contact data decays at about 2.1% a month, roughly 22.5% a year, according to HubSpot's database decay research. Whatever you paid for the list, a fifth of it stops being true before the annual plan renews.
Choose Dripify if

Your list is already good, you want the campaign running while you're in meetings, and you'd rather pay more per seat than keep a browser tab alive. For most people who land on this page, this is the right answer.
Choose Waalaxy if
You're one person, you're starting out, and the gap between €19 and $59 a month is a real decision. The templates teach you what a sequence looks like, and you can leave whenever you want.
If neither is the problem
You've run sequences before. The copy is fine, the acceptance rate is fine, and the pipeline still isn't. Then the sender wasn't the thing you needed to change.

Gojiberry is an AI-powered multichannel prospecting platform. It tracks more than 30 buying-intent signals across socials and the web, surfaces the leads who are in market right now, and triggers personalized outreach across channels. Dripify and Waalaxy begin once the list exists. We begin one step earlier.
🎯 Signals, not static lists
Funding rounds, hiring pushes, role changes, competitor engagement. The account enters the queue when something moves, not when a scraper found it.
🤖 The sourcing is the product
Agents watch public signals around the clock, score each account on fit with what you sell, and surface only the ones worth a message this week.
💬 Copy written from the trigger
Each message starts from the event that surfaced the account, which is why it reads like a person noticed something rather than a merge field firing.
💰 One price for the workspace
Sourcing, enrichment and outreach in a single $99 line. A fourth teammate joins and the invoice stays where it was.

Timing is the whole argument, and there's a public number behind it. Median job tenure in the United States is 3.9 years, and 22% of employees have been in their role under a year, per the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Every one of those moves is a new budget, a new stack decision and a short window. A sequencer sends into that window by accident. We aim at it.

Where we lose: point Gojiberry at a market where nothing public ever moves. No hiring, no funding, no role changes, no visible activity. The signal layer has nothing to work with, and a cheap sender pointed at a list you built by hand will beat us. Those markets exist, and if you're in one, buy Waalaxy and spend the difference on research.
Wispra now sources six in ten of its weekly demos from intent signals.
Mindflow lifted outbound reply rate by switching to intent-triggered outreach.
GTE Localize booked more than a hundred meetings after moving off cold email volume.
2x
Baur Software doubled its network while keeping outreach written by hand.
Where this came from

Before Gojiberry there was Coco.ai, and before Coco.ai there was Roman spending his days prospecting on socials the way everyone does it. He kept a spreadsheet of accounts that had done something worth noticing, checked it by hand every morning, and wrote to the ones that had moved. The messages that worked were never the best written ones, they were the best timed ones.

Coco.ai became the place where that hunch got tested against real pipelines, and the part that kept working was the part nobody wanted to do by hand. Gojiberry is that morning ritual, running without him. If you've ever kept a list like that in a spreadsheet, you already understand the product.
If you'd rather see the wider category before deciding, we keep a running list of sequencing tools and where each one breaks.

Neither vendor can promise you anything, because the platform keeps its enforcement rules private and changes them without notice. What's structural is this: Dripify acts from its own servers, so the traffic arrives from an address that isn't yours, while Waalaxy acts inside your browser session, from your own address, in a page the platform can read. Each leaks a different signal. The behavior that gets accounts restricted is the same on both, and it's volume you haven't earned: a spike in invitations, a low acceptance rate, a pile of requests nobody answered.

Waalaxy, by a wide margin, and it isn't close. Three seats on Dripify Pro come to $177 a month on annual billing, so $2,124 for the year. Three seats on Waalaxy Business come to €103.50 a month billed yearly, so €1,242, or €207 a month if you'd rather not prepay twelve months. Add the inbox add-on on the Waalaxy side and the gap tightens, though it doesn't close. Neither figure includes Sales Navigator, which most teams running either tool already pay for.

For a founder sending a few dozen emails a week alongside social touches, yes. Business at €69 includes cold email sequences, multiple sender accounts and 500 finder credits a month. Past that volume it stops being a fit. A dedicated sender gives you inbox rotation, warmup, deliverability reporting and per-domain reputation, and none of that is Waalaxy's job. If email is your main channel and social is the follow-up, buy the sender first.

Yes. You can import from a standard search, from a CSV, or from a saved list, and campaigns run the same either way. What you lose without Sales Navigator is the filtering, and that's not a small loss: the difference between a good campaign and a bad one usually happens before the sequence starts. Budget for it if you're pricing seats, because at $99 a seat it's often the largest line in the stack.

Two directions, two reasons. People leave Waalaxy for Dripify when they're tired of the browser being part of the infrastructure, usually after a campaign stalls over a weekend. People leave Dripify for Waalaxy when the per-seat invoice arrives for a third rep and the value doesn't scale with it. A third group leaves both, and it's the group whose acceptance rate is fine while the pipeline stays empty.

Neither, and we'd rather say so than sell you a compromise. Both bill per user, so five client accounts means five seats and five separate inboxes to check. Tools built for this bundle sender accounts under one subscription instead. If you run client profiles, price a per-sender platform at your real account count, and start with our comparison of HeyReach against Waalaxy.

Technically yes, practically no. Running two automation tools against one account stacks their daily activity on top of each other, and the platform sees one account behaving twice as hard as it did last week. That's the pattern restrictions follow. If you're testing, run them on separate accounts or run them in separate months.

It replaces the work that happens before either one. Gojiberry reads buying signals wherever they surface, checks each account against your ICP, and hands you the ones that deserve a message, then triggers outreach across channels. Teams run it instead of a sender when the sequence was never the weak part, and alongside one when they want to keep a motion they've already tuned. Pricing is a flat $99 a month for the workspace, so a third seat changes nothing on the invoice.
Try it on your own market
Tell Gojiberry who you sell to and it goes looking for qualified prospects. No sequence to build, no browser tab to babysit.

La Growth Machine made a name for itself by automating multichannel outreach across email, socials and more. It is a solid tool. But the sales-tech world moves fast, and what felt revolutionary last year is table stakes today. Newer platforms now compete on smarter AI, better intent data and cleaner workflows.

Maybe you are hitting a wall with the feature set, hunting for something more cost-effective, or you want a tool that leads with intent rather than raw volume. Whatever the reason, evaluating alternatives to La Growth Machine is a smart move.

This guide breaks down 12 platforms that could be the right fit for your team. For each one we cover who it is for, its core strength and where it falls short, so you can pick the next engine for your outbound motion with confidence.
La Growth Machine or Gojiberry?
3 quick questions to see which tool actually fits your real outbound needs.
Free . No signup . 60 seconds

Think of Gojiberry less as a simple automation tool and more as an AI-powered copilot for B2B prospecting. That makes it one of the most compelling alternatives to La Growth Machine, especially for teams focused on high-intent lead generation.

Gojiberry is an AI-powered, multi-channel prospecting platform. It tracks 30+ buying-intent signals across socials and the web, surfaces leads who are in-market right now, and triggers personalized outreach across channels. Instead of just automating messages, its core strength is spotting when a prospect is ready to buy.

The platform runs 24/7, detecting triggers such as job changes, funding announcements, competitor engagement and specific keyword activity. Once a lead is identified, Gojiberry filters it against your Ideal Customer Profile, enriches the record with verified contact data, and pushes it into your CRM or an automated outreach sequence.

What sets Gojiberry apart is an end-to-end workflow that fuses intent detection with multi-channel outreach. Teams report this pairing removes hours of manual prospecting and lifts reply rates. It integrates with tools like HubSpot, Pipedrive, Instantly and Lemlist, so it slots into your existing stack rather than replacing it.

Over 500 sales teams use the platform. Reported outcomes from case studies include a 6x ROI, a 3x lift in reply rates, and results like booking 5 demos from just 30 leads, which makes it a strong fit for founders, small B2B sales teams and growth operators who need a predictable pipeline.
Do
Let the AI agents source prospects showing genuine buying intent so your outreach lands timely and relevant.
Do not
Rely on it for very low-activity niches, since its edge is tied to the volume of signals available.
Actionable step
Set an agent to watch competitor engagement across socials. Anyone interacting is a warm lead. Gojiberry grabs the info, enriches it and drops it into your sequence.
Pro from $99/mo. Elite and Enterprise tiers add unlimited contacted prospects and deeper integrations. A free trial is available.
Multichannel sequences with strong deliverability tooling.

Lemlist grew from a cold-email tool into a full multichannel platform, and its biggest draw is the end-to-end workflow in one interface. You can find leads from its 600M+ database, enrich them, and launch personalized email and LinkedIn sequences without juggling a dozen tabs.

It is especially well regarded for built-in deliverability tools like lemwarm, which warms up sending accounts to protect inbox placement. That makes it a strong pick for SMBs and scale-ups that want one tool for lead gen and outreach.
Use the AI to rewrite copy and generate icebreakers, speeding up campaign creation.
Expect WhatsApp in standard plans; it is an add-on.
Pull 50 ICP-matched leads and build a 3-step sequence (email, a LinkedIn profile visit, follow-up), then track which step drives the most replies.
Email Pro from $55/user/mo; Multichannel Expert $79/user/mo (includes LinkedIn actions). 14-day free trial.
Gojiberry finds people already showing buying intent, then feeds them to your outreach. Warm leads, delivered weekly.
Simple, cost-effective automation for LinkedIn-first prospecting.

Waalaxy is the go-to for individuals and small teams running LinkedIn-first prospecting. It works as a cloud-based automation tool, which is safer and steadier than browser extensions that can get flagged. Users run campaigns with profile visits, connection requests and messages without a complicated setup.

Its simplicity is the selling point, which makes it one of the most accessible alternatives to La Growth Machine for solo founders and early-stage teams. You can import leads from LinkedIn, Sales Navigator or Recruiter Lite and manage automated follow-ups with almost no learning curve.
Use the free plan to automate basic profile visits before committing.
Rely on it for robust native email campaigns.
Import 20 prospects from a LinkedIn search and run a 2-step sequence: visit the profile, then send a short personalized connection note two days later.
Advanced plan around $44/mo (includes email finding); Business around $66/mo adds CRM sync.
Safety-first LinkedIn automation built for agencies.

Expandi has a reputation as a premium platform for LinkedIn automation, prioritizing account safety and streamlined workflows, especially for agencies. It uses smart limits and human-like behavior to reduce the risk of LinkedIn restrictions.

Its differentiator is an agency-centric design: a single full-featured plan that makes managing multiple client accounts on one dashboard straightforward, which agencies handling outreach for several brands appreciate.
Use the agency dashboard to manage multiple client or team accounts from one place.
Expect native email outreach; plan to integrate a separate tool.
Run a Connector campaign for connection requests plus a Messenger campaign to follow up, using dynamic placeholders.
Around $99/user/mo for the single all-inclusive plan; 7-day free trial.
Cloud outreach with agency and white-label controls.

Zopto is a mature, cloud-based automation platform aimed at sales agencies and larger teams. What sets it apart is robust agency features: white-labelling, multi-user management and a global inbox, which suit organizations running campaigns across many clients or departments.

It is built for scale, with hands-on customer success and omni-channel sequencing that combines LinkedIn actions with email from a central dashboard. That agency-level control makes it a notable alternative to La Growth Machine for service businesses.
Use A/B testing to compare message variations and see what resonates.
Choose this as a solo user on a tight budget.
For a new client, brand the dashboard with their logo and target a specific group before sending connection requests.
From around $197/mo for the Personal plan; agency and team tiers add seats and features.
Modular multichannel with an AI SDR and voice.

Reply.io is a modular sales-engagement platform. Its core strength is email sequencing, but the real differentiator is a flexible add-on structure: start with email, then bolt on LinkedIn automation, a native dialer with SMS, or an AI SDR to run campaigns.

That build-your-own approach makes it a strong alternative to La Growth Machine for teams that want control over tooling and budget, assembling only the channels they use. Base plans include unlimited email account connections and warmup.
Use the Chrome extension to source contacts from LinkedIn and add them to sequences in one click.
Underestimate add-on costs for LinkedIn automation and calls/SMS.
Give Jason AI a clear ICP and goal, let it find prospects and manage outreach for a week, then review.
Free plan for one user; paid from $49/user/mo by contacts engaged. 14-day trial.
Straightforward, scalable cold email.

Mailshake is a veteran in cold email, known for a practical, no-frills approach. It is designed for teams that want a powerful email tool without the complexity of a massive all-in-one suite, focusing on deliverability, personalization and scale.

It is a solid choice for SMBs that value predictable costs and ease of use, with a clean UI, strong onboarding and reliable automation. That makes it a good alternative to La Growth Machine when email is your primary channel.
Generate copy variations with the AI writer and A/B test for reply rate.
Sign up expecting to trial it free; you buy a plan to start.
Connect Gmail or Outlook, turn on warmup, and let it run a week before your first send.
Email Outreach $45/user/mo; Sales Engagement $85/user/mo, billed annually.
Deliverability-focused cold email with fair scaling.

Woodpecker is a reliable, scalable cold-email platform favored by agencies and high-volume teams. Its strength is deliverability: inbox rotation and automated warmup to keep emails landing where they should.
Pricing is based on prospects contacted rather than seats, which is cost-effective for growing teams. Free real-time catch-all verification via Bouncer helps keep lists clean without extra cost.
Add multiple inboxes and use rotation to protect your domain reputation.
Expect its social automation to be as deep as multichannel suites.
Upload 50 prospects on the trial and review how clean your verified data is.
From $24/mo for up to 500 contacted prospects, unlimited team members. Free trial.
High-volume cold email with deep deliverability tooling.

Smartlead is engineered for high-volume cold email with an obsessive focus on deliverability. It lets you connect unlimited email accounts and warm them simultaneously, all managed from a central master inbox, which suits agencies running large-scale campaigns.

Features like SmartDelivery automatically test and route emails through the best-performing sender accounts. This data-driven approach makes it a compelling alternative to La Growth Machine for teams that put technical email performance first.
Use the master inbox to manage every reply across connected accounts in one place.
Expect a beginner-friendly interface out of the box.
Connect three inboxes, enable SmartDelivery, and let the AI pick the best sender per prospect.
Basic $39/mo (2,000 active leads); Pro $94/mo with unlimited seats. Free trial.
Flat-cost, high-volume email sending.

Instantly exploded in popularity by focusing on high-volume email with simple, predictable pricing. Its core value prop is unlimited email accounts and warmup across all outreach plans, which removes a big barrier to scaling.

This email-first approach fits teams that prioritize volume over multichannel complexity. For organizations that live by their email metrics, it provides the engine to send at scale without runaway per-inbox costs.
Use A/B/Z testing to find winning copy faster.
Overlook the active-leads cap on the entry tier.
Connect five addresses, enable warmup at a low daily increment, and build reputation over two weeks.
Growth from $37/mo (1,000 active leads); Hypergrowth $97/mo (25,000).
All-in-one prospecting with a flexible credit system.

Snov.io is an all-in-one cold-outreach platform combining lead generation, data verification and email campaigns. Its strength is a flexible credit system usable across tools, from prospecting to verification, which is cost-effective for SMBs juggling multiple needs.
It suits reps who want a straightforward, integrated workflow: search the database, validate contacts, and push them into a drip sequence. A no-cost email warmup adds value.
Use the free plan and monthly credits for small, targeted searches.
Assume LinkedIn automation is included; it is a paid add-on.
Run the Chrome extension on a target domain, verify found emails with credits, then add valid contacts to a drip.
Free plan (50 credits); Starter $39/mo (1,000 credits); Pro $99/mo (5,000).
A vast B2B database plus engagement in one stack.

Apollo.io is a dominant force in sales tech, packaging a massive B2B database, enrichment and engagement tools into one data-forward platform. Its value prop is a unified way to find leads and reach them via email and a built-in dialer, a go-to for US-market coverage.

The strength is its all-in-one nature: reps prospect, enrich contacts with intent data, and launch sequences without leaving the app. That consolidation makes it a powerful, if sometimes complex, alternative to La Growth Machine.
Use advanced filters to build targeted lists by tech stack, headcount and hiring data.
Be surprised if free-tier credits and plan features change.
Export 25 verified contacts on the free plan and run a simple two-step sequence to feel the workflow.
Generous free plan; paid from $49/user/mo billed annually.
There is no single best platform, only the one that is best for your goals. The fastest way to choose is to name the biggest thing holding your outreach back right now, then match a tool to it.
Emails land in spam
Look at Smartlead or Woodpecker, both obsessed with deliverability.
Manual LinkedIn prospecting eats your day
Waalaxy or Expandi are built to solve this safely.
You need data, email and calls in one place
Apollo.io or Reply.io offer the broader suite.
You are tired of cold outreach with no replies
This is the shift: a tool like Gojiberry leads with buying intent, the next evolution in sales.
The future of sales is not automating more tasks. It is automating the right tasks, so your team can focus on building relationships and closing deals.
Get fresh, high-quality leads delivered to Slack or your inbox every week. Free trial, no credit card required.

Teams usually switch for one of three reasons. First, specialization: they want a tool that goes deeper into one channel, such as email deliverability (Smartlead) or safer LinkedIn automation (Expandi).
Second, cost: as they scale, they prefer predictable pricing based on contacts (Woodpecker) or flat unlimited-seat plans (Instantly).
Third, strategy: they move away from pure volume toward an intent-based model (Gojiberry) to improve lead quality and conversion.
Generally no. Platforms like Apollo.io and Reply.io offer CRM-like features for managing contacts inside their ecosystems, but they are engagement tools, not full CRMs.
For pipeline management, reporting and a single source of truth, integrate them with a dedicated CRM like HubSpot or Salesforce.
It matters a lot for account safety and efficiency. Cloud tools run 24/7 from a dedicated IP, so they keep working when your computer is off.
They also avoid injecting code into pages the way browser extensions do, which detection systems increasingly flag. No automation is risk-free, but cloud solutions are widely seen as steadier.

If reply rates are your bottleneck, look at an intent-first tool. Gojiberry surfaces prospects showing active buying signals and enriches them before your team reaches out, so sequences run on warm leads rather than cold lists.

Follow-Up Email Generator: free tool for more replies

If you want to spend less time building prospect lists and more time talking to qualified prospects, Gojiberry takes care of the prospecting work for you. It watches more than 30 buying signals, checks companies against your ICP, and finds the accounts worth contacting.
You want the database so look at Apollo first

Social automation on a small budget, French, with a free tier you can test the channel on before you pay anything. Once the sequences run and the replies stay flat, the problem has moved to the list and that is where we come in.
European data quality drives you so price Cognism

Verified mobile numbers and a clear line on where the data comes from put Cognism ahead on European coverage. Ask for the quote, then read it twice, because the platform fee sits on top of the seats. Gojiberry is European too and it charges one flat price.

Zeliq is a French all-in-one prospecting platform: a database of more than 450 million contacts, multi-source enrichment, and email plus social sequencing, from around 59 euros per user per month. That reads well until you count your seats. A team of five on the middle tier pays close to 495 euros a month, and the meter follows headcount rather than results, which is the moment most small teams start looking around.

This page gives you eleven alternatives sorted by how you leave Zeliq: five platforms that replace it outright, four apps that replace one piece of it for less, and two entry points if you prospect alone. We checked every price in August 2026 and we say which one matches which bottleneck, because the reason you are leaving decides where you should go.
Gojiberry finds your leads
Zeliq charges every seat. Gojiberry charges 99 dollars a month for the whole team and finds the accounts already showing buying signals.
Table of contents

Pick by bottleneck rather than by category. If the bill is what pushes you out, four tools below cost less for the same job. If the list is what pushes you out, only one of them decides who deserves the message, and Gojiberry is the one we would start with because a team of two to ten rarely runs out of contacts. It runs out of hours to sort them.

How to read this table. We checked every price in August 2026, on each vendor's own pricing page where the vendor publishes one, and we flag the rest as reported figures in the block that follows. Most of these bill per seat. The number above is what one person pays, so do the multiplication for your own headcount before you compare anything, because that is where a 59 euro line becomes a 495 euro line.

We opened each vendor's own pricing page in August 2026 and took the numbers from there, tier by tier, noting the monthly price, the annual price and what the meter runs on. That last part matters more than the sticker. Six of these tools bill per user, two per workspace, two on credits, and Gojiberry charges one flat price for the team. Two tools with the same headline number land four times apart at five people.

Where a vendor hides its prices we say so rather than guessing. Cognism quotes rather than publishes, and the Zeliq figures here come from a third party consultancy rather than from Zeliq, so we attribute them in the sentence every time. You will not find a scorecard of measured reply rates here, because we have not run that test on an identical list. We pay for the tools we write about, no vendor read a word of this before publication, and our customer results sit in published case studies.
These five cover the database, the enrichment and the sending, exactly like Zeliq does. You cancel one subscription and you start another, with nothing left to wire together yourself.

Gojiberry finds who to contact instead of handing you a database to search. It watches more than 30 buying signals across socials and the web, job changes, funding rounds, hiring, competitor engagement, checks every account against your ICP, then contacts the ones that pass. We build it in France and we charge one price for the team.

Price. Free to start. Pro costs 99 dollars a month for the team with 2 AI agents and up to 1,800 prospects contacted per month, on no commitment. Custom above five people and for agencies. Five seats change nothing.
Strength. It answers the question the other ten leave to you: who is worth writing to this week and why now.
Limit. We do not sell you a 450 million contact database to browse. If searching a list yourself is the job you want, Apollo does that better than we do.

Same shape as Zeliq, a large contact database with sequencing and enrichment on top, except Apollo publishes its prices and gives you a free plan to start on. For a team that likes the Zeliq model and dislikes the invoice, this is the shortest move.
Price. 49 dollars per user per month on annual billing, 59 dollars month to month, with a free plan below that. We broke the credit tiers down in what Apollo really costs.
Strength. Cheaper per seat than Zeliq for a comparable job, and you can test it before you talk to anyone.
Limit. European coverage runs thinner than the American data, and the credit rules confuse new users often enough that it comes up in every review round.

The premium European option. Cognism verifies mobile numbers by hand, screens against do not call lists across Europe, and states plainly where its data comes from. If your pipeline runs on cold calls into Europe, nothing else on this list matches the connect rate.

Price. Cognism quotes rather than publishes. Procurement databases and consultancies report a platform fee somewhere between 15,000 and 25,000 dollars a year, plus roughly 1,500 to 2,500 dollars per user per year on top. Treat those as reported figures and get your own quote in writing.
Strength. Data accuracy and compliance, in that order. For a phone heavy team in Europe the premium pays for itself.
Limit. The platform fee lands before the first seat, so the per user maths gets worse the smaller you are. A team of five leaving a 59 euro tool is not the buyer Cognism prices for.

All-in-one with intent signals built into the platform rather than bolted on. Data, sequencing across several channels, deliverability monitoring and AI agents sit in one place, which is genuinely close to what Zeliq sells, one tier up in ambition and in price.

Price. The Startup plan costs 600 dollars a month for two users, so 300 dollars per user per month, and it bills annually with no monthly option. Growth starts at four users and Elite at ten, both on quote. Neighbouring tools sit in the best Amplemarket alternatives.
Strength. The only platform here that ships intent and execution in one contract.
Limit. Priced for bigger teams. Two seats and an annual commitment is 7,200 dollars before you have sent anything, which prices out most of the teams reading this page.

French, multichannel, hosted in Europe. It sequences across socials, email and messaging in a single flow, enriches contacts along the way, and the interface assumes you sell in Europe rather than translating an American product into French.
Price. Third party comparisons report between 50 and 100 euros per user per month depending on tier. That is per seat, like Zeliq, so the arithmetic works the same way at five people.
Strength. The closest thing here to Zeliq on the sending side, from a company under the same regulation as you.
Limit. The contact database is smaller than Zeliq's, so you bring more of your own targeting. And the per seat model reproduces exactly the problem you left over.

Here is the section. Assembled together, these four cost 15 to 25 percent less than a Zeliq licence and cover most of what a small B2B team needs. They also arrive as four subscriptions, four logins and four places for something to break, because you wire the stack together yourself and you maintain it yourself. If nobody on your team enjoys that work, read the previous section again.

Clay replaces the enrichment piece. It runs waterfall enrichment across many providers in a spreadsheet style table, so when one source misses an email the next one tries, and you pay for the result rather than for the subscription. Teams whose real problem is data quality end up here.
Price. 167 dollars a month on Launch with annual billing, 185 dollars month to month, metered in credits per workspace rather than per person. The wider field sits in the best Clay alternatives.
Strength. Nothing else here gets you a comparable hit rate on European contacts, because it queries several providers instead of one.
Limit. It is the steepest learning curve on this page and it sends nothing. Budget an afternoon a week for whoever owns it.

French email enrichment and cleaning, hosted in France, and it finds contacts by deduction rather than by holding a database of personal data. That design decision is the product: there is no stored contact base to be caught out by, which makes the GDPR conversation with your legal team a short one.
Price. Third party comparisons report between 24 and 299 euros a month depending on volume, metered on credits rather than on seats.
Strength. GDPR by design rather than by policy page, and the European email hit rate holds up against tools costing five times more.
Limit. Emails only. No mobile numbers, no sequences, no list building. It cleans what you bring it.

French, and it works where your reps already spend the morning. A browser extension pulls mobile numbers and email addresses straight off social profiles, one prospect at a time or across a whole list, and pushes them into your CRM without a second screen.
Price. Third party comparisons report a free tier and paid plans up to 79 euros a month, metered on credits.
Strength. The cheapest route to European mobile numbers, and a rep can be using it five minutes after installing it.
Limit. It reveals contacts and stops there. Pair it with something that sends and something that decides who is worth revealing in the first place.

Email volume at the lowest cost per send. Connect as many mailboxes as you like, warm them up inside the same product, and rotate the sending across all of them. This is the piece of Zeliq you replace when your problem is throughput rather than targeting.
Price. 47 dollars a month on the outreach only plan. The database and the CRM sell separately, so read the line items before you compare it against an all-in-one.
Strength. Cheapest credible way to run real email volume, and the deliverability tooling is the reason people stay.
Limit. It sends. It does not find. On its own it is half of what Zeliq gave you, at less than half the price.

Two tools for a solo founder or a team testing outbound for the first time. Both are French, both cost less than a single Zeliq seat, and both let you find out whether the channel works before you commit to anything.

The cheapest entry point on this page. It runs from the browser, the setup takes an afternoon rather than a week, and the free tier is enough to see whether outbound works for your market at all before you pay a euro.
Price. Third party comparisons report from 19 euros per user per month, with a free plan below that. The entry tier covers socials, and email steps arrive one tier up.
Strength. A founder can run a real campaign the same day for less than a third of a Zeliq seat.
Limit. The entry tier is thinner than it looks, and the per user price climbs quickly once a second person joins.

French too, and the one to pick when your emails work because of how they are written. Personalised images, video thumbnails and custom variables sit inside the sequence, with warmup bundled in rather than sold on the side.

Price. 69 dollars a month per workspace on the email plan with unlimited users, then 109 dollars per user per month on multichannel. The billing model flips at that point, which is the thing to check before you commit. We put it against the volume side of the market in Smartlead vs Lemlist.
Strength. A workspace price with unlimited users makes it the cheapest option here for a four person team that only needs email.
Limit. Multichannel bills per user, so that same four person team suddenly multiplies by four.
Stop guessing who to contact
Gojiberry watches more than 30 buying signals, checks every account against your ICP, and sends you the ones worth writing to.

If you left Zeliq you did not leave Europe. Six of the eleven tools above answer to the same regulation you do, and the difference between them is not marketing. It is where the servers sit, what the vendor holds about the people you contact, and which language you get an answer in when something breaks on a Friday afternoon.

What really separates them. Dropcontact takes the strictest position, since it deduces contact details rather than storing a base of personal data, which removes an entire paragraph from your processing register. Cognism takes the most operational position: the data exists, and Cognism screens it against do not call lists in more than fifteen countries so your reps can dial without checking each number by hand. Kaspr and La Growth Machine sit in the middle, French and hosted in Europe, with the usual GDPR paperwork.

And Gojiberry is French, which matters here for a reason that is not the flag. We watch public buying signals rather than resell a contact database, we host in Europe, and there is one processor to declare instead of four. When you assemble a stack out of four tools you inherit four data processing agreements, four sub processor lists and four support queues in four time zones. That is the hidden cost of unbundling that no pricing page shows you. If your shortlist reaches beyond these eleven, we ran the same exercise on a neighbouring query in the best Topo.io alternatives.

Zeliq is a French all-in-one prospecting platform. You search a contact database, enrich what you find from several sources, then sequence email and social messages without leaving the interface. It launched as a modern answer to the older American suites, it sells mostly in Europe, and it prices itself per user, which is the detail that brings people to this page.
Where Zeliq is strong
Where Zeliq costs you

Zeliq itself does not publish a full grid, so the figures below come from a third party consultancy that documents its own Zeliq deployments rather than from Zeliq. Treat them as reported and confirm your own tier in writing.
What it costs once you multiply by your team
Every line above is per user. The same source reports that monthly billing runs around 20 percent above annual, so the number you sign is not the number you read.

Five people on Growth comes to around 495 euros a month. That is the arithmetic that sends teams to this page, and no discount structure changes it, because the meter counts seats rather than results.

Then add what the same source documents as hidden costs. Onboarding lands between 1,500 and 4,500 euros depending on the setup. And extra credits arrive beyond roughly 2,000 enriched contacts per rep per month, which an active rep passes inside a quarter.

The same consultancy, which claims more than thirty Zeliq deployments, reports a satisfaction score of 4.6 out of 5. That is a healthy number and it matches the two things people praise most often: the interface and the speed at which a new rep becomes productive.

That source lists the limits too, and they are worth repeating because they are consistent. Reporting sits behind Outreach and Salesloft, so a sales manager who lives in dashboards will feel it. The integrations marketplace is smaller than Apollo's, which bites the day you need a connector nobody built. And American data is weaker than Apollo's, which is the trade you accept for stronger European coverage.

Sources and date: we took Apollo, Clay, Instantly, Lemlist and Amplemarket prices from each vendor's own pricing page in August 2026. Zeliq, Waalaxy, La Growth Machine, Kaspr and Dropcontact figures come from third party comparisons and consultancies, and we attribute them in the sentence each time. Cognism quotes rather than publishes.
Four reasons come up on every page ranking for this query. Three of them are billing problems and the fourth one is the reason people switch twice.

Every seat is a full subscription. Hire a second rep and the line doubles, whether or not that rep books anything. There is no workspace price and nothing that rewards the team growing. Five people on Growth is around 495 euros a month for software that still leaves the targeting to you.

Enrichment runs on credits and the ceiling sits at roughly 2,000 enriched contacts per rep per month before extra credits appear. None of that is hidden, it is just hard to model in advance, so the second invoice does not match the first one.

European coverage is the strong side and it is good. Push outside it and the hit rate drops, and the same happens inside narrow verticals the database never indexed deeply. Sell to French manufacturers and you are fine. Sell to American healthcare and you top up from a second source.

This is the deep one and it is not a flaw in the product. Zeliq gives you a database to search, which assumes you already know who to search for. Nothing in it watches for a job change or a funding round and tells you that this account moved this week.
Find the line that sounds like your month rather than the column that sounds like your company.

A third party consultancy that documents its own deployments reports a free tier, then Starter around 59 euros per user per month, Growth around 99 and Pro around 149, with Enterprise on quote. The same source puts monthly billing around 20 percent above annual.

Multiply before you compare. Five people on Growth lands near 495 euros a month, and that source also documents onboarding between 1,500 and 4,500 euros plus extra credits beyond roughly 2,000 enriched contacts per rep per month.
Waalaxy, reported from 19 euros per user per month with a free plan below that. Kaspr also runs a free tier, and Dropcontact starts at a reported 24 euros a month on credits.

Cheapest on the sticker is rarely cheapest in use, though. Those three each replace one piece of Zeliq, so the real comparison is the stack you end up with. At five people, one flat price of 99 dollars a month beats every per seat combination on this page.

Cognism, if your pipeline runs on cold calls. It verifies mobile numbers by hand and screens against do not call lists across more than fifteen countries, which no other tool here does. The catch is the platform fee, which arrives before the first seat.

For emails rather than dials, Dropcontact holds the strongest European hit rate and hosts in France. Kaspr and La Growth Machine sit just behind, both French. And Gojiberry is French too, which is why the compliance answer here is one processor rather than four.

Yes, several, and they are worth using properly rather than for an afternoon. Apollo runs a free plan on its database, Waalaxy runs one on social sequences, Kaspr gives you a monthly allowance of credits, and Gojiberry lets you start free.
What a free tier tells you is whether the channel works for your market. What it will not tell you is whether the tool scales with your team, since every limit that matters sits on the paid tiers.

You can, and the maths works. Kaspr for the mobile numbers, Dropcontact for the emails and the CRM cleaning, then La Growth Machine or Instantly for the sending. That stack costs 15 to 25 percent less than a Zeliq licence and covers most of what a small B2B team needs.

What the maths leaves out is the maintenance. Four subscriptions means four logins, four data processing agreements and four places for something to break, and somebody on your team owns that work every week. Count that hour before you count the saving.

Export two things first, because they are the only two that are yours to take: your contact lists and your sequence copy. Sequence structures do not transfer between tools, so plan on rebuilding them by hand rather than hoping for an import.

Then let running sequences finish where they are instead of cutting them off mid flow, and start new ones on the other side at a low daily volume for the first week. Cancel the old subscription only once a full sequence has completed on the new tool and the replies land where you expect.

Yes, and a fair number of teams start that way. Gojiberry decides who is worth contacting and Zeliq keeps doing the sending, so nothing in your current setup breaks while you find out whether signal based targeting changes your reply rate.
Most teams drop one of the two after a quarter, and which one depends on what was failing in the first place. If the sending was fine and the results were not, the seats go and Gojiberry stays.
Your buyers are moving now
Someone in your market just changed jobs or started following a competitor. Gojiberry spots it, checks they match your ICP, and writes first.
These two answer different questions, and it is worth being precise about which one you are asking before you compare a price.

Both companies are European, so nobody wins the GDPR argument here. Zeliq hosts in Europe, answers in French and sits under the same regulation we do. If a comparison page tells you otherwise it is selling you something. What separates the two is the billing model and the direction of the work.

Zeliq bills every seat, which comes to around 495 euros a month for five people against 99 dollars for the team. And Zeliq hands you a database to search while Gojiberry tells you who moved this week. One asks you to know the answer before you start. The other one brings you the question already framed, with the signal attached.

What that looks like in practice, from customers who agreed to be named. Wispra rebuilt its outbound around intent signals and now sources 60 percent of its weekly demos that way. Mindflow stopped spraying its ICP and writes only to accounts that moved, reporting a reply rate above 30 percent. GTE Localize shifted from email outbound to intent driven outreach and passed 100 meetings booked. Baur Software runs the same motion on a smaller team and doubled its network without losing the personal tone.
This started as a problem we had

Before Gojiberry, Roman prospected by hand on socials for Coco.ai. Not running sequences: hunting the signals himself, one browser tab at a time. Watching who had just changed jobs, who had started engaging with the category, who had said something that suggested they had the problem. Then writing to those people with a reason that was true.

It worked, which is the part worth saying plainly, because it is why the product exists. And it did not scale. One person can follow about thirty accounts properly. Past that the method collapses, and what collapses first is the reason for writing. You stop noticing the signal, you keep the cadence, and within a month you are doing mass outreach with a first name variable in it.

Gojiberry runs that routine on its own, which is also why the product targets a team of two to ten people rather than an enterprise sales floor. We built it for the size of team where nobody has a spare afternoon to rebuild the list, and we priced it for that team rather than for each person in it.
Let Gojiberry find them
Tell Gojiberry who you sell to and it starts finding companies showing buying signals. One price for the team, no seat to add.

How did an e-commerce startup 10x its revenue in just 6 months? It wasn't magic, and it definitely wasn't a massive ad budget. It was a completely different way of thinking.

Welcome to the world of ecommerce growth hacking. In a market where customer acquisition costs are soaring and margins are shrinking, the old playbook just doesn't cut it anymore. You need to be smarter, faster, and more creative. This guide is your new playbook. We're going to break down 7 proven growth hacking strategies specifically designed for e-commerce, packed with real examples and actionable steps you can use today. No fluff, just results.
So, what’s the big deal with "growth hacking" anyway? Isn't it just a buzzword for marketing? Not quite.

Think of traditional marketing as following a well-worn map—it’s reliable, but often slow and expensive. Growth hacking is about forging a new, faster path through the wilderness. It's a mindset focused on one thing: rapid growth using limited resources.
The core difference lies in the process:

This approach is built on a simple but powerful loop: Test → Measure → Iterate. Instead of launching one huge campaign and hoping for the best, a growth hacker runs dozens of small experiments. They might test a new headline, a different button color, or a unique discount offer. They measure the results obsessively, kill what doesn't work, and pour resources into what does.

For online stores with razor-thin margins, this mindset isn't just a nice-to-have; it's a survival strategy. It forces you to ask one question over and over: “What’s the most efficient way to get more customers right now?”
Ready to see how it works? Let's dive in.
What if every new customer brought you another one for free? That’s the power of a viral loop.
A great example is Warby Parker and their “Home Try-On” program. Customers shared photos with friends to get opinions. Each buyer became a distribution channel.
Tools: ReferralCandy, GrowSurfROI benchmark: €5 in rewards can generate €50+ in new sales.
Ads give you a spike. Content gives you an asset.
Instead of interrupting people, you attract them with helpful content:
Decathlon is a great example: their buying guides and tutorials reportedly drive a huge share of their organic traffic and a meaningful portion of sales.
ROI benchmark: €0 ad spend, long-term compounding traffic.
Your email list is your most valuable asset. With automation, it becomes your best salesperson.
The classic example: abandoned cart emails. A simple reminder can recover up to 30% of lost sales. For many Shopify stores, email drives 30–40% of total revenue.
Tools: Klaviyo, Brevo, MailchimpROI benchmark: Often €30–€40 for every €1 spent.
Forget celebrities. The real leverage comes from micro-influencers (10k–100k followers) with high engagement and niche authority.
Brands like Shein and Zara scaled massively using this model.
ROI benchmark: €500 in products + commissions can generate €5,000+ in sales.
About 97% of visitors leave without buying. Retargeting gives you a second chance.
Show:
Amazon and Zalando reportedly generate a huge share of conversions from retargeting alone.
ROI benchmark: Often €5 in sales for every €1 spent.
A customer is good. A customer who becomes an advocate is gold.
Brands like Peloton built powerful communities (Facebook groups, challenges, shared progress) that drive massive retention and referrals.
ROI benchmark: Hard to measure short-term, huge impact on LTV and retention.
Top e-commerce brands don’t guess. They test everything:
Even a small +5–10% lift compounds massively over time. Amazon reportedly runs thousands of tests per year.
ROI benchmark: Compounding gains of +20–30% conversions per year are common.
