Your match
Gojiberry is the fit

You want the accounts picked for you and you want to start this week. Gojiberry watches for buying signals, scores each account against the buyer profile you describe, then writes first. Nothing sits between you and the product.
Amplemarket is the fit

Ten reps, a process, someone who owns the tooling: that’s the shape the product was designed for, and it does that job well. Come back to us when you’d rather spend $99 a month than $600, or when you want the targeting layer without the annual contract.
A sending tool is the fit

Your list is already built and the bottleneck is throughput. Instantly or Lemlist will move more messages for less money than any platform here. Once the volume is running and the replies stay thin, the problem moves upstream to targeting, and that’s our half of the job.

Amplemarket is a full outbound platform. One contract buys a database of more than 200 million contacts, over 100 contact-level buying signals, multichannel sequences and a deliverability suite. It’s a good product, and the reviews say so.

Then you ask the price. Six hundred dollars a month for two seats, billed annually, after a sales call. For three people who want to start on Tuesday, that’s a wall. Here are twelve alternatives, what they cost, and who each one suits.
Gojiberry finds your prospects for you
Same idea as the enterprise platforms, without the demo call and the annual contract. $99 a month, running from day one.
Table of contents

Amplemarket sells a platform to teams that already run a process. The twelve tools below split the same job differently: four replace the whole motion, four sell you data, and four move messages once you know who to write to. Prices below were read on the vendors’ own pages on August 10, 2026, so they’re current as of today.

Every price on this page comes from the vendor, read on August 10, 2026. Published tiers were taken from the pricing page or the vendor documentation. For the tools that publish nothing, the figures are buyer-reported contract data, labeled as such in the section, because a quote isn’t a price list. We opened self-serve accounts where one exists, and for the sales-gated platforms we worked from vendor documentation and public reviews.

We pay for every plan ourselves, no vendor read a word of this before publication, and Gojiberry is our product. That’s exactly why its limits are written the same way as everyone else's, in the same place in the card.

One thing you won’t find here: a scorecard of reply rates by tool. We haven’t run twelve tools against one identical list under controlled conditions, and an invented percentage would be worth less than this sentence admitting it. When we run that test, the numbers go up here.
The order runs from the closest replacements for a small team toward the pieces you’d assemble yourself. Every card is capped at the same length, including ours, so the comparison stays readable.

Gojiberry is an AI-powered multichannel prospecting platform. It tracks more than 30 buying-intent signals across socials and the web and runs personalized outreach on several channels. It’s built for a team with no ops person and no plan to hire one.

Pro is $99 a month, self-serve, with two agents and up to 1,800 prospects contacted a month. Teams of five and up move to a Custom plan. That’s $1,188 a year for three people, on one bill. Wispra sources 60% of its weekly demos this way, read the case study.

Few tools start finding accounts this fast for this little. Then you notice the trade. There’s no 200-million-row database to browse, because the product decides who is worth contacting instead of handing you a search bar.

Apollo puts a 210-million-contact database and a sequencer behind one login, which is why it’s the first purchase for most small teams. You can find someone, reveal the email and drop them into a sequence without leaving the tab.

Basic is $49 per user a month on annual billing, Professional $79, Organization $119 with a three-seat minimum. Monthly billing adds roughly 20%, so you’re better off annual. Three reps on Professional is $2,844 a year before any credit top-up.
Few tools pack this much into a low seat price, and few will have you watching a credit balance you didn’t budget for.

Clay is a workbench rather than a product you switch on. You build a table, wire in providers, run a waterfall until an address comes back, then push the row somewhere else. The output is worth exactly what you’re able to build.

Clay replaced Starter, Explorer and Pro in March 2026. New accounts get Free, Launch at $185 a month or Growth at $495, all with unlimited seats and a split between Data Credits and Actions. Failed lookups still spend credits, so a stale input list costs you before it’s enriched.
Flexibility is where it wins. Time to first result is where it loses.

UserGems watches the contacts you already have. When a champion changes jobs or an account shows contact-level intent, it alerts the rep and drafts the follow-up. Amplemarket runs a dedicated comparison page against it, which tells you how directly they’re competing.

UserGems now publishes its tiers. Core is $2,750 a month, or $33,000 a year, covering 3 admins, 20 end users and 30,000 records, plus a one-time implementation fee you’ll negotiate separately. Advanced and Elite list at $69,000 and $120,000.
The contract decides this one. Below twenty reps with a thin CRM, you’re buying a signal layer with nothing to feed it. Above that line, few tools work a customer list harder.

Cognism sells numbers you can dial. Its Diamond Data set is human-verified and screened against do-not-call lists, and its European coverage is why teams pick it over US-first databases. It enriches people you can already name, and it won’t discover a market for you.

Cognism publishes no price. Its two prospecting packages, Standard and Pro, are shown with five seats in the starting configuration, and every deal is an annual quote. Buyers report a platform fee before any seat cost, so check their current pricing page and ask about that fee first, because it doesn’t scale down for a small team.
The five-seat shape ends the conversation for most teams of three. For the ones it doesn’t end, no phone data here lands as reliably in Europe.

ZoomInfo holds the deepest record of US companies and the people inside them: org charts, technologies, funding history, web visitors, intent topics. It’s a database first, with the sending tools bolted on later.

Nothing is published. Buyers report entry contracts near $15,000 a year, with a median around $32,000 once seats, credits and intent stack up. A free Lite tier exists if you’d like to see the data before any of that.
Start with the budget question. Under $15,000 a year for data alone, this isn’t a conversation you can have. Above it, nobody knows the US market better.
Lusha is a lookup tool. You’re on a company page or a profile, you click, and you get an address and sometimes a mobile. It makes no attempt to run your outbound.

A free tier gives a few dozen credits a month. Paid plans sat around $50 a month on annual billing when we looked, with a promotion running on the page, so check their current pricing page before you build a budget on it.
It collapses contact research into two clicks, at the cost of leaving you to work out who’s worth those clicks.

Outreach runs the whole revenue cycle for large sales organizations: sequences, a dialer, conversation intelligence, deal management and forecasting, with the governance you’d expect at fifty reps. The 2026 Amplify packaging adds AI agents metered on credits.

Nothing is published. Buyers report roughly $100 to $160 per user a month on annual contracts, plus implementation and a consumption layer for the AI agents. Check their current pricing page for the tier list.

Onboarding alone costs more than most teams of three spend on software in a year, and that’s before a single seat is billed. At fifty reps with someone owning the process, that same rigor is the thing you are paying for.

Salesloft covers similar ground from a coaching angle, now bundled with Clari's forecasting stack after the 2025 merger. Cadences, call recording, deal management and analytics live in one workspace for managers who run to a number.

Quote only, annual only. Reported list pricing runs $125 to $180 per user a month, negotiated down at volume, with the dialer on top. Vendr puts the median contract near $31,000 a year, and you won’t see a number without asking.
Managers who spend the week coaching get real value here. Then you count the seats. Under ten reps, you’re paying for work nobody has the hours to consume.

Lemlist built its name on personalization people notice: custom images, dynamic landing pages, video. The socials, the dialer and a lead database came later, along with lemwarm for deliverability. The email plan is now priced per workspace rather than per seat.

The email plan is $69 a month for the whole workspace, $55 on annual billing, with a 650-million lead database and credit-based finding. Multichannel is $109 per user a month, $87 annual. Three people sending email only won’t pay less anywhere else in this comparison.
Nothing sends a warmer first message for a smaller bill, and nothing does less to tell you who’s on the other end.

Instantly is sending infrastructure. Unlimited mailboxes, unlimited warmup, one inbox for every reply, and rotation logic that keeps volume off a single domain. The leads and the CRM aren’t included, they’re separate subscriptions.
Growth is $47 a month, $37.60 on annual billing, capped at 5,000 sends and 1,000 active contacts. Hypergrowth is $97. Add lead credits and the CRM and you’re nearer $120 to $210 a month.
It moves more email per dollar than anything else in this comparison, and it’s assuming you arrived with the list already built.

Reply.io puts email, socials, calls and SMS into one sequence builder, and sells Jason, an AI sales rep, as a separate product on top. It’s the cheapest route into genuine multichannel if you buy only the channels you’ll use.

The email plan starts near $49 per user a month on annual billing and multichannel is $89, with channels billed as add-ons. Jason is priced separately and starts in the hundreds. Check their current pricing page, because the seat price isn’t the bill.
Breadth is where it wins. The add-on line of the invoice is where it loses.
You shouldn't have to guess who to contact
Gojiberry watches more than 30 buying signals across socials and the web, checks each account against your ICP, and sends you the ones worth writing to.

Nothing here is a knock on the product. Amplemarket consolidates five purchases into one contract, and the customers who use all five parts say the math works. The catch is the shape of the buyer it was designed around: a sales organization with reps, a process and someone whose job includes the tooling. If that isn’t you, the mismatch starts at the invoice.

More than most of its competitors, which is what the price buys. The database carries over 200 million AI-verified contacts across 20 million companies, with more than 70 million records refreshed weekly, under 3% bounce rates and 96.5% phone accuracy on the vendor's own numbers.

Assembled separately, that list is three to five subscriptions. For a team already paying for a data provider, a sequencer, a warmup service and a signals tool, consolidation is a real argument, and it’s the one the vendor leads with.

What hurts

The Startup plan is $600 a month on an annual term and includes two users, which works out at $300 per seat, or $7,200 for the year. Growth covers four users and Elite ten, both priced on request. Every tier carries the same database, the same signals and the same deliverability suite, so you’re buying seats and volume rather than features.

Credits meter the usage: 15,000 email credits and 480 phone credits per user per year, renewing annually instead of monthly, with extra phone credits at $0.50 each. Revealing a contact you already revealed costs nothing, so you’re not paying twice for the same person.
Run the math for a team of three

Amplemarket Startup covers two of your three people. The year costs $7,200 before the third seat, which is quoted, and before any credit top-up. Gojiberry Pro is $99 a month, so the same year costs $1,188, on a card, cancellable, with the whole team working from one workspace.

The two numbers don’t buy the same thing, and pretending otherwise would be useless to you. Amplemarket includes a contact database and a dialer we don’t sell. What $1,188 buys is the part a small team runs day to day: who to contact this week, and the messages going out to them. Mindflow lifted reply rates 31% on that basis, the numbers are here.

The public reviews split along a predictable line. Teams that use the whole platform rate it highly and talk about dropping three or four other subscriptions. The recurring complaint, cited by roughly a quarter of reviewers on aggregator sites, is that the cost doesn’t match the value for smaller companies.

Two other themes come up often enough to plan around. There’s a learning curve, with most teams describing a few weeks before they’re fully running, and onboarding is community-based on Startup while Growth and Elite get a dedicated contact. Gartner named it a Cool Vendor in generative AI for sales in 2024, which tells you the product is taken seriously by people who look at these things for a living.
Four reasons come up again and again, and none of them is that the product doesn’t work.
The floor is too high
$7,200 committed before the first email goes out is a real number for a company with three salespeople. Most of them have a total tooling budget below that.
You can’t try it on a Tuesday
A trial exists, but the plans are annual and the two upper tiers need a call. Teams that want to test something this week go elsewhere and never come back.
It expects a process
Sequences, workflows, analytics and governance pay off when somebody owns them. Without someone owning them, half the platform sits unused and still shows up on the invoice.
The seats don’t match
Two users included means a third person costs extra, and a founder who sells part-time is a full seat like everyone else.

There’s a fifth reason that has nothing to do with any vendor. B2B contact data goes stale at roughly 2.1% a month, about 22% over a year, so the list you paid to build in January is measurably worse by December. Buying a bigger database doesn’t fix that. Watching for the moment someone moves does.
Six situations, six answers. Find yours and skip the rest.
I sell on my own and I’m starting
Gojiberry. The agent does the part you have no hours for, which is deciding who to write to. Apollo's free tier is the alternative if you’d rather search a database by hand.
We’re three and nobody owns ops
Gojiberry. One $99 subscription against $7,200 committed, and the workflow assumes nobody is available to maintain it. This is the situation the product was built around.
We’re ten and we have a budget
Gojiberry. At that headcount the consolidation argument holds, the seats are used, and the depth stops being decoration. We’d rather say so than lose you on a claim you can check in a minute.
I need European phone numbers
Cognism. Verified mobiles, compliance-screened before they reach a rep, with EMEA coverage nothing here matches. Expect a five-seat starting package and an annual quote.
I want to build my own enrichment
Clay. Providers in a waterfall, an AI researcher on every row, and results pushed anywhere. You’re buying a workbench and the time to learn it.
My problem is sending, not targeting
Instantly or Lemlist for the volume, then Gojiberry above them once the replies stay thin. More sending against a weak list gets you to a spam complaint threshold faster, nothing more.

One number worth keeping in mind while you choose. Median job tenure in the United States is 3.9 years, and 22% of employed people have been in their role under a year. Your buyers are moving constantly, and each move is a reason to write. Any tool that only searches a static database is answering a question you didn’t ask.
Your competitors' customers are moving right now
Someone in your market just changed jobs or started following a competitor. Gojiberry spots it, checks they match your ICP, and writes before anyone else does.

Both products work from signals, so this isn’t a comparison between a tool that sees intent and one that does not. Amplemarket advertises more than 100 signals and we advertise more than 30. The difference is who each product was priced and shaped for.

Same idea, without the sales call and the annual commitment. That’s the whole pitch, and it only matters to you if your team is the size this page keeps describing. Four clients have put numbers on what the signal-first approach does for them.

Roman, one of our cofounders, spent his days prospecting on socials before Gojiberry existed. He did intent research by hand at Coco.ai: who had just changed roles, who had started following a competitor, who had begun asking about the category in public. It worked, and it did not scale. One person can follow about thirty accounts properly. Past that the method falls apart, and you go back to blasting a list.

Gojiberry is that manual routine running on its own. It’s also why the product targets a team of two to ten rather than a sales floor. We built the thing we needed when we were three people and nobody owned the tooling, and the pricing reflects who was in the room.

There’s no single answer, and any page that gives you one is selling something. For a team of two to ten with no ops person, Gojiberry is the closest replacement for what Amplemarket does at a price that fits. For phone outbound in Europe, Cognism. For US data depth, ZoomInfo. For raw sending volume, Instantly.

Several tools here have free tiers: Apollo, Clay, Lusha and ZoomInfo Lite all let you look before paying. None of them runs an outbound motion for free. Gojiberry has a free start with no card required, which is the closest you’ll get to testing the full workflow at no cost.

The Startup plan is $600 a month on an annual term and includes two users, so $7,200 for the year. Growth includes four users and Elite ten, both quoted on request, so you won’t see a number without a call. Each seat carries 15,000 email credits and 480 phone credits a year, and extra phone credits cost $0.50 each.

Apollo if budget is the constraint and you’ll accept watching a credit balance. Amplemarket if you are consolidating three or four tools and the deliverability suite and signals matter more than the seat price. Apollo starts at $49 per user a month annually against $600 a month for two seats, so the decision is rarely close for a small team.

On a strict monthly total, Instantly at $47 and Lemlist at $69 for the whole workspace come in lowest, but they’re both senders, and neither one decides who gets the message. Counting the full job, Gojiberry at $99 a month covers targeting and outreach together, which is where a three-person team loses most of its time.

Some do. UserGems is built entirely on signals, ZoomInfo and Cognism price intent separately, and Gojiberry tracks over 30 signals of its own. The senders don’t, which is the dividing line between the two halves of the list.

Export your contacts and your sequence copy before you cancel anything, because access usually ends on the renewal date and you won’t get it back. Then run both tools in parallel for two weeks on separate segments. Watch reply rates, not open rates, and only cut the old contract once the new one is producing meetings.

Yes, and plenty of teams do. Gojiberry finds the accounts and can hand them to a sender you already pay for, or run the outreach itself. If your sending setup works, don’t replace it, put the targeting layer above it.

The frontier AI labs are no longer just selling to the Fortune 500. On May 13, 2026, Anthropic shipped Claude for Small Business, a packaged version of Claude Cowork aimed at the 25-employee shop, not the 25,000-employee enterprise.
It automates a lot. Specifically: the back-office.
But there's one thing this launch doesn't touch, and it's the thing most small sales teams spend their week fighting: the sales pipeline itself.
Here's what was shipped, what it actually does for you, and the gap it leaves wide open.
Claude for Small Business is a toggle inside Claude Cowork, flip it on, and you get a bundle built around the 30+ tasks that eat the most time out of an owner's week.

Anthropic indicates it doesn't train on customer data by default on Team/Enterprise plans, which matters because half of the SMB owners they surveyed cited data security as their #1 blocker to AI adoption.

What's actually new here isn't the technology, Claude has been able to do most of this for a year. What's new is that a frontier lab is building specifically for the 25-person business. AI tooling has been priced and shaped for the enterprise for the past two years. That's the shift.
📎 Anthropic's official announcement: Claude for Small Business
The 15 workflows cluster cleanly by function. Here's what's getting automated:
Finance: payroll runs, monthly close, cashflow forecasting, invoice chasing.
Operations: employee onboarding, contract routing through DocuSign, vendor follow-ups.
Marketing: campaign drafting via Canva, lead triage and attribution through HubSpot.
Customer service: inbox routing, response drafting, escalation rules.

A concrete example, straight from Anthropic's framing: scheduling payroll by reconciling QuickBooks cash position against incoming PayPal settlements, automatically, with the owner approving the run before the payment leaves the account.

For a small team currently losing 5-10 hours a week to that kind of work, this is a meaningful unlock. The owner-in-the-loop pattern is the right trust model for moving real money. Anthropic shipped a solid product here.
💡 The pattern to notice

Every workflow above shares one thing: it operates on data that already exists in your tools. Invoices already in QuickBooks. Leads already in HubSpot. Contracts already drafted. Claude orchestrates what's there. It doesn't go fetch what isn't.
Try Gojiberry free →
Here's the part that gets glossed over in every "Anthropic launches X" recap I've read this week.

The HubSpot connector does lead triage and campaign attribution. It works leads that already exist in your CRM, sorting them, scoring them, attributing them to the right campaign. That's useful. But it's not prospecting.
What Claude for Small Business does not do:

This is a distinction worth pausing on: managing demand ≠ creating demand. Anthropic automated the revenue ops layer that fires after a lead enters your system. The hardest part for a small team, keeping the top of the funnel filled, week after week, is still entirely on you.
And here's the thing: this is a deliberate, sensible choice by Anthropic.

Anthropic shipped the safe, defensible layer. That's the right call for a frontier lab. But it leaves the prospecting layer wide open, and that's a layer that performs very differently when built as a specialized tool versus bolted onto a horizontal agent.
For context on what specialized prospecting looks like today, our breakdown of the AI SDR landscape in 2026 covers the dedicated players.
The real news isn't the feature list. It's the validation.

A frontier AI lab, the same one shipping enterprise infrastructure for the world's biggest companies, now believes SMB agentic automation is a real, mature market. That's the headline. Everything else is implementation detail.

The adoption curve backs this up. Per SBA Office of Advocacy data referenced across tech press coverage, the AI usage gap between large enterprises and SMBs closed from 1.8× to 1.2× between early 2024 and August 2025. The smaller players are catching up fast.
So what does that mean for someone running sales in a 10-50 person company?

If the back-office is being automated now, then AI ownership of the pipeline is the next frontier. Not in 2030. In the next 12-24 months. SMBs that wait will be prospecting by hand against competitors whose AI is already filling the top of the funnel for them.

This is the same dynamic that played out with email marketing in 2010-2015, with CRM in 2015-2020, and with cold outreach automation in 2020-2024. Each layer got specialized tooling, then mainstream adoption, then a meaningful gap between teams that adopted early and teams that didn't.
For a take on how this shift is already playing out at the top of the market, see our recent piece on what the Altman-vs-Musk dispute tells us about cold outreach.
Get warm leads on autopilot →
Forget the hype cycle. Here's what to actually do this quarter:

On the right: everything that happens after a lead lands in your CRM, qualification, attribution, follow-up sequencing, deal stage updates, reporting. That column is increasingly being automated by tools like Claude. Plan for it.

On the left: everything that happens before a lead lands in your CRM, list building, intent signal monitoring, enrichment, cold outreach, reply handling. That column is still 100% your responsibility, and it's where the leverage lives.

Most small teams build their stack in the wrong order: CRM first, then sequencing tool, then "we'll figure out prospecting later." But "later" is the bottleneck. If your post-lead workflow is about to get automated for free with Claude, your competitive moat moves up the funnel. The teams that figure out specialized prospecting now will have a 12-month head start.
For the signals to look at when building this layer, our guide to 13 buying-intent signals is a starting point.
Anthropic just made this the standard. If a sales AI vendor pitches you full automation with no human checkpoint before outbound goes out, that's a red flag. The trust model has moved.

It's an ops tool with sales-adjacent features. Use it for what it's great at, moving paperwork, reconciling numbers, drafting comms, routing contracts. Pair it with a dedicated prospecting layer for the top of the funnel. The two work together.

That's where Gojiberry sits: a specialized layer that surfaces buying signals across the web, enriches contacts with verified emails and phone numbers, and puts them in your hands weekly. It's the top-of-funnel companion to the back-office automation Anthropic just shipped. Same trust model, you validate before anything goes out, applied to the prospecting half of revenue.
Anthropic just proved the agentic-AI-for-SMB thesis is real, and drew the map. The back-office is solved. The pipeline is the open frontier.

If you're running sales in a small company, the question isn't whether AI will eventually own pipeline. It will. The question is whether you'll be ahead of that shift or behind it when the wave breaks.
Gojiberry surfaces buying-intent signals, enriches contacts, and serves warm leads ready to action. You validate, AI executes.

You want timing over volume. That's the swap Gojiberry makes: it watches the market for movement, checks each account against your profile, and writes first.

A dedicated extraction platform

Throughput is your bottleneck, and Apify handles it better than anything else here. Once the rows land somewhere, you'll still need to know which twenty of them deserve a message this week. That half is ours.
Phantombuster still earns its slot
You've built workflows that work and you'd rather tune them than rebuild them. Keep them. The piece worth adding is the one that tells you who to feed into them on Monday morning.

Phantombuster is a cloud automation platform. You point one of its prebuilt scripts at a source, it extracts what it finds, and you're billed for the hours it spent running. Plenty of teams leave anyway, and the reasons repeat. Automated collection puts the connected account at risk, the execution meter turns a fixed budget into a variable one, and nothing in the output tells you which of those thousand rows deserves a message on Monday.

So we went through ten of them and sorted them into the three groups people shop in: tools that decide who to contact, tools that send the messages, and tools that pull the data. Every price below came off the vendor's own page in August 2026. Where one of them beats us, we say so.
Gojiberry finds your prospects for you
No scraping, no proxies, no account at risk. Gojiberry spots who's started looking for what you sell and writes the opening message.
Table of contents

Three families cover the whole shortlist. Extraction tools pull data off pages, outreach tools send the messages, and intent tools decide who should receive them. Phantombuster lives in the first family, which is why swapping it for a sending tool doesn't end well.

Two of those rows beat us outright, and pretending otherwise would waste your afternoon. If the job is pulling structured data off web pages at volume, Apify does something Gojiberry does not do at all, and we're not a scraper by design. If the job is a clean export of a saved search for under $20 a month, Evaboot wins on price and nothing here comes close.

Every price on this page came off the vendor's own pricing page or its documentation in August 2026, never off a comparison site. Third-party listings on this category go stale within a quarter. We opened self-serve trials where one exists, ran a small extraction on Phantombuster, Apify and Octoparse to see what the free tiers really allow, and read buyer reviews for the tools that gate access behind a call.

One thing you won't find here: a scorecard of measured extraction speeds or match rates. We haven't run one identical list through all ten tools under controlled conditions, and an invented percentage would be worth less than this sentence admitting it. We pay for every plan ourselves, no vendor read a word of this before publication, and Gojiberry is our own product, which is why its limits are written the same way as everyone else's.

The order runs from tools that change what you're doing to tools that do the same thing faster. First the three that decide who to contact, then the four that handle sending, then the three built for extraction.
Intent and prospecting first. These three answer the question an extraction tool leaves open: out of everyone who matches your filters, who's worth a message this week?

Gojiberry is an AI-powered multichannel prospecting platform. It tracks more than 30 buying-intent signals across socials and the web, surfaces the accounts in-market right now, and triggers personalized outreach across channels. Nothing here asks you to extract anything: the list is the output instead of the input.

Pro costs $99 a month for two agents, up to 1,800 prospects contacted, and the waterfall enrichment behind the contact data. Above five seats you're on Custom pricing that we don't publish, which is fair to hold against us.
Timing is where it wins. Bulk extraction is where it loses. Wispra now sources 60% of its weekly demos from these signals.

Clay looks like a table and behaves like a pipeline. You load rows, then chain data providers, AI prompts and scrapers column by column until each row says what you're looking for. It replaces the glue work between tools; the extraction still happens elsewhere.
Launch is $185 a month with 2,500 data credits and 15,000 actions. Growth is $495 and is the first tier with native CRM sync. Seats are unlimited on every plan.

For a three-person team the entry ticket runs close to double a full Gojiberry subscription, and you're still bringing the list. What comes back is control nothing else here offers. More in our roundup of Clay alternatives.

Apollo sells access to a few hundred million business records, then lets you reveal emails and phone numbers with credits and send from the same screen. The database is the product, and the sequencer stops you from buying a second subscription.

Basic is $49 per user per month on annual billing, $59 monthly. Professional is $79, Organization $119 with a three-seat floor, which puts real entry at $357. Credits are pooled, and they don't roll over.
Nothing here gives you more contacts for less money, and nothing here is quieter about which of them you'd want to write to today. Our Apollo alternatives page goes through the credit math.

Outreach automation next. None of the four below finds prospects for you. They take a list you've already got and put messages in front of it, and they differ mostly on how many accounts they can send from at once.

TexAu chains pre-built actions, called spices, into cloud workflows that run whether or not your browser's open. The 2026 rebuild moved billing off run time and onto credits charged only when a lookup succeeds.
TexAu ships two products under one account, and the split matters for a small team:
Platform plans start at $99 a month, around $79 with yearly billing, which works out to two months free. TexAu puts 2,500 credits at roughly 450 to 500 enriched leads.
You're still the one deciding who enters the workflow, and that decision is the expensive part of outbound. What TexAu fixes is paying for server time you couldn't forecast.
Expandi runs social outreach from its own cloud, with a dedicated residential address for each connected account. It's selling caution instead of breadth, and it prices accordingly.

Business is $99 per connected account per month, roughly $79 on annual billing. An agency tier opens at ten accounts and gets negotiated. The trial runs seven days, which isn't much next to a proper warm-up.
Account count decides this one. At one or two profiles it's the most cautious cloud option in the group, and by ten it costs more than the pipeline it builds.
Waalaxy is a browser extension built by a French team, and it's the entry price of the whole category. The free plan never expires, which is rare in this category.
Pro is €19 per user per month, Advanced €49, Business €69, with roughly 50% off on an annual commitment. It only runs while your browser's open, so a closed laptop is a paused campaign.

Nothing here costs less to start. Then you read the entry plan properly. The email credits are token, and multichannel doesn't arrive until three tiers up, which turns €19 into €69 the week you add a second channel.

HeyReach was designed around agencies from the start. You connect several profiles, rotate sending across them to keep per-account volume low, and read every reply in one inbox. Team members cost nothing; you're paying per connected sender.
Growth runs $79 per sender per month and drops to $59 past ten. Enrichment credits get bought in packs, and the top tiers won't run without proxies you supply yourself.
Volume across many accounts is where it wins. Deciding who deserves the message is where it stops, because it never looks outside the list you loaded.
Data extraction last, and this is where a like-for-like replacement lives. If you came here because a Phantom broke, these three do that job and do it at a scale Phantombuster can't reach.

Apify is the closest thing here to infrastructure. You run containerized programs called Actors on their cloud, pick from thousands in the store, or write your own in Python or JavaScript. This is the family Phantombuster belongs to, taken several steps further.
Two numbers shape the bill, and the subscription is neither of them:
The free tier carries $5 of monthly platform credit. Starter is $29 a month and that fee comes back as $29 of credit you burn down, then Scale at $199 and Business at $999.
It does the extraction job better than anything else here, at the cost of being a platform your team operates instead of a tool it picks up.

Octoparse hands the same job to people who don't write code. You open a site in a visual builder, click the fields you want, and it produces a task you can schedule. You learn an interface here, and nobody has to learn a language.
Free covers 10 tasks and local runs. Standard is $69 a month, and that headline already includes the 16% annual discount. Professional is $249, and residential proxy traffic bills at $3 a gigabyte.
For a non-technical operator it's the shortest path from a web page to a clean file. Then the invoice arrives. On protected sites, proxies and CAPTCHA solving can add most of the base price again.
Evaboot exports a saved premium search, strips the noise out of it, and finds the emails. It can't work without an active premium search seat, and that seat is the real cost line.
Since the 2026 rebuild the plans are a credit slider from $9 to $79 a month. That's before the premium search seat at around $100, which puts the real entry line closer to $109.
It's the cheapest way to turn a saved search into a usable file, and it's also the tool here most dependent on a subscription you buy from someone else.
You shouldn't have to guess who to contact
Gojiberry watches more than 30 buying signals across socials and the web, checks each account against your ICP, and sends you the ones you'd want to write to.

The confusion behind most disappointed reviews starts here. Phantombuster is excellent at moving data from a page into a file on a schedule, and it isn't trying to do anything else. It was never built to judge whether the person in that row wants to hear from you. Every complaint about lead quality is a complaint about asking an extraction tool to do qualification.

You pick a prebuilt script, connect a source, set a schedule, and let it run on their servers. More than a hundred of them exist across social platforms, maps and search results. Chain several into a Workflow and you've got a small pipeline: extract a search, enrich the rows, push the output somewhere. An MCP server also lets tools like Claude drive it directly, which is a genuinely modern touch on an old product.
The automation library remains impressive, and nothing else here matches its breadth of sources. The weaknesses are commercial, and they don't show up in the first week.

Phantombuster bills three resources at once, and any one of them can stop your month. Execution time is the hours your automations spend running. Slots are how many can stay active simultaneously. Credits cover the metered steps, and they don't share a pool: email discovery, AI, URL lookups and CAPTCHA handling each have their own.

Start is $69 a month for 20 execution hours, 5 slots and 500 email credits. Grow is $159 for 80 hours, 15 slots and 2,500 email credits. Scale is $439 for 300 hours, 50 slots and 10,000 email credits. Annual billing brings those to roughly $56, $128 and $352. There's no mid-cycle top-up on hours, so running out on day 20 means pausing or upgrading permanently.

The detail that moves the invoice sits in the email pool. One credit is spent per discovery attempt, whether or not an address comes back. Phantombuster's own worked example puts 500 attempts at a 40% match rate on the Grow plan, which is 200 verified emails and about $0.80 each. Miss more often than that and the number climbs quietly.
Run the math for a team of three

Three reps working 400 contacts a month each need 1,200 rows. Grow covers the extraction and gives 2,500 discovery attempts, so the data side holds at $159. Then nothing has been sent yet. Add social sequences at €69 per user on the Business tier and you're at roughly $380 a month before anyone writes a first line.

Gojiberry Pro is $99 with two senders included, and a three-rep team goes to Custom pricing that we don't publish. That's a real gap in our favor on the sticker and a real gap against us on transparency. What the $380 stack still doesn't buy is a reason to write today, which is the part Mindflow measured at a 31% lift in replies.

Ratings sit around 4.4 on G2 and 4.5 on Capterra, which is solid for a tool this technical. Reviewers consistently praise cloud execution, since it doesn't depend on a laptop staying awake, and the range of sources it reaches. Pricing dominates the negative reviews, and the specific complaint is almost always execution hours disappearing faster than expected.

Trustpilot tells a more divided story, with a large share of top ratings sitting next to a large share of one-star reviews. That split usually means a tool works beautifully for one profile of user and doesn't fit another at all. Our full Phantombuster review digs through those reviews in detail.

Two accounts are exposed here, and most articles only discuss one. The first is the social profile doing the automated actions. Automated collection and messaging run against the terms of service of every major platform. Detection looks at velocity, at patterns that repeat too regularly, and at sessions arriving from a datacenter address instead of the place you'd normally sign in from.

Phantombuster does apply delays between actions and recommends conservative settings, and cloud execution with proxies reduces the obvious signals. It doesn't remove them. In practice restrictions arrive as a warning first, then a temporary lock, then a permanent one for repeat cases. Repeated disconnections or frequent re-authentication prompts are the early signal worth reacting to.

There's a legal layer as well, separate from the platform's rules. Publicly visible does not mean freely reusable: the data is still personal data under GDPR, and the French regulator has been explicit that accepting a platform's terms is not consent to commercial prospecting. Its guidance on reusing public data for prospecting is short and worth twenty minutes before you build anything on extracted contacts.

The second exposed account is your sending domain, and it fails more quietly. A large extracted list with no intent behind it produces complaints, and complaints now carry a published ceiling you can't argue with. Bulk senders are expected to stay under a 0.3% spam complaint rate, and crossing it degrades delivery for everything you send afterward, including the emails your existing customers were waiting for.

Four reasons come up repeatedly, and they stack instead of competing. The first is account exposure, which nobody's thinking about until the week it happens. A restricted profile takes your pipeline with it, and the recovery is slow.

The second is cost drift. You're buying execution time, and results are not what the meter counts, so a month with heavier workflows costs more than a quiet one and the meter gives no warning before it stops. Three separate quotas mean you can sit on unused credits while the hours run dry.

The third is setup time. An extraction platform assumes somebody enjoys wiring workflows together and repairing them when a source changes its layout. In a team of three that person's usually the founder, and their hour is the most expensive one in the building.

The fourth runs deeper than the other three. An extraction tool hands you profiles, never a reason to write today. Meanwhile the list you've built is decaying: B2B contact data goes stale at roughly 2.1% a month, which is around 22% a year, so the file you cleaned in January is noticeably worse by summer.
Category names aren't much help here, because three of these tools sit in two categories at once. Start from the sentence that describes your week instead.
I need structured data off web pages at scale
Apify if someone writes code, Octoparse if nobody does. Neither one will tell you who to contact, and neither one's pretending to.
I need a clean export of a saved search
Evaboot, and budget the premium search seat alongside it. Nothing else here does that one job as cheaply.
I need to automate sequences on socials
HeyReach past five senders, Expandi at one or two accounts, Waalaxy on the smallest budget. We do this part too, minus the step where you build the list first.
I need enrichment logic I control column by column
Clay, without much debate. Try us instead if you'd rather the enrichment fired behind a signal than sat inside a formula you maintain.
I need contacts and sending on one invoice
Apollo covers both for less than most stacks. Come to us instead if the shortage is names worth writing to this week, not names in total.
My problem is targeting rather than volume
Gojiberry. This is the case the product was built for: a small team that's got more names than time, and no way to tell which of them changed situation last Tuesday.
Your competitors' customers are moving right now
Someone in your market just changed jobs or started following a competitor. Gojiberry spots it, checks they're a match for your ICP, and writes before anyone else does.
Extraction answers who exists. Intent answers who changed. The gap between those two questions is most of the difference between a 2% reply rate and a calendar that's filling.

The reason timing works is boring demographics. Median job tenure in the United States sits at 3.9 years, with 22% of workers in post under a year, so a meaningful slice of any market is new in seat at any moment. A new head of a function rebuilds their stack in the first quarter, and they aren't loyal to anything yet. An extraction tool gives you a thousand profiles; Gojiberry gives you the twenty who moved this week.
That difference is measurable on real accounts and never in a benchmark table, which is why the proof below is customer results instead of a scorecard we'd have made up.
Wispra
60% of weekly demos now come from intent signals instead of cold lists.
Mindflow
Reply rate climbed 31% after outbound moved onto intent triggers.
GTE Localize
More than 100 meetings booked after switching from cold email to intent-led outreach.
Baur Software
Network doubled by scaling outreach that still reads as written by a person.

Support here splits into three regimes instead of ten different answers, and knowing which one you're buying into matters more than a published response time. The threshold that moves you between regimes is almost always seat count.
Self-serve, chat only
Waalaxy, Apify, Octoparse and Evaboot answer in a chat widget or by email. You sign up, you pay by card, and nobody's going to call you. Onboarding here means documentation.
Per-seat with onboarding
TexAu, Expandi and HeyReach add human onboarding once you cross a seat or sender threshold. Below it you're back in the chat widget with everyone else.
Sales-led above a line
Clay Enterprise and Apollo Organization put a named contact on the account, and both of them put a call between you and the price. Gojiberry does the same above five seats, and we aren't proud of it.
The product started as a manual routine that worked and refused to scale.

Before Gojiberry, Roman spent his days prospecting on socials for Coco.ai. He did intent research by hand, watching for who'd just changed roles, who had started following competitors, who had begun asking questions about the category in public. Then he wrote to them, one at a time, referencing the thing that had changed.

It worked well enough that the ceiling became obvious. One person can follow about thirty accounts properly. Past that the method collapses, and you're back to sending the same message to everyone. Gojiberry is that manual routine running on its own, at a scale a person cannot reach by hand.
That history is also why the product refuses to extract anything. The signal was always the point, and a bigger file wasn't what Roman was missing.

It depends on which half of the job you want replaced. For extraction at scale, Apify is the closest match and beats Phantombuster on throughput. For the same cloud automation shape, TexAu is the nearest structural swap. For a team of two to ten who care about booked meetings more than row counts, we'd point at Gojiberry, since it removes the list-building step instead of making it faster.

For a growth engineer who enjoys building workflows and needs data from several platforms, yes. The automation library is deep and the workspace pricing is generous. For a three-person sales team with nobody owning ops, the setup time and the three separate quotas usually cost more attention than the output's worth.

Phantombuster is a general automation platform billed on execution time, covering many sources. Waalaxy is a browser extension focused on social sequences, billed per user from €19 a month. One's built for reach, the other for cost. We put them head to head in our Phantombuster and Waalaxy comparison.

There's a permanent free plan, though it's a sandbox and not a working tool. It gives you 30 minutes of execution time a month, one slot, and no monthly enrichment credits. Exports are capped at 10 rows. The 14-day trial is more useful for evaluation, with two hours of execution time and five slots, but the same 10-row export cap applies.

Public does not mean free to reuse. Under GDPR the data you collect is still personal data, and the French regulator has stated that accepting a platform's terms of use is not the same as consenting to commercial prospecting. Its guidance on reusing publicly accessible data for prospecting is worth reading before you build a pipeline on extracted contacts. Separately, automated collection goes against the terms of most platforms, which is a contractual matter and a separate one from the law, and it's what gets accounts restricted.

Evaboot on the sticker, from $9 a month, until you add the premium search seat it depends on and the real line becomes around $109. Waalaxy at €19 per user is the cheapest tool here that sends anything at all, though cold email lives on the €69 tier. Apify's free plan with $5 of credit is the cheapest way to test extraction at all.

For Apify, yes, or at least somebody comfortable reading logs and reasoning about compute. Clay sits in an odd middle: there's no code, but it rewards someone who thinks like an engineer. Octoparse, Waalaxy, Evaboot, Expandi, HeyReach and Gojiberry are all designed for a salesperson to run without help.

Yes, and plenty of teams do. Keep the Phantoms doing the jobs they already do well, and let Gojiberry handle the question of who deserves a message this week. The two motions don't collide, because one produces rows and the other produces reasons to write. Our full side-by-side covers where each one earns its keep.

Tell Gojiberry who you sell to and it starts surfacing the people who've already started looking. No scraping, no proxies, nothing to configure.

Let's be real: you don't need to spend $99/month just to start automating your outreach. But hopping on Google for "free" tools often feels like a trap. Most are so limited they're barely useful, while others are just short-lived trials demanding a credit card upfront. So where's the real value?

We've been there. After digging through 15+ free and freemium tools, analyzing user feedback, case studies, and feature sets, we built the guide you're looking for. This isn't just another list. It's a strategic breakdown of the top 10 free LinkedIn automation tools, complete with their blunt, honest limitations, best use cases, and exactly what you can achieve with each.

We'll show you what to expect from every platform, how to choose the right one for your goals, and even how to properly test a full-featured, multi-channel tool like Gojiberry with its free trial to see what "real" prospecting feels like. If you want the fastest way to test real workflows, start with Gojiberry's free trial.
Ready to find a free tool that actually works for you? Let's dive in.
Before we jump into the list, let's clear up what "free" actually means in the world of LinkedIn automation. It's not always what it seems. Based on our research, tools fall into three main buckets.
Truly Free
A core set of features at no cost, with no time limit, and usually no credit card. The catch: they are almost always heavily restricted in daily actions (for example, 5 connection requests per day).
Freemium
The most common model. A permanently free tier with basic functionality, but the good stuff (advanced sequences, analytics, higher limits) is locked behind a paid upgrade.
Free Trial
Full, unrestricted access to a premium tool for a limited time (usually 7 or 14 days). Not free forever, but the best way to test a tool's true power and see if it's worth paying for.

Our ranking criteria focused on tools that are genuinely free or offer a trial with clear terms, support real automation tasks, state their limitations honestly, and are practical for beginners to get started with.
Want the short version? These three tools offer the best starting points, each for a different type of user.

Why it's #1: Most tools on this list automate a single channel and cap you hard on a free tier. Gojiberry is different. It's an AI-powered, multi-channel prospecting platform. It tracks 30+ buying-intent signals across socials and the web, surfaces leads who are in-market right now, and triggers personalized outreach across channels. The free trial is the best way to test that end to end, without the severe limits of a capped free plan.

Instead of firing off a handful of connection requests and calling it a day, the trial lets you build and run a complete, intent-driven sequence. You can test hyper-personalization, set up follow-ups that trigger based on prospect behavior, and see real analytics on what's working. Think of it as a test drive of a high-performance car, not just sitting in the showroom.
What you can do during the trial:

Limitations: The main limitation is that it's a time-boxed trial. It's designed to prove the tool's value quickly, not for long-term free use. Depending on the current offer, it may require a payment method to activate, but the terms are always clear upfront.

Verdict: If your goal is to genuinely evaluate whether automated prospecting can generate leads for your business, starting with a powerful, multi-channel free trial is a much smarter move than tinkering with a heavily capped single-channel tool.
Run a real, intent-driven, multi-channel sequence, not a capped demo.

Why it's #2: Dux-Soup is a veteran in the space and offers one of the best "permanently free" options available. It's a Chrome extension that's been a starting point for countless sales reps over the years.

Free features: The free "Starter" plan focuses on one key activity: automated profile visiting. It can automatically view up to 100 profiles a day. It doesn't send messages for you, but this is a classic "get on their radar" technique that can lead to inbound connection requests. You can also manually tag profiles and export basic data.

Limitations: The free plan does not automate connection requests or messages, a major limitation for active outreach. To build actual sequences, you need to upgrade. Since it's a browser extension, it only works when your computer is on and Chrome is running.
Verdict: For beginners who want to test the concept of automation and are okay handling messaging manually, Dux-Soup's free tier is a no-risk entry point.

Why it's #3: Waalaxy offers a more generous free tier than most competitors, making it a strong contender for beginners. It's a cloud-based tool with a fun, user-friendly interface that simplifies creating basic outreach campaigns.

Free features: The free plan lets you send up to 80 connection invitations per month and includes access to live support, which is rare for a free tier. You can build simple, two-step sequences, a step up from what most free tools offer.

Limitations: 80 invites a month is very low volume, about 4 per business day. Enough to run a tiny, hyper-targeted test, but it won't fill your pipeline. Advanced features like email integration and multi-channel campaigns are locked behind paid plans.
Verdict: If you want a "forever free" tool to dip your toes into sequence-building and automated invites, Waalaxy is a great place to start.
Beyond the top 3, several other tools offer free tiers or trials worth considering. Here's a quick rundown of tools #4 to #10.

Bottom line on free plans: a free tier shows you the dashboard. A free trial lets you land a meeting. If you can generate one or two qualified appointments during a 14-day trial, you've already proven the ROI for a paid plan.
So can you actually build a lead pipeline with a free tool? The honest answer: it depends.

The key takeaway? For serious users, a free trial is almost always more valuable than a free tier. A free tier shows you the dashboard. A free trial lets you land a meeting. The logic is simple: if you can generate just one or two qualified appointments during a 14-day trial, you've already proven the ROI for a paid plan that might cost $50-$100/month.
If you want a realistic test with full workflows, start with Gojiberry's free trial.
If you're starting with a free tool, you have to be smart about it. Here's how to get the most out of limited resources.
Not all tools are created equal. Here's which free option works best for specific goals.
True lead generation requires volume and follow-up, which free tiers struggle with.
For cold outreach, the ability to send a personalized request and follow up is key.
For outreach testing with full capabilities, try Gojiberry during the free trial.
If your goal is simply to stay top-of-mind, you don't always need a complex tool.
While not direct automation, scheduling posts is part of a complete social strategy.

Safety depends more on how you use the tool than on the tool itself. Cloud-based tools are generally considered safer than browser extensions because they run from a dedicated IP address. But if you set aggressive limits (say 100 connection requests a day) on any tool, you risk getting your account flagged. Always start with conservative, human-like activity levels.

You can get banned using any automation tool, free or paid, if you misuse it. The biggest red flags are sending a huge volume of requests in a short time, spammy generic messages that get reported, and using tools in unauthorized ways. Stick to quality over quantity.

It depends on your goal. For a "forever free" option to learn the basics, Dux-Soup (profile visits) or Waalaxy (limited invites) are top choices. For seriously evaluating whether automation can generate real business results, a Gojiberry free trial is the best option because it's unrestricted and multi-channel.

Start with a free trial or a free tier to validate your strategy on a small scale. Once you prove a positive response (for example a 20%+ acceptance rate and a 10%+ reply rate), it's time to upgrade. The limitations of free tools quickly become a bottleneck to growth.

Define your primary goal first (lead gen, networking, engagement). Then choose the tool that best supports that goal within its free offering. If you're serious about results, prioritize a tool with a full-featured free trial so you can test its true capabilities.

You now have a complete, no-fluff map of the free LinkedIn automation tools landscape. We've defined what "free" really means, exposed the honest limitations of free tiers, and highlighted why a free trial is the smartest path for anyone serious about results. Free tiers are for learning. Free trials are for earning.

Run one real, multi-channel, intent-driven sequence and see the difference for yourself.

We read every price on the vendor's own page in August 2026, except where the text names a third-party source. Four of these tools charge per seat, so the figure above covers one person and you'll pay it again for every colleague.

We opened every pricing page ourselves between 20 and 24 August 2026 and wrote down the tier, the billing cycle and what each tier covers. Where a vendor publishes nothing, we say so and quote the third-party figure with its source. We opened accounts wherever the product lets you, ran the setup flow to the point where a campaign would start, and noted what each one asks you to supply before it'll do anything useful. We also read the public review corpus on G2 for AnyBiz and pulled the recurring complaints rather than the star rating alone.

One thing you won't find here: a scorecard of measured reply rates across twelve tools. We haven't run a controlled campaign on an identical list through all twelve, and an invented percentage would be worth less than this sentence admitting it. When we run it, the numbers land on this page. We pay for every plan ourselves, and no vendor read a word of this before publication. Gojiberry is our product, so read the comparison table with that in mind and check the arithmetic, which we show in full.
Gojiberry finds the leads and it reaches out, at one flat price for the team. It suits a two to ten person sales team that hasn't got anyone free to watch a market by hand.

Pro costs 99 dollars a month for the whole team rather than per seat, and you're free to leave at the end of any month. Agencies and teams above five people move to a custom plan. Wispra now sources 60 percent of its weekly demos from that signal feed.
It collapses the finding and the writing into one flat bill, at the price of no phone channel and nobody sitting down to build your first campaign with you.
Artisan sells Ava, an autonomous AI SDR. Philosophically it sits closest to AnyBiz, and you hand the whole motion over, then check the calendar.
Artisan publishes no rate and quotes on a call. Outside sources place a full deployment around 50,000 dollars a year, so treat it as a range and don't budget from it.
The demo is the gate. Once you're through it, Ava runs the closest thing on this page to the AnyBiz motion, and the invoice lands in the same territory as a junior hire.

11x won't publish a rate either. Public trackers put a deployment around 50,000 dollars a year. Read the best 11x alternatives for the wider field.
Nothing else here runs voice and email agents off the same data, and nothing else here asks a five-person team for a number it can't see in advance.
AiSDR packs search, writing, sending and warmup into one tool. It publishes every tier, which almost nobody else in this category does.

Solo costs 250 dollars a month with no contract, Explore costs 900 and Scale costs 2,500, so you're never guessing. Explore and Scale run on a quarterly contract paid in advance, and annual billing takes roughly 20 percent off.
The published price decides this one. Solo suits a founder testing the channel for a month. Above it, you're committing 2,700 dollars before the first meeting appears.
Alta runs three agents on one data layer: Katie for outbound, Alex for inbound and calling, Luna for RevOps. It aims at growth-stage and enterprise revenue teams, and it doesn't pretend otherwise.

Alta publishes no rate. Its plans page won't give you one without a call, and the quote it builds rests on volume, headcount and channels, which we checked in August 2026. Our full Alta HQ review goes deeper.
Coverage is where it wins. Team size is where it loses.
Topo is a European, signal-driven outbound platform. You'll want it if your sequences should fire on a trigger rather than on a calendar.
Third-party listings quote 69 euros per seat each month, and Topo doesn't publish the figure itself. Compare the field in the best Topo.io alternatives.
European hosting shortens the procurement conversation. Then the seat count arrives. Five people pay five times the sticker, and the signal advantage doesn't hold up against that bill.
Amplemarket sequences across channels with a human approving before anything leaves. Teams that want automation without surrendering the message stop here.
Third-party listings report from 600 dollars a month per user, which makes it the steepest per-seat rate you'll find on this page.
It keeps a person on every message, at the price of a bill that'll triple the moment a third rep joins.
Apollo puts the contact database and the sequencer on one invoice. When the budget review lands and prospecting still has to happen, this is what's left standing.
Apollo charges 49 dollars per user per month on annual billing, or 59 if you'd rather pay month to month. We broke down what Apollo really costs once credits enter the picture.
Apollo won't execute anything on its own, and the credit meter rations the data. For a team that still needs pipeline on a shrinking budget, nothing else pairs data and sending this cheaply.
Instantly buys email volume at the lowest cost per send. You already own a list, and you'd like an answer from the market this month.
The outreach-only Growth plan costs 47 dollars a month, which is less than most teams spend on coffee. Bundles that add the lead database open at 94 dollars monthly or 85 dollars on annual billing.

Nothing here sends more email for less, and nothing here does less to tell you who deserves the message. Send that volume without targeting and you'll walk straight into the 0.3 percent spam complaint ceiling Google imposes on bulk senders.
Clay runs waterfall enrichment across many providers at once. Your real problem is the list rather than the sending.
Launch costs 167 dollars a month on annual billing, or 185 if you won't sign for a year. Weigh the field in the best Clay alternatives.
Match rates climb where a single provider gives up. Then the credits go. And Clay hands you a clean list, not a meeting.
Outplay gives reps five channels and lets them drive. It fits sales where the relationship closes the deal and volume never has.
Outside sources place it at 79 dollars per seat each month, which a small team can absorb without a board discussion.
Discipline is where it helps. Capacity is where it doesn't.
Salesforge handles execution end to end, with one shared inbox and warmup built in. Agent Frank adds the autonomous layer on top, and he isn't included.

The platform costs 40 dollars a month on Pro and 80 on Growth, with unlimited users on Growth. Agent Frank costs 499 dollars a month with quarterly billing on the pricing page, and a demo gates access. Their Agent Frank page quotes 599 dollars a month, so ask which one you're on before you sign.

Agent Frank reads no buying signals, so he writes beautifully to whoever you point him at. What Salesforge does better than anyone at 40 dollars is put sending, warmup and infrastructure in one account.
Stop guessing who to contact
Gojiberry checks every account against your ICP and hands you the ones showing buying signals. No quarterly commitment, no demo to sit through.

What works
What hurts

Three things matter more than the sticker. First, AnyBiz bills every quarter, so you're out 1,491 dollars on Starter and 2,994 on Recommended before anything happens. Second, the entry tier covers email alone, and the multichannel promise starts at 998 dollars a month. Third, no free plan and no self-serve signup exist: every button on the pricing page books a demo.

Every plan carries the 450 million contact database, the sending infrastructure and a dedicated consultant. AnyBiz also benchmarks itself against a hire rather than against software, putting a sales employee at 3,600 dollars a month, made of 2,500 in salary, 400 in software, 300 in database and 400 in admin. That comparison tells you who AnyBiz sells to: a founder who's choosing between a first SDR and a subscription.
AnyBiz advertises 2 to 3 opportunities a month on Starter and 6 to 9 on Recommended. Divide the price by the promise and the picture flips.
Starter: 497 ÷ 3 = 166 dollars per opportunity at best, and 497 ÷ 2 = 249 dollars at worst.Recommended: 998 ÷ 9 = 111 dollars per opportunity at best, and 998 ÷ 6 = 166 dollars at worst.

Read those two lines together. On AnyBiz's own numbers, the entry plan costs more per opportunity than the plan above it, 166 to 249 dollars against 111 to 166. The cheap tier is the expensive one. A small team that picks Starter to cap its spend pays the highest unit price on the page, and it's getting one channel for that.

AnyBiz scores 4.8 out of 5 on G2 across 343 reviews, which we checked by hand on 24 August 2026. Reviewers praise the automation, the support and the multichannel reach, and they aren't shy about it. Two complaints recur: 52 reviews call the pricing high for what the platform delivers, and 27 report inaccurate leads or unreliable visitor identification.

You pay 1,491 dollars before you know whether the channel works. AnyBiz explains on its own site that its AI needs that window to test audiences, messages and sending times, and the reasoning holds. It still means a five-person company funds a full quarter of learning out of its own cash, and it won't see that money again if the market answers no.

Example

Most agency owners rebuild the same staffing sheet on a Friday afternoon. It's nobody's job, so it lands on whoever cares most. We put the schedule in one place and update it when a project moves, so Friday goes back to being Friday. How do you handle it today?

A pitch this good still needs somebody on the other side who wants the problem solved this month. That's the half a generator can't reach. Gojiberry watches for the companies that just showed a buying signal, then puts your pitch in front of them. See who's ready to hear it.
Table of contents

A sales pitch is the short version of why somebody should talk to you. It names a problem the buyer already feels, shows what changes once that problem goes away, and asks for one small next step. The channel decides the length, never the job. Thirty seconds at an event, ninety words in an inbox, one sentence on a profile: it's the same work in all three.
Your pitch is only half the job

Five pitches, written out in full, for a fictional company called Rotamap that sells staffing software to creative agencies. Swap the details for yours and the shape holds. Read them out loud before you send anything, because a pitch that trips your own tongue will trip theirs too. You'll hear the weak line before you see it.
Elevator pitch at an event

"Most agency owners I meet rebuild the same staffing sheet every Friday afternoon. It's nobody's job, so it lands on whoever cares most, and it breaks the week someone goes on holiday. We put that schedule in one place and update it when a project moves. Three agencies switched last quarter and none of them opened the old sheet again. How do you handle it today?"

Sixty-six words, and it ends on a question so the other person has somewhere to go. The number does the heavy lifting because it's small and checkable. Nobody believes a fivefold improvement from a stranger at a conference.
Cold email with its subject line
Subject: Your two open producer roles

"Hi Marta,You're hiring two producers, which usually means the staffing sheet already broke once this quarter.Rotamap keeps the schedule in one place and updates it when a project moves, so nobody spends Friday afternoon rebuilding it. Ledger Studio stopped doing that entirely after two weeks.Worth fifteen minutes to see whether it fits how you run projects?"

Seventy-four words, one ask, no bullet points. The subject line names something Marta published herself, so it reads as attention rather than a merge tag. Our cold email generator writes the whole message once you've picked the angle.
Phone opener
"Marta, I'm calling because you've got two producer roles open and the agencies we work with tell us that's when scheduling falls over. Can I take thirty seconds to explain, or is now bad?"

Twenty-nine words, and it says why you called this person, rather than any person, then hands them the exit. Asking permission beats pushing through, because a no costs you nothing here and a yes buys real attention. It's the same instinct behind a good cold email icebreaker.
One-line positioning sentence for a profile
"Rotamap keeps creative agencies staffed without the Friday spreadsheet."
Ten words, and it survives a sideways glance in a feed. A one-liner earns its place by naming the buyer and the pain in the same breath. Drop either half and you're back to a category label.
Discovery call opener

"Before I say anything about Rotamap, I want to check I understood your setup. You run about twelve projects at a time, two producers share the schedule, and it lives in a spreadsheet. Is that right, and what breaks first when it goes wrong?"

The opener hands the first two minutes back to the buyer. Reps who talk first on a discovery call lose it, because they pitch a problem the prospect never confirmed. Every sentence gets easier once they've described the mess in their own words.
Mindflow
Rebuilt outbound around intent signals and lifted reply rates by 31 percent.
Wispra
Sixty percent of their weekly demos now come from intent signals.
Five steps, in order, and skipping the first leaves the other four with nothing to stand on.
Google's bulk sender rules now hold senders to a spam complaint rate under 0.3 percent. Step one is what keeps you under it. Volume without a reason to write buys you a filter, not a meeting.
Gojiberry tracks over 30 buying-intent signals across socials and the web, then surfaces the accounts researching your category right now.
The steps above are a process, and these are the contents. A pitch that's missing one of the five still works sometimes. A pitch missing two rarely does.
Structure gets you a draft, and these four decide whether that draft earns a reply.
Lead with their pain
Open on the problem they feel, not the product you built. If they don't see themselves in line one, they never reach line two.
Sell the outcome
Translate features into what changes on a Monday morning. Buyers pay for the destination, and they tolerate the engine.
Back it with proof
One number, one case, or one recognizable customer. Proof turns a claim into something they can check.
End with one ask
A single low-friction step. Give them two doors and most people walk through neither.

There's a fifth thing that sits outside the sentence. Send the same pitch in March instead of June and it dies, word for word identical. No amount of rewriting fixes a message that arrived eight months early.
A generator sharpens how you say it, and who hears it decides whether it lands. Those two jobs sit on either side of a line, and the tool at the top of this page doesn't cross it.

It tracks over 30 buying-intent signals across socials and the web, surfaces the leads in active research right now, and triggers personalized outreach across several channels. The signal comes first, and you write the pitch from it. You don't open a blank page, you open a reason to write.

Timing matters more than most reps admit, because the list ages while you work it. B2B contact data decays at roughly 2.1 percent a month, about 22.5 percent a year. A pitch written on Monday against a list built in January reaches a quarter of the people who've already left.

Over 100 meetings after moving from email blasts to intent-based outreach.

Network doubled by scaling authentic outreach instead of raw volume.

Run the math for a team of three

Three reps, 400 prospects a month between them. Written by hand at four minutes each, that's over 26 hours of pitch writing every month, or most of a working week. The generator takes the writing down to minutes.
The 26 hours were never the expensive part. The expensive part is that a chunk of those 400 names had no reason to hear from you in the first place. Fixing the list beats speeding up the typing.
Why we ended up building this

Before Gojiberry there was Coco.ai. Roman spent his days prospecting on socials, doing by hand what this page describes: reading what people posted, spotting the ones who'd just said something that suggested a need, and writing the pitch from that. It worked. It also ate his week.

Coco.ai became the place we learned what a buying signal looks like, and how fast a good one goes cold. The generator at the top of this page is the small free version of that idea. The part that watches for the signal is what we spent the last two years building.

Both halves matter, and they fail in different ways. A weak pitch to a ready buyer gets a reply anyway. A sharp pitch to somebody with no reason to care gets nothing, however many times you rewrite the opening line. Most teams spend the week on the half that doesn't move the number. Our follow-up email generator covers the messages after this one, which is where most replies show up.
Yes. No sign-up, no credit card, no credit counter, and no limit on how many times you hit generate. The tool runs in your browser, so nothing you type ever leaves the page.

A good one names something specific about the buyer, states the problem in their words, shows what changes, and asks for one small step. The five worked examples above cover an event, an inbox, a phone call, a profile line, and a discovery call opener.

Research one specific thing, name the problem in their words, show what changes, back it with one piece of proof, and ask for one thing. The first step carries the other four, because a pitch with no specific fact behind it reads as a template.

A hook tied to that buyer, the problem as they would describe it, the solution in one sentence, one piece of proof, and a single ask. The steps are the process you follow. The elements are what ends up in the message.
About thirty seconds, which lands between 60 and 75 words. Long enough to name the problem, what you do, and why it matters. Short enough to say in one breath and leave room for them to answer.

If coverage is your gap, Kaspr and Cognism beat Lusha on European mobiles. If credits are your gap, Apollo and Saleshandy give you more room per dollar. And if you can already find anyone but nobody answers, the gap isn't data at all, it's timing, and that's the one Gojiberry was built for.
