We ran this the way a small team would. Every self-serve product on the list got started on its own free or entry plan, pointed at the same target list of French and British software companies between ten and two hundred people, and asked the same three things: find the person, find a way to reach them, and tell me whether now is a good moment. For the tools with no self-serve door, Cognism and ZoomInfo, we worked from published material and public reviews on G2 and Capterra. Every price quoted here came off the vendors' own pricing pages in July 2026.

We pay for every plan ourselves, and no vendor read a word of this before publication. Gojiberry is our own product, so read that entry as informed rather than neutral. One thing you won't find here: a scorecard of measured hit rates. We haven't run a controlled reveal test across twelve tools on an identical list, and an invented percentage would be worth less than this sentence admitting it. When we run it, the numbers land on this page.

Twelve tools, and they don't all do the same job. Eight are places to look someone up. Two are senders you'd pair with one of the eight. One is a workbench you assemble yourself. And the first one doesn't ask you to look anyone up at all. They're ordered by how close each sits to what you already do, so the entries near the top are the ones you could swap in this week.

Gojiberry is an AI-powered multichannel prospecting platform. It tracks more than 30 buying signals across socials and the web, surfaces the leads in active research right now, and triggers personalized outreach across several channels. It answers the question Lusha never asks: who deserves a message today?
Gojiberry starts free, and paid plans include 2 social senders instead of charging per reveal. There's no credit weighting to model here.
Timing is where it wins. Lookup is where it loses: hand it a name and ask for the mobile, and a database beats us. Wispra now sources 60% of its weekly demos from intent signals.

Kaspr is a browser extension that reveals phone numbers and emails from the profile you're viewing, backed by a database weighted toward Europe. If your dialing is French, German or Dutch, it's the closest like-for-like swap you can make.

There's a free plan with a small monthly credit allowance, and paid plans start around $49 a user a month. Phone and email draw on separate pools here, so check their current pricing page before you plan a month around a number.

You still choose the account yourself, and you'll still need a second tool to send anything. What changes is the hit rate on a French mobile, and for a team dialing Paris every morning that alone can justify the switch.

Apollo puts a database and a sequencer on one invoice, which for a founder paying two vendors is the obvious consolidation. Its free tier is the most generous of the twelve, and plenty of small teams never leave it.

Paid plans start around $49 a seat a month on annual billing, roughly a fifth more month to month. Overages move the invoice far more than the tier you pick, so it's the mobile meter you want to watch in week one.
It collapses two subscriptions into one and answers the credit math, at the price of checking a title before you dial, because enough reviewers report stale ones that you'll learn to.
Cognism sells human-verified mobiles and compliance, mostly to teams selling into Europe. It's the one tool here where a person has picked up the phone to check the number before it reaches you.

There's no self-serve tier, and no published price. Expect a quote, an annual contract and a budget in five figures a year for a small team. Ask about seat minimums before you get attached to the data.
The contract ends the conversation for most teams of two to ten. For the ones it doesn't end, no European phone data here comes close.
RocketReach is a lookup engine sitting on a large profile database, and it's one of the cheapest ways onto one. The limit sits in the tier list: the entry plan doesn't include phone numbers.

Essentials runs about $33 a month on annual billing and hides phone numbers entirely. Mobile reveals don't appear until the tier above, near $75 a month annual, and monthly billing costs a good deal more.
Buy the entry plan expecting phone data and you'll be back within a week. As an email research tool at that price, it holds up fine.
UpLead sells accuracy as the product. Every email is verified at the moment you pull it, and a bounce comes back to your credit balance rather than costing you twice.
Plans start around $99 a month on annual billing, and credits don't roll over. It isn't the cheapest entry here, and the refund policy is most of what you're paying for.
The credit frustration this whole article is built around has one direct answer, and this is it. Database size is the trade, since it's smaller than Apollo or ZoomInfo.
Hunter finds work emails from a domain rather than from a profile, and it doesn't charge per seat. For a team of three sharing one credit pool, that pricing model is worth real money.
There's a free plan covering a handful of searches a month. Starter sits near $34 a month on annual billing, closer to $49 month to month, and Growth lands around $104 with the API attached.
No phone numbers at all. If your motion is email and you sell to companies rather than to named individuals, nothing here costs less for what it does.
LeadIQ is built for reps who live in the CRM: capture the contact, push it, move on. It's also the only other tool here that tells you when someone changes jobs.
There's a free tier, and paid plans start around $36 a user a month with a steep step up to the pro tier. Credits pool across the account rather than per seat, which helps a small team.
Nothing else in these twelve comes as close to a timing signal, and the CRM workflow is quick. Then you notice what it watches: contacts you already knew about. A much smaller world than your market.
Clay is a spreadsheet that calls a hundred data providers, one column at a time. Nothing here gets you more coverage per dollar, and nothing here asks more of you before it works.

Free covers a hundred data credits a month. Launch is $185 a month and Growth is $495, and the dual meter, data credits for results and actions for operations, is the part you'll have to model before you commit.
Budget a week before it earns anything back. A founder with no ops help usually stalls somewhere around the second table.
ZoomInfo is the enterprise end of this market: the deepest database, the most intent data, and a procurement process to match. It's on this list so you can rule it out with a number.
Quote only, annual contract, and budget from roughly $15,000 a year before seats and add-ons. Seat minimums are usually where a team of five doesn't get through the door.
The seat minimum decides this one. Below twenty reps with nobody owning ops, the contract costs more than the pipeline it would find you. Above it, ZoomInfo earns its keep.

Saleshandy is a cold email platform first, with contact data bolted on as an add-on. It's here because the cheapest exit from a two-subscription setup sometimes runs the other way: keep the data you have, change the sender.

Outreach plans start near $25 a month for a couple of thousand prospects. Lead Finder is a second line on the invoice from around $29 a month, so you'll want to price the pair rather than the headline.
Nothing here moves more email for less money, and nothing here does less to tell you who should be receiving it.
Instantly is the other sender here, known for unlimited mailboxes and the volume playbook that comes with them. Contact data is an add-on in this one too.
The Growth plan is $37 a month, or about $30 on annual billing. Contact data starts near $47 a month on top of that, so you're really starting at $77 rather than at $30.

Volume is the entire proposition, and it delivers on it. Since February 2024, Google has asked bulk senders to keep user-reported spam complaints under 0.3%, and sending at volume without targeting is the fastest way to test that ceiling.
You shouldn't have to guess who to contact
Gojiberry watches more than 30 buying signals across socials and the web, checks each account against your ICP, and sends you the ones worth writing to.

Lusha is a contact data platform with a browser extension at the center of it. You open a profile, you click, and it returns a verified work email and, if you're willing to spend the credits, a direct phone number. It sits on a few hundred million business profiles, and it's strongest in the United States, in the United Kingdom, and in Canada.

The reason it spread through sales teams isn't coverage, it's friction. Two clicks, no export, and no list to build the night before, night after night. Speed is the whole product, and speed, unfortunately, is also the whole ceiling.
What works well
Where it stops
Lusha charges you twice for the same contact: once for the seat, then again for the action. The seat is the number on the pricing page. The action is the one that'll decide your month.

An email reveal costs one credit. A phone number costs ten. A contact where you want both burns eleven, so a plan advertising 400 credits is really about 36 complete contacts a month. That rate also doubled at some point from five credits to ten, which means every pricing guide written before the change understates the cost by half.

The self-serve tiers run from roughly $20 to $60 a seat a month on annual billing depending on the tier and where you drag the credit slider, and monthly billing adds something like 25% to 35% on top. Above a handful of users you're pushed onto a quote-based plan with an annual commitment. Plan names and allowances have moved more than once this year, so treat any figure you read, including ours, as a starting point and check their current pricing page before you budget.

Run the math for a team of three. Say each rep wants a mobile for 40 people a month. That's 400 credits of phone reveals per rep, per month, before a single email address. Three reps on a 400-credit plan run dry in the first ten days.

Then the reset. Unused credits don't roll over, so the month you prospect lightly subsidizes nothing at all, and the month you push hard costs extra. Budget the credits first, the seats second, because the seats are the smaller line. GTE Localize booked 100+ meetings after moving that budget from lookups to timing.
We didn't collect our own reviews, so this is a reading of what's public on G2 and Capterra rather than a survey. Three themes repeat with real consistency.

Praise lands in the same place every time: speed and simplicity. People describe onboarding a new rep in an afternoon. That counts for something in this category. Complaints cluster just as tightly, and they're almost always about credits, with the ten-to-one phone rate named directly. The second complaint is coverage: reviewers selling into Southern Europe, the Nordics or APAC report hit rates well below what they see in the US.
The third theme shows up at renewal rather than at signup. The invoice doesn't match what people remember agreeing to, usually because credit consumption grew faster than headcount did.

Credits that don't stretch. The ten-to-one phone rate is the single most cited reason for leaving. A plan reads as hundreds of credits, resolves to a few dozen full contacts, and nobody discovers this on the pricing page. They discover it on the 12th, when the meter stops.

Coverage that thins outside the US and UK. The database is strong where it's strong and thin where it isn't. This gets worse over time on its own, because B2B data decays: HubSpot puts the rate at around 2.1% a month, roughly 22.5% a year. A weak region doesn't stay static, it degrades.

Nothing happens after the reveal. You get a contact, and a blank cursor. So one workflow ends up costing two subscriptions, and the pair usually lands somewhere north of $100 a seat a month once the sender is on the invoice.

No sense of timing. This is the deepest gap and the one nobody puts in a support ticket, because it doesn't feel like a product defect. It feels like sales being hard. Median job tenure in the US sits at 3.9 years, with 22% of workers in post under a year, which means your market reshuffles constantly and a reveal tool has no opinion about any of it.
Pick by the gap you have rather than by the feature list you'd enjoy reading.
Coverage is the problem

European mobiles that don't show up? Kaspr if you want the same extension habit at a self-serve price, Cognism if the numbers are worth an annual contract. Gojiberry if the harder question is which accounts to dial at all.
Credits are the problem
Apollo gives you more room per dollar with sending included. Saleshandy is cheaper still if the volume you need is email. Gojiberry charges per plan, so no meter runs when you open a lead.
You pay twice for one workflow

Consolidate on Apollo, or pair Instantly with Hunter and keep each piece cheap and replaceable. If the second subscription is a social sender rather than an email one, our LeadIn alternatives roundup covers that half.
You find everyone, nobody replies

That's a timing gap. Gojiberry reads the signals and hands you the shortlist, and LeadIQ is the lighter option if job changes alone would do it. We put the signal tools against each other in the Trigify alternatives roundup.
Maximum coverage per dollar
Clay, provided you have a week to build tables and someone who enjoys it. The ceiling is high, and so is the floor.
Past twenty reps with an ops hire
ZoomInfo. Below that headcount, the contract costs more than the pipeline it finds you.
None of those six is your gap if what you want is an agent running the whole motion instead of a tool you drive yourself. That's a different shortlist, and it lives in our 11x alternatives roundup.

Whatever you land on, run it in parallel for two weeks before you cancel anything. Point both tools at the same fifty accounts, count what each one returns, and count what each one costs you to get there. Two weeks of overlap is cheaper than a year on the wrong plan.

It depends which half of the job you mean. For European mobiles, Kaspr and Cognism are better. For getting data and sending on one invoice, Apollo is better. For knowing who to contact in the first place, that's a different category, and it's where Gojiberry sits: Mindflow lifted reply rates 31% by writing to accounts that had just moved rather than to a static list.
Nothing on this page is better than Lusha at what Lusha does, which is turning a profile into a phone number in two clicks.

Apollo for most small teams, because it covers the sending too and its free tier is far more usable. Lusha wins on the narrow thing: mobile numbers in the US, UK and Canada, where reviewers consistently rate its accuracy above Apollo's. If you dial into those markets every day, that difference is worth paying for. If you send email and want one bill, Apollo is the easier call.

Several, and they're not all equal. Apollo's free tier is the most generous of the twelve and includes sending. Hunter's free plan covers a handful of searches a month with no seat limit. Kaspr and LeadIQ both give you a small monthly credit allowance. Gojiberry starts free as well.
Free tiers are for judging data quality against your own market, not for running outbound. Test them on twenty accounts you know well, so you can tell a wrong answer from a right one.

Because a phone number costs ten credits and an email costs one. If your motion involves dialing, you're spending at ten times the rate the plan's headline number suggests. A 600-credit plan is 60 phone numbers.

Two other things drain the pool faster than people expect: unused credits reset at the end of the billing cycle with no rollover, and features beyond straight reveals can draw from the same balance. Check what counts as a billable action on your specific plan.

Cognism, on the strength of human-verified numbers and do-not-call screening across European registers, with Kaspr close behind at a fraction of the commitment. We're reporting the consensus from public reviews and vendor documentation. We haven't run a controlled coverage test of our own across these databases.
If your market is France, Benelux or the DACH region, test both against fifty accounts you already know before you sign anything.

Browser extensions that read profile pages sit in a gray area with most professional networks, whose terms generally prohibit automated data collection. Reveal tools like Lusha are widely used and rarely the direct cause of a restriction on their own. What draws attention is volume and pace: hundreds of profile views a day from one account looks automated whether or not it is.
Keep your activity at human pace, and treat any tool that promises unlimited scraping as a risk to the account you've spent years building.

No, and you shouldn't. Run the new tool alongside it for two weeks on the same target accounts, then compare what each one returned and what each one cost. Most of these tools have free tiers or monthly billing precisely so you can do that.
Cancel once you have evidence, not on the strength of an article. Ours included.

Apollo, Hunter, Saleshandy and Instantly all send. Gojiberry sends across email and socials, and drafts the first message from the signal that surfaced the lead. Lusha, Kaspr, Cognism, RocketReach, UpLead, LeadIQ, Clay and ZoomInfo don't send anything on their own.

If you're pairing a finder with a sender, budget for both from the start. A $34 email finder plus a $30 sending platform costs a real $64 a month, so $64 is the figure a consolidated plan has to beat.
Your competitors' customers are moving right now
Someone in your market just changed jobs or started following a rival. Gojiberry spots it, checks they match your ICP, and writes before anyone else does.
These two aren't competing for the same job, which is exactly why the comparison is worth making. One answers how to reach a person. The other answers which person.

Lusha waits for you to pick the account. Gojiberry picks it from live signals. Gojiberry is an AI-powered multichannel prospecting platform: it tracks more than 30 buying signals across socials and the web, surfaces the leads in active research right now, and triggers personalized outreach across several channels. That's the whole difference, and it decides everything downstream, including what you spend.

Where we lose: point Gojiberry at a specific person whose mobile you need in the next ninety seconds and a database wins. We're not a lookup tool and we won't beat Lusha on phone coverage in its home markets. What we're claiming is that the lookup was never the hard part.
Wispra
60% of weekly demos now come from intent signals rather than from list building.
Mindflow
A 31% lift in outbound reply rate after switching to intent-based targeting.
GTE Localize
100+ meetings booked after moving from email outbound to intent-led outreach.
Baur Software
Network doubled by scaling authentic outreach instead of raw sending volume.

Support matters more at this company size than anyone admits, because you don't have an ops person to absorb a broken integration. Here's the shape of it across the twelve, without numbers we didn't measure.
Self-serve tools

Apollo, Hunter, RocketReach, Saleshandy, Instantly and Kaspr answer through chat or a ticket queue, in business hours, in English. Fast for a billing question, slower when it's something that needs an engineer.
Enterprise platforms
Cognism and ZoomInfo give you a named contact and structured onboarding. That's the thing you're buying with the annual contract, and it's worth real money when data breaks.
The middle
UpLead, LeadIQ and Clay hand you a human once you clear a seat or spend threshold. Below it, you're in the same queue as everyone else.

What we haven't done is time a first human reply from a paying account across all twelve vendors. That's a real test and it deserves real numbers, so we'd rather leave the table empty than fill it with estimates. When we've run it, it goes here.

Before Gojiberry there was Coco.ai, and before Coco.ai there was Roman spending most of his week prospecting on socials by hand. He wasn't short of contact data. He was short of a reason to write to any particular person on any particular Tuesday, so he started checking by hand for the things that suggested somebody had begun looking: a new role, a funding round, a competitor's post getting attention from the wrong crowd.

It worked, and it capped out at about thirty accounts a person. That ceiling is why the product exists and why it assumes a team of two to ten rather than a sales floor with an ops hire. Coco.ai was where the founders learned that finding the number was never the hard part.

Which brings the whole thing back to a question you can answer this week rather than next quarter. You already know how to write a good first message. The only thing missing is knowing who's ready to read one.
Try it on your own market
Tell Gojiberry who you sell to, and it brings back qualified prospects. No list building, no manual lookups.

Sending discipline is your constraint, and Agent Frank runs warmup, inbox rotation and follow-up better than most of this list. He works from a list you hand him though. If you want the list to arrive already sorted by who moved, that half is ours.
Regie.ai fits a floor your size

At thirty reps the seat minimum stops mattering and the dialer starts paying for itself. Worth knowing before you sign: our flat price covers the same headcount for a fraction of that contract, without the parallel dialer.

Topo runs outbound from one platform: buying signals, multichannel sequences, and an AI agent on top. OMR publishes 69 euros per user per month, and Topo's own pricing page shows no number at all. Three reps costs 207 euros a month, and every hire you make moves that number.

We went through twelve alternatives, checked what each one charges in August 2026, and sorted them by the bottleneck they fix. You'll find flat-price agents, per-seat platforms, a research engine and one workbench you assemble yourself.
Gojiberry finds your leads
Topo charges per seat. Gojiberry charges 99 dollars a month for the whole team, watches more than 30 buying signals, and hands you the accounts worth your time.
Table of contents

Pick by bottleneck rather than by feature list. If you can't tell who's in market, start with Gojiberry or Coldreach. If you can't get the volume out safely, start with Salesforge or AiSDR. If you're short of names, start with Apollo.

Prices checked on each vendor's own pricing page in August 2026. Several of these bill per seat, so the entry figure covers one person and your team multiplies it. Where a vendor publishes nothing, we say so in its section rather than guess.

We spent August 2026 on this comparison. For every tool we opened the vendor's own pricing page and copied the number it publishes, signed up wherever the product let us in without a call, read the public reviews on G2 and OMR, and settled each contradiction on the vendor's site rather than on a competitor's comparison page. That last rule mattered here: Salesforge writes that Topo stops at lead discovery, while Topo's product pages list multichannel sequences, managed email infrastructure and reply suggestions. We went with Topo.

One thing you won't find below: a scorecard of reply rates across twelve tools. We haven't run the same campaign on the same list through all twelve, and an invented percentage would be worth less than this sentence admitting it. When we run it, the numbers land on this page. We pay for every plan ourselves, and no vendor read a word of this before publication.

Twelve tools, grouped by what they replace. Six of them run the whole motion for you. Three hand you the data and let you drive. Two are execution platforms you point at a list. And the first one doesn't start from a search at all.

We built Gojiberry for the team that can't justify a seat license. It watches more than 30 buying signals across socials and the web, screens every account against your ICP, and opens the conversation on the channel where the signal fired. One price covers everyone who sells, so a fourth hire doesn't change the invoice.
Gojiberry costs 99 dollars a month for the whole team, and you won't need a card or a call to start. Three reps pay 99 dollars, not 297.
Point us at a market where nobody publishes anything and a database will beat us. Point us at a market that moves and you won't find anything here that reaches the right account sooner.

Artisan sells Ava as a virtual BDR that owns the top of the funnel end to end. She pulls contacts from a 300 million record database, researches each one, writes the sequence, warms the inboxes and handles replies up to a booked meeting. Since the Ava 2.0 rebuild in May 2026 you don't need a call to sign up and launch a campaign.
Intern runs 250 dollars a month on annual billing with 12,000 credits, Employee 600 with 30,000, and monthly billing adds about 10 percent. The power dialer's 67 dollars per seat on top.
It folds four subscriptions into one and doesn't ask anything of you before you try it, at the price of a meter that sets your budget instead of your plan.

11x splits the job between two agents. Alice runs outbound prospecting across email and socials, Julian answers and places calls. The pitch is a digital worker rather than a tool, and the contract matches the pitch. 11x sells on annual terms after a scoping call, so you won't be starting here on a Tuesday afternoon.

11x lists 36,000 dollars a year on its Growth plan and quotes everything above it. Julian carries a separate line, and buyers report first-year totals well past the sticker once implementation lands. We've gone deeper in the best 11x alternatives.

That number ends the conversation for a team of three, and it should. For a company that's already running ten reps with someone owning tooling, the two-agent split covers a channel the rest of this category skips.

AiSDR runs an agent called Ami across search, writing, sending and warmup. The plan provisions your domains and mailboxes, which removes the week most teams lose to deliverability setup. Every tier sits on the pricing page, so you don't need a call to build the budget.

Solo starts at 250 dollars a month for 200 researched contacts and one user, with no commitment. Explore costs 900 dollars a month on quarterly billing, Scale 2,500, and you'll save roughly 20 percent on annual billing.

Nothing else here gets you sending faster with less setup. Then the quarterly invoice arrives. Twenty-seven hundred dollars up front is a real decision for a five-person company that hasn't sent a campaign yet.

Apollo puts a large contact database and a sequencer behind the same login. You filter a list, reveal the contacts, and you're sending without exporting anything. For a team whose only problem is running out of names, it stays the cheapest complete answer here.

Apollo charges 49 dollars per user per month on annual billing, 59 dollars monthly, and keeps a free plan for a first look. Three reps land at 147 dollars a month. We've ranked the rest of the field in the best Apollo alternatives.
Nothing here gives you more names for less money, and nothing here does less to tell you which of those names isn't worth the send.

Coldreach sits closest to what we do. You describe the buying signal in plain English, it watches your market for that signal, and it doesn't write until it's read the company. Every message opens on a verified reason instead of a merge tag.
Starter costs 899 dollars a month, Growth 1,099, Pro 1,499 and Enterprise 1,999. If you'd rather hand the whole thing over, the managed version runs 3,000 dollars a month.
Timing is where it wins. Price is where it loses a two-person team.

Salesforge separates the platform from the agent. The platform runs human-led campaigns with warmup and inbox rotation. Agent Frank runs the same motion on his own, or waits for your approval on each message. Two products means two prices, which explains the gap you'll see quoted around the web.
The Salesforge platform starts at 48 dollars a month. Agent Frank costs 599 dollars a month on quarterly billing, or 499 on annual, and you'll add from 33 dollars for mailbox infrastructure.
Frank reads no buying signals, so he'll write beautifully to a company that signed with your competitor last quarter. On sending discipline alone, nothing here beats him.

Regie builds outbound around content and sequences, with agents that source leads, draft the copy and feed a power dialer. It aims at established sales floors, and the packaging doesn't hide it. Both published tiers carry a seat minimum and an annual term.

AI SEP costs 180 dollars per user per month with a ten-seat minimum, which puts the floor near 21,600 dollars a year. Force Multiplier Rep runs 499 dollars per user with a five-seat minimum, and you'll add about 150 dollars per user for the parallel dialer.
The seat minimum decides this one. Below ten reps you're paying for licenses nobody opens. Above it, the dialer and the content engine earn their line on the invoice.

Clay hands you a spreadsheet sitting on top of a hundred data sources, then steps back. You build the waterfall, write the prompts and push the output into whatever sends. You'll get more control here than anywhere else on this list, and you'll pay for it in hours.
Launch costs 167 dollars a month on annual billing, 185 dollars monthly, and credits meter every enrichment run. We've compared the field in the best Clay alternatives.
It replaces a data vendor and a research analyst at once, provided somebody on your side would rather build the machine than sell. If nobody volunteers, you've bought a spreadsheet.

ZoomInfo holds the deepest B2B dataset in this comparison, with org charts, technographics and intent topics layered over the contacts. Topo names it as one of the three American platforms it positions against. The commercial terms haven't moved in years: annual contract, quoted price, no self-serve door.
ZoomInfo publishes nothing. Buyers report around 15,000 dollars a year on the entry plan, climbing with seats and credits. We've pulled the reported numbers together in what ZoomInfo really costs.
Fifteen thousand dollars buys coverage a small team will never exhaust. Then the term arrives. You can't leave mid-year, and a company of three shouldn't sign for data it will use twice a week.

Amplemarket bundles contact data, intent signals, sequencing and deliverability into one platform and one contract. It sits in the same lane as Topo, and it's one of the few names here that publishes an entry price. Seats arrive in blocks rather than one at a time.

Startup costs 600 dollars a month on an annual term and includes two users. Growth and Elite go to quote, and extra seats bill separately. We've listed the cheaper routes in the best Amplemarket alternatives.
Six hundred dollars for two seats works out at 300 a head, which is roughly four times what Topo costs per person. The difference: you'll see Amplemarket's number before the call.

Lemlist is European like Topo, and it made its name on personalization: custom images, dynamic landing pages, and sequences that mix email, social steps and call tasks. It's now selling buying signals as credits on top of the sending plan. The email plan prices the workspace rather than the rep.

The email plan costs 69 dollars a month for the whole workspace. Multichannel moves to 109 dollars per user, which changes the arithmetic for a team of three. We've put it head to head in Smartlead vs Lemlist.

For one person running a real multichannel sequence, it's the cheapest route on this page. Three people on multichannel costs 327 dollars a month, and at that point the flat-price agents deserve a second look.
Gojiberry watches more than 30 buying signals across socials and the web, checks every account against your ICP, and tells you who moved this week.

Topo is a French AI sales platform. The company runs out of Paris and Delaware, Y Combinator backs it, and it sells one subscription covering the prospecting platform, an AI outbound agent and a human support layer. More than 200 teams run the agent next to their reps, and Topo doesn't sell the pieces separately.
A fair amount, and more than several comparison pages suggest. We wrote this section from Topo's own product pages rather than from anyone else's summary of them.
What Topo does well
Where it gets tight

Topo's own pricing page shows no number. It describes a single platform plan that includes three user licenses, 6,000 credits a year, two domains and six mailboxes, then asks you to talk to the team. OMR publishes 69 euros per user per month, which is the only public figure we found in August 2026.

Run the math for a team of three. At OMR's figure that lands on 207 euros a month and 2,484 euros a year. The three-license floor means a two-person company pays for a seat nobody logs into, and a fourth hire adds 828 euros a year before that person books a single meeting.

The credits deserve the same arithmetic. Six thousand a year, one per enriched lead, works out at 500 leads a month for the whole team, or about 167 per rep. For comparison, Gojiberry charges 99 dollars a month for everyone who sells, and our customer stories run on that same plan.

G2 rates Topo 4.9 out of 5 across 121 reviews, checked in August 2026. Reviewers there praise ease of use, speed to first value and the support, and the recurring complaints cluster on a learning curve and some integration friction. OMR lists Topo with zero reviews, so a buyer comparing across sites finds one glowing source and silence next to it. Topo's own site claims 150 customers and the same 4.9 average.

Topo detects buying signals and it executes campaigns, so the reasons below have nothing to do with a missing feature. They're about what the model costs a small team and what a buyer can check before signing.
The price follows headcount, not results

At 69 euros per user per month, growing from three sellers to five adds 1,656 euros a year to the bill before anyone books a meeting. The plan bundles three licenses, so the floor stays at three whether you're filling them or not.
The credits run on a yearly clock

Every plan ships 6,000 credits a year, one per enriched lead. That caps the whole team near 500 new names a month. Execution isn't the ceiling here, since Topo handles replies, warmup and multichannel sending. The ceiling is how many fresh accounts the year allows.
The feedback comes from one place
G2 shows 4.9 out of 5 across 121 reviews and OMR shows none. A near-perfect score on a single site, no published price and no free trial doesn't leave a buyer much to weigh before the call.
Personalization thins out as volume climbs

Google has held bulk senders to a 0.3 percent spam complaint rate since February 2024, and HubSpot puts B2B data decay at 2.1 percent a month. Push more volume through a list that ages while you work it and both numbers move against you. That one's on every agent here, ours included.
One bottleneck, one recommendation. Find yours and skip the rest.
You're 2 to 10 people and you want one price for the team
Gojiberry. Ninety-nine dollars a month covers everyone who sells, the signals decide who gets a message this week, and a fourth hire won't change the invoice.
You want an agent that handles calls too
11x.ai. Julian is one of the few phone agents shipping in this category. Budget for the annual term before you've fallen for the demo.
You want to launch fast without building a stack

AiSDR or Artisan. Both provision the sending infrastructure and neither one needs a call before you start. Artisan meters credits, AiSDR meters contacts. Gojiberry starts self-serve too, at a sixth of what Artisan's Employee plan costs.
The trigger matters more than the volume

Coldreach. You write the buying signal yourself and it researches every company before it drafts. You'll start at 899 dollars a month. Gojiberry runs the same play on a fixed signal set for 99, so budget decides between the two.
You already send at volume and want full execution

Salesforge. Agent Frank plus the warmup stack handles more sending per dollar than anything else here, once you've fed him a list. Plenty of teams pair him with Gojiberry, which supplies the accounts worth writing to.
You want to build your own lists
Clay. Nothing here gives an operator more room. Hand it to someone who enjoys the work, because a table nobody owns won't survive the quarter.
You mostly run short of contacts
Apollo. Forty-nine dollars per user buys the database and the sequencer, and the free plan tells you fast whether the data covers your market. If it doesn't, you've lost nothing.

Lemlist, at 69 dollars a month for the whole workspace on the email plan. Apollo comes next at 49 dollars per user per month, which beats Lemlist for one person and loses to it at three. Among the tools that find the accounts for you rather than waiting for a list, Gojiberry is the cheapest at 99 dollars a month flat, and Clay sits at 167 if you'd rather assemble the workflow yourself.

OMR publishes 69 euros per user per month. Topo's own pricing page shows no figure and routes you to a scoping call, so treat OMR's number as the best public estimate rather than a quote. What Topo does publish: every plan includes three user licenses, 6,000 credits a year, two domains and six mailboxes. At OMR's rate a team of three pays 207 euros a month, or 2,484 euros a year.

Gojiberry, and we'll show our reasoning rather than assert it. A team that size rarely has someone owning tooling, so per-seat pricing and annual contracts hurt twice: once on the invoice, once on the ramp. Gojiberry charges one flat price, starts without a call, and hands over accounts that moved this week. If sending volume is your actual constraint instead of targeting, Salesforge costs less per message and does that job better.

Most of them do. Artisan, 11x, AiSDR, Coldreach, Salesforge and Regie all manage replies up to a booked meeting, with an approval mode on several. Apollo, Clay, ZoomInfo and Lemlist expect a human in the thread, though Lemlist and Apollo at least keep the inbox where you're already working. Topo handles replies too, which is worth saying out loud since a few comparison pages claim otherwise.

Yes. Topo runs as a French company, Topo SAS, with a US entity in Delaware and offices in Paris and San Francisco. It positions itself as the European answer to ZoomInfo, Clay and Apollo. Lemlist is the other European name in this comparison, and Amplemarket keeps a strong European footprint. We're French too, which matters when procurement asks where the data sits.

Export three things before your renewal date: your account and contact lists, your sequence copy, and the exclusion list that keeps you off customers and open opportunities. Topo syncs activity back to HubSpot and Salesforce, so your CRM already holds most of the history. Then warm the new domains for two weeks before you send anything at volume, because a fresh domain you push hard lands in spam and you'll spend months digging out.

Yes, and a few teams do it deliberately during a renewal window. Gojiberry surfaces the accounts showing buying signals and starts the conversation; Topo keeps running whatever sequences you've already built. Point them at different segments so the same person doesn't get two messages in a week, and compare the reply rates after 30 days. That comparison usually settles the renewal question on its own.
Your buyers are moving now
Someone in your market just changed jobs or started following a competitor. Gojiberry spots it, checks they match your ICP, and writes before anyone else does.
Both products start from buying signals, so a feature-by-feature reading won't settle it. The split shows up in how each one bills.

Here's the line that decides it. Topo bills every seat and Gojiberry bills the team. At one rep the gap barely registers. At three it turns real, and at five it pays for a contractor. That's the whole argument, and we'd rather make it once than dress it up.
What the flat price buys in practice shows up in the numbers our customers report:
Wispra
Intent signals now drive 60 percent of the demos booked each week.
Mindflow
Reply rates climbed 31 percent after the team moved to intent-based outbound.
GTE Localize
The team booked 100+ meetings by swapping email blasts for intent-led outreach.
Baur Software
Baur doubled its network by scaling outreach that still reads as human.

Before Gojiberry, Roman spent his days prospecting on socials for Coco.ai. He hunted signals one tab at a time: who changed jobs, who started following a competitor, who posted about a problem we solved. The method worked. It also capped out at roughly thirty accounts, because that's how many one person can follow properly before the tabs start lying to them.

The timing part turned out to matter more than the volume part. US workers hold a job for a median of 3.9 years, and 22 percent of them started their current role inside the last twelve months. Every one of those moves is a reason to reach out, and no human catches them by hand. So we built the routine into a product, and we priced it for the team Roman was on: two to ten people, all of them selling.
That's also why the plan has no seat count. A tool that punishes you for hiring a second rep has picked the wrong customer, and we picked ours on purpose.
Tell Gojiberry who you sell to and it starts finding companies showing buying signals. One price for the team, no seat to add, no annual contract.

Your fit: Cognism or Apollo
No amount of orchestration fixes a source that doesn't hold your market. Buy the data directly instead of assembling it, then decide whether you still need the table on top.

Clay.com is the GTM tool where you build a table, point it at a dozen data providers, and then let it fill in the columns. It's very good, and it costs $185 a month before a single provider credit is spent.

At two to ten people with no ops person, the wall comes in two parts. Somebody has to own the tables, and that somebody is already carrying a quota, badly. Then the credits land on top of the subscription. Below: the ten tools we looked at, what they cost in July 2026, and which one fits.
Gojiberry finds your prospects for you
No table to build and no waterfall to configure. Gojiberry watches your market and sends you the accounts that started looking for what you sell, before they're anyone else's lead.
Table of contents

Nothing here does everything Clay.com does, and most teams who leave weren't using the rest.  The table below sorts the ten by which part they replace, from the enrichment layer through to skipping list building altogether.

Entry prices, and entry prices decide very little in this category. Credits and provider costs decide the budget, which is what the cost section further down is for. It's the second invoice that surprises people.

We spent July 2026 on this comparison, reading every tool through the eyes of a two-to-ten person sales team with no ops function. Every pricing page was opened and dated. Every product with a self-serve signup was created on a free or entry plan and used far enough to see what a first enrichment costs and how long the setup takes. The three vendors that gate access behind a sales call were read through public documentation, buyer-reported contract figures and reviews from the last twelve months. Several prices circulating in competing comparison posts predate Clay's March 2026 repricing, which is why we didn't reuse them.

What you won't find here is a table of measured hit rates. We haven't run a controlled enrichment test across ten tools on one identical list, and a number we invented would be worth less than this sentence saying we didn't. When we run it, the results land on this page. We pay for every plan ourselves, no vendor read this before publication, and Gojiberry is our own product, so read that section as informed rather than neutral.

Five of the ten are places to buy data. Three replace the enrichment layer without the spreadsheet. One is a canvas for people who wanted to keep building. And the first one doesn't ask you to build a list at all.

Gojiberry is first because it's ours and because it answers the complaint that brought most readers here. The nine after it aren't ranked against each other, they're grouped by which part of Clay.com they stand in for.

Gojiberry is an AI-powered multichannel prospecting platform. It tracks more than 30 buying signals across socials and the web, surfaces the accounts that started looking for what you sell, and writes the first message. There's no table to build and no waterfall to configure.

$99 a month per workspace, not per seat and not per credit. That covers 2 social senders, two agents running around the clock, and up to 1,800 prospects contacted a month. The invoice doesn't move when a third rep joins.
If somebody on your team enjoys building tables, Clay is the better tool and we'd rather say so here than bury it. What we replace is the building, and that only pays off when nobody wants the job.

Apollo bundles a contact database with a sequencer and a dialer, all under one subscription. It's the swap people make when the Clay.com bill lands and the workflow they built turns out to be a list they could have filtered in one screen.

Free plan, then Basic at $49 per user per month on annual billing, Professional at $79 and Organization at $119 with a three-seat minimum. Credits are the part to model: an email costs one, a phone number costs eight, and what you don't spend doesn't roll over.
Coverage per dollar is the best here, and coverage still isn't targeting. You'll pay a fraction of the Clay bill and remain the person deciding who deserves a message.

FullEnrich does the one part of Clay most small teams use: the waterfall. It queries more than 20 data providers in sequence for a single contact, and stops at the first one that returns something verified. There's no table around it.

Starter is $29 a month for 500 credits, and Pro sits near $55 for 1,000, with about 30% off on annual billing. A work email costs one credit and a mobile costs ten, so that's 500 addresses or 50 phone numbers.
Narrower than Clay by design, and cheaper by an order of magnitude. If enrichment was the only reason you opened Clay, this is the whole reason you'd close it.

Gumloop is a visual builder for AI workflows rather than a data tool. You drag nodes onto a canvas, wire scraping and model calls together, and end up with something that behaves like the Clay table you'd have built by hand.

Free covers 5,000 credits a month on one seat. Pro opens at $37 a month with 20,000 credits and unlimited seats, and Enterprise is quoted. Credit burn depends on which model each node calls, so an AI-heavy flow costs several times what a scraping flow does, and you won't know which one you built until it runs.

Gumloop swaps Clay's spreadsheet for a canvas and keeps everything else, the building included. Wrong answer for anyone who came here tired of building. Right one for anyone who liked building and hated the invoice.

Freckle sells itself as Clay without the learning curve, and the pitch mostly holds. You type what you want in plain English, an ISO certification, an open sales role, a current pricing tier, and its agents go and find it across more than 40 providers. You don't configure anything.

Free covers 100 credits, then paid plans price by monthly volume: $99 for 2,500 credits, $189 for 5,000, $349 for 10,000, up to $999 for 40,000. A phone number costs five credits, which moves the math fast if calling's your channel.
It's built for the person Clay was never built for. Then the ceiling arrives: HubSpot and Salesforce only, no sequencing, and no signal layer at all.

ZoomInfo is what a Clay table spends weeks approximating: one vendor that already owns the data. The database is the deepest of the ten, and the intent layer tells you which accounts are researching your category. It's priced like it too.

There's nothing published. Reported quotes open near $14,995 a year for three seats and 5,000 credits, with the middle tier around $24,995. Annual only, three-seat minimum, and procurement data puts the median signed contract above $31,000 a year.

At three reps this is a category error rather than a comparison. Past twenty reps with somebody owning ops, it does in one subscription what a Clay build spends a quarter getting close to, and it doesn't need a maintainer.

Cognism is the answer when the reason your waterfall keeps coming back empty is Europe. Its Diamond Data® records are mobile numbers a person has called to confirm before they're ever handed to your dialer.

There's no pricing page and no self-serve signup. Buyers report a platform fee plus per-seat licensing landing around $15,000 to $25,000 a year for five to ten seats, on annual contracts only, with renewals reported to climb at each cycle.
The contract closes the door on most teams of two to ten. Behind that door, no waterfall you'd assemble yourself will match it on European mobiles.
Lusha is the opposite of a workflow. You're on a prospect's profile, you click the extension, and a mobile and a direct email appear in about two seconds.

Lusha doesn't publish flat tiers, it runs a credit slider. Starter sits near $37 a month per user on annual billing, Pro near $52, and Premium jumps to roughly $300 a month for five seats. An email costs one credit, and a phone number costs several.
Nothing here gets you a number faster. It has no opinion at all on which of your 400 accounts deserves the call, which was the question Clay was supposed to help with.

Seamless.AI runs as a live search rather than a stored database, assembling a contact when you ask, instead of serving a row it collected last year. Phone coverage is what people buy it for, and it's the part that holds up.

The Basic tier was removed in 2026, so there's no published paid price left. Free is 50 lifetime credits. Pro is quote-only with a five-seat minimum on an annual contract, reported by buyers between roughly $4,700 and $9,000 a year for five seats, and credits are charged even when a lookup returns nothing.
Five seats and a twelve-month commitment is an odd floor for a tool a solo founder would happily use. Read the renewal clause before signing, because that's what most of the reviews are about.
Hunter has done one job since 2015: find and verify professional email addresses from a company domain. No tables, no waterfall, no canvas, and it hasn't tried to become any of those.

Free covers 50 credits a month. Starter is $34 a month billed annually for 2,000 credits, and Growth is $104 for 10,000, with monthly billing adding around 30%. Unlimited team members share one pool on every tier, so a second rep doesn't cost anything.
It's the cheapest thing here you'll wire in once and never think about again, at the price of never getting a phone number out of it.
Gojiberry watches more than 30 buying signals across socials and the web, checks each account against your ICP, and sends you the ones you'd want to write to.

Clay.com is a go-to-market data platform built around a spreadsheet. Each row is a company, or a person, each column is an enrichment step, and the steps run through more than 150 providers, in whatever order you set. It's the most capable tool in this category and the reason it keeps winning technical teams. We took it apart at length in our Clay review.

You import a list, or build one from Clay's own sources, then stack columns on top: find the email, then the mobile, then the funding round, then whether they're hiring for the role you sell to. Claygent, the AI research agent, reads company sites and writes a first line from what it finds. Conditional logic skips steps that don't apply, and the finished rows push into your CRM or your sender. Anything you can describe as a sequence of lookups, you can build in Clay, which is both the pitch and the problem.

Clay repriced in March 2026 and the old Starter, Explorer and Pro tiers are gone for new buyers. What's left is a free plan with 100 credits a month, Launch at $185 a month with 2,500 Data Credits and 15,000 Actions, Growth at $495, and a quoted tier above that. Seats are unlimited on all of them, which genuinely softens the entry price for three people.

The credit system is where forecasting gets hard. Clay bills in two currencies: Data Credits for the enrichment itself, Actions for everything the table does around it. A single row running an email waterfall, a mobile lookup and a Claygent research step draws on both. The repricing did fix one real complaint, because a lookup that comes back empty doesn't cost a credit any more, which is worth 20% to 30% on enrichment-heavy tables. CRM sync moved down from the old $800 tier to Growth at $495.

Then there's the layer under the subscription. You either buy Clay credits, which bundle the provider cost at Clay's margin, or you bring your own keys and pay each provider directly. Bringing your own is cheaper per lookup, and it adds a handful of subscriptions to manage. A working figure for a small team running weekly enrichment is $250 to $350 a month all in, against a $185 headline.

The praise and the complaints are unusually consistent, and they're the same sentence read from two ends. People who love Clay describe building something in an afternoon that would have taken an engineer a week. People who leave describe the afternoon becoming every afternoon. The second recurring theme is the credit meter, and the third is the repricing, which landed badly with teams who had built their stack around the old $149 tier.

$185 is the number on the pricing page. The number on the card is that, plus provider costs, plus whatever the Actions column adds, and it moves every month because it tracks how much you enriched. A tool you can't forecast is a tool somebody has to watch, and in a team of three that person is also carrying a quota. The March repricing helped by dropping the charge on failed lookups, and it also tripled the entry tier for anyone signing up now.

The first useful table takes a day. The version that handles the edge cases takes a week, and then a provider changes its response format, and it takes another afternoon. None of that is Clay being badly built. It's the cost of a tool that can do anything: you have to tell it what to do, in detail, forever.

Clay needs a person who finds formulas and provider chains satisfying, rather than annoying. In a five-person company there's usually exactly one, and they become the bottleneck for everyone else's lists. When they go on holiday the pipeline goes with them, and when they leave the company the tables become an artifact nobody can read.

Here's the part that doesn't show up in a pricing comparison. A perfect table tells you who exists and what's true about them. It doesn't tell you which of those 400 accounts is in the market this quarter, and that one variable decides your reply rate.

The data is also rotting while you build. B2B contact records decay at roughly 2.1% a month according to HubSpot's database decay research, which compounds to about 22% a year, and most of that is people changing jobs rather than companies closing. The Bureau of Labor Statistics puts median tenure at 3.9 years with 22% of workers in post under a year. A job change breaks a row in your table and creates a reason to write. Which of those two your tooling notices is the whole difference between the first entry above and the nine under it.

And volume against a list nobody wanted has a ceiling now. Google requires bulk senders to keep spam complaints below 0.3%, so a bigger, better-enriched list sent to people with no reason to answer doesn't cost you a quarter, it costs you the domain.
Pick by which part of Clay.com you were using. Four cases cover almost everyone who's landed here.
You want a cheaper Clay
FullEnrich, Gumloop or Gojiberry

FullEnrich if the waterfall was the only column that mattered, at $29 a month charged on success. Gumloop if you liked building, and the invoice was the problem. Freckle if the person doing it would rather type a request in English. And count the hours before you count the subscriptions, because at $99 flat Gojiberry undercuts Clay before anybody spends a morning on it.
You just want reliable data
Apollo, ZoomInfo or Lusha

Stop assembling and buy it directly. Apollo gives the most coverage per dollar and throws in the sending. ZoomInfo is the depth play if you're past twenty reps. Lusha is the fastest route from a profile to a phone number.
Nobody on the team has time to build
Gojiberry

This is the gap we built for, and it's a different gap from the price one. The signal picks the account, the ICP check filters it, and the first message comes out of whatever triggered it. Nothing to maintain between Tuesdays.
You sell into Europe under GDPR
Cognism

Phone-verified mobiles with do-not-call screening on the way out, which no waterfall you assemble yourself will match on European numbers. Budget for an annual contract, and look at Lusha instead if that's out of reach.
Whichever way you go, run it beside Clay for two weeks before cancelling. The tables you built are worth more than the subscription, and two weeks tells you which of them you'd genuinely miss.
Your market is moving while the table fills
Somebody you sell to just changed roles, or started following a competitor. Gojiberry spots the move, checks the fit against your ICP, and writes while it's still news.

The two tools answer different questions, which is why a feature count would mislead you. Clay.com answers what's true about this company. Gojiberry answers which company is moving right now. The full head-to-head lives in our Gojiberry vs Clay comparison.

Clay optimizes for depth. Gojiberry optimizes for timing. If you're contacting 400 perfectly enriched accounts to book six meetings, a 41st column won't change that. Knowing which 20 of the 400 started looking this month will.

The limit is the same sentence in reverse. We don't do research projects, and there are questions a Clay table can answer that we can't touch. If somebody on your team likes building tables, keep Clay and read this as a comparison you've already won.
A 31% lift in outbound reply rate after moving to signal-based targeting.
60% of weekly demos now come from intent signals rather than built lists.
100+ meetings booked in two months after leaving list-based outbound.
Network doubled while scaling outreach that still reads as human.
Where Gojiberry came from

Before Gojiberry there was Coco.ai, and before Coco.ai there was Roman doing outbound by hand. He spent his days on the socials watching for the things that mean somebody is about to buy: a new role, a funding round, a comment under a competitor's post. He ran intent search one browser tab at a time. He also hit a ceiling around thirty accounts, which is roughly how many any one person can watch properly.

That ceiling is the product. Coco.ai is where the founders learned which signals predicted a reply and which ones merely looked interesting, and Gojiberry is that learning turned into an agent. It's also why the pricing assumes a team of two to ten rather than a sales floor. We built it for the situation we were standing in.

On sticker price, FullEnrich at $29 a month for 500 credits, or Hunter at $34 billed annually if all you need is email. Gumloop's Pro tier is $37 with unlimited seats. All three are under a quarter of Clay's $185 entry.
Cheapest per meeting is a different question. A $29 tool that still needs somebody to decide who goes on the list costs you the same morning Clay was costing you.

Several, and all of them are evaluation tiers rather than working plans. Clay's own free tier gives 100 credits a month, Gumloop gives 5,000, Freckle gives 100, Hunter gives 50, and Apollo's free plan is the most usable of the group.
Budget one afternoon to run the same 50 contacts through two or three of them. Hit rates on your market matter more than anyone's published accuracy number.

Not technical in the engineering sense. You need somebody comfortable with formulas, conditional logic and API-shaped thinking, which in a team of five is usually one specific person, and they'll own it forever.
That's the dependency worth pricing before you buy. Clay is excellent when that person exists and enjoys it. When they leave, the tables leave with them.

It depends on which half of Clay you were using. For enrichment, FullEnrich or Freckle. For data plus sending under one bill, Apollo, and we ranked twelve of those in our guide to Apollo alternatives. For European phone numbers, Cognism if the contract fits and Lusha if it doesn't.
If the real answer is that nobody on the team has time to run any of it, that's the gap Gojiberry was built for.

Export each table to CSV first, then map the columns you care about, one at a time, to whatever comes next. Most teams find that two or three columns out of thirty were driving every decision, which makes the migration smaller than it looks. You won't miss the other twenty-seven.
Keep the enrichment provider keys you brought yourself. Those move with you, and they're often the part you'd have to re-buy.
Yes, and plenty of teams do. Clay handles the one-off research projects nothing else can, while a cheaper tool covers the weekly enrichment that doesn't need orchestration.
Watch the total rather than the two line items. Clay at $185 plus a sender plus provider credits gets past $300 a month quickly, and that's the number to compare against a flat plan.
Try it on your own market
Tell Gojiberry who you sell to, and it starts finding qualified prospects for you. There are no tables, no provider keys and no credits to watch.

Three different products share this page. Some hand you a database to filter. Some hand you a workflow to enrich and route. And some tell you which accounts moved this week, so you write to twenty companies instead of two thousand. Buy the wrong one and you'll blame the tool.

So here are thirteen tools sorted by the job they do, each priced from the vendor's own page in August 2026: the number, the billing period, the seat minimum. The grouping follows Google's own answer on this query rather than our preference.
Twenty accounts moved in your market this week
Table of contents

B2B prospecting means finding the companies that fit what you sell, working out who decides inside them, and starting a conversation. Three jobs sit under that sentence: choosing which accounts deserve your week, finding a way to reach the right person there, and picking the moment to write. Every tool below automates at least one of the three, and none of them automates all three well.

There's a fourth job no software touches, which is knowing what to say. A tool can tell you a company just hired a head of revenue operations. You still decide whether that matters to your product. It's also worth knowing that the list you buy starts rotting the day you export it, because B2B data decays at roughly 2.1% a month, so a database you bought in January is meaningfully wrong by summer.

We opened every vendor's own pricing page in August 2026 and recorded three things per tool: the entry price, the billing period, and any seat minimum. Where a vendor publishes plans but hides the upper tiers, we say which tiers you can read and which ones need a call. Where a vendor publishes nothing, that's the finding, and we wrote it down rather than borrowing a number from a competitor's blog. For company location we used each vendor's own legal pages and, for the French and British entities, the public company registers.

One thing you won't find here: a scorecard of measured match rates. We haven't run a controlled reveal test across thirteen tools on one identical list, and an invented percentage would be worth less than this sentence admitting it. When we run that test, the numbers land on this page. We pay for the plans we use, no vendor read a word of this before publication, and Gojiberry is our own product, which is why it sits first in its group rather than first on the page.

These tools answer a timing question rather than a coverage question. They watch for events that suggest a company entered a buying window, then hand you the account with the reason attached. Teams that already own a database and still get silence usually belong here. Our guide to 13 intent signals to find high-intent leads without cold outreach lists the events worth watching, and our roundup of Trigify alternatives covers the rest of the signal-tracking market.

Gojiberry is an AI-powered multichannel prospecting platform. It tracks more than 30 buying-intent signals across socials and the web, surfaces the leads who are in-market right now, and triggers personalized outreach across channels. Fresh funding, a relevant hire, a role change and engagement with a competitor each open a different message, and the ICP filter screens the account before anything goes out.

It fits a founder or a sales team of two to ten who already know who they sell to and want the tool to answer when rather than who. If your ICP is still fuzzy, the filter has nothing sharp to work with and you'll get less out of it.

Here's the difference inside this group: we close the loop. Common Room aggregates signals and hands them to your stack, and Leadfeeder names the companies on your own site. We start the outreach from the signal itself, so the reason you're writing and the moment you write come from the same event. What we don't do matters just as much. We're not a contact database, so we won't build you a 50,000-row export. We're not a bulk email sender and we're not a CRM. Teams that need those keep them and put us in front.
Price
Free plan, then $99 a month on Pro. Custom above that.
Seat minimum
None. The price covers the account, with 2 social senders.
Where the company sits
France.
Wispra
60% of weekly demos now come from intent signals.
Mindflow
Reply rate above 31% on intent-based outbound.
GTE Localize
100+ meetings after moving from cold email to intent.
Baur Software
Network doubled by scaling authentic outreach.

Common Room pulls signals from communities, product usage, your website and social platforms into one view per person and per account. It resolves the same human across a Slack workspace, a GitHub repo, a social profile and your product, scores the account, then pushes it out to the rest of your stack.

It suits revenue operations teams at software companies with a real community or a product-led motion, and it needs somebody to own the configuration. Small teams rarely have that person, and the plan sizing assumes they do.

Nothing else in this group resolves identity across community sources the same way. If your pipeline starts in an open-source repo or a Slack group, nothing else here stitches those identities together as well. The entry tier is the only one with a public number, and at $30,000 a year it's a different conversation from the rest of this page.
Essential at $2,500 a month on annual billing, so $30,000 a year. Advanced and Enterprise go through sales.
Essential includes 5 seats and up to 100,000 contacts.
United States.

Leadfeeder names the companies that visit your website through reverse IP lookup, shows which pages they read, and pushes the account into your CRM. It counts a company once a month however often it comes back, and it filters out bots and consumer connections.

It fits teams that already get real B2B traffic and watch it leave without a form fill. Anyone browsing from home stays invisible to it, so how much of your traffic it can name varies a lot by market and by how remote your buyers are.

Its whole premise sets it apart: it reads your own first-party traffic instead of a database or a public feed. The corporate history is worth knowing too, since the company merged with Echobot in 2022, traded as Dealfront from 2023, then unified back under the Leadfeeder name on 24 March 2026.
Free plan up to 100 identified companies a month. Discover from €79 a month on annual billing, €113 month to month. Activate €369 annual. Scale €599, annual only. Enterprise on quote.
None. Every plan includes unlimited users.
Germany, as Dealfront Group GmbH. The product started in Helsinki.

Apollo bundles a large contact database with sequencing, a dialer and reporting behind one seat price. You filter a list, reveal the contacts, and send from the same screen, which is why it ends up as the default first purchase for so many teams.

It fits an outbound team of three to twenty who want one login rather than four. Solo founders often find the interface heavier than the job needs, and anyone working the phone watches the credit meter closely, since a mobile number costs several times what an email costs.

One thing no other tool on this page manages: find, enrich and send on a single subscription. Everything else on this page expects you to bring at least one other tool. Our Apollo pricing breakdown walks through where the credits go.
Free plan. Basic $49 per user a month on annual billing, $59 monthly. Professional $79 annual, $99 monthly. Organization $119 annual, $149 monthly.
None on Basic and Professional. Organization needs 3 users.

ZoomInfo sells the deepest commercial B2B dataset in the market, with org charts, direct dials, intent topics and a stack of modules layered on top. Large sales organizations buy it for coverage and for the workflows their operations team builds around it.
It fits companies with a procurement process and a data budget. A two-person team can't buy it in any practical sense, and that's a positioning choice rather than an accident.

Its edge is depth in North America. What it won't do is show you a price. ZoomInfo publishes a free Lite tier and no list price for any paid plan, sells on annual contracts, and buyers consistently report a three-seat floor. If that rules it out, our page on alternatives to ZoomInfo covers the cheaper end of the same job.
No published price on paid plans. Every quote goes through a call. A free Lite tier exists.
Not published. Buyers report 3 seats on the entry tier.

Cognism built its name on European contact data, phone-verified mobile numbers and a compliance-first posture that includes do-not-call screening across European lists. Teams selling into DACH, France and the Nordics reach for it when a US database comes back thin.
It fits a team that calls, sells across several European markets, and has a compliance officer in the room. It expects an annual contract and a conversation before you see anything at all.

Against Ocean.io the gap is verification: Cognism confirms mobile numbers by phone rather than inferring them, and it screens against European do-not-call registers. That's the whole reason a European enterprise buyer signs the contract, and it's also why the contract exists in the first place.
No published price. Cognism quotes every deal through sales on an annual contract, with no self-serve trial.
Not published.
United Kingdom, as Cognism Limited in London.

Ocean.io starts from your best customers instead of from a filter. You give it three to five seed domains, it returns companies that look and behave like them, and then it reveals verified emails and direct phone numbers for the people inside.

It fits a team selling into a niche that filters badly by industry code, and it prices in a way a small team can start with. The database is smaller than the giants, so coverage thins out in some segments and you'll want to test yours before you commit.

Cognism has no equivalent to the lookalike search, and it charges by seat where this one doesn't. You pay for credits rather than for people, which changes the math the moment your team grows past two.
Credits from $0.063 each with a 9,000-credit minimum, which the page shows as $47.25 a month and $567 for the year. Pay-as-you-go costs more per credit.
The site names Ocean Global, Inc. in San Francisco, so the United States.

That matters more than it sounds: median job tenure in the United States runs 3.9 years, and 22% of employees have been in post under a year, so a fifth of your target list is new in role and open to a conversation.

It fits a rep who researches by hand and wants a contact detail on demand, and it stays popular with teams that call. Phone reveals cost several times what an email reveal costs, so a phone-first motion drains an allocation fast and the slider becomes the real price.

Eleven of the thirteen publish a number you can read without talking to anybody. Here's what each one asks for at the entry point.

Two publish nothing at all, and several others publish only their first step. Common Room quotes Advanced and Enterprise. 11x quotes Pro and Enterprise. Clay, Ocean.io and Leadfeeder each keep an unpriced Enterprise tier on the last rung.

For a two-person team the consequence is concrete. Without a published price you can't compare two vendors, you can't put a line in next quarter's budget, and you burn a discovery call plus a demo before you learn whether the answer was ever going to be yes. A published number costs you four seconds and tells you whether to keep reading.

Google treats European compliance as its own category on this query, so it deserves a straight answer. The difference isn't whether a vendor claims GDPR compliance, because every one of them does. The difference is which company signs your contract.

Sign with a vendor established in the European Union and GDPR applies to that entity directly, your counterparty sits in the same legal space you do, and your own regulator can reach it. Sign with a US vendor and the vendor covers the transfer through contractual mechanisms such as standard contractual clauses or the EU-US Data Privacy Framework, while the parent company stays subject to US law. That second arrangement is legal and extremely common. It's also more paperwork for whoever owns privacy at your company, and one more question your enterprise customers will raise during their own security review.

Here's where these companies sit, based only on what we could confirm from their own pages and from public registers. European entities: Gojiberry in France, PhantomBuster as The Phantom Company SAS in Paris, Leadfeeder as Dealfront Group GmbH in Germany, and Cognism as Cognism Limited in London, which puts it in the United Kingdom rather than the European Union. United States entities: Apollo, ZoomInfo, Clay, Common Room, 11x and Sales Navigator.

Ocean.io deserves its own line. It sells strong European company coverage and plenty of buyers file it as a European option, yet the entity printed in its own footer is Ocean Global, Inc. in San Francisco. We couldn't confirm the entity behind Lusha or LeadMagic from their own pages, so we left both out of the lists above rather than guess.

Never take a certification on trust. Before you sign, ask the vendor to put three things in writing: the legal entity on the contract, the region where the data sits, and the list of sub-processors. A badge on a marketing page tells you what the vendor wants you to believe. The data processing agreement tells you what you can hold them to.

Take three salespeople contacting 400 prospects a month between them, which is a normal load for a small team that also demos and closes. Buy the research layer and the reveal layer separately and you're at $119.99 a license for Sales Navigator, so $360 a month, plus around $50 for enrichment. That's $410 a month for the ability to find people, before anybody decides who deserves a message.

Buy the all-in-one instead and Apollo runs $147 a month for three seats on Basic, with the credits deciding the real bill. Buy the agent and 11x starts at $3,750 a month on an annual commitment. Gojiberry is $99 a month flat for the account, and it answers a different question from all three: not who exists, but who moved.

None of those numbers is wrong for somebody. The mistake is stacking all three because each one looked cheap in isolation, then wondering in March why the tooling line grew faster than the pipeline did.
The order you buy in matters more than the logos. Four steps, and each one maps to a different type of tool.

Steps one and four cost nothing and carry most of the outcome. There's also a hard reason to keep volume down: Google requires bulk senders to stay under a 0.3% spam complaint rate, and blasting an unfiltered list is the shortest route to that threshold. Teams that skip the thinking buy bigger tools to compensate, then get the same silence back at a higher price.
Three questions route you to a group rather than to a logo. The quiz at the top of this page walks you through them, and here's what each answer means.

If you have contacts and no replies, the bottleneck is timing and you want the signals group. Come to us instead if you'd rather the tool told you the twenty accounts worth a message right now, at $99 a month with no seat minimum.

Per-seat pricing punishes growth, and Apollo, Sales Navigator and Cognism all bill that way. Clay, Ocean.io, Leadfeeder and Gojiberry price the account instead, so a third rep costs you nothing extra.

If your customers audit your sub-processors, the shortlist narrows to European entities before you compare a single feature. Gojiberry, PhantomBuster and Leadfeeder sit there, and Cognism sits in the United Kingdom.
