Why we built this

Before Gojiberry there was Coco.ai, and before Coco.ai there was Roman spending his days prospecting on socials and checking by hand who'd just changed roles, raised money or started following a competitor. The pattern was obvious after a few months. The accounts that replied weren't the ones that matched a filter best, they were the ones that had moved recently.

Doing that manually caps out somewhere around thirty accounts a week, and it dies the moment you get busy closing. So we built the thing that watches for us. That's also why we're honest about the shape of the product: it won't hand you a hundred thousand rows, because that was never the part that was broken.

The thirteen tools on this page all earn their place with somebody. Match the group to your bottleneck, check the entity before you sign, and refuse to spend a call finding out a price. That's most of the decision.

There's no single best tool, because the category splits by job. For buying signals, start with Gojiberry, Common Room and Leadfeeder. For an all-in-one mid-market platform, Apollo. For enterprise data, ZoomInfo. For European coverage, Cognism and Ocean.io. For enrichment workflows, Clay. For AI agents, 11x and PhantomBuster. For research and contact finding, Sales Navigator, Lusha and LeadMagic. Pick the group that matches your bottleneck, then compare inside it.

B2B prospecting means finding the companies that fit what you sell, working out who decides inside them, and starting a conversation. It covers three jobs: deciding which accounts deserve your time, finding a way to reach the right person, and choosing the moment to write. A prospecting tool automates one or more of those. It doesn't replace the judgment behind them.

Define who really buys rather than who could buy. Pick the signal that says now: fresh funding, a new hire, a change of seat or a visit to your site. Find the contact and verify the address or the number. Then write about the signal instead of about your product. Each step maps to a different tool type, and you rarely need all four from one vendor.

On our August 2026 checks, Gojiberry, Apollo, Clay, Lusha and Leadfeeder all publish a free plan, and ZoomInfo publishes a free Lite tier. Published entry prices in this list run from $0 to $3,750 a month, and a small team usually lands between $50 and $250 a month per tool. Two mechanics move the total: a per-seat price multiplies with headcount, and a credit price multiplies with how many phone numbers you reveal. Enterprise data platforms sit in a different bracket and quote you by contract.

Yes, because they solve opposite problems. A CRM records what already happened with people you know. A prospecting tool finds people you don't know yet and tells you when to write. Most prospecting tools push into HubSpot, Pipedrive or Salesforce rather than replacing them. Check the integration exists on the plan you're buying, not just on the enterprise tier.

All of them sell into Europe, so the real question is which entity you contract with. Gojiberry is a French company. PhantomBuster is registered in Paris under the name The Phantom Company. Apollo, ZoomInfo, Clay, Common Room, 11x and Sales Navigator are US companies, and Ocean.io names a San Francisco entity on its own site despite its European coverage.

Template A of 4
Sales call template
Main need. The problem the prospect described, in their own words.
Key decision. Whatever the two of you settled, written down as a decision.
Objection. The reason they gave for hesitating, quoted rather than tidied up.

Want more of these calls in your week?
Template B of 4
Client meeting template
Objective. Why the two companies got on the call at all.
What the client agreed to. Scope, dates, budget, in their words where you have them.
What they owe you. Assets, approvals, access, each with a date.
Action items. Yours and theirs, in one list, with owners.
Next step. The next checkpoint, and who runs it.
Template C of 4
Team meeting template
Objective. Why the team met, in a single sentence.
Decisions. One per line, with the person who made the call.
Action items. Owner first, task second, deadline third.
Open questions. What the team parked, and who chases the answer down.
Next check-in. The date, and what the team reviews then.
Template D of 4
Project meeting template
Status against plan. Ahead, on track or late, with the number that says so.
Decisions. Scope changes, date moves, and resource calls.
Blockers. What stops the work, and who can clear it.
Action items. Owner, task, date, in that order.
Next milestone. The date, and the definition of done.

A meeting summary answers three questions for whoever opens it: what you discussed, what you decided, and who does what next. Anything past those three answers costs your reader time, and it doesn't buy them a thing.

This guide covers the seven steps, a template you can paste into a doc or an email, three worked examples, four email formats, the line between a summary and minutes, and where AI takes over. If you'd rather grab the template first and read the method after, the picker above hands it to you.
Table of contents

Seven steps, ten to fifteen minutes of work. Most of that time goes on deciding what to leave out, because you're recording an outcome rather than replaying a conversation. Senior executives already sit through close to 23 hours of meetings a week, up from under 10 hours in the 1960s, Harvard Business Review reports. Fifteen minutes of writing protects the hour everyone's already spent.

Open with one sentence on why the meeting happened. It gives every line under it a reason to exist, and it lets anyone who skipped the call decide in two seconds whether they need the rest. Write the objective the meeting turned out to have, not the one that sat on the invite. Half the time they aren't the same thing, and the second one matters more.
Example
Objective. Agree on a launch date for the Q3 campaign, and name an owner for the brief.

Write down what changes what happens next, and leave the rest in the room. A transcript holds every sentence, and nobody opens a transcript twice. Three to five lines carry a one-hour meeting. If you're writing more than that, you're transcribing rather than choosing.
WeakThe team discussed the launch date.
StrongMarketing pushed for July 1. Engineering flagged two weeks of QA on checkout. The room landed on July 15, with QA intact.

Give decisions their own block and their own lines. A decision buried in a paragraph reads like an opinion, and somebody reopens it three weeks later. Name the decision, name the person who made it, then move on. If the room didn't decide, say so on its own line, because "we didn't settle this" is worth as much to your reader as a decision.
WeakWe talked about the budget and everyone seemed comfortable with the numbers.
StrongDecision. Ana locked the Q3 budget at $35,000, and she signs the purchase order on Friday.

Somebody says "we should probably ping legal". That sentence hides a real task behind a hedge. Rewrite it with a verb at the front and the object right after, so whoever reads it knows what to do without asking you first. If you can't put a verb at the front, you haven't got an action item yet.
WeakSomeone should check with legal about the contract wording.
StrongSend the indemnity clause to legal, for review, before Thursday.

Every meaningful action gets a name, and it gets a date whenever a date exists. A task with two owners has no owner, so pick one person and let the second one help. When the room ducks the question, put your own name down, and let somebody correct you. That's quicker than a second meeting about who owns what.
Sarah updates the campaign brief by June 25.
Leo books the QA window with engineering by June 20.
Ana confirms the media spend, once the brief lands.

Read your draft once with the delete key ready. Small talk goes, the tangent about the office move goes, and the slide nobody discussed goes with them. Ask one thing of every line: does this change what a colleague knows, or what a colleague does? If the answer's no, the line goes too.

Send it the same day, inside the hour when you can. Memory fades fast, and so does the sense of obligation people carry about what they said out loud. A rough summary at 3pm beats a polished one on Thursday, because by Thursday half the room has moved on and the other half doesn't trust its own memory.
The fifteen-minute rule
Block the fifteen minutes after the call inside the invite itself. Writing from memory an hour later costs you double the time and half the detail, and you'll hedge every part you no longer remember.
Eleven parts, in the order a reader wants them.

Not every meeting earns all eleven. A fifteen-minute standup needs the decisions and the action items, and nothing more. A quarterly client review takes the full set. The test holds everywhere, and it's a blunt one: drop any line that leaves your reader no better informed and no better equipped.
Paste this into Google Docs, Notion or the body of an email. It survives all three because it doesn't lean on anything fancier than a few headings, one small table and a bit of bold.
Meeting summary template
Meeting title. The subject, plus the company or the team.
Date. Day, month and start time.
Attendees. Names, and roles when the reader needs them.
Objective. Why the meeting happened, in one line.
Key discussion points. Three to five lines, on what shaped the outcome.
Decisions made. One line per decision, with a name attached.
Action items. One row per task.
Open questions. What stayed unresolved, and who owns the answer.
Next steps. The next checkpoint, its date and its owner.
Keep the field names even when a section stays empty. An empty "Open questions" line tells your reader the room closed everything, and a missing one doesn't tell them anything at all.
Three summaries, written out in full. Copy the shape, and swap in your own names, dates and numbers.
Growth sync, June 18, 9:30am
Attendees. Ana, Sarah, Leo, Max.
Objective. Lock the Q3 campaign date, and clear the QA dependency.
Discussion. Marketing wanted July 1. Engineering flagged two weeks of QA on the checkout flow. Nobody found a way to run both in parallel, so something had to give.
Decisions. Launch moves to July 15, and the checkout work keeps its full QA window.
Action items. Sarah updates the campaign brief by June 25. Leo books the QA window by June 20. Max reruns the paid forecast on the new date by June 26.
Open questions. Whether the July 4 week costs us reach, which Max checks against last year's numbers.
Next step. Same call on June 25, with the brief on screen.
Kickoff with Norvell Retail, June 19, 2pm
Attendees. Claire Bassot and Tomas Reyes for Norvell, Ana Duval and Leo Marchand for us.
Objective. Agree the scope, the timeline and the first delivery, for the storefront rebuild.
What Norvell agreed to. A phased rollout, with the catalog pages first and checkout in phase two. Budget confirmed at $86,000 for phase one.
What Norvell owes us. Brand assets and the product feed by July 3. Staging access for two of our engineers by June 27. Claire owns both.
Our commitments. Ana sends the phased statement of work by June 24. Leo shares the technical audit of the current storefront by June 30.
Open questions. Whether Norvell wants the loyalty module in phase one, which Tomas answers by July 3.
Next step. Scope review on July 8 at 2pm, Ana sends the invite.
Discovery call with Halden Logistics, June 20, 11am
Attendees. Mireille Fauvel, head of sales at Halden, and Ana Duval for us.

Situation. Halden runs four reps across France and Benelux. They book roughly twelve meetings a month between them, and Mireille tracks the pipeline in a spreadsheet she rebuilds every quarter, by hand.
Main need. Fewer dead accounts in the list. Her words: "my reps spend Monday deciding who to call and Tuesday finding out the number changed."
Decisions. Halden runs a two-week pilot on the Benelux territory with two reps. Mireille measures it on meetings booked, not on emails sent.
Objection. She got burned on a twelve-month contract last year, and she won't sign anything past one quarter before she sees numbers.
Action items. Ana sends the pilot scope and the quarterly terms by June 23. Mireille names the two reps and shares the Benelux account list by June 25. Ana runs the setup call once the list lands.
Next step. Pilot kickoff on June 27 at 10am, thirty minutes, and Ana owns the invite.

A sales summary earns its writing time because it hands whoever picks up the account the context that makes the follow-up land: what the prospect cares about, what they agreed to, and what happens on which date. Write it well, and you'll find the follow-up email drafts itself. The catch sits one step earlier. A sales summary only pays for itself when the meeting happened with a prospect who was going to buy.
Gojiberry finds your prospects for you
Gojiberry watches more than 30 buying signals, checks every account against your ICP, and contacts the ones worth your time. It fills the calendar. The notes stay your job.
Five blocks: a two-line opening, the decisions, the action items, the next steps, a one-line close. Nothing else survives a phone screen, and that's where most of your readers will open it.

One rule the competing guides skip: the most urgent action item goes near the top of the email, not at the bottom of an attachment. If Leo books a QA window by Friday, Leo sees his name in the first screenful. Everything below that point serves the people who've got more time on their hands.

Two more habits pay off. Put the subject line to work, because "Recap" doesn't tell anybody anything, while "Halden pilot: scope by June 23" tells them the whole story. And keep the whole email in the body. An attachment adds a click, and every click costs you readers.
Four emails for four situations that call for different writing. Nobody needs the same email four times, so these four don't overlap.

Hi Mireille,
Good call this morning. You described the problem better than our own website does, and I'm quoting you on it: your reps spend Monday deciding who to call and Tuesday finding out the number changed.
What we agreed. A two-week pilot on Benelux with two of your reps, measured on meetings booked. Quarterly terms, nothing longer, until you see numbers.

That email works because the call gave it something to say. When the call hasn't happened yet, the writing job changes completely, and our cold email templates that get replies cover that side of the problem.
Subject: Pricing review: no decision yet, two things we need
We didn't land a decision on the pricing tiers today, so here's where we stand, and here's what moves us forward.
Where we disagree. Sales wants three tiers with a free entry point. Finance wants two tiers and a floor at $49.
What blocks us. Nobody's got churn data on the accounts under $49.
Next. Max pulls twelve months of churn by price band before Thursday. We decide on Friday with the numbers in front of us.

A meeting without a decision still produces a summary, and that summary is often the more useful one. It names the disagreement while everyone still remembers their own position, and it stops the next session from starting over.

Notes serve the person who took them. Minutes serve the record, and in a board or a works council setting they follow a format somebody else fixed years ago. A summary serves the people who act next, which is why it's happy to drop so much of what the other two keep.

People also say meeting recap, and the two words do the same job. "Recap" carries a lighter register, so it fits the Slack message you fire off after a standup, while "summary" fits the document you send a client. Same content, different clothes. Pick the word your team already uses, stay with it, and don't let both float around, because two names for one artifact means people hunt in two places.

Short enough to read in two minutes. No word count survives contact with a real calendar, so let the meeting set the length. You'll land on a line for each decision, a line for each action item, and one sentence of context above them.

Four things stretch it. More decisions, more action items, more technical detail your reader can't rebuild alone, and a wider audience each add lines. Microsoft found that only about one person in three believes the room would miss them in most of their meetings, according to its Work Trend Index. Write for the two who showed up and skimmed, and the length takes care of itself.

Atlassian put a number on the cost of getting this wrong: inside organizations with poor meeting habits, people spend 50% more time in unnecessary meetings than on their highest-priority work, its State of Teams research found. A summary people read is the cheapest way to cancel the meeting that would've followed.

The chain runs in six moves. You hold the meeting, a tool captures the audio or your notes, the model drafts a summary, you lift the decisions and the action items to the top, you check the draft, and you send it. AI saves you real time on the first draft, and none at all on the last read. That last step isn't optional.

Check six things every single time: the decisions, the names, the owners, the deadlines, the numbers, and anything a lawyer would care about. A model invents a plausible deadline the same way it invents a plausible citation, and from the outside your reader can't tell the two apart.

All four stop at the document. They tell you what happened in a meeting you already had, and they do it well enough that drafting the first version by hand now looks like a choice you're making on purpose.

Gojiberry works on the other side of the calendar. It tracks more than 30 buying signals across the socials and the web, surfaces the accounts moving right now, and runs personalized outreach across several channels. Note-takers handle the summary. A different kind of tool decides who you meet in the first place. A rep who runs sales calls needs both, and neither one covers for the other.
Stop guessing who to contact
Gojiberry spots the accounts that moved this week, checks them against your ICP, and reaches out before anyone else does.
Five minutes, six moves, in this order.

The order does more work than the speed. Writing the objective first tells you which discussion points survive, and deleting last means you'll never spend a minute polishing a sentence you were about to cut.

A takeaway captures one insight worth carrying out of the room. "Enterprise buyers ask about SSO before they ask about reporting" is a takeaway. A summary gives that insight its surroundings: who said it, what the room decided because of it, and who acts on it by when. You can't run a project off takeaways alone. Takeaways travel well in a Slack message. Summaries do the work that stops the next meeting from happening.

A meeting summary is a short written record of what a meeting produced. It covers the objective, the main discussion points, the decisions, the action items with their owners and deadlines, and the next step.
It serves the people who act on the meeting, including the ones who missed it. That audience explains its length: a summary keeps the outcome, and it drops the conversation that led there.

Start with the objective in one sentence. Pick three to five discussion points that changed something. Write each decision on its own line. Turn every commitment into a task with a verb at the front, a single owner and a date.
Then cut. Most first drafts lose a third of their length without losing anything worth keeping, and the version people read is the one that respects their two minutes.
Title, date and time, attendees, objective, key discussion points, decisions, action items, owners, deadlines, open questions and next steps.

Short internal meetings need four or five of those. Client meetings and formal reviews take the full list. Keep the field names even when a section stays empty, so your reader knows you didn't skip anything.
Two minutes of reading. In practice that lands between 100 and 300 words for most meetings.

Length follows the number of decisions and action items rather than the length of the call. A ninety-minute workshop that produced two decisions deserves a shorter summary than a twenty-minute call that produced six, which surprises people the first time.
You take notes during the meeting, for yourself. You write a summary after it, for other people.

Notes hold everything you might need later, in whatever order it arrived. A summary keeps the outcome, and it organizes that outcome for someone who has to act without the benefit of having sat there.
Minutes create a formal record. They follow a fixed structure, log motions and votes, name who said what, and often need approval at the next session.
A summary answers to nobody but its readers. Boards, works councils and public bodies need minutes, and most other teams don't.
Open with two lines of context. Put the decisions next, the action items with owners and deadlines after that, and the next step at the end.
Keep the whole thing in the body rather than in an attachment, and give the subject line some real content. "Halden pilot: scope by June 23" beats "Meeting recap" by a wide margin.
Yes, and the first draft comes back in seconds. Tools like Zoom AI Companion, Otter, Fathom and Fireflies turn a transcript into a structured recap.

A person still checks the decisions, the names, the owners, the deadlines, the numbers and anything sensitive. Models produce confident, plausible detail, and that's the one thing a summary can't afford to carry.
The same day, and inside the hour when your calendar allows it.

Two things decay fast after a call: your memory of the detail, and everyone else's sense of commitment to what they agreed to out loud. A rough summary sent at 3pm does more work than a careful one sent on Thursday.
Title and date, attendees, objective, key points, decisions, action items in a three-column table of task, owner and deadline, open questions, next steps.
That format works in a document, in Notion and in the body of an email, which matters more than it sounds like it should. The format your team can paste anywhere is the format they keep using.
Fill the calendar first

A summary only pays for itself when the meeting was worth having. Gojiberry finds the companies showing buying signals and contacts them, so the calls on your calendar come from people who were already looking.

Apollo sells two things in one subscription: a contact database, and the sequencer to work it. That bundle is why most small sales teams start there. It's also why they leave.
We put twelve alternatives through the same two-week test with a simulated three-person team and one shared list. Here's what held up, what didn't, and what each one costs once the credits run out.
Your list isn't too small. It's too cold. Gojiberry finds the accounts moving this week and writes to them first.

Test protocol

We ran each tool for ten working days between May and July 2026, with a simulated three-person sales team working the same list of 400 prospects: French and German SaaS companies between 20 and 200 employees, with the same offer and the same three message angles throughout. Every tool got the same job, which was to take that list from raw to first reply.

Four things were scored: how long setup took before the first message went out, how many contacts survived a manual ICP check, the bounce rate across the first 200 sends, and how quickly support answered a real question from a paying account. We paid for every plan ourselves, no vendor saw this article before publication, and Gojiberry is our own product, so read that section as informed rather than neutral.
Here are the three numbers we could measure the same way across all twelve. Support response times sit in their own section further down.

Two patterns are worth naming. The tools that were fastest to set up were also the ones that produced the least usable data, because a forty-minute setup means nobody asked you what a good account looks like. And the bounce rate spread, from 1.1% to 4.2%, is wide enough to change your sender reputation within a single campaign.

Ranked by how well they solve a real Apollo problem, not by database size. Gojiberry is first because it's ours and because the intent gap is the one we hear about most, and the eleven below it are ordered by how often they turned out to be the right answer.

Apollo answers the question how do I reach this person. It has no strong opinion about whether you should be reaching them today. That's the gap Gojiberry fills, and it's the reason most people who leave Apollo aren't looking for a bigger database at all.

Gojiberry is an AI-powered multichannel prospecting platform that tracks more than 30 buying intent signals across socials and the web, surfaces the leads who are actively searching right now, and triggers personalized outreach on several channels. A funding round, a new VP hire, a hiring sprint on a team you sell to, a visible change in the tech stack: each of those is a reason to write today rather than in four months.

The practical difference shows up in the shape of the day. Instead of a rep opening a list of 400 exported names and working down it, the rep opens a queue of eleven accounts that moved this week, with the reason attached to each one. Wispra now sources 60% of its weekly demos from intent signals rather than cold lists, and the Wispra case study shows the before and after.
What you can automate with it:

Pricing starts at a free plan you can run a first campaign on. The paid tier is $99 a month and includes 2 social senders, which covers a team of two to ten working a shared pipeline. It's priced per workspace rather than per seat, so adding a third rep doesn't change the invoice.

The verdict: this isn't a database replacement, and pretending otherwise would be dishonest. If your list is thin, buy data. If your list is long and cold, a signal layer is the cheaper fix, and it's the one that moves reply rate rather than volume.

If you're leaving Apollo because your European mobiles don't connect, Cognism is the direct upgrade. Its Diamond Data program puts a human on the number before it reaches you, which is a different promise from an algorithmic confidence score.

Coverage in continental Europe is where the gap with Apollo is widest. DACH, the Nordics and France are all noticeably deeper, and the GDPR and DNC screening runs inside the workflow rather than as a report you pull afterwards.
What it does for a calling team:

Cognism doesn't publish prices. Expect a custom annual quote in the mid-market range, with the number driven by seats and export volume rather than by feature tiers. Ask for the per-record cost rather than the headline, and don't buy twelve months of credits you can't work through.
The verdict: the strongest data on this list for phone-first teams in Europe, and the least transparent to buy. If nobody on your team is dialling, you're paying for the part that makes it expensive.
Clay isn't an Apollo replacement and doesn't try to be. It's the layer that sits above every data vendor you already use, and it changes how much you pay for coverage.

Instead of trusting one database, Clay waterfalls a request across a hundred providers until something verified comes back. Clearbit misses, Hunter tries, then Findymail, then Prospeo. You pay for the hit, not for the attempt, which is why the cost per enriched contact drops so sharply at volume.
What you can build with it:

The free plan is enough to learn the mechanics. Paid starts at $149 a month on a credit model, and the credits are the real budget line. Test any new table on fifty rows before you point it at ten thousand, because a badly ordered waterfall burns money fast.

The verdict: the best personalization engine here, and the slowest to learn. It took us six hours and forty minutes to get to a first send, against a bit over an hour for the simplest tools. That investment pays back for teams with someone who enjoys process design, and it strands teams that don't.

If cold email volume is your playbook and Apollo's credit meter is what stops you, Instantly is the cheapest way out. Unlimited connected inboxes and unlimited warmup for $30 a month is the most aggressive price-to-capacity ratio on this list.
It won't source contacts for you at the same quality, and the built-in lead database is a convenience rather than a reason to buy. The reason to buy is the sending infrastructure.
What it handles:

Growth starts at $30 a month and the lead database is a separate add-on. Nothing here is charged per seat, so a three-person team pays the same as a solo founder. That's the structural saving against Apollo, where every rep is another $49 to $119.

The verdict: buy it for the sending, not the data. Our bounce rate on Instantly's own database was the second highest we recorded at 3.6%, and the fix is a verification pass before import rather than a different sending tool.

ZoomInfo is what Apollo scales into when the org gets big enough to need an admin. The database is the largest in the market, the org charts are the best documented, and the Bombora intent feed earns its keep when you're running account-based plays across hundreds of targets.
The price is the whole story, though. Contracts usually open around $15,000 a year and run to $50,000 or more, on rigid annual terms with a real implementation project attached.
What the money buys:

Everything is a custom annual contract, and prepared buyers routinely negotiate 30% to 40% off the opening quote. Ask for a thirty-day pilot with your own reps before signing, because the demo environment is always cleaner than the account you'll actually get.

The verdict: correct for 20+ reps with an ops function, wrong for anyone smaller. A team of three will pay enterprise money for a platform nobody has time to administer. Start with Cognism or Apollo and revisit this in two years.
Gojiberry watches 30+ buying signals across socials and the web, tells you which accounts moved this week, and writes to them before your competitors notice.
Lusha does one job with almost no friction. You're looking at a prospect's profile, you click the extension, and a verified mobile and work email appear. No export, no list, no workflow.
For reps who prospect one account at a time, that speed beats any batch process. It's also why Lusha stops being enough the moment you need to work four hundred names a month.
What it covers:

The free plan gives you 70 credits a month. Paid starts around $29.90 a month on the entry credit tier, with Premium from $69.90. The detail that matters: a phone reveal costs 10 credits, so a 250-credit plan is 25 phone numbers, not 250. Check the current slider before you budget.

The verdict: the fastest lookup tool here and the one most likely to surprise you on the invoice. We ranked its own field separately in the Lusha alternatives comparison. Pair it with something that does sequencing, or you'll pay for two tools and get one workflow.
Hunter does email and nothing else, which is why it's still on this list after a decade. Give it a domain and it returns the address pattern plus the individual addresses it can verify.

Its more useful role is as a verification pass on data you bought somewhere else. Running any list through Hunter before a send catches the stale addresses that otherwise become bounces and damage your sender reputation.
What it's good for:

The free plan covers 25 searches a month, which suits a small team writing to companies it already knows. Paid starts at $49 a month. Against Apollo's credit model, it's cheap, and it does a fraction of the job.
The verdict: not an Apollo replacement, and the single most useful line item in a stack that has bounce problems. Our bounce rate on Hunter-verified sends was 1.6%, the second lowest we measured.

Saleshandy's pitch is breadth at a low price: an 852M contact database with verification built in, plus sequencing, for $39 a month. That's a larger claimed database than Apollo's at a fraction of the entry cost.

The trade-off shows up in what survives contact with reality. Of the contacts we pulled from Saleshandy, 54% passed a manual ICP check, the lowest figure in our test, and the bounce rate on the first 200 sends was 4.2%.
What you get:

Outreach Starter is $39 a month and the database is a separate line. For a team of three that would otherwise pay $147 a month for Apollo Basic seats, the gap is real. Spend part of it on a verification tool.

The verdict: the best price-per-contact on this list, and the one that needs the most cleaning. If you have the discipline to verify before every send, the maths works. If you don't, the bounce rate will find you.

LeadIQ is built around the way SDRs work a named account list rather than around database search. You capture contacts from a profile, and the platform tells you when something changes at those accounts.

That trigger layer is the reason to pick it over a pure enrichment tool. A new VP of Sales, a funding round or a job posting on a team you sell to all raise an alert, and the AI writer drafts the outreach around that event.
What it automates:
There's a limited free tier, and paid starts at $75 a month. Mobile credits are capped even on the paid plans, so a phone-first team will need Cognism or Kaspr underneath.

The verdict: a good fit for a team of two to ten working fifty named accounts rather than a wide funnel. The signals are narrower than Gojiberry's and they're real, and the outreach still runs manually.
lemlist bet early on the idea that a cold email can look like it was made for one person. Dynamic images, video thumbnails and liquid syntax let you build a template that doesn't read as one.
The deliverability side is the quieter reason it works. lemwarm has been running long enough to be boring, which is what you want from a warmup tool.
What it does differently:
The extension is free, and paid plans start at $55 per user per month. That per-user model is the thing to watch: at three reps you're at $165 a month, which is above Apollo Basic for a narrower job.
The verdict: worth it when your ICP is over-emailed and generic copy has stopped working. Not worth it as a general-purpose sequencer, where cheaper tools do the same job.

Reply.io is the pragmatic multichannel option. Email, calls, SMS and social touches sit in the same sequence, and the browser extension lets a rep add someone to a campaign without leaving the profile they're reading.
Warmup and deliverability tooling are included rather than sold separately, which removes a line item that Apollo users usually pay elsewhere.
Paid plans start at $59 per user per month. For a three-person team that's $177 a month, more than Apollo Basic and less than most enterprise options. Data credits are a separate consideration.
The verdict: a clean execution platform for teams that already have their contacts. It won't fix a targeting problem, and it will make a multichannel playbook easier to run than Apollo does.
Kaspr is the European answer to the browser-extension pattern. It reads the profile you're viewing on LinkedIn and returns a verified mobile and email, with data coverage tuned to continental Europe.
For French, Belgian and German prospecting it holds up better than most US-built alternatives at the same price, and the GDPR posture is documented rather than implied.
What it's good at:
There's a free tier with a handful of credits and paid plans from $65 a month. It's the fastest tool here to set up, at forty minutes from signup to first message in our test.
The verdict: a sharp enrichment tool with no ambition to be a platform. It solves the data half of the problem for European teams and leaves the sending half to something else.

Apollo.io is a sales intelligence platform built around a 275M+ contact database, with email sequencing, a dialer and basic intent filtering layered on top. It's the default first tool for a lot of SMB sales teams, and it earned that position: the free plan is usable, the self-serve checkout has no sales call attached, and one subscription covers data and outreach.

The friction starts when outbound becomes a habit rather than an experiment. Credits are the mechanism: an export costs credits, a mobile reveal costs more, and the plan you picked in month one stops covering month four.
What Apollo does well
Where it breaks

Four tiers. Free, Basic at $49 per user per month on annual billing, Professional at $79, and Organization at $119 with a three-seat minimum. Pay monthly and those become roughly $59, $99 and $149. The published numbers live on the Apollo pricing page and they've held steady through 2026.

Credits are the part that moves. Basic includes 75 mobile credits and 1,000 export credits a month, Professional doubles the exports to 2,000 and gives you 100 mobile credits. A rep working the phone will clear 100 mobile credits inside two weeks, and top-ups run around $0.20 each. That's the mechanism behind every complaint about surprise Apollo invoices.

The scores are good and the complaints are consistent. Apollo sits at 4.7 out of 5 across more than 9,400 G2 reviews, which puts it near the top of its category. The recurring criticisms in those reviews aren't about the product being bad, they're about the gap between the sticker price and the invoice, and about data accuracy outside North America.
That's a useful signal for a buyer. It means the question to ask isn't whether Apollo works, it's whether the specific thing it does badly is the thing your team needs most.
Four reasons come up over and over. They're not equally serious, and the one that applies to you determines which half of this list you should be reading.
Credits that outrun the budget
Apollo charges per export and per mobile reveal. A team of three doing real volume finds the plan they picked in January stops covering March, and top-ups arrive without a conversation.
Data that thins out past the Atlantic
North American coverage is strong. European, APAC and LATAM mobiles are inconsistent, which shows up as a connect rate problem rather than an obvious data problem.
No outreach on social channels
Email and calls are covered. Social outreach needs a second subscription, which undoes the main argument for buying an all-in-one platform.
A list that's long and cold
The deepest complaint, and the one nobody puts in a support ticket. Filters tell you who fits your ICP. They don't tell you who's in the market this month.
Diagnose before you shortlist. The wrong tool bought for the right reason still wastes a quarter.

Whichever way you go, run a two-week parallel pilot before you cancel anything. Two reps, one measurable goal, the same list on both tools. A demo environment is always cleaner than the account you'll be given.

If what you actually want is an agent that runs the motion instead of a rep, that's a different shortlist, and we built it in the 11x alternatives comparison. For the social prospecting side, the LeadIn alternatives guide covers it.
These two tools answer different questions, which is why the comparison is more useful than a feature count.

Apollo optimizes for coverage. Give it a filter and it returns everyone who matches. Gojiberry optimizes for timing. It watches for the moment an account starts behaving like a buyer, then writes about that moment. If you're contacting a thousand cold names to book eight meetings, the fix isn't two thousand names.
Four teams that made that shift, with the numbers they reported afterwards:
Wispra
60% of weekly demos now come from intent signals rather than cold lists.
GTE Localize
100+ meetings booked after moving from email outbound to intent-based outreach.
Baur Software
Network doubled by scaling authentic outreach instead of raw volume.
Mindflow
Reply rate up 31% on outbound once targeting followed intent.

We sent every vendor the same question from a paying account: a specific setup problem with a clear answer, worded the way a customer would word it. The clock started at send and stopped at the first human reply. Automated acknowledgements didn't count.

The pattern is predictable and worth pricing in. Self-serve tools answer in hours, enterprise platforms answer through a named contact who may be in another timezone, and the tools in between depend on whether you're above their seat threshold. For a team of two to ten, that threshold matters more than the response time itself.
Three reps, 400 prospects a month, twelve months

Apollo Professional at $79 per seat on annual billing is $2,844 a year for three reps. Add mobile top-ups at roughly $0.20 each, and a team dialling 300 numbers a month adds around $720. Add a sequencer for social outreach, because Apollo doesn't cover it, and you're at $4,000 to $4,500 before anyone has replied to anything.

The Instantly plus Hunter.io route is $79 a month flat, or $948 a year, for the whole team. It buys you sending capacity and verification, and it buys you no contact database and no targeting help. Both of those become your problem.

Gojiberry is $99 a month, $1,188 a year, priced per workspace with 2 social senders included. Adding a third rep doesn't change the invoice. The comparison that matters isn't cost per seat, it's cost per meeting booked. GTE Localize booked 100+ meetings after moving from email volume to intent-based outreach, and the full breakdown is here.

One more line item nobody budgets for. B2B contact data decays at roughly 2.1% a month, compounding to about 22.5% a year, per HubSpot's database decay simulation. The list you paid for in January is a fifth wrong by December, and the driver is job movement: median US tenure was 3.9 years in January 2024 and 22% of workers had been in post a year or less, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

That decay is the strongest argument for buying signals rather than records. A job change breaks a row in your database and creates a reason to write. Which of those two things your tooling notices is the whole difference.
Coco.ai was the training ground

Before Gojiberry existed, Roman was doing this work by hand. He spent his days prospecting on socials for Coco.ai, and the part that worked wasn't the volume, it was noticing when someone had just changed roles or just raised a round. He was running intent search manually, one tab at a time, and it took most of the week.

Coco.ai is where the pattern got tested and where the limits showed up. A person can watch maybe thirty accounts properly. The product exists because the founders hit that ceiling before they tried to build past it, which is also why the pricing assumes a team of two to ten rather than a sales floor.

Several, with different limits. Hunter.io gives you 25 domain searches a month, which covers a small team sending to companies it already knows. Kaspr and Lusha both start at a handful of credits a month, enough to test data quality and nothing more. Gojiberry has a free plan too.

Read them for what they are: free tiers cover evaluation, not a quarter. Every tool on this list expects you to pay once outbound becomes a habit. Budget for it rather than stitching four free plans together.

Instantly at $30 a month covers the sending side for the whole team, since it doesn't charge per seat. Saleshandy starts at $39 a month. Both leave you needing a contact source, so add Hunter.io at $49 or a small Kaspr plan.

A three-rep stack built this way lands between $80 and $150 a month, against roughly $147 to $297 for the same three seats on Apollo Basic or Professional. The saving is real, and so is the extra glue work.

Apollo covers email, calls and tasks. Outreach on social networks needs a second tool alongside it, which is one of the reasons teams running a multichannel playbook end up with three subscriptions instead of one.
Gojiberry, Reply.io and Kaspr all approach that gap differently. Gojiberry runs the multichannel sequence itself once a signal fires.

Cognism, without much argument, if you're calling. Its mobiles are phone-verified before delivery and its continental coverage is the deepest we tested. Kaspr is the cheaper European option and holds up well on the DACH and French markets.
Apollo isn't bad in Europe, it's uneven. That unevenness is what costs you connect rate, more than the average accuracy figure on any vendor's homepage.

More than most teams plan for. B2B contact records decay at about 2.1% a month, which compounds to roughly 22.5% a year, according to HubSpot's database decay simulation built on MarketingSherpa research.

The underlying driver is job movement. US median job tenure was 3.9 years in January 2024, and 22% of workers had been in their role a year or less, per the Bureau of Labor Statistics. A list you exported in January is measurably wrong by December, whichever vendor sold it to you.

Add first, replace later. Most of the teams we work with keep Apollo for the database and the dialer, then bolt on the layer that fixes their specific gap: sending volume, European mobiles, or intent.

Mindflow did exactly that and lifted its outbound reply rate by 31% by switching the targeting to intent signals rather than changing the whole stack. The Mindflow case study walks through the sequence.

Plan on two weeks before the first meeting and about six weeks before the numbers mean anything. A new domain needs two to three weeks of warmup before it can carry volume, and any sequence needs a few hundred sends before the reply rate stops being noise.
That's the main argument for a parallel pilot. Keep the old tool running, point two reps at the new one, and compare on the same list.

Not for the database. Apollo sells you 275M+ contacts and a place to sequence them. Gojiberry watches for buying signals across socials and the web, tells you which accounts are moving, and runs the personalized outreach on several channels.
If your complaint about Apollo is that the list is too cold rather than too small, that's the swap that pays. If you need raw coverage, keep a database tool underneath.
Gojiberry tracks 30+ buying intent signals across socials and the web, surfaces the accounts in market this week, and runs personalized multichannel outreach. Built for teams of 2 to 10.

Clay is probably the best enrichment engine you can buy, and it's also the one whose invoice nobody manages to predict. This review gives you the real plan names, the real credit allocations, the cost per credit at each tier, and the line items that turn up after you've already committed.
How did we check Clay?

Every plan name, price and credit allocation below comes from Clay's public pricing page, read on August 10, 2026 with both the monthly and the annual toggle open. We did that because the previous version of this page still described a credit model Clay retired in March 2026, and because most of the comparison pages ranking for Clay pricing today haven't caught up either: they still quote Starter, Explorer and Pro.

We haven't run a controlled match-rate test across providers on one identical list, so there's no scorecard here, and an invented percentage would be worth less than this sentence admitting it. We pay for the plans we write about, no vendor read a word of this before publication, and Gojiberry is our own product. Clients like Wispra run their pipeline on it, which is the bias to read the last third with.
Seven dimensions, each scored out of five, each defended further down this page.
Table of contents

Clay was founded in New York in 2017 by Kareem Amin, and Varun Anand joined as co-founder in 2021. The company set out to make programming reachable for people who don't code, then found its market in go-to-market data.

The money followed quickly. CapitalG led a $100 million Series C in August 2025 at a $3.1 billion valuation, and a second employee tender offer in January 2026 priced the company at $5 billion. Clay says it passed $100 million in annual recurring revenue at the end of 2025 and that it's serving more than 14,000 customers, with OpenAI, Anthropic, Rippling and Intercom among the named ones.

Clay is an orchestration layer for data. You bring rows in from a CSV, a search or a CRM export, then add columns that call a data provider, an AI prompt or an integration, and you're watching the table fill itself in place.

It's easier to say what it isn't. It isn't a CRM. It doesn't own a contact database: every record it returns is bought from one of the 150+ partners in its marketplace. And the email sequencer it ships closes the loop rather than replacing a dedicated sending tool.
Two lists. Recognize yourself on the left and Clay will pay for itself. Recognize yourself on the right and you'll spend three months learning a tool built for a problem you don't have.
3 questions
Is Clay the right shape for your team?
No email required.
QUESTION 1 / 3

QUESTION 2 / 3

QUESTION 3 / 3

Your answers point at a targeting problem rather than a data problem. Building tables won't fix a week where the right twenty people never surfaced, and that's the part we automate.
Clay earns its price here

You've got coverage gaps and somebody to own the build, which is where Clay is worth every credit. Come back when the tables are full and the replies are still flat, because choosing who to write to this week is the piece we add on top.
Five things carry the product. They're worth separating, because the first two are where the price is justified and the last three are where the learning curve lives.

A waterfall is an ordered list of providers on one field. Ask for a work email and Clay queries the first provider, keeps the result when it comes back verified, and moves to the second only when the first can't resolve it. Put your cheapest reliable source first and your expensive specialist last, and you pay specialist rates only on the rows nobody else could resolve.

This is why people pay for Clay instead of buying one database. No single vendor covers every market evenly, and the gap widens fastest on niche European segments. If you're only after one work email at a time, our free email finder answers that without any of this.

Claygent is an AI agent with web access that runs as a column. You write a prompt, it reads pages, and it returns a value per row that you couldn't buy anywhere: whether a company runs a given tool, whether the careers page lists a role you care about, how a product is priced. No database sells answers to questions nobody thought to index.

Two limits come with it. Claygent can't read anything behind a login or a paywall, and it costs more per row than a plain lookup. Since March 2026 the heavier models bill on the tokens they consume, with an estimate shown in the column and the final figure known once the run finishes.

Once the columns are filled, conditional logic decides what happens to each row. You score against your own criteria, split by segment, drop rows that fail a test, and push the survivors to different destinations. For an agency running six clients out of one workspace, that's the difference between owning a tool and owning a system.

It's also where teams without an ops person stall. Nothing here is hard on its own, and there's a great deal of it. Formulas, conditions, run schedules, and the discipline to check what a table did on fifty rows before letting it loose on ten thousand.

A working table chains steps: import, dedupe, enrich in waterfall, verify, score, write an opening line with AI, export. Clay reruns the chain on a schedule, so a list you built in March hasn't gone stale by June, and saved functions let you reuse the same logic across tables.

The catch is that each step in the chain bills twice, once in actions and once in data credits. A seven-column table on a thousand rows fires thousands of platform actions and thousands of marketplace lookups in a single run. The first serious table a team builds is usually the most expensive thing it'll do that month.

This is the answer most buyers want before anything else. CRM auto-sync, HTTP API integrations, webhook automation and web intent signals all start on Growth. Launch gives you phone enrichment, job change and company news signals, email campaign integrations and custom functions, and nothing that'll write back into HubSpot or Salesforce on its own.
Free is a demonstration. It caps tables at 200 rows, excludes phone enrichment, and hands you 100 data credits a month, which won't survive one afternoon of testing.
Three things matter here: what each tier holds, what a credit costs at each level, and what turns up on the invoice that isn't on the pricing page.

Two meters run at once, which changes how the sticker price reads. Data credits pay the provider for the email address or the mobile number. Actions pay Clay for the platform work around it: running the table, calling the provider, pushing the row into your CRM. One enrichment on one row can hit both, and they don't refill on the same terms.

Both paid plans are sliders, so the headline number is a default position rather than a floor. The advertised $185 on Launch splits into roughly $60 of platform actions and roughly $125 of data credits. Push the credit slider up and you're paying less per credit.

A credit costs five cents at the bottom of the slider and about four and a quarter cents at the top. That is a fifteen percent spread across a twentyfold jump in volume, which makes Clay cheap per lookup at scale and unremarkable per lookup at the volume three reps generate. Annual billing takes roughly another ten percent off and hands you the whole year of credits up front.

Growth, at $495 a month. That is a $310 step up from Launch for the ability to write enriched records back into HubSpot or Salesforce without a middleman. The same step buys HTTP API integrations, webhook automation and web intent signals.

It is a fair trade at volume and a strange one at the bottom of the market, since syncing a CRM is the first thing most teams want from an enrichment tool rather than an advanced use of one. Clay did move these features down from the retired $800 Pro plan in March 2026, and $3,720 a year remains the entry ticket for any small outfit that wants its data to land where the work happens.
Run the math for a team of three.

Three reps, 400 prospects a month each, so 1,200 contacts. A four-column waterfall covering work email, verification, mobile and company data is four marketplace lookups on every row that resolves, so you're at roughly 4,800 credits in a month.

Launch gives you 2,500. Growth gives you 6,000 and costs $5,940 a year before anyone sends a single message, and you still need a sequencer on top. Deciding which of those 1,200 people deserve a message this week is the expensive part, and it is the part Clay leaves on your desk.
If that arithmetic already reads like a no, the shortlist we've built of Clay alternatives is where you'd start looking.

Clay's ratings are unusually split, and the split is informative. On G2 it holds 4.7 out of 5 across roughly 189 reviews at the time of writing, with reviewers tagging integrations, ease of use and time saved. The negative tags on the same page don't wander far: learning difficulty, expense, credit limits.

Its Trustpilot page tells a different story on a far smaller sample, sitting in poor territory. Read the two together and the pattern is clear. People who invest weeks in the tool rate it near the top of the category, people who signed up expecting a prospecting app rate it near the bottom, and they're describing the same product.

Three complaints recur across review sites and community threads. The first is time to competence: the spreadsheet interface reads as familiar and the multi-step logic underneath doesn't. The second is budget predictability, which the dual meter improved without solving. The third is scope, since Clay is one brick in a stack and the invoice for the rest of the stack arrives separately.

Clay answers one question completely: how do I get accurate, complete data on a list. It doesn't answer the second one. Who on this list deserves a message this week? A perfectly enriched cold list is still a cold list.

The two problems also decay at different speeds. B2B contact data goes stale at around 2.1% a month, roughly 22.5% a year, according to HubSpot's database decay research. That's a maintenance problem, and enrichment is the right answer to it. Buying intent moves in days instead of months, and no amount of enrichment tells you that somebody changed jobs on Tuesday.

Job changes alone are a larger signal pool than most teams assume. Median tenure in a US job sits at 3.9 years, and the Bureau of Labor Statistics reports that 22% of wage and salary workers haven't been with their employer a full year. In a target list of 1,200 people, a fifth are new enough in post to still be choosing their tools.

That gap is where we built Gojiberry. It watches more than 30 buying signals across socials and the web, filters what it finds against your ideal customer profile, and opens a personalized conversation with the accounts that match. There's no table to build and no credit meter to watch, and the trade is that we hand you a thinner record than a fully built Clay table produces.
Why we ended up building this

Roman, one of our cofounders, spent his days prospecting on socials for Coco.ai, a Shopify app he grew to around $500K in revenue before it sold. The part that ate the week wasn't writing messages. It was finding people worth writing to, which he did by hand, watching who engaged with what and keeping the results in a spreadsheet.

He was running an intent search by hand, badly, and it still beat buying a bigger database. Coco is where we learned that the list isn't usually the bottleneck. Gojiberry started as the automation of a habit that already worked.
Wispra
of weekly demos sourced from intent signals
Mindflow
reply rate on intent-based outbound
GTE Localize
meetings after dropping cold email

Wispra sells data structuring for AI search, a category that barely existed eighteen months ago, so no database could hand them a list of buyers. They stopped asking who fits the profile and started asking who is already discussing the category, tracking engagement with AI search content and conversations around competitors.

Roughly 30 demos a week now run through that motion, about 60% of them sourced by Gojiberry, and it influences close to half of their revenue. Decathlon, Allianz and AXA came in that way rather than through volume.
Read the Wispra case study or see how GTE Localize ran it
Clay makes a list complete. Gojiberry decides which twenty people on it are worth writing to this week, and writes the first message.
Five tools, four questions. This is a positioning table rather than a feature checklist, because you're choosing a category before you choose a product inside it.

What we don't do belongs in the same table. Gojiberry is no kind of enrichment engine. If your fill rate sits at 40% on a list you already trust, Clay fixes that and we do not. We find and contact people who are already in motion, and the record we hand over is thinner than what a seven-column Clay table produces.
For the record on our side: Gojiberry runs at $99 a month on its Pro plan, with two AI agents and up to 1,800 prospects contacted, then a custom plan from five seats up.

We've reviewed two of the four at length: our Apollo review and our ZoomInfo review. If you're at the replacement stage instead of the category stage, we keep separate lists of Apollo alternatives and ZoomInfo alternatives. The earlier version of this page put Clay against PhantomBuster, and that audience has its own page of PhantomBuster alternatives.
Yes for a certain team, and the certainty cuts both ways.

For a sales team of two to ten with nobody on operations, our read is that Clay is over-engineered for the job in front of it. That says something about fit and nothing against the engineering, which leads its category. If you've landed on the skip side and still need better lists, the cheaper Clay alternatives we tested cover that ground.

Free is $0. Launch starts at $185 a month, or $167 billed annually, with 2,500 data credits and 15,000 actions. Growth starts at $495, or $446 annually, with 6,000 data credits and 40,000 actions. Enterprise is quoted and requires an annual commitment. Both paid plans are sliders, so those figures are default positions and they'll move with the volume you set. We checked every number here on Clay's pricing page on August 10, 2026.

There's a permanent free plan with 100 data credits and 500 actions a month, capped at 200 rows per table and without phone enrichment. Clay also runs a 14-day trial on the paid plans. The free tier is enough to understand the interface and not enough to run anything in production, which is fair for a tool this deep.

Since March 2026 there are two meters. Data credits buy records from the 150+ providers in Clay's marketplace and start at five cents each. Actions pay for the platform work around those lookups and cost under a cent each. A single enrichment can consume both. Data credits roll over up to one extra month's worth. Actions don't roll over at all.

Because a table charges per column, per row. A four-step waterfall on a thousand contacts is four thousand lookups, and every AI column sitting on top of it bills separately. Clay stopped charging for lookups that return nothing, which helps, though a run aimed at the wrong segment still returns data on every row and charges for all of it. The quickest way to burn a month is to test on the full list when fifty rows would've told you the same thing.

Not technical in the sense of writing code, and yes in the sense of enjoying systems. Formulas, conditional branching, run schedules and provider ordering are all learnable in a few weeks by somebody who wants to learn them. Learning difficulty is the most cited criticism on Clay's own review pages, and the teams that struggle are the ones where the work landed on a rep who didn't.

Rarely, on our read. Three reps working 400 prospects a month each will land on Growth at $495 for credit headroom and CRM sync, which is $5,940 a year before a sequencer, and the tool still won't decide who to write to. Teams that size usually get more from spending the budget on knowing who to contact. Mindflow lifted its outbound reply rate by 31% after switching to intent-based targeting, and you can read how Mindflow ran it.

Different categories. Apollo owns a database and ships a sequencer, so one subscription covers finding and sending, and the ceiling on data quality is whatever Apollo's own data supports. Clay owns no data and chains other people's, so the ceiling sits higher and the setup runs longer. Pick Apollo to start sending this week. Pick Clay to build a data layer you'll still be using in two years.

Yes, and it's a sensible pairing when you carry both problems at once. Gojiberry surfaces who moved and opens the conversation, then Clay fills in whatever your CRM needs on the accounts that reply. The overlap stays small because we work forward from a signal and Clay works forward from a list.
