Instantly splits its product into separate meters. One subscription moves your email. A second one, priced in credits, opens the contact database. The CRM doesn't carry a price of its own and rides on those same two subscriptions. The number on the pricing page covers the first meter only.

Every page that ranks above this one buries that structure or skips it. So this comparison runs on one question: what's the full bill once you add everything the job needs? Full bills, never sticker prices, all checked on the vendors' own pages in August 2026.
Your mailboxes work. Your list is the problem.
Table of contents

Entry prices below run on monthly billing unless the cell says otherwise. Every figure comes from the vendor's own pricing page in August 2026. The Instantly row sits second so you can read the gap without scrolling.
What we did and what we skipped

We opened every vendor's live pricing page between 25 and 29 August 2026 and copied the figures by hand, tier by tier, noting whether each rate bills monthly or annually. Half the confusion on this query comes from pages that quote an annual rate without saying so, and from pages that copy a competitor's blog instead of the source. Where a product sells itself in self-serve, we started an account and clicked through the sending setup. Where a sales call gates the product, we say so in the entry rather than guessing. We also read public reviews on G2, Trustpilot and Reddit for each tool, looking for complaints that repeat across all three rather than one loud thread.

One thing you will not find here: a scorecard of measured reply rates. We have not run a controlled send across nine platforms on an identical list, and an invented percentage would be worth less than this sentence admitting it. When we run that test, the numbers land on this page. We pay for every plan ourselves, and no vendor read a word of this before publication. Gojiberry is our own product and it sits first, so read that entry with the same suspicion you would apply to any vendor writing about itself.
Instantly's pricing page carries four tabs. Two of them price a meter you can buy on its own, and those two decide almost every bill. The third sells bundles. The fourth sells a managed service.

Sending and warmup. The Growth plan costs $47 a month if you pay monthly, or $37.60 a month if you pay for the year. It connects unlimited email accounts, warms all of them, and allows 1,000 uploaded contacts with 5,000 sends a month. Move to Hypergrowth at $97 monthly, or $77.60 annually, and you'll get 25,000 uploaded contacts. Light Speed sits at $358 monthly and $286.30 annually.

Contact data. Instantly meters its 450M-record database in credits, and those credits carry their own subscription. You'll pay another $47 a month for Growth Credits, or $37.60 annually, and 1,500 to 2,000 credits arrive with it. Supersonic runs $97 monthly for 5,000 to 7,500, and the Hyper tier starts at $197.

The CRM. Instantly's CRM page publishes no price of its own. It promises one subscription with unlimited seats and points you back at the sending and lead products, so treat it as a feature of the two meters above rather than a third line item.
Now run the math for a team of three. Say each rep works 400 prospects a month, a normal load for a small team, and touches each one four times. That's 1,200 new contacts and 4,800 emails a month.
Run the math for a team of three

The 4,800 sends fit inside Growth's 5,000-email allowance with almost nothing to spare. The 1,200 contacts do not fit inside Growth's 1,000-contact allowance at all. So the team moves sending to Hypergrowth at $97 a month and adds Growth Credits at $47 to source the list. The working price lands at $144 a month, against a $47 sticker.

Pay annually and the same pair costs $115.20 a month. Buy the Starter bundle instead and you pay $94 monthly or $85 annually, which packages 5,000 emails, 1,000 contacts and 1,500 credits, and throws in the AI Sales Agent. Read those two numbers side by side and the bundle only wins on the annual line, and only because of the agent.

One more detail worth checking yourself before you sign. On the day we looked, Instantly's Hypergrowth card advertised 125,000 emails a month while the feature comparison table further down the same page said 100,000. Two numbers, one plan, one page. Confirm which one your contract says.
None of this makes Instantly expensive for what it does. It does make the sticker price and the working price two different numbers, and that gap is why you're reading a page like this one.

Instantly holds a 4.8 out of 5 on G2 across more than 4,000 reviews, and it's earned that score. Its Trustpilot average sits closer to 3.8, and the gap between the two tells you where the friction lives. Four complaints repeat across G2, Trustpilot and the r/coldemail threads.

Growth allows 1,000 uploaded contacts. A single rep working a normal week fills that in three weeks. Reviewers describe the same arc every time: the plan looks generous during the trial, then the ceiling arrives in month two and you're paying double. The send allowance and the contact allowance run out at different speeds, which makes the plan hard to size in advance.

This is the loudest theme in recent reviews. Teams sign up for the outreach price, then switch on the lead database, then the AI reply agent that lives on a higher bundle, and the invoice stops resembling the page they bought from. Nobody's accusing Instantly of hiding the tabs. The complaint is that the entry price advertises one meter while the job needs two.

Reddit threads through early 2026 describe healthy warmup scores inside the app alongside campaigns landing in spam, and done-for-you domains arriving with weak reputation. Warmup activity and real inbox placement are two different measurements, and the dashboard reports the first one. Every sender on shared infrastructure carries some version of this risk, so it's a category problem that Instantly happens to be large enough to attract complaints about.

Instantly runs email. It doesn't automate social touches, and it won't fold them into a sequence. Teams selling into markets where buyers ignore cold email either add a second tool or move to a platform that covers both channels. That last complaint drives more switching than the other three combined.
If your problem is the copy rather than the platform, our 12 cold email templates that get replies will help faster than any migration you're considering.

The order runs from the tool that changes the input, through the tools that replace the sending, to the ones that widen the channels. Read the price paragraph in every entry before the bullet list, because that's where these products differ most.

Gojiberry is an AI-powered multichannel prospecting platform. It tracks more than 30 buying-intent signals across socials and the web, surfaces the leads who are in market right now, and triggers personalized outreach across several channels. Instantly decides how much you send. We decide who's worth writing to.

Start on the free plan, then $99 a month, flat, for the whole team. You won't find a per-seat multiplier or a credit meter running underneath. A three-person team pays $99. A ten-person team pays $99.

Instantly will tell you how many people opened. It won't tell you which of your 1,200 contacts changed something this week. That's the whole product, and it's the variable left to change once the sending already works.

Smartlead is the closest like-for-like swap for Instantly, and the two products argue over the same customer. Unlimited mailboxes, unlimited warmup, a unified master inbox and an API that agencies build on. Its pricing ignores how many people log in, and that's why lead-gen agencies keep landing here.

Base costs $39 a month for 2,000 contacts and 6,000 sends. Pro jumps to $94 for 30,000 contacts and 90,000 sends. Unlimited Smart runs $174 and Unlimited Prime $379. Annual billing takes 17% off every tier. You'll want to budget the $59 warmup add-on if you sit below Unlimited Smart, plus mailboxes at roughly $4.50 each.

Ask Instantly for a branded client portal and it'll point you at a bundle upgrade. Smartlead sells the same thing as a $29 add-on from Pro upward. We wrote the full comparison in Smartlead vs Instantly, and a wider roundup in our Smartlead alternatives guide.

Saleshandy answers the exact complaint that opened this article. Sending, warmup and contact data sit on one subscription, so you won't stack modules. Every outreach plan carries lead credits instead of selling them on a second meter.

Starter costs $34 a month billed annually, or $41 monthly, for 2,000 active prospects, 6,000 emails and 1,500 lead credits. Pro moves to $76 annually or $99 monthly, for 30,000 active prospects, 100,000 emails, 4,000 credits and ten seats. Scale sits at $149 annually. The email infrastructure add-on runs $3.49 per mailbox a month with a 25-mailbox floor, and you'll pay $14 a year per domain.
One invoice carries the sending allowance and the contact credits at the entry tier. Instantly splits those across two subscriptions, and you can't undo that split from inside the product.

Lemlist built its name on personalization that survives a second look. Custom images, video thumbnails and landing pages that carry the prospect's own details. It has since grown into a sequence builder that mixes email, social steps, calls and WhatsApp in one flow. The multichannel plan is the one almost everybody buys, and it prices per seat.

The email plan costs $69 a month and Multichannel Expert costs $109 per user a month at the monthly rate, with roughly 20% off for annual commitment, which brings the multichannel seat to about $87. Verification runs $0.05 an email and phone numbers $0.20. Three reps on Multichannel Expert reach $327 a month before you've burned a single credit.
A social touch and an email inside the same branch: Instantly doesn't build that, and Lemlist has built little else for five years. For the detailed head-to-head, read Smartlead vs Lemlist.

Apollo puts a large B2B database and a sequencing engine behind one login, and it opens a free account that never expires where rivals put a countdown. That combination settles the second question most buyers arrive with. The database is why people buy it. The credit pool decides whether the price you signed for is the price you'll pay.

Free costs nothing. Basic runs $49 per user a month annually, or $59 monthly, for 30,000 credits a year. Professional costs $79 annually or $99 monthly for 48,000 credits. Organization reaches $119 annually or $149 monthly, and the three-seat minimum means you'll write $357. We broke the credit math down in full in our Apollo pricing guide.
A database seat that costs nothing for as long as you want it. Instantly sells no such thing, so Apollo carries the free answer here.

Salesforge charges neither per seat nor per mailbox, which makes it the structural opposite of Lemlist. It runs inbox and social outreach inside one sequence, pools every reply into an inbox it calls Primebox, and bundles warmup instead of selling it. Growth carries unlimited users, so headcount doesn't move the invoice.

Pro costs $40 a month billed annually, or $48 monthly, for 1,000 active contacts, 5,000 emails and one social sender. Growth costs $80 annually or $96 monthly for 10,000 active contacts, 50,000 emails, unlimited social senders, unlimited users and API access. The trial caps at 25 emails, so you'll tour the interface rather than run a campaign.
Instantly won't add a social step to a sequence at all. Salesforge treats both channels as one motion, and it does it in 21 languages.

Woodpecker predates most of this list and its pricing shows a different philosophy. You don't buy a tier. You drag a slider to the number of prospects you plan to contact each month and the price follows at $7 per 100 contacted prospects, with everything else thrown in free.

At 500 contacted prospects the bill reads $35 a month, and annual commitment cuts that by a third. That position includes 16,000 emails, 4,000 stored prospects, four warm-ups and 100 Lead Finder credits. Extra mailboxes cost $4 to $6 each, and you'll pay $59 a month for a dedicated server.
Buy the volume you need rather than the tier above it. Nothing in Instantly's four tabs lets you do that, and Woodpecker prices nothing else.

Reply.io has sold sales engagement since 2014, and the age shows in both directions. The sequence builder handles email, social touches, calls, SMS and WhatsApp with conditional branching that newer tools have yet to match. It also splits those channels across plans and add-ons, so the seat you're quoted rarely equals the seat you buy.

Email Volume starts at $49 per user a month annually, or $59 monthly, for 1,000 active contacts with unlimited email and warmup. Multichannel costs $89 annually or $99 monthly. The Agency plan runs $166 a month, annual only. Switch on the social and calling modules and you're closer to $187 for a working seat.
A call, an SMS and an email in one conditional branch. Instantly never claimed those channels, and Reply.io has run them since 2014.

Snov.io bundles an email finder, a verifier, drip campaigns, warmup and a light CRM into one cheap panel. Nothing in it leads its category, which is beside the point. For a founder running the first 500-prospect campaign, one subscription covers the entire workflow.

The Trial renews 50 credits and 100 campaign recipients. Starter costs $39 a month paid monthly, or $29.25 annually, for 1,000 credits, 5,000 recipients and three warm-up mailboxes. Pro tiers climb from $99 for 5,000 credits to $738 for 100,000. Per-credit cost varies about fourfold across tiers, so if you undersize the plan you'll quietly double your cost per lead.
Under $40 buys a solo founder prospecting and sending without a second subscription. The nearest Instantly pairing costs $94.
Nine senders. One list problem.
Every tool above moves email well. None of them tells you which accounts changed this week. Gojiberry watches over 30 buying signals and hands you the ones worth writing to.

Yes, four of them, and the gap between a permanent tier and a trial decides which one helps you. A free plan renews. A trial counts down, then locks the door. Most pages covering this question don't separate the two.

Instantly itself sells paid tiers on its pricing page today, so plan for a bill from day one. The four permanent tiers above split into two jobs: Apollo and Snov.io find people for you, while Gojiberry plus Reply.io reach them. A founder validating an offer can run Apollo's free credits into Reply.io's no-cost account and spend nothing for a month.

Snov.io Starter at $29.25 a month on annual billing carries the lowest sticker. Saleshandy Starter follows at $34 annually. Woodpecker lands at $35 for 500 contacted prospects, and Smartlead Base at $39. Not one of those four numbers survives the second job.

Now the caveat, because the ranking flips the moment you add the second job. Smartlead's $39 buys sending and nothing else, so a team that also needs contacts pays $39 plus whatever a data tool costs, which puts the working total above $80. Snov.io's 1,000 credits find roughly 1,000 people once, then the balance resets to zero.

Saleshandy's $34 includes 1,500 lead credits and 6,000 sends on the same invoice. Compare working totals rather than entry prices and it wins the cheap slot outright, which is why it sits third on this list rather than eighth.
The cheapest tool and the cheapest pipeline are different questions

A $34 subscription that sends 6,000 emails to a list you guessed at costs more than a $99 subscription that sends 600 to accounts that just changed something. Google now holds bulk senders to a spam complaint rate under 0.3%, and volume against a cold list is the shortest route to that threshold. Read Google's sender guidelines before you buy on price alone.

Email only points you at Smartlead, Woodpecker or Saleshandy. Add social touches and the field narrows to Salesforge, Lemlist plus Reply.io. Add a dialer and only the last two survive. Gojiberry runs email and social senders together, so it belongs in the second group. Answer this one first, because it'll eliminate more tools than the other two combined.

List the invoices. A data subscription, a verifier, a warmup service, a Zapier plan for CRM sync. Saleshandy folds the first two into one bill and Woodpecker throws in verification free. If you already pay for Apollo or a similar database, buy a pure sender and stop there. Paying twice for contacts is the overspend we see most, and it's the easiest one to miss.

This is the question that matters. If your reps can't get volume out of the door, buy a bigger sender and the problem goes away. If your volume is fine and your replies are not, no sender on this page fixes anything, because they all move the same message to the same list. Come to us instead if that second sentence describes your quarter.
Senders fixed the sending. Nobody fixed the choosing.

These two products answer different questions, and comparing them on sends misses the point. Instantly asks how much email you can move. We ask which accounts deserve it, and that's a different product. A team that needs both usually keeps a sender and points it at what we surface.

Where we lose: point Gojiberry at a 50,000-address blast and it will disappoint you. That's not the product. Instantly, Smartlead and Salesforge all handle that job better, and an agency running six clients should buy one of them.

We haven't timed a first human reply from a paying account across nine vendors. That test deserves real numbers, so we'd rather leave the table empty than fill it with estimates. What we can describe is the shape of each support model, because the vendors publish it.
Self-serve chat
Instantly, Smartlead and Snov.io answer in-app, with priority queues reserved for higher tiers. Support responsiveness draws the most critical reviews across all three.
Tiered human contact
Saleshandy adds live chat at Pro and a dedicated account manager at Scale. Reply.io and Lemlist follow a similar ladder, so the seat you buy decides who picks up.
Founder-led onboarding
We are small enough that a human walks every new team through setup, which is an advantage we will lose as we grow. Judge it while it lasts.
of Wispra's weekly demos now come from intent signals rather than a static list.
reply rate at Mindflow after they moved outbound onto buying intent.
meetings for GTE Localize after they swapped email blasts for intent-led outreach.
2x
network for Baur Software, who scaled authentic outreach rather than volume.

One number explains why timing beats volume. B2B contact data decays at roughly 2.1% a month, which strips about 22.5% off a list over a year. Median job tenure in the United States runs 3.9 years, and 22% of employees haven't reached their first year in the job. Your list rots while you work it, and every one of those role changes is a reason to write.
Why we built this instead of another sender

Roman spent his days prospecting on socials before Gojiberry existed. He tested buying signals by hand, one account at a time, scrolling for the funding post or the new head of sales and writing the moment he found one. The reply rates were excellent and the method did not scale past one person. The bottleneck was never the sending. It was the twenty minutes of research that made each message worth sending.

Coco.ai came first and taught us the rest. Running outbound for a product nobody had heard of, we watched a well-built cold email sequence return almost nothing against a list we had guessed at, then watched the same sequence work against forty accounts that had just changed something. We built Gojiberry to do that research automatically, for teams of two to ten who cannot spare a full-time researcher.

Four of the nine open a real free tier instead of a countdown. Gojiberry asks for no card at all. Apollo grants 900 credits a seat each year, two sequence slots and 250 daily sends. Reply.io keeps a no-cost account for building and inspecting sequences. Snov.io renews 50 credits and 100 campaign recipients every cycle. Smartlead, Saleshandy, Lemlist, Salesforge and Woodpecker hand you seven to fourteen days instead.

Instantly's pricing page sells paid tiers only, and the cheapest of them costs $47 a month for sending. The company has run trials in the past, so check the current signup flow before you assume one exists. If a permanent free tier is what you need, Apollo, Reply.io, Snov.io and Gojiberry all publish one.

Instantly runs cold email at scale. It connects unlimited mailboxes, warms them, rotates sending across them, and manages replies in one inbox. Separate subscriptions open a 450M-record contact database and a CRM layer. It does not automate social channels, and it does not track buying intent.

Snov.io Starter carries the lowest annual sticker at $29.25 a month, and Saleshandy Starter follows at $34. Compare working totals instead and Saleshandy wins, because its $34 includes 1,500 lead credits and 6,000 sends on one invoice while the cheaper option meters data separately. The cheapest email-only tool stops being cheapest the moment you add a contact database.

No. Instantly automates email and leaves the other channels to you. Salesforge, Lemlist and Reply all run both channels inside a single sequence, and Gojiberry pairs the inbox with 2 social senders on every plan. This gap drives more switching than any pricing complaint we read.

Because the two products solve the same problem with the same core promise. Both connect unlimited mailboxes for a flat fee, both warm every inbox, and both pool replies into one view. The differences sit at the edges: Smartlead sells white-label client portals and charges $59 for its premium warmup pool, while Instantly bundles an AI sales agent and sells contacts on a second meter. The head-to-head earlier in this article covers the rest.

Only if the sending is what broke. If your emails land in the inbox and nobody answers, a new sender moves the same message to the same people. Fix the list first: our free cold email generator and follow-up email generator will tell you fast whether the copy or the targeting is the weak link.
More mailboxes will not fix bad targeting
Gojiberry watches more than 30 buying signals and hands you the accounts that deserve a message this week. Your sending tool then does the job it is good at.

For raw budget and a big database in one login, Apollo is the sensible start, and UpLead is the cleaner-data sibling. When your list is fine but replies stay thin, that timing problem is the one we solve, and you can point Gojiberry at your market for free.

ZoomInfo is one of the deepest B2B contact databases on the market, and it earned that reputation fairly. The data's broad, the org charts are detailed, and the intent feeds are real. For a large sales floor with someone to run it, that depth pays off.

The trouble starts when a small team signs the same contract. It opens around $15,000 a year on rigid annual terms, the records decay whether you're working them or not, and nobody on a three-person crew has time to run a platform built for fifty reps. This guide walks through twelve alternatives that fit a smaller team, what each one replaces, what it costs, and where it falls short.
Gojiberry finds your prospects for you
A bigger database tells you who exists. Gojiberry tells you which of them started looking for what you sell this week, and writes the first message.
Table of contents

If your list is healthy but too few people reply, the gap is timing, and Gojiberry is the pick. If the list itself is thin, you need data, so Apollo, UpLead, or Cognism earn a look first. Here's the full field, with what each one replaces and where it starts.

We built one ICP list of small B2B companies, the kind a two-to-ten-person team sells to, and ran each tool against it over three weeks in July 2026. For every product we checked the live pricing page, tried the self-serve tier where one existed, pulled sample contacts, and read recent reviews on G2 and Reddit. We pay for every plan ourselves, and no vendor read a word of this before publication, which is why Gojiberry's limits are written down like everyone else's.

One thing you won't find here: a scorecard of measured hit rates. We haven't run a controlled reveal test across twelve tools on one identical list, and an invented percentage would be worth less than this sentence admitting it. When we run it, the numbers land on this page. Support gets the same treatment: we haven't timed a first human reply from a paying account across all twelve, so we describe how each vendor sets up support rather than posting response times we didn't measure.

Here's the field in order, and the order runs from the closest replacements for a small team toward the pieces you bolt together yourself. Eight of these are databases you search to look people up. Two are enrichment engines you point at a list you already have. One is a finder inside a professional network. And the first one doesn't ask you to look anyone up at all, it brings the leads to you.

Gojiberry is an AI-powered intent-based prospecting platform. It's the one tool here that brings leads to you rather than sending you off to hunt. It tracks more than 30 buying signals across socials and the web, surfaces in-market accounts, and drafts the first message. Built for crews of two to ten, not a fifty-seat floor.

There's a free plan, then paid access is $99 a month with two social senders. No annual lock-in, no credits ticking down, and a third rep doesn't change the bill. Mindflow lifted replies 31 percent this way.
If your list is empty you need data first, and Gojiberry won't fill it for you. Point it at a real market and it does the one thing a database can't: tell you who's ready now.

Apollo pairs a large contact database with the tools to work it, so you build a list, sequence it, and dial from one tab. For a small team shrinking the stack, that bundle's the draw. The database runs past 200 million contacts, and the free tier is usable for testing.

There's a free plan, then Basic runs $49 per user a month annually, Professional $79, and Organization $119 with a three-seat minimum. The sticker is half the story: the credit meter moves the invoice on active outbound.

The credit math turns ugly the moment you need mobiles at volume, and it catches most teams by month two. For email-first prospecting on a budget, nothing here fits more into one login. We go deeper in our full Apollo review.

Cognism built its name on compliance and phone data, and for anyone selling into Europe that focus is the whole point. Its verified mobile coverage is the strongest here for EMEA. The database is GDPR-minded, and intent comes through a Bombora feed layered on top.
Cognism doesn't publish a price, so it's quote-based and sold as an annual package. Expect it to sit above the self-serve tools here, which is what you pay for the phone accuracy.

The contract decides this one. Below a real outbound budget with someone to negotiate it, the annual commitment costs more than a small team gets back. Above that line, no European phone data here connects like it.

Clay is a workbench you build on rather than a database you query. You wire dozens of data providers into a waterfall that enriches a list step by step. For a team with someone who enjoys building systems, it's the most flexible option here, and Google's overview names it among the top ZoomInfo alternatives.

There's a free tier with 100 credits, then Clay reworked its plans in March 2026: Launch is $185 a month and Growth $495, both usage-based with unlimited seats. Credits burn per step, and failed lookups still cost you.

Nothing here bends to a custom workflow the way Clay does. Then you price the ramp: weeks to learn, credits per step, someone to own it. A lot of overhead for a small team that wants leads without a build. See also our Clay alternatives breakdown.

UpLead sells verified B2B data with an accuracy guarantee, and that's the reason to pick it over cheaper bulk sources. It verifies each email in real time as you export, and refunds the credit if one bounces. A single credit returns both the email and the mobile for a contact.

A 7-day trial gives you 5 credits, then Essentials is $74 a month on annual billing for 170 credits, and Plus is $149 for 400. Essentials and Plus are single-seat, so a team of two lands on the custom Professional plan.
It's the cleanest data here for the money, and also the tightest, since 170 credits and single-seat plans run dry on any real outbound week.

Lusha's the fast, simple lookup most reps reach for first. Its browser extension pulls a verified direct dial or email in a click while you prospect. It does one thing well, person-level contact data on demand, and it syncs straight into Salesforce and HubSpot.

There's a free plan with a small monthly allowance, then Pro starts around $29 per user a month on annual billing and climbs on a credit slider. Watch the phone-credit math, since numbers eat ten credits each.

The sticker reads $29 a month. The number that matters is per phone reveal, at ten credits each, which turns a Pro plan into a few dozen dials before the meter's empty. More options in our Lusha alternatives guide.

Lead411 pairs a contact database with growth triggers, and it's the one here that flags company events worth a call. Hiring sprees, funding rounds, and leadership changes surface right in the search. Its Chrome extension pulls verified emails and direct dials while you prospect.

A 7-day trial gives you 50 exports, then Spark is $75 per user a month on annual billing for 200 exports, with Bombora intent sitting on the Ignite tier at roughly $3,000 a year. Exports are capped per plan, so heavy list-building climbs the tiers fast.
If hiring and funding triggers are how you time outreach, Lead411 is a fair-value way to get them. If you only want contacts, the export caps and the intent add-on price make it a slow build.

RocketReach leads on database size, with more than 700 million profiles in its system. For teams that need a wide net on a small budget, that reach is the appeal. The interface is simple, and the Chrome extension pulls contact info straight from profiles and company sites.

There's a free tier with 5 lookups, then Essentials starts near $33 a month on annual billing for email-only lookups, with phone numbers on Pro from around $75. Team plans are per seat and annual, so a five-rep crew climbs quickly.
Accuracy sits around the mid-80s, so plan a verification pass on what you pull. For sheer reach on a small budget, though, few databases here run wider.

Seamless.AI is a real-time search engine for B2B contacts, built for speed. Its extension finds and saves leads straight from a profile, and the AI validates data as it goes. If you need to build a large list quickly, it moves fast, though data quality can vary.
There's a free plan with a lifetime credit allowance, then Pro and Enterprise are quote-based and Pro carries a five-seat minimum. Pricing isn't published, so a real number takes a sales call.
The seat minimum ends it for most small teams. Pro is quote-only and needs five seats, which prices out a crew of two or three before the demo. Clear that bar and the real-time search is quick.

SalesIntel takes a human-first approach to data, re-verifying its dataset on a rolling cycle. Its research-on-demand service will go find a contact you can't, usually within hours. That focus on accuracy makes it a premium pick for teams that can't afford bounces.
SalesIntel doesn't publish pricing, so it's quote-based and sold on an annual contract aimed at mid-market and up. You'll talk to sales to see a number.

Few tools here verify data by hand the way SalesIntel does. Then you see the model: mid-market and up, quote-based, an annual commitment. A big swing for a team counting hundreds of prospects a month.

Breeze Intelligence is what Clearbit became after HubSpot bought it. It's an enrichment engine that lives inside HubSpot, appending firmographic and technographic data to your CRM records. If you're already on HubSpot, it fills in company size, industry, and roles without manual research.

There's no standalone product and no free tier anymore. Credits start at $45 a month for 100, but a paid HubSpot subscription sits underneath, so the real floor is around $75 a month, and buyer intent needs a Professional plan.
The add-on reads $45 a month. The real floor is the HubSpot plan underneath it, which turns a small enrichment line into a platform bill, and buyer intent needs Professional on top.

Sales Navigator is the paid prospecting layer inside the professional network most of your buyers already use. It's a finder rather than a data provider: it surfaces and saves the right people, but hands you no email or phone directly. Advanced search and real-time alerts make it strong for spotting who to work.

Core runs $119.99 a month per seat, about $90 on annual billing, with Advanced at $159.99 for team features. Every plan is per seat, so a ten-rep team lands in the $12,000 to $18,000 a year range, and you still need a separate tool to get the email addresses themselves.
It points you at exactly the right person, then leaves you to find their email somewhere else. That second half is the expensive one.
You shouldn't have to guess who to contact
Gojiberry watches more than 30 buying signals across socials and the web, checks each account against your ICP, and sends you the ones worth writing to.

ZoomInfo is one of the largest B2B data platforms on the market, a database of hundreds of millions of contacts wrapped in a go-to-market suite with intent feeds, org charts, and deep CRM integrations. It's the enterprise standard, and it's priced and built like one. Most of the alternatives above exist because that scale is overkill for a small team.

You search a deep database by firmographics, technographics, and title, then export verified contacts into your CRM or sequencer. On top of the data sit org charts that map who reports to whom, a Bombora-powered intent feed that flags accounts researching your category, website visitor identification, and workflow tools that route new records to the right rep. For a large team, it's a single source for finding, enriching, and prioritizing accounts.

ZoomInfo publishes no pricing, so every number comes from a sales quote built around your seats, credits, and modules. Buyer-reported figures put the entry Professional plan around $14,995 a year for three seats with about 5,000 credits, Advanced near $25,000, and Elite past $40,000. Vendr's marketplace data pegs the median contract at roughly $31,875 a year.

A few things shape the real number. Contracts are annual only, with a three-seat minimum and an implementation project attached. Credits meter every contact view and export, and running out mid-year means buying more. Renewals often carry a 10 to 20 percent increase, and there's a 60 to 90 day cancellation window before auto-renewal. The opening quote is a starting point, and prepared buyers routinely negotiate a large discount off it.

The praise is consistent: the data is deep and the coverage is broad, and for a well-staffed team it delivers. The complaints are just as consistent. Reviewers on G2 and Reddit point to the price, the rigidity of the annual contract, credit limits that bite mid-year, auto-renewal surprises, and data that ages faster than the term. The pattern is less about quality and more about fit, since enterprise tooling asks for enterprise time and budget a small team doesn't have.

The contract and the entry price. This is the one everyone names first. A deal opening around $15,000 a year, locked annual, three-seat minimum, is enterprise money for a team that doesn't have an enterprise. When a third of the seats go unused and the renewal climbs, the math stops working.

Records that decay whether you use them or not. B2B data ages fast. HubSpot puts the decay rate near 2.1 percent a month, which is roughly a fifth of your database gone every year. You're paying to store contacts that are quietly going out of date, and a bigger database only means more of them to maintain.

The platform needs someone to run it. ZoomInfo is built for a sales floor with an ops function behind it, tuning filters, managing credits, keeping integrations clean. On a three-person team, that person is also the one selling, onboarding, and doing support. The tool that needs the most administration lands with the team that has the least time for it.

A database tells you who fits, never who's moving. This is the deepest reason, and the hardest to see on a demo. A database answers who matches your ICP. It can't tell you which of those accounts started hiring, switched tools, or lost the champion you'd been working, this week. People change jobs every few years, 22 percent within their first year in a role, and every one of those moves is a buying signal a static list will never surface.
The right tool depends on the gap in front of you. For most teams of two to ten, the gap isn't the size of the list, it's knowing which names on it are worth a message this week.

Whatever you shortlist, run it beside your current setup for two weeks before you let a ZoomInfo contract lapse. A parallel pilot on your real ICP tells you more than any demo, and on a monthly plan it costs one month instead of a year of the wrong tool.

It depends on what better means for you. For raw database depth, nothing beats ZoomInfo. For a small team, a cheaper, more focused tool usually delivers more, since you stop paying for coverage and admin you can't use. If your list is thin, a data tool like Apollo or Cognism serves you well. If your list is fine but replies stay thin, an intent tool like Gojiberry does more for the money.

The names that come up most are Apollo, Cognism, and Clay, which Google's own overview highlights as the main three. Beyond those, UpLead, Lusha, Lead411, RocketReach, Seamless.AI, and SalesIntel all compete on contact data, while intent-first tools like Gojiberry compete on timing rather than database size. Which one is the real competitor depends on whether your gap is data or timing.

No. The platform is actively developed and the database is still the deepest around. What's dated for many buyers is the model: a big static list on a rigid annual contract, when the harder problem in 2026 is knowing which accounts are in-market now. For most small teams the data isn't the issue. A list can't tell you who's moving this month.

Yes, several. Apollo, Lusha, RocketReach, and Seamless.AI all have free tiers, and Gojiberry has a free plan to start. They're built for testing rather than scale, so use the free credits to check data quality and fit on your own ICP before you pay for anything. A free tier is the cheapest way to run the two-week pilot the guide above recommends.

For pure data on a budget, Apollo's free-to-$49 range is the lowest entry, and RocketReach starts near $33 a month. But cheapest per contact doesn't equal cheapest per meeting booked. Gojiberry is $99 a month flat, and a third rep on the workspace doesn't raise the bill, so for a crew of three the per-person cost drops as you add people, which is the opposite of the per-seat data tools.

Cognism, without much debate. Its phone-verified mobile coverage across EMEA is the strongest here, with GDPR and CCPA screening built in and do-not-call checks for the US and Europe. If connecting with European decision-makers by phone is the job, that's the one to trial first.

Carefully, and early. ZoomInfo contracts are annual and auto-renew, usually with a 60 to 90 day cancellation window before the renewal date, so the first step is finding that date and the notice deadline in your agreement. Miss it and you're locked in for another year. The safe play is to line up and validate a replacement during the notice window rather than after it, so you're never without data mid-switch. There's also a data-handling clause on exported contacts to check before you leave.

It depends on your list. If your database is thin or aging, you need data, so a replacement or a cheaper data tool is the move. If your list is already solid and the problem is that too few contacts convert, keep the data and add a timing layer beside it. Plenty of teams run a lean data source for coverage and Gojiberry on top to catch who's in-market.
Your competitors' customers are moving right now
Someone in your market just changed jobs or started following a rival. Gojiberry spots it, checks they match your ICP, and writes before anyone else does.

These two solve different problems, so the comparison isn't head to head. ZoomInfo is a database you search; Gojiberry is a signal engine that brings the right accounts to you. Here's how they line up for a small team.

The line that sums it up: ZoomInfo optimizes for coverage. Gojiberry optimizes for timing. A database points you at everyone who fits. Point enough untargeted email at a big list and you become the fastest route to Google's 0.3 percent spam-complaint threshold, which has throttled bulk senders since February 2024. Fewer messages sent to in-market accounts is how you stay under it.

Put the two models next to each other over a year and the gap is less about the sticker than about how each one scales.

The metric that counts is cost per meeting booked, not cost per record. A cheaper list that books nothing costs more than a pricier signal that books three. On a three-person team, the ZoomInfo entry is roughly $15,000 before a single meeting, while Gojiberry runs $1,188 for the year with the first message written, and adding people doesn't move that line.
The Coco.ai origin

Before Gojiberry, our cofounder Roman ran prospecting by hand for Coco.ai. He spent his days on socials, testing what intent-based outreach could do one tab at a time, watching for the accounts that had just changed something worth a message. It worked, and it didn't scale.

The ceiling was human. One person can watch maybe thirty accounts properly before the signals blur and the timing slips. That number is why Gojiberry exists, and why its pricing assumes a team of two to ten rather than a sales floor. We built the thing that watches the accounts for you, so a small crew can act on timing without living in a browser tab.
None of that needs a data team or an annual contract. You tell Gojiberry who you sell to, and it starts surfacing the accounts worth writing to, on your own market, from day one.

You want the outbound family
Nobody's arriving on their own yet, so something has to go out and find the accounts. Gojiberry finds prospects showing buying signals and matching your ICP, then contacts them for you.
A chat agent works that traffic, and it stops there

Your visitors deserve a fast answer, and the four tools further down handle that well. They won't grow the number of visitors. Gojiberry turns your ICP into a prospecting list and identifies the companies worth contacting.
Someone builds it, then someone maintains it
Builder platforms give you the parts, and the parts cost weeks before they return a single lead. Before you start, let Gojiberry handle the prospecting and the lead discovery for you.

Three families of tools answer to the name AI lead generation agent, and they don't solve the same problem. Outbound agents go and find people who've never heard of you, inbound and chat agents talk to the visitors already on your site, and builder platforms hand you the parts so you assemble the agent yourself. This page sorts the three families first, then compares the tools inside each one, because most of the confusion on this query comes from mixing them up.
Gojiberry finds your leads
Gojiberry runs two AI agents that watch more than 30 buying signals, check every account against your ICP, and contact the ones worth your time. 99 dollars a month for the team.
Table of contents

Every tool on this page calls itself an AI agent for lead generation. That label hides the one distinction that decides your shortlist: where the lead comes from. Answer that and you’ll ignore two thirds of this page without regret.

An outbound agent starts from your ICP rather than from a list you built. It searches directories, job boards and social platforms. It enriches what it finds. It ranks accounts by how ready they look and sends the first message. You describe who you sell to, and the agent hands back names with a reason for writing today, which is what you’d otherwise build by hand on Monday morning. Nobody has to visit your site first, which makes this the only family that works from a standing start.

An inbound agent sits on your website, your WhatsApp or your Instagram and answers questions in real time. It checks whether the person matches your criteria. Then it books the meeting or passes the thread to a human. It converts demand you've already earned. Its value tracks your traffic, so a quiet site turns the smartest chat agent into an expensive widget.

A builder platform gives you a visual canvas, model access, integrations and a scheduler. You design the workflow and connect the sources. You write the prompts. Then you keep the thing alive as APIs shift underneath it. You're buying capability rather than an outcome, and the subscription line rarely represents what it costs you.

One line routes most readers. An inbound agent has nothing to chew on until the traffic arrives, and traffic takes months of content, ads or reputation to build. If you’re starting from zero, you want an outbound agent, because it creates the conversation instead of waiting for one.
Four cases cover almost everyone. Find the line that sounds like your month.
How we checked the numbers on this page

We opened every vendor's own pricing page in August 2026 and took each figure from there, tier by tier, writing down what the meter runs on: contacts researched, leads contacted, seats, resolutions or executions. Then we read what each vendor puts in writing about commitments and add-ons, because that's where a bill moves after month two. Comparison articles on this query still quote plan names that vendors retired a year ago, so we ignored them.

One thing you won't find here: a scorecard of measured reply rates across thirteen tools. We haven't run a controlled test on an identical list, and an invented percentage would be worth less than this sentence admitting it. So there are no scores out of ten, and where the only answer is that it depends on your market, we say that instead. Gojiberry is our own product and it gets the same treatment as the rest. We pay for every plan ourselves, no vendor read a word of this before publication, and our customer results sit in case studies published one at a time.
Read the pricing model before you read the price

Five of the six tools below sell to teams that employ a RevOps function, and they price accordingly. Artisan sizes every plan on a sales call. 11x publishes one tier and quotes the two above it. B2B Rocket shows several conflicting grids at once. AiSDR and Leadspicker publish everything, and both put their real working tier well above what a small team budgets for software.

Gojiberry is the only tool here showing a flat price built for a team of 2 to 10. That says nothing about the quality of the others. It says they aim at a different buyer, and you deserve to know which buyer a product wants before you sit through its demo.

Gojiberry runs two AI agents for small B2B teams that start with no traffic and no list. The first watches more than 30 buying signals across socials and the web: job changes, funding rounds, hiring, competitor engagement. It checks every account against your ICP, so nothing lands in front of you that shouldn’t. The second writes to the accounts that clear the filter, with the signal attached as the reason for getting in touch today.

A free plan gets you started, then Pro costs 99 dollars a month for the whole team: 2 AI agents and up to 1,800 prospects contacted per month, with no commitment, so you’re free to stop in month two. Above five people, and for agencies, the plan turns custom. Teams running this motion report what it changes: Wispra now sources 60 percent of its weekly demos from intent signals.

Nothing else on this list decides who deserves the message. What we need from you is a market that leaves traces, and if your buyers don’t post, don’t hire and don’t raise in public, an intent layer finds less to work with.

Artisan sells Ava, an AI BDR that runs the whole outbound motion for teams that would rather hand the job over than operate a tool. Ava sources from a bundled contact database, writes the sequences, answers replies and books the meeting, and an autonomy setting decides how much she sends before you’ve read it.

The pricing page shows three tiers and no figure on any of them: Team at roughly 2,500 leads contacted a month, Scale at roughly 6,000, then Enterprise, and you won’t find a number next to any of them. The vendor states that it sizes a plan on your lead volume, your mailboxes and your dialer seats.
Every plan ships with a CSM and a guided rollout, and none of them ships with a price. You can't put a line in next year's budget without booking the call first.

11x sells Alice, an outbound digital worker aimed at sales orgs carrying a revenue number they can’t hire against. Alice prospects, personalizes, handles replies and books meetings. The real pitch sits in the infrastructure the vendor manages for you: mailboxes, domain setup, warmup, inbox rotation and monitoring all live inside the plan rather than beside it.

Growth starts at 3,750 dollars a month billed annually, covering up to 5 end users and 2,000 new prospects a month. The FAQ on that same page quotes 36,000 dollars a year as the entry point, so ask which number applies to you. Pro and Enterprise both go to quote. If that’s outside your range, we mapped the best 11x alternatives separately.

Bundling the mailboxes, the warmup and the rotation into one subscription removes the four line items that usually surprise people. Then you read the entry price, and 3,750 a month prices Alice against an SDR salary rather than against the software budget you’re working from.

AiSDR does what almost nobody else in this category does: it publishes every tier. The agent researches each contact, writes, follows up and hands you the replies, and the meter counts AI-researched contacts rather than seats, so a team of two and a team of twenty pay the same for the same volume. Setup takes hours instead of a quarter, and you don’t meet a salesperson on the way in.

Solo costs 250 dollars a month for 200 AI-researched contacts and one user, Explore costs 900 for 800 contacts, and Scale costs 2,500 for 2,500. Annual billing takes roughly 20 percent off each one. Only Solo runs contract free, and the two tiers above it want a quarterly commitment paid up front before you’ve sent a single email.
Publishing every tier is rare enough here to count as a feature on its own. The catch sits between the tiers, where each step up roughly triples the allowance and the invoice that’s attached to it.

Leadspicker puts autonomous discovery, waterfall enrichment and multichannel outreach in one platform, and it runs most social actions through its own infrastructure rather than through your account. Robots research people, watch job portals and monitor buying intent, then feed a sequence that spans email and social. Agencies read the seat structure first, because the plans count email seats and social seats separately, and they don’t move together.

Explorer costs 199 a month with 4,000 credits, Growth 479 with 16,000, Scale 1,599 with 80,000, then Enterprise goes to quote. Annual billing saves up to 20 percent and releases the credits up front. You start free without a card, and the vendor prices one credit at one euro cent, so you can cost an enrichment before you’ve run it.

Two meters run at once here, the plan and the credits, so you can’t forecast month one properly. What makes that survivable is the public price list: verified email at two credits, a phone number at fifty, everything else in between.

B2B Rocket bundles a large contact database, AI BDR agents, unlimited email sending, done-for-you domains and mailboxes, a unified inbox and a light CRM into one subscription. Outreach spans email, social, WhatsApp and SMS, and the agents answer replies on their own. At the top of the range it stops being software and becomes a managed service, with the vendor's GTM engineer running your campaigns.

Read this one twice, because the pricing page shows several plan sets at the same time: a self-serve ladder at 599, 999 and 1,399 dollars a month billed annually. A quarterly set at 799, 1,299 and 1,799. A cheaper Starter, Growth and Scale ladder at 59, 99 and 149. And a managed VIP tier at 8,000 dollars a month. Ask in writing which grid applies to you, because you can’t tell from the page.

The pricing page contradicts itself. Four grids, three billing rhythms, and a managed tier at 8,000 a month sitting next to a 59 dollar plan. There's a real product underneath, and working out what it costs you takes an afternoon you'd rather spend selling.

These four solve a different problem, and we'd rather say so than pretend they compete with the six above. They work the demand you already have. If people land on your site or open a chat with you every day, this is your family. If they don't, no widget on the page changes that.

The reference for support-led conversation, now built around Fin, its AI agent that answers, resolves and hands off. Seats cost 29, 85 or 132 dollars per person per month on annual billing, and Fin bills 0.99 dollars per outcome on top, so the AI line tracks your success rather than your headcount, and a busy month doesn’t come cheap.

Live chat built for ecommerce and small teams, with Lyro as the AI layer. A free plan exists, Starter costs 29 dollars a month and Growth 59, then the ladder jumps straight to 749 for Plus with nothing in between. Lyro arrives as a separate add-on from 39 dollars a month, so you’re budgeting two meters rather than one.

Built for teams whose buyers open WhatsApp, Instagram or Messenger rather than an inbox, which usually means B2C. Starter costs 79 dollars a month, Growth 159 and Advanced 279 on annual billing, and you’ll pay more month to month. Your bill moves on Monthly Active Contacts, and AI usage sits inside the Growth plan rather than beside it.

The closest thing here to a revenue agent rather than a support agent: it engages B2B SaaS visitors, qualifies them against your criteria, routes them to sales and helps users activate inside the product. The vendor prices its Discover and Convert plan at 999 dollars a month, and it doesn’t publish a cheaper self-serve tier below that.

Three platforms dominate this route. Read the subscription, then double it in your head, because you’re buying capability rather than an outcome, because the build and the upkeep cost far more than the licence. Someone designs the workflow and writes the prompts. Someone connects the sources. Someone repairs the whole thing every time an API shifts.

A no-code canvas for AI agents with a real free plan at 1 agent and 1,000 runs a month, then Individual at 20 dollars a month, or 16 on the annual plan, and Business on quote. The subscription buys the platform alone: model usage bills on top at provider cost, so your total tracks how hard your agents work, and you won’t see it until they’ve run.

A multi-agent workforce builder with two meters, Actions for platform work and Vendor Credits for model compute. Free covers 200 Actions a month, Pro costs 19 dollars a month on annual billing and Team costs 234, or 349 month to month. Extra Actions run around 80 dollars per 1,000, and that's the line nobody models in advance.

The most flexible of the three and the cheapest to run, if you’re able to host it. The Community Edition costs nothing beyond your server, while the cloud tiers bill executions: Starter at 20 euros a month billed annually for 2,500 runs, Pro at 50 for 10,000, Business at 667 self-hosted for around 40,000, then Enterprise on quote.
Stop guessing who to contact
Gojiberry watches job changes, funding rounds, competitor engagement and more than 30 other signals, then writes to the accounts that match your ICP.
Five capabilities separate an AI agent from a sequencing tool with a chatbot bolted on. Check each one against the demo you're about to sit through.

The agent searches directories, job boards and social platforms on its own schedule and builds the list from your ICP description, so nobody rebuilds a saved search on Monday morning. Timing is what this buys you. Median job tenure in the United States sits at 3.9 years, with 22 percent of employees in post under a year, which means your market reshuffles its buying committees constantly, and somebody’s got to notice.

The agent cross-references company news, funding, headcount moves and website signals. Then it fills the contact details from several providers in sequence until one returns a verified address. That work never finishes, because B2B databases decay by around 2.1 percent every month, close to a quarter of the list you’re working from each year. If you want the specialists that do only this part, we ranked the best Clay alternatives.

The agent ranks accounts by how ready they look to buy rather than by how well they match a static filter. A company that just hired three people into the team you sell to sits above an identical company that hasn’t moved this quarter. Readiness beats resemblance, and this is the capability that moves reply rates rather than send volume.

The agent writes from what the prospect did rather than from a merge field, then follows up across email and social at the cadence you set. Getting that first line right matters more than the channel count, and it’s what protects your domain: Google holds bulk senders to a spam complaint rate below 0.3 percent. We published the cold email templates that get replies for exactly this reason.

The agent handles the back and forth about timing, then drops the meeting into a calendar with the context attached. Most vendors in the outbound family ship this now. Very few ship it well enough to run with nobody reading the thread first, and the ones that ship it well give you an approval step for a reason you’ll appreciate.

Ask that question on a public forum and the top answer usually arrives as a joke. The reaction tells you something accurate about the category: plenty of teams bought an AI SDR in 2024, sent thousands of emails, booked nothing, and they haven’t forgotten.

So here's the state of the evidence. Every figure circulating on this query comes from the vendors themselves, and ours are no exception. No independent body audits reply rates in this market. Nobody runs one identical list through ten agents and publishes what came back. Treat any percentage you read here, on a competitor's page or in a review site's summary as a customer story rather than a benchmark, and ask for the sample size before you believe it.
Here are ours, published one customer at a time, with the customer named.
Wispra
Rebuilt its outbound around intent signals and now sources 60 percent of its weekly demos that way.
Read the case study
Mindflow
Stopped spraying its ICP, wrote only to accounts that had moved, and reached a reply rate above 30 percent.
GTE Localize
Shifted from volume email to intent-driven outreach and passed 100 meetings booked.
Baur Software
Runs the same motion on a smaller team and doubled its network without losing the personal tone.
Now the limit that decides whether any of this works for you

A signal engine reads what your market leaves behind: a job change, a funding round, a hire, a post, an interaction with a competitor. When your buyers leave those traces, the method works and the numbers above make sense.

When your buyers leave no trace online, no signal engine invents activity that isn't there. Sell to rural contractors who never post, to public bodies that announce nothing, or to a market of forty companies you already know by name, and an intent layer adds very little. Come to us instead when your market moves in public and you can't watch all of it.
The three families bill on three different units, which is why comparing headline prices across them won’t tell you much. Read the middle column first.
The two lines that catch small teams out

Per resolution pricing on the inbound side punishes a good month. At 0.99 dollars per outcome, an agent that resolves 2,000 conversations adds roughly 1,980 dollars to a bill that started at a seat price of 85.

Quarterly and annual commitments hide the real entry cost on the outbound side. A 900 dollar plan paid quarterly in advance asks for 2,700 dollars before the first meeting lands. Data subscriptions sit outside most of these plans too, and we broke that pattern down in what Apollo really costs.

It depends entirely on where your leads come from, which is why this page sorts the families before it ranks anything. If you’ve already got visitors, an inbound agent converts that traffic and a chat tool serves you best.

If nobody knows you yet, only an outbound agent helps, because it finds the accounts and starts the conversation. For a team of 2 to 10 in that position, Gojiberry runs both agents on one flat price, which is why it opens our outbound list.

Yes, and thousands of teams do it every day. AI handles the parts of prospecting that reward patience rather than judgement: watching hundreds of accounts for a change, cross-referencing several data sources, drafting a first message that reflects what’s happened at that company this month.

You still own the parts that decide deals. You set the ICP, you approve the positioning, and you take the call. An agent nobody supervises produces volume, not pipeline. GTE Localize passed 100 meetings by keeping that division clear.

Computer science sorts agents by how they decide, and the list hasn’t changed much in twenty years. Simple reflex agents react to a trigger. Model-based reflex agents keep an internal picture of the world. Goal-based agents plan toward an objective. Utility-based agents weigh trade-offs. Learning agents improve from feedback. Multi-agent systems split the work across specialists, and hierarchical agents put one agent in charge of others.

Sales tools borrow that vocabulary loosely. A prospecting agent usually combines a goal-based core with a learning layer, and a multi-agent setup just means one agent finds the accounts while another writes to them.

Several vendors open the door for nothing. Gojiberry runs a free plan and Leadspicker lets you start without a card. Tidio keeps a permanent free tier. MindStudio gives you one agent and 1,000 runs a month, and n8n costs nothing beyond your own server if you self-host the Community Edition.
Read what free covers, though, because it doesn’t cover much. Free tiers in this category test the interface rather than the channel, and most of them run dry inside a fortnight of real use.

AI SDR describes a job. AI agent describes an architecture. Vendors say AI SDR when the product replaces a sales development rep's whole routine, from list building to booking, and they price it against a salary.

AI agent covers anything that decides and acts on its own, including a chat widget or a workflow you built yourself. Every AI SDR counts as an AI agent, and most AI agents do something far narrower than an SDR's job. Judge the capabilities rather than the label.
For the outbound and inbound families, no. You describe your ICP, connect a mailbox and a CRM, approve the messaging, and the agent runs. Most teams launch in an afternoon.

For the builder family, yes, and more than the marketing suggests. Someone designs the workflow, writes the prompts, connects the sources and repairs it whenever an API shifts. Count that person's hours as part of the price, because they usually outweigh the subscription several times over.
This started as a problem we had

Before Gojiberry, Roman prospected by hand on socials for Coco.ai. He wasn't running sequences: he did the intent research himself, one browser tab at a time. Watching who'd just changed jobs, who'd started engaging with the category, who'd said something that suggested they had the problem. Then writing to those people with a reason that was true.

It worked, which is the part worth saying out loud, because it's why the product exists. And it didn't scale. One person can follow about thirty accounts properly. Past that the method collapses, and what collapses first is the reason for writing. You stop noticing the signal, you keep the cadence, and a month later you're doing mass outreach with a first name variable in it. Gojiberry is that routine running on its own, for the size of team where nobody has a spare afternoon.

That constraint explains the shape of this page. A team of 2 to 10 doesn't need an AI employee priced against a salary, and it doesn't need a canvas to build one on either. It needs the list to arrive already sorted, on a price that stays the same when the third rep joins.

When something changed for the prospect. Day-of-week and hour-of-day effects are small and they don't hold up consistently from one study to the next, and a relevant email on a bad day still beats an irrelevant one on a good day. Fix the reason before you tune the schedule.

Not because a model wrote them. Placement comes down to sending reputation, volume, links, and relevance. Since February 2024, Google has held bulk senders to a spam complaint rate under 0.3%, and you'll cross that line by mailing people with no reason to hear from you, whoever typed the words. In most markets, yes, inside rules. In the US, CAN-SPAM allows B2B cold email as long as your headers are accurate, you include a real postal address, and you don't ignore opt-outs. In the EU and the UK, GDPR and PECR expect a legitimate-interest basis, targeting that holds up to scrutiny, and an easy, visible way out. Companies almost never let people pick their own address. IT sets one convention, sometimes two, and everybody hired after that gets slotted into it. That's the whole reason pattern guessing works at all. Find one person's address at a company and you've usually found the shape of everyone else's.

The convention tends to drift in a predictable direction as the company grows. Early on it's first@, because there are eleven people and no two of them share a first name. Then a second Sarah joins, the collisions start, and the company moves to first.last@. Past a few thousand employees you often land on flast@, which packs more names into fewer characters. And at a ten-person shop, the founder is frequently still john@company.com because nobody changed it.

The practical version looks like this. You want the VP of Sales, and nothing comes back for them. So you stop looking for the VP, and you look for anyone else at that company who's already published an address: a support alias on the contact page, a press contact, an engineer who signed a changelog. 11x sells digital workers: Alice runs outbound end to end, Julian handles the calls. It's demo-gated, starts at $36,000 a year on 11x's own Growth plan, and standard contracts run twelve months, which rules it out for most teams of two to ten.

Below are ten tools that don't work that way. Seven are agents that run outbound for you. Three are pieces you bolt on yourself, and they're here because on a small team they often solve the problem for less.
Most AI SDRs send more cold email to the same cold list. Gojiberry changes the list: it surfaces the people already showing intent.
