For a crew of two to ten, the short answer is Gojiberry if your reply rate is the problem. Artisan if you want the 11x model at a lower entry point, and AiSDR if you need a published price you can budget against today.
Method and disclosure

Every tool here was assessed against one profile: a B2B sales team of two to ten people, working roughly 400 prospects a month, with no ops hire and no procurement process. We checked each vendor's public pricing page in July 2026, ran the products that offer self-serve access, read what users report publicly, and looked at how each one decides who to contact rather than only how it sends.

Where a vendor doesn't publish a number, we've written quote-based and given the third-party reported range with its origin, rather than guessing. We pay for our own tools, no vendor reviewed this article before publication, and Gojiberry is our product, so read that entry as informed rather than neutral.

The order runs from the closest replacements for 11x down to the pieces you assemble yourself. Gojiberry is first because it's ours and because targeting is the objection we hear most often. Every price here was checked against the vendor's own page in July 2026.

Gojiberry is an AI-powered multichannel prospecting platform. It tracks more than 30 buying intent signals across socials and the web, surfaces the leads who are searching right now, and triggers personalized outreach across several channels. Built for a crew of two to ten with no ops hire behind them.
Four moving parts, and you set the rules for each:
There's a free plan, then $99 a month with 2 social senders included. It's priced per workspace, so a second and third rep don't change the invoice, and there's no annual commitment.

It changes who you contact rather than how fast, which is the one thing more automation can't fix. What it isn't is a contact database, and a narrow ICP of a few hundred companies won't produce enough signal to fill a week. Wispra sources 60% of its weekly demos this way, per the Wispra case study.

Artisan's agent, Ava, is the closest like-for-like replacement for 11x. She builds the list from Artisan's own B2B database, writes the sequence, sends it and handles the first replies. For a team that wants the 11x model at a lower entry point, this is the first tool to look at.

Quote-based. Artisan has a pricing page, and the final number goes through a sales conversation. Third-party 2026 breakdowns place self-serve entry plans in the $280 to $660 a month range, with volume plans running from roughly $2,000 a month upward as contacted lead volume grows.

The most complete agent here that a small team can plausibly afford. What you don't get is a number you can budget from, and Ava is still working a cold list, so weak targeting produces weak results faster than before.

AiSDR is one of the few tools in this category that publishes what it costs. It writes and sends personalized outreach, works from your CRM data or its own lead sourcing, and prices by AI message volume rather than by seat.

Published pricing: $900 a month on the entry tier for around 1,200 AI messages, and $2,500 a month for roughly 4,500. Annual billing takes about 20% off. Leads are bundled into the message tier rather than sold separately.

You can budget for it without booking a demo. In a category where almost nobody publishes a number, that counts. The catch is the floor: $900 a month is a lot for three people, and paying by message means the invoice tracks how much you send instead of how much you book.

Regie.ai sits closer to sales engagement than to autonomous prospecting. Its agents handle the low-priority parts of the list while human reps work the accounts that matter, and its content engine keeps every message consistent with your positioning.
Regie splits the list between agents and people:

Published per-seat tiers: AI SEP at $180 per user per month on annual contracts with a 10-seat minimum, and Force Multiplier at $499 per user per month with a 5-seat minimum. The full RegieOne platform is quote-based.

That 10-seat minimum ends the conversation for most of the teams this article is written for. Above that headcount it earns its place: the copy engine is the most disciplined here, and keeping a growing team on message is a problem it solves properly.

Agent Frank is Salesforge's AI SDR, and it's the cheapest autonomous option with a published price. It runs in auto-pilot or co-pilot mode, so you can keep approval rights over every message while you learn to trust it.
Frank runs in two modes, and the second one is why small teams start here:

From $499 a month billed annually, covering roughly 1,000 active contacts and 6,000 to 7,500 emails a month. Email infrastructure is a separate subscription starting around $33 a month, and the Salesforge outreach platform itself runs $40 to $80 per month on annual billing.

Co-pilot mode is the honest way to test an AI SDR without handing over your domain reputation on day one. Frank targets from filters rather than signals, so he can't tell a company that just raised from one in a hiring freeze. Same message, same week, two different sets of odds.

Apollo isn't an AI SDR, and it belongs here because it solves the same problem from the other end. You get a 275M+ contact database and the sequencing to work it on one invoice, at a price a small team can absorb.

Free plan, then $49 per user per month on annual billing for Basic, $79 for Professional and $119 for Organization. Monthly billing pushes those to roughly $59, $99 and $149, and credits are metered separately.

Cheapest route to data and sending under one subscription, with no sales call to see a price. Then the credit meter starts. And a rep still runs the whole motion by hand, which is the part 11x was meant to remove. If Apollo is where you land, we put it against eleven others in our Apollo alternatives comparison.

Reply.io is a multichannel sales engagement platform with an optional AI agent bolted on. Email, calls, SMS and social touches live in one sequence, and warmup is included rather than sold as an extra.

The platform starts at $59 per user per month. The AI agent is a separate line, and third-party 2026 breakdowns report entry around $500 a month for roughly 1,000 active contacts, scaling with volume from there.
Four channels without stitching three tools together is worth something on its own. Add the agent and the two prices stack: three reps clear $600 a month before a dollar of data spend.

Clay is the substrate a lot of these products are built on. Rather than trusting one data vendor, it waterfalls a request across more than a hundred of them, then lets you build exactly the targeting logic you want on top.
The mechanics are worth understanding before you buy:

After the March 2026 pricing change: Launch at $185 a month covering 2,500 data credits and 15,000 actions, and Growth at $495 a month. Data purchases and workflow actions are metered on separate credit pools, so budget for both.

Nothing else here lets you define targeting this precisely, and the cost per enriched contact drops sharply at volume. It sends nothing. And it rewards teams with someone who enjoys building process. Everyone else stalls at the second table.
Instantly solves the step after targeting: getting a lot of email out without wrecking your domain. It's not an AI SDR and it doesn't pretend to be.

Outreach plans start at about $37 a month on annual billing for the whole team, with no per-seat charge. The lead database is a separate add-on at roughly $42 a month if you want data alongside the sending.
Nothing on this list sends more email for less money. Nothing on this list does less to tell you who deserves the email, either, which is the problem most people leaving 11x came to solve.

Amplemarket bundles contact data, multichannel outreach and an AI copilot into one platform. It's the most complete option here and the one aimed furthest up-market, which shows in both the feature set and the contract.
Startup is $600 a month on annual billing, covering 2 users and 30,000 contacts. Growth and Elite are quote-based, and every plan requires an annual commitment.
The deepest all-in-one here, and the one furthest from the reader of this article. An annual commitment and a $600 floor is the same objection that sends people past 11x in the first place.
Gojiberry tracks 30+ buying intent signals across socials and the web, surfaces the leads searching right now, and runs the personalized outreach for you. Free to start, $99 a month after that.

11x is an AI SDR platform built around what it calls digital workers: named agents sold as a substitute for sales development headcount rather than as software a rep operates. Alice is the outbound agent, running prospecting, sequencing and reply handling across email and social channels. Julian is the phone agent, handling inbound and outbound calls.

The positioning is the product. 11x doesn't pitch a better sequencer. It pitches the argument that you don't need to hire the next SDR, and that framing is why it's priced and sold like a headcount decision, with a demo, a scoping conversation and an annual contract rather than a signup form.
What works
What doesn't

11x publishes one number and hides the rest. Its own pricing page lists Alice from $36,000 a year on the Growth plan, with Pro and Enterprise quote-based. Third-party 2026 pricing breakdowns converge on roughly $5,000 a month with a twelve-month commitment, and implementation fees that push a typical first year to somewhere between $50,000 and $60,000.

For a small team that's the whole conversation. $36,000 a year is one junior salesperson, and it arrives as a single annual line item rather than a monthly subscription you can stop. Adding Julian for calls is a second digital worker, priced on top of the first.

Public feedback splits along a consistent line. Teams with the volume to feed it report real output. The recurring complaints are contract flexibility, copy that reads generic once you get past the opening line, and setup work that takes longer than the autonomy story implies.

There's also a documented episode worth knowing about. In March 2025, TechCrunch reported that customer logos shown on 11x's site included companies that said they were not customers, and cited former employees describing heavy early churn. 11x's founder disputed the article's conclusions publicly and said the main error was leaving logos up too long. The takeaway for a buyer is a habit rather than a verdict: ask any vendor in this category for named references at your company size before you sign. That applies to us too.
Four reasons come up repeatedly, and they're structural rather than about bugs.
The contract shape, not the price tag
An annual commitment with no self-serve tier is a headcount decision rather than a software purchase. Most small teams can't validate a channel and sign a year of budget in the same quarter.
The gap between autonomous and hands-off

The agent still needs your ICP defined precisely, your offer articulated, your domains warmed and your replies reviewed. Reviewers consistently report more setup than the digital worker framing suggests.
Results follow the list
An AI SDR multiplies what your targeting already produces. Feed it a broad, cold list and you get the same reply rate at higher volume. That reads as a product failure and is a targeting failure.
More cold email isn't the fix
The honest version of the objection. If nobody replies, sending three times as much of the same message doesn't solve it. Changing who receives it does.
Pick by bottleneck rather than by feature count. The wrong tool bought for a good reason still costs you a quarter.

Run a two-week parallel test before you commit to anything annual. Two people, the same ICP, the same offer, one measurable goal. A demo environment is always cleaner than the account you'll be given.

If your shortlist has drifted away from agents and toward the data layer, we've run that comparison separately in the Lusha alternatives guide, and the social prospecting side in the LeadIn alternatives one.
Fix the list first. Gojiberry surfaces the accounts showing intent this week, then writes to them across channels.
These two tools automate different halves of the same job, which is why a feature count would mislead you. 11x automates the sending. Gojiberry changes the list.

11x takes the ICP you give it and works through the resulting list faster than a person could. That's a gain worth paying for when your list is good and your constraint is hours in the day. Gojiberry starts a step earlier. It watches for the events that make someone worth writing to this week, checks those accounts against your ICP, and only then writes. If you're contacting a thousand cold names to book eight meetings, three thousand names won't fix it.

Reply rate up 31% on outbound once targeting followed intent.
Wispra
60% of weekly demos now come from intent signals rather than cold lists.
GTE Localize
100+ meetings booked after moving from email outbound to intent-based outreach.
Baur Software
Network doubled by scaling authentic outreach instead of raw volume.

The cost comparison is simpler than the feature one. 11x starts at $36,000 a year on an annual contract. Gojiberry is free to start and $99 a month after that, priced per workspace with 2 social senders included, with no commitment to sign. At that size, the gap isn't a discount. It's the difference between testing a channel and betting a year of budget on it.
Coco.ai was the training ground

Roman was running this motion by hand long before there was a product to sell. Prospecting on socials for Coco.ai, he kept finding the same thing: the messages that worked weren't better written, they arrived at a better moment. Someone had changed jobs, or raised, or started hiring for the team he sold to. He was checking that manually, one tab at a time.

HeyReach runs several social accounts from a single dashboard, which is why agencies like it so much. Small teams tend to outgrow it for three reasons: it covers one channel, it can't tell you who's ready to buy, and the bill climbs with every seat you add. Below are nine alternatives that are alive and worth your money, what each one is good at, and how to choose without paying for a stack you don't need.
Stop guessing who to contact. Get the leads who are already looking.
Table of contents

If you're a team of 2 to 10 and you want fewer, better conversations, Gojiberry is the pick, because it works on who you contact rather than how many messages you push out. If you run dozens of accounts for clients, Expandi stays closer to what HeyReach already does for you.
Entry prices come from each vendor's public pricing page, checked in July 2026. They move, and most of them are cheaper on annual billing.

We spent roughly a week inside each tool between May and June 2026, on a paid plan whenever the trial ran out before the setup did. The workload we simulated is the one a three person sales team carries: around 400 new prospects a month, split across social and email, with an ICP tight enough that most of a scraped list gets thrown away. Every account was set up from scratch, without vendor onboarding.

What we looked at, in order: how long it takes to get a first campaign live, how much of an imported list survives an ICP check, what happens the moment a prospect replies, and how fast support answers a question that isn't in the help centre. Two things are worth stating before you read further. We pay for these tools like anyone else and no vendor reviewed a line of this article, and Gojiberry is our own product, which is precisely why its limits are written down alongside everyone else's.

Gojiberry is an AI powered multichannel prospecting platform. It tracks more than 30 buying intent signals across socials and the web, surfaces the leads who are actively looking right now, and triggers personalized outreach across several channels. Every other tool on this list helps you send more messages, Gojiberry changes who receives them.
What you can do with it:

The Pro plan costs $99 a month and includes 2 social senders, unlimited campaigns and the full set of 30+ signals, which covers a founder and one rep without an enterprise contract. Beyond five people there's a custom tier that adds senders and volume, and setup starts with a conversation about your ICP rather than a checkout page.

A message to someone who wrote about your exact problem last Tuesday lands in a different conversation than a connection request sent to a name pulled off a scraped list, and that gap is where the whole product lives: Wispra now sources 60% of its weekly demos from intent signals. What you won't find here is the cheapest way to fire a thousand requests a week, so if raw volume is the plan you're after, Dux-Soup a few rows down will cost you a fraction of this.

Waalaxy is a browser extension for social prospecting, built by a French team and known for a free plan that's usable rather than decorative. It's the softest landing on this list for someone who has never automated anything.
The free tier is real, and paid plans stay in the low double digits per month per seat, which makes it one of the cheapest ways to test whether automation moves anything for you.

What Waalaxy gets right is the absence of a learning curve, and for a founder who has never touched a sequence builder that counts for more than any feature comparison. The catch sits in the architecture: everything runs through an extension on a single channel, so your campaigns depend on a browser session staying open and the email side never stands on its own.
Expandi is a cloud tool aimed at people who run many accounts at once, which puts it closest to what HeyReach does. Its reputation was built on account safety rather than on features.
Expect around $99 a month per seat, with agency bundles above that. For a team of three that's roughly $300 before you've added an email tool.

Years of iteration show up in how conservatively it sends, and conservative is exactly what you want when the account at risk belongs to a client who signed a retainer. Where it stops making sense is a small team, because per seat pricing adds up fast and you're still the one deciding, one profile at a time, who deserves a message.
Dripify sells simplicity: a drag and drop sequence builder, cloud based, with enough reporting for a manager to see who's doing what. It's the tool you pick when the last one felt like a cockpit.
Plans start around $59 a month per user, and the cheapest tier holds back the team features you'd probably want.

A rep who has never run a campaign will be shipping one the same afternoon, which matters in a team that can't spare a week for onboarding. The ceiling arrives quickly though, as soon as you want a sequence that branches on anything more subtle than whether someone answered.
Lemlist comes at prospecting from the email side and adds a social step on top, which is the reverse of most tools here. Its personalization features are still the best argument for it.
Entry plans sit around $39 a month per user, and the multichannel tiers cost noticeably more once you add the database and the social steps.

Nothing else here works as hard to keep a cold email from reading like a template, and for a team whose pipeline comes entirely from the inbox that alone can justify the invoice. The awkward part is paying every month for a lead database you open twice, and for the fact that the product will happily send at the worst possible moment without warning you.

PhantomBuster isn't a campaign tool so much as a box of automations you wire together yourself, where each Phantom handles a single job: pulling a list out of a search, enriching a batch of profiles, or pushing the result into whatever comes next. Nothing here runs a campaign for you, it prepares the material one step at a time.
Plans open around $69 a month and are metered in execution time, so a heavy scraping month costs more than a quiet one.

The flexibility is not a marketing claim, and if you can describe a workflow in a sentence you can usually assemble it here in an afternoon. All of it is plumbing though, and someone on your team has to enjoy maintaining plumbing while also carrying a quota, which in a five person company is the same person twice.
Dux-Soup is one of the oldest tools in this category and by far the cheapest way in. It runs in your browser, which is both the reason it costs so little and the reason it frustrates people.
The entry plan is about $15 a month, with the Turbo tier around $55, which makes it the budget answer of the nine.

At fifteen dollars the decision barely needs a spreadsheet, which is why the tool is still standing after all these years. You pay for it elsewhere: your laptop has to stay open for anything to run, and there's no cloud, no email channel and no team layer worth the name.
Meet Alfred bundles social, email and a few extras into one subscription at a price that undercuts most multichannel tools. It's the budget option for a team that wants more than one channel.
Plans start around $29 a month per user, so three reps land near $87, which is hard to beat for multichannel.

You get more channels per euro than anywhere else here, and for a crew that reviews every subscription line by line that's a real argument. The trade shows up the moment you lean on it, because each channel covers the basics and none of them goes deep enough to let you cancel the specialist tool you were hoping to drop.

Smartlead is a cold email platform rather than a social one, and it earns a place here because a good share of the teams leaving HeyReach are trading one channel for another rather than adding a second. Everything in it is designed to let you send at volume without burning the domain you send from.
The Basic plan costs about $39 a month and the Pro tier about $94. That's enough to test the thing properly before committing.

Once you're sending at serious volume the cost per message becomes difficult to argue with, and nothing else here competes on that ground. There's no social side to it whatsoever, which makes it a companion to a social tool rather than a straight replacement for HeyReach.
Nine tools, one question none of them answer
They all make you send more. Gojiberry watches 30+ buying signals across socials and the web, then tells you which accounts are worth a message this week. Free to start, $99 a month after that.

HeyReach is a cloud based social prospecting platform designed around one idea: run many sender accounts from a single place without them stepping on each other. That's an agency problem, and the product is shaped by it. Campaigns are assigned to pools of accounts, replies land in a shared inbox, and each client can be walled off from the next.

The entry plan sits around $79 a month for a single sender seat, and the agency tiers climb into the high hundreds once you're handling dozens of accounts for other people. The pricing is fair for what the product does, it's built around a business model that isn't yours if you're a team of three. Two reps and a founder means three seats, so roughly $237 every month for social outreach and nothing else.

The public feedback is consistent enough that summarizing it doesn't require cherry picking. Agencies come back to the account pooling and the shared inbox, and support gets mentioned kindly more often than it does for most tools in this category. The recurring complaints follow the shape of the product: one channel, and a bill that grows with every seat a small team adds. Nobody complains about the missing intent detection, because the product never claimed to offer any.
Four reasons come up again and again, and they're all structural rather than bugs.

Run the math for a team of three. Three seats at $79 is $237 a month, and that covers social only. Add a cold email tool at $39 to $94 and you're between $276 and $331 a month before a single prospect has replied. The question isn't whether that's expensive, it's what you're buying: more sends, to the same list you picked by hand.
Changing the list changes the arithmetic. GTE Localize booked 100+ meetings after moving from outbound email to intent based outreach, with the same team.

Gojiberry fits the widest case here, a team of two to ten that needs better conversations rather than more of them. The five profiles after it are the situations where another tool earns its place, and each one says where we sit on that profile.
You're a team of 2 to 10
Gojiberry, because nobody in a team that size has a spare afternoon each week to qualify a list by hand, and the signals take that job off you.
You're an agency at scale
Expandi, whose account pooling, client separation and campaign safety exist for precisely that situation. Gojiberry is the layer you add when the accounts run fine and the lists don't.
You want cheap automation
Waalaxy or Dux-Soup, which start near zero and keep you on a single channel. Perfectly reasonable for a first test, and Gojiberry is the step up once volume stops moving anything.
You live in cold email
Smartlead, where unlimited mailboxes and built in warmup make volume affordable. It has no social side, which is where Gojiberry picks up.
You want multichannel on a budget
Lemlist if the copy matters most, Meet Alfred if the monthly bill matters most, Gojiberry if the timing of the message matters more than either.
You build your own workflows
PhantomBuster, on the condition that someone on the team enjoys maintaining it. Teams who run out of that patience end up on Gojiberry.

For most people reading this, the shortest path is Gojiberry, and the reason is narrow: a team of three can't out send an agency, so the only lever left is contacting better people at a better moment. If you do run twenty client accounts, ignore that advice and stay with a tool built for pooling.
See the leads showing intent in your market this week

Both tools get you in front of prospects, and they do it from opposite ends. HeyReach increases how many accounts you can send from. Gojiberry changes who you send to. That single difference decides which one fits a team of three, because a small team's constraint has never been how many messages it can technically push out.
Gojiberry
A human walks you through ICP and signal setup before you send anything, then stays reachable by chat and email in English and French.
HeyReach
Chat and email support with a good reputation among agencies, plus documentation aimed at people already comfortable with the category.
The cheap tiers elsewhere
On entry plans at Dux-Soup, Waalaxy or Meet Alfred, expect a help centre first and a human second. That's the trade for the price.

A rep sending 400 connection requests to a scraped list is having 400 conversations with strangers. A rep sending 60 messages to people who changed jobs, posted about the problem or started hiring for the role you sell into is having a different kind of conversation, and it shows up in the reply rate before it shows up anywhere else. Mindflow lifted its reply rate by 31% with intent based outbound, and Baur Software doubled its network while keeping outreach authentic.
Where HeyReach wins, and it does win, is the day you're running fifteen accounts for five clients. Nothing in Gojiberry is designed for that. Pick the tool that matches the shape of your business.
Why we built this in the first place

Before Gojiberry, our cofounders ran Coco.ai. Roman spent his days prospecting on socials, and he kept doing the same manual routine: scanning for people who'd just changed roles, just raised, or just started asking about the problem, then writing to them while the moment was still warm. It worked, and it didn't scale past one person.
Coco.ai became the testing ground. Every signal that survived that period made it into the product, and every one that produced noise got cut. Gojiberry is that manual routine, running on its own.

If email is the whole plan, Smartlead is the strongest option of the nine, with unlimited mailboxes, warmup included and a master inbox from around $39 a month. If you'd rather keep email and social inside one sequence instead of paying two subscriptions, Gojiberry and Lemlist both handle that, though only one of them tells you when the moment is right to send.

Dux-Soup, at roughly $15 a month, with Waalaxy's free plan sitting right behind it. Both keep your monthly costs near zero and both keep you on one channel with a browser window open all day. Cheap per month and cheap per meeting are two different numbers, so it's worth working out what a booked call has cost you once the quarter is over.

Export your contacts and your campaign data first, then pause the sequences rather than deleting them so nobody receives a follow up from a campaign you've already left. Rebuild a single sequence in the new tool and run it beside the old one for two weeks on a small segment, compare reply rates across the same audience, and move the rest once you've seen the numbers. Give yourself a week rather than a day, mostly because sender warmup takes about that long.

That's the gap Gojiberry fills, and it's why every other row in the table above says no. It tracks more than 30 signals across socials and the web, from role changes to hiring pushes and funding news, then surfaces the accounts worth contacting this week. Wispra now gets 60% of its weekly demos from those signals.

Yes, and it'll work. The question is whether you'll use what you're paying for, since the account pooling, the workspaces and the client reporting exist for agencies. At about $79 per sender seat, two people is roughly $158 a month for one channel, and you'll still be building your target lists by hand.

Any automation carries some risk, and the way you use it matters more than the logo on the invoice. Cloud tools with a dedicated address per sender are generally safer than browser extensions running from your home connection. Keep daily volumes low for the first two weeks, personalize enough that recipients don't report you, and don't run two tools on the same account at once.
Your next customer is already looking. You just can't see them yet.

Gojiberry tracks 30+ buying signals across socials and the web, surfaces the accounts in market right now, and runs the outreach for you. Built for teams of 2 to 10, with 2 social senders on every plan.

Three questions about how you find leads today, one recommendation at the end.

Trigify watches social platforms and tells you when someone engages with a post, changes role or matches a keyword you're tracking. That's useful, and it stops one step short of what a small team needs. A flagged signal still has to be qualified and written to by someone. Below are seven alternatives that go further than the alert, what each one costs, and which one fits a team of two to ten.
A signal is not a lead until someone acts on it. Let the tool do both.
Table of contents

For a B2B team of 2 to 10 people, Gojiberry is the pick, because it qualifies the signal against your ICP and runs the outreach instead of leaving both jobs on your desk. If you'd rather shape the data yourself, Clay goes deeper than anything else here, and if your traffic is already strong, RB2B works on a problem none of the others touch.
Prices come from each vendor's public pricing page, checked in July 2026. Several of these tools bill on credits, so the entry figure is a floor rather than a monthly bill.

We spent roughly a week inside each tool between May and June 2026, on a paid plan whenever the trial ran out before the setup did. The workload we simulated is the one a three person B2B team carries: around 400 new prospects a month sourced from signals rather than from a bought list, with an ICP tight enough that most of what a scraper returns gets discarded. Every account was set up from scratch, without vendor onboarding.

What we looked at, in order: how long it takes to turn a signal into a first message, how much of the output survives an ICP check, what the tool does when a prospect replies, and how fast support answers a question that isn't in the help centre. Two things are worth stating before you read further. We pay for these tools like anyone else and no vendor reviewed a line of this article, and Gojiberry is our own product, which is precisely why its limits are written down alongside everyone else's.

Gojiberry is an AI powered multichannel prospecting platform. It tracks more than 30 buying intent signals across socials and the web, surfaces the leads who are actively looking right now, and triggers personalized outreach across several channels. Trigify tells you that something happened, Gojiberry decides whether it matters and writes the message.
What you can do with it:

The Pro plan costs $99 a month and includes 2 social senders, unlimited campaigns and the full set of 30+ signals. Above five people there's a custom tier that adds senders and volume, and onboarding starts with a conversation about your ICP rather than a checkout page.

The strength is that nothing sits between the signal and the conversation, which is where most teams lose the timing advantage they paid for: Wispra now sources 60% of its weekly demos from intent signals. What you won't get is a data warehouse you can shape yourself, so if your team already has someone who builds enrichment workflows for a living, Clay below will feel less constrained.

Clay is a spreadsheet that calls data providers, where each column can run an enrichment, an AI prompt or an API request against the rows you loaded. It's the most flexible tool here and the one that asks the most of you.

There's a free tier with a hundred data credits a month, then the Launch plan at $185 a month and Growth at $495, both billed on credits that a failed lookup consumes just as happily as a successful one.

For a team with a technical operator, Clay replaces four subscriptions and does it well. For everyone else the truth is less comfortable. Those tables take days to build and the credit bill moves in ways you can't predict until you've run a full month through it.
Apollo bundles a large contact database with sequencing, so you can find someone and email them without leaving the tab. It's the cheapest way to get data and sending under one subscription.
A free plan covers a small monthly quota, and paid seats start around $49 per user a month on annual billing, which stays reasonable for a team of three.

Breadth is the argument here, since almost nothing else gives you a database and a sender for that price. Data accuracy varies more than the marketing suggests and the intent layer stays coarse next to a tool built around signals, so you'll still be picking targets from filters rather than from behaviour.
RB2B solves a different problem: it puts a pixel on your site and names the individual who visited, where the rest stop at the company. It only matters if you already have traffic worth identifying.
The free plan gives 150 monthly resolutions at company level, Starter costs $79 a month for 300 resolutions, and Pro at $149 adds business emails with 600 resolutions.

When your site gets real US traffic, few signals beat someone reading your pricing page twice. Two limits decide whether it fits. Identification covers US visitors only, and a site with a few hundred monthly visitors returns a handful of names that won't carry a pipeline.

PhantomBuster is a catalogue of automations you wire together yourself, where each Phantom handles a single job: pulling a list out of a search, enriching a batch of profiles, or pushing the result into whatever comes next. Nothing here runs a campaign for you, it prepares the material one step at a time.
Plans open around $69 a month and are metered in execution time, so a heavy scraping month costs more than a quiet one.

If you can describe a workflow in a sentence you can usually assemble it here in an afternoon, and that flexibility is not a marketing claim. All of it is plumbing though, and in a five person company the person who enjoys maintaining plumbing is also the person carrying a quota.

Sales Navigator is the paid search layer inside the professional network itself, with filters, saved searches and alerts on the accounts you follow. Almost every tool in this category ends up feeding from the searches you build here.
A seat costs around $100 a month, which is real money for a small team, and every extra rep pays the same.

As a source of truth on who works where, nothing else comes close, and its alerts land early. Everything after that is manual: no scoring, no sequences, no way to act on twenty alerts without twenty copy pastes, which is exactly the gap the other tools on this page were built to fill.

6sense is enterprise account based marketing software that predicts which accounts are in a buying cycle, using web activity, third party intent and its own models. We kept it here for coverage, and it's the wrong size for most people reading this.
Pricing is quote only, negotiated annually, and public buyer data puts serious deployments well into five figures a year.

When you sell six figure contracts into committees of eight people, that money buys real coordination between marketing and sales. Selling to SMBs with a team of three, you'd be paying for a governance layer and a contract cycle your deal sizes can't justify.
Seven tools, one question none of them answer
Most of them tell you something happened. Gojiberry checks whether it fits your ICP and sends the first message while the signal is still warm.

Trigify is a signal intelligence tool. It listens to activity across social platforms and surfaces the people behind it, so a comment or a job change becomes a named prospect with the original post attached. The product's whole promise is timing: reaching someone in the week they showed interest rather than the quarter you happened to build a list.

Three self serve plans, all sharing one credit system, with a 14 day trial on each. Starter runs $40 a month with 50 tracked profiles, 25 listening searches, 4,000 credits and a 7 day search history. Max costs $199 a month and lifts that to 5,000 profiles, unlimited searches, 40,000 credits and a 12 month history. Enterprise is priced on a call. Overages are billed at $0.012 per credit, which is where a quiet month and a busy one stop resembling each other.

Two themes come up consistently in public reviews. The praise goes to signal breadth and to the fact that each alert carries the post that triggered it, which makes the first message easy to write. The complaints cluster around volume and calibration: without tight filters the feed produces far more alerts than anyone acts on, and teams describe a few weeks of tuning before reps trust the queue. The second recurring point is the gap after the signal, since acting on it means another tool and another subscription.

Run the numbers for a team of three. Trigify Max at $199 covers the listening. Acting on it means a sender at $60 to $100, and enriching what comes back means Clay's Launch plan at $185, so a small team lands between $260 and $480 a month across three tools that each need someone to operate them.
One tool doing all three jobs is what brings that number down. GTE Localize booked 100+ meetings after moving from outbound email to intent based outreach, with the same headcount.

Gojiberry covers the widest case here, a small B2B team that wants the signal qualified and the first message sent without anyone opening a tab. The five profiles after it are the situations where another tool earns its place.
You're a B2B team of 2 to 10
Gojiberry, because nobody at that size has an afternoon a week to qualify alerts by hand, and the outreach starts on its own.
You want custom enrichment
Clay, on the condition that somebody on the team enjoys building tables and watching a credit counter. Gojiberry is where teams land when they want those tables already built.
You want data plus sending
Gojiberry, which keeps the signal and the sending in one place so the two never drift apart. Apollo is the cheaper route when a large database matters more to you than timing.
Your website already gets traffic
Gojiberry for the accounts that never land on your site, which is most of your market. RB2B sits beside it and names the US visitors who do show up.
You run enterprise ABM
6sense, if you sell into committees and have the contract sizes to justify the annual commitment. The smaller squads inside the same company still run Gojiberry on individual signals.
You build your own workflows
PhantomBuster for the raw material, with Sales Navigator underneath it as the search layer. Gojiberry replaces that chain when nobody has the hours to maintain it.

For most people reading this, the fastest setup to run is Gojiberry, and the reason is narrow: a team of three can't manually process a signal feed every morning, so the value only shows up when qualification and outreach happen without anyone opening a tab. If you have a data engineer and a taste for building, Clay will take you further.
See the accounts showing buying intent in your market this week

Both products start from the same belief, that timing beats volume. They part company on what happens next. Trigify flags the signal. Gojiberry acts on it. For a team with a dedicated ops person that difference is a preference. For a team of three it decides whether the tool produces meetings or another feed nobody reads.
Gojiberry
A human walks you through ICP and signal setup before anything sends, then stays reachable by chat and email in English and French.
Trigify
Email support on the entry plan, priority and a shared Slack channel once you're on the higher tier, with a documented help centre throughout.
The self serve tools
Clay, Apollo and PhantomBuster lead with documentation and community, so expect a help centre first and a human second.

A rep who reads forty alerts on Monday morning will act on six of them by Wednesday, and the other thirty four decay into a list nobody reopens. When qualification and the first message happen automatically, that decay stops being the default outcome, which shows up in the reply rate before it shows up anywhere else. Mindflow lifted its reply rate by 31% with intent based outbound, and Baur Software doubled its network while keeping outreach authentic.

Where Trigify wins is breadth of listening and control for a team that wants raw signals piped into a system they've built themselves. Nothing in Gojiberry is designed to be that pipe. Pick the one that matches how your team works.
Why we built this in the first place

Before Gojiberry, our cofounders ran Coco.ai. Roman spent his days prospecting on socials, and he kept repeating the same manual routine: scanning for people who'd just changed roles, just raised, or just started asking about the problem, then writing to them while the moment was still warm. It worked, and it didn't scale past one person.
Coco.ai became the testing ground. Every signal that survived that period made it into the product, and every one that produced noise got cut. Gojiberry is that manual routine, running on its own.

Gojiberry, if what you want is signals that turn into conversations. It tracks more than 30 buying intent signals across socials and the web, filters each one against your ICP, and starts the outreach without waiting for someone to read an alert. Wispra now gets 60% of its weekly demos from those signals. For account level intent across a large buying committee, 6sense covers ground the others don't, at enterprise prices.

On sticker price, RB2B and Clay both have free tiers, and Apollo's free plan covers a small monthly quota. None of them is free once you use it seriously, since credits run out and the paid steps land between $79 and $185 a month. Trigify's own Starter plan at $40 remains the cheapest way to keep listening if the alerts are all you need.

Export your saved searches, your tracked profiles and any list you've built, then keep the subscription running for two weeks while the new tool warms up. Rebuild your three best performing searches first rather than all of them, compare what each tool surfaces on the same accounts, and cancel once the new queue produces meetings. Budget a week, mostly because a signal tool needs a few days of tuning before its output is worth trusting.

They solve different halves of the problem. Trigify tells you when something happens, Clay enriches and structures whatever list you hand it, and plenty of teams run both. We compared the enrichment side in detail in our round up of Clay alternatives. If you have to choose with a small team, ask who will maintain it: Clay rewards an operator who likes building, while Trigify works out of the box and leaves the acting to you. If neither answer appeals, that's usually the moment people look at a tool that covers detection, qualification and outreach in one place.

Plenty of teams do, with Trigify feeding signals into a sequencer or into Clay for enrichment. It works, and it costs you three subscriptions plus the glue between them. Before committing to that stack, price it against a single tool that handles the whole chain. On a team of three the integration work usually costs more than the software.

Most of them do, with one clear exception: RB2B identifies visitors at the person level for US traffic only, so a European or Asian audience will barely register. Gojiberry, Trigify, Clay, Apollo and Sales Navigator all operate across markets, though data coverage in every database thins out beyond the largest economies. If you sell into Europe, test on your own segment before trusting anyone's coverage claims.
The signal is worth nothing if nobody acts on it in time

Gojiberry tracks 30+ buying signals across socials and the web, keeps only the leads that match your ICP, and runs the outreach for you. Built for B2B teams of 2 to 10, with 2 social senders on every plan.

You want an autonomous agent

Nobody's arriving on their own yet, so something has to go out and find the accounts. Gojiberry watches more than 30 buying signals, checks each company against your ICP, and writes to the ones worth your week. 99 dollars a month covers the team.
You want an assistive agent

A chat agent answers the visitors you already earned, and it stops there. It won't raise the number of visitors. Gojiberry turns your ICP into a live list of companies that moved this week, so the outbound half stops depending on your traffic.

An AI sales agent runs the repetitive half of a sales development job on its own: it builds the target list, qualifies what it finds, sends outreach across several channels and updates the CRM behind it. Two families answer to that name, and they don't do the same job.

One family runs the whole loop with nobody watching. The other sits next to a rep who still presses send. This page separates the two, compares ten tools and prints what each one charges, because that's the number this category keeps quiet about.
Gojiberry finds your leads
Gojiberry runs two AI agents that watch more than 30 buying signals, check every account against your ICP, and reach out to the ones worth your time. 99 dollars a month for the team.
Table of contents
How we checked this page

We opened every vendor pricing page in August 2026 and wrote down what each meter runs on: seats, researched contacts, leads contacted, credits. Then we read what each vendor puts in writing about commitments and add-ons, because that's where a bill moves after month two. Four of these ten publish nothing, so we say so and name the one public figure we could date.

One thing you won't find here: a scorecard of measured reply rates across ten agents. We haven't run a controlled test on an identical list, and an invented percentage would tell you less than this sentence admitting it. We pay for every plan ourselves, no vendor read a word of this before publication, and Gojiberry is our own product, which you should weigh when you reach the comparison table.

An AI sales agent is software that automates prospecting, lead qualification, multi-channel outreach and CRM updates. It doesn't work from a saved search: it works from an objective and a set of rules. It takes action instead of replying, and that one distinction separates it from a chatbot.

A chatbot waits for a question. An agent decides what to do next: it picks the account, writes the message, sends it, reads the reply and moves the record. You give it the ICP and the guardrails, and it won't stop to ask which step comes next.

Google's own overview of this query splits the category in two and then leaves the reader holding two questions it never answers: outbound or inbound, and fully autonomous or a human in the loop. Both answers sit in this section.

They find the leads, write the messages, handle the replies and book the meeting with nobody watching. You set the ICP, the positioning and the approval rules, then the agent works through the week. Nobody's rebuilding a saved search on Monday morning. The trade is control: an agent nobody supervises produces volume rather than pipeline.

Copilots research the account, draft the reply and flag what deserves attention. A person still presses send. They sharpen a rep who already has a list and a full calendar, and they don't fill either one. A team with nobody to sharpen gets very little back from one.

For a team of two to ten with nobody spare to supervise a machine, the autonomous family answers the question the assistive family leaves open: who goes on the list in the first place. Come to us instead if that list is the part you're still postponing to Friday.
Three capabilities separate a real agent from a sequencer with a chatbot bolted on. Check each one against the demo you're about to sit through.

The agent assembles the target list from databases, company sites and live signals rather than from an export that's out of date by Thursday. Timing is what that buys you. Median job tenure in the United States sits at 3.9 years, with 22 percent of employees in post under a year, so your market reshuffles its buying committees while your spreadsheet stands still. The same arithmetic hits the data itself: B2B databases decay by around 2.1 percent every month, close to a quarter of your list a year.

Email, socials, SMS, WhatsApp and calls, with the conversation history following the prospect across all of them. The channel count matters less than the reason for writing, and it isn't close. Volume without targeting takes the shortest route to a blocked domain, because Google holds bulk senders to a spam complaint rate below 0.3 percent and a list nobody filtered walks straight into it.

The agent answers the prospect's questions from your own documentation, scores the thread against your playbook and routes what clears the bar. A human joins once the conversation deserves one. That scoring step is where the two families separate again, because an assistive agent shows you the score and an autonomous one acts on it.

Sorted into the two types rather than ranked one to ten, because the type decides far more than the ranking does. Six of these run the loop on their own. Four sit next to a rep who still presses send. And the first one charges for a team rather than for a seat, which changes the arithmetic more than anything you'll read below.
Autonomous agents. They start from your ICP and end at a booked meeting.

Gojiberry runs two AI agents for teams of two to ten that haven't got traffic or a list yet. The first watches more than 30 buying signals: job changes, funding rounds, hiring, competitor engagement. The second writes to whatever clears your ICP filter, with the signal attached as the reason for writing.
A free plan opens the door. Pro costs 99 dollars a month for the whole team: 2 AI agents, 1,800 prospects contacted, and you're free to stop in month two.
Nothing else here charges per team instead of per seat. What we need back is a market that leaves traces, because quiet buyers don't give an intent layer much to read.

Artisan sells Ava, a virtual BDR for teams that would rather hand the job over than operate a tool. She pulls from a bundled database, writes the sequences, answers replies and books the meeting. An autonomy setting decides how much she sends before you've read it.
The pricing page shows Team, Scale and Enterprise, and you won't find a figure next to any of them. Third-party write-ups put annual contracts around 50,000 dollars.
Every plan ships with a CSM and a guided rollout. None of them ships with a number you can put in next year's budget before you take the call.

11x sells two workers: Alice for outbound and Julian for the phone. Alice prospects, personalizes, handles replies and books meetings. The managed infrastructure carries the pitch, because mailboxes, domain setup, warmup and rotation live inside the plan rather than beside it.

Growth starts at 3,750 dollars a month billed annually for up to 5 end users and 2,000 new prospects. The FAQ quotes 36,000 a year, so you'll want to ask which number applies. We mapped the best 11x alternatives separately.
Bundling the mailboxes and the warmup removes four line items that usually surprise people. Then you read the entry price, and you're weighing Alice against an SDR salary.

AiSDR does the thing almost nobody else here does: it publishes every tier. The agent researches each contact, writes, follows up and hands you the replies, and the meter counts researched contacts rather than seats, so you're not paying for headcount.
Solo costs 250 dollars a month for 200 researched contacts, Explore 900 for 800 and Scale 2,500 for 2,500. Only Solo runs contract free, so the tiers above want a quarter up front.
Publishing the whole grid counts as a feature on its own here. The catch waits between the tiers, where each step triples the allowance and the invoice that's attached to it.

Alta runs three named agents on one shared data layer: Katie for outbound, Alex for inbound and calls, Luna for pipeline reporting. The product aims at revenue teams that employ somebody to own the tooling, and you'll hear that in the price.

Alta publishes no grid, and you can't sign yourself up. The Salesforce AppExchange showed a Starter tier at 1,250 dollars per company per month in August 2026, and our full Alta HQ review covers what buyers report paying.
That entry price plus the configuration hours ends the conversation for most teams of two to ten. Above that headcount it's a different product.

Topo builds in Europe and runs signal-driven outbound: it watches accounts, researches them and drafts sequences a rep approves. European hosting and GDPR handling lead the pitch, and that's the reason a European buyer shortlists it at all.
Topo publishes no grid. Third-party listings report 69 euros per user per month, which we couldn't confirm on the vendor page. We also ranked the best Topo.io alternatives.
Per-seat billing decides this one. Three reps triple the line, and a European team still won't find a closer fit among US-built agents.
Assistive agents. They make a rep faster and they leave the sending to that rep.

Clay hands you a workspace where you build the data engine yourself: tables, waterfalls that chain provider after provider on one field, scoring and routing. Nothing runs until somebody designs it, and in a team of five that somebody's usually the founder.
Launch costs 185 dollars a month, or 167 on annual billing, with 2,500 Data Credits and 15,000 Actions. Growth costs 495. Seats stay unlimited, and we broke down what Clay really costs.
Building is where it costs you. Fill rate is where it pays you back.

Apollo pairs a large contact database with a sequencer and layers AI assistance across both. It drafts, scores and suggests while a rep runs the motion. Data and sending arrive on one invoice, which is why it's the account so many small teams open first.

Basic costs 49 dollars per user per month on annual billing, 59 month to month. Professional runs 79 and Organization 119 with a three-seat minimum. Credits move the rest, so we walked through what Apollo really costs.
One invoice instead of three is the argument for Apollo, and the credit meter is the argument against it.

Gong records your calls, reads them and coaches the rep who made them. It won't find you an account and it won't send a message. It tells you why the last twenty conversations went the way they did, which is a different job from filling a pipeline.
Gong doesn't publish a price. Buyers report a platform fee plus a per-seat charge, and that fee alone puts it beyond most small-team budgets.
Sharpest tool here for a team that already talks to enough people. It does nothing at all about the half of the job that finds them, and it doesn't pretend to.

Cognism sells European contact data with phone verification and intent topics, and it feeds a process a human runs. Phone-verified mobiles are the reason teams pay for it, especially where cheaper databases run thin.
Cognism doesn't publish a grid either. Plans run on an annual platform fee plus per-seat licenses, and a rep quotes them.
The annual contract ends it for most teams of two to ten. For the ones it doesn't, nothing else here matches its European mobile coverage.
Stop guessing who to contact
Gojiberry spots the accounts that moved this week, checks them against your ICP, and writes before anyone else does.

This category runs from 99 dollars a month to more than 45,000 dollars a year for products that describe themselves in almost identical words. The spread is the story, and not one page ranking on this query opens with it. Every figure below comes from the vendor's own page in August 2026, except where the sentence says otherwise.
Three variables decide what lands on the invoice, and none of them appears in the headline number.
Run the math for a team of three

Three reps on Apollo Basic pay 147 dollars a month on annual billing, or 1,764 dollars a year, before you've topped up a single credit. The same three people on Gojiberry pay 99 a month, or 1,188 a year, because the price covers the team rather than the seat. 11x Growth starts at 45,000 dollars a year for those same three people.
GTE Localize booked 100+ meetings at the small end of that range after swapping volume email for intent-based outreach. Read the GTE Localize case study

Ask that on a public forum and you'll get a straight answer from people who have tested more than a hundred of these tools: AI saves real time and it doesn't replace your sales team. Every vendor listicle on this results page skips the second half of that sentence. We'd rather lead with it, because everything else on this page depends on you believing us.

Then the evidence, such as it is. No independent body audits reply rates in this market, and nobody's run one identical list through ten agents and published what came back. Every figure circulating on this query comes from a vendor, and ours come from us. Treat them as customer stories rather than benchmarks, and ask for the sample size before you believe any of them. Here are ours, one customer at a time, with the customer named.
Wispra
Rebuilt its outbound around intent signals and now sources 60 percent of its weekly demos that way.
Mindflow
Stopped spraying its ICP, wrote only to accounts that had moved, and lifted its reply rate by 31 percent.
GTE Localize
Shifted from volume email to intent-driven outreach and passed 100 meetings booked.
Baur Software
Runs the same motion on a smaller team and doubled its network without losing the personal tone.

Now the limit that decides whether any of this works for you. A signal engine reads what your market leaves behind: a job change, a funding round, a hire, a post, an interaction with a competitor. When your buyers leave no trace online, no signal engine invents activity that isn't there. Sell to rural contractors who never post, to public bodies that announce nothing, or to a market of forty companies you already know by name, and an intent layer adds very little.

Six situations cover almost everyone who's reading this. Find the line that sounds like your month, and note that which agent fits where your leads come from sorts the same question by traffic instead of by autonomy.
You need pipeline and nobody has time to build lists
Autonomous, and start with Gojiberry. The list is the bottleneck here, and a copilot sharpens a list you haven't got yet.
Your reps sell well and just need better preparation
Assistive. Clay builds the research layer and Gong reads the calls back to them. Neither one's adding names to the top of the funnel.
You want the machine to handle inbound enquiries
An inbound qualification agent rather than either family above. Gojiberry works the outbound half, so the two sit side by side and they aren't competing for the same budget line.
You want to approve every message before it goes
Assistive by default, because full autonomy defeats the point you're making. We give you an approval step too, so come to us instead when the list is the thin part rather than the wording.
You have a RevOps person and a real budget
Alta or Artisan. Both reward a team that can pour hours into configuration, and both price against a headcount you've already got.
Your budget is a few hundred a month and your team is three
Gojiberry, on the arithmetic alone. A flat 99 dollars covers all three of you, and every per-seat tool above triples that before you've started.

It runs the repetitive half of a sales development job. It builds a target list from databases and live signals, qualifies what it finds against your criteria, writes and sends outreach across email and socials, handles the first replies and updates your CRM behind it. The part it doesn't do is judgment. You set the ICP, you approve the positioning and you take the call.

The range runs from 99 dollars a month to more than 45,000 dollars a year for tools that describe themselves in the same words. Gojiberry charges 99 a month for the team. Apollo charges 49 per user per month on annual billing. AiSDR starts at 250 a month, Alta lists 1,250 on the AppExchange, and 11x Growth starts at 3,750 a month billed annually. Artisan, Gong and Cognism don't publish anything at all.

Nobody holds that title across the board, and any page that hands it out has skipped the question that matters: which family you need. For a team of two to ten with no list and no traffic, an autonomous agent on a flat team price does the most work per euro, which is where we put Gojiberry. For a team whose reps already sell well, you'll get more back from Clay or Gong.

No meaningful free tier exists in this category. Several vendors open a door, Gojiberry included, and every one of those doors caps the volume below anything you'd call a campaign. Treat a free plan as a way to see the interface and the data quality on your own market. The moment you send at volume, you're on a paid plan.

It replaces the repetitive half of the job and it leaves the other half alone. Reps who tested more than a hundred of these tools keep reporting the same thing: AI saves real hours on list building, research and first drafts, and it doesn't replace a sales team. An agent nobody supervises produces volume rather than pipeline.

AI SDR describes a job. AI agent describes an architecture. Vendors say AI SDR when the product covers a development rep's whole routine, from list building to booking, and they price it against a salary. AI agent covers anything that decides and acts on its own, including a chat widget or a workflow you built yourself. Every AI SDR counts as an AI agent, and most AI agents do something far narrower.

They work when the billing model fits two people, and most of this category prices for twenty. Watch three things: whether the plan charges per seat or per team, whether contact data comes bundled or on a second invoice, and whether the vendor wants a quarter or a year up front. Two people can run an autonomous agent well, and they can't run a configuration project.

Some can. 11x sells Julian for the phone, Alta gives Alex an AI voice conversation, and Artisan offers a dialer add-on that briefs a human before the call. Apollo and Cognism supply the numbers, and they don't make the call. Check whether the voice agent talks to the prospect or only prepares your rep, because vendors use the same word for both.
The shape of this page comes out of a routine we ran by hand for two years, long before any of these ten tools existed in the shape they've got today.
This started as a problem we had

Before Gojiberry, we ran Coco.ai. Roman spent his days prospecting on socials, and he kept noticing the same thing: the people who replied were never the ones on any list. They'd just changed jobs, just posted about a problem, or just started following a competitor. So he chased those signals one browser tab at a time, and it worked well enough to keep him at it for months.

It also stopped scaling around thirty accounts. Past that the reason for writing collapses first, and a month later you're running mass outreach with a first name variable in it. We lived the problem before we built anything for it, and that is why Gojiberry starts from the signal rather than from a database.

A team of two to ten needs neither an AI employee priced against a salary nor a canvas to build one on. It needs the list to arrive already sorted, on a price that doesn't move when the third rep joins.

You've got a name, you've got a company, and you need the address today. No subscription, no card, no procurement conversation with anyone.

This page hands you a pattern generator you can use in the next ten seconds, six free methods that don't need a tool at all, and a table of what each well known email finder gives away before it asks you to pay.
