Table of contents
Six methods, ordered by how fast they pay off. The first three cost you a browser tab. The last three take longer, and they reach the people the first three don't.

Start where the company already publishes contact routes, because one of them names a person. The contact page is the obvious one, and it's usually a generic alias, so keep going. The pages that carry named addresses are the ones a lawyer wrote.
For a company of fewer than fifty people, two minutes of clicking beats any tool.
Google indexed the address years ago, so you've just got to ask it the right way. Run these five queries and swap in the domain you care about.

The PDF one earns its place more often than the others. Conference decks, annual reports and press kits carry addresses that nobody thought to strip, and Google's already read them. The quoted-name query works when the person spoke at an event, co-signed a paper, or sat on a panel.

You need a name before you need an address, and business social profiles are where that name sits attached to a job title. Read the profile, check the about section, look at what the person posts, and note who they work with. Some people put their address in the about section themselves, and that ends the search right there.
Read profiles by hand. Automated extraction breaks the terms of every platform that hosts them, and a restricted account costs you far more than the twenty minutes you'd have saved.

Companies pick one rule, then apply it to everyone. Find a single confirmed address at the company and you've found the rule for all four hundred employees. A press contact reading maria.lopez@company.com tells you the CFO sits at firstname.lastname too.

Roughly two thirds of B2B domains use first.last or first initial plus last. The generator above builds the six patterns that cover most of the rest, so paste your name and domain in, then work down the list until one of them doesn't bounce.

A finder does the pattern work, and it checks its own database at the same time. Our own free email finder takes a name and a domain, needs no account, and returns the formats that company most likely uses. It doesn't verify anything, and that's the trade you make for free and unlimited.
The next section puts the free quotas of the other finders side by side, because three of them advertise a number in their own page title, and those numbers don't line up.

When the website gives you nothing and the finders return nothing, the address usually sits somewhere a person published it on purpose. That's a smaller haystack than it sounds. These six places carry named addresses that no database indexes.
Phone numbers hide in the same places, and they turn up the same way. Our guide to free phone number lookups walks through that version of the search.

Three of these tools put a free number in their own page title. Nobody puts the seven numbers next to each other, so the numbers stop meaning anything. Here they are, each one read off the vendor's live pricing page on September 3, 2026.

Read the Apollo row twice. Its free tier advertises a large email allowance and caps you at ten export credits a month, so ten contacts a month leave the platform. The number you can look up and the number you can take away with you aren't the same number.

Skrapp has the same shape of catch. Fifty credits a month sounds generous next to VoilaNorbert's fifty-at-signup, and the free tier blocks list exports entirely, so you copy addresses out by hand. VoilaNorbert's fifty never come back, which makes it a trial wearing the word free.

Where these numbers come from. We opened all seven pricing pages on September 3, 2026 and read the free column. We didn't run a match-rate test across the seven, and an invented percentage would be worth less than this sentence saying so.
Gojiberry publishes this guide and runs a free email finder of its own, which sits in the first row.
A name and nothing else is the hardest starting point, and it's the one most people have. Five steps take you from a name to something you can send to.

Names repeat, and job titles move. Three people called David Chen work in sales somewhere, and two of them left the company you care about. Pin down the job title, confirm the current employer, and do it before you spend a minute on the address, or you'll write a perfect message to the wrong David. A perfect address for the wrong David costs you the same bounce as a wrong address.

The domain the company sends mail from often differs from the domain it markets on. A group that owns six brands routes everyone through the parent domain. Check an address in a footer or a press release first, because the marketing domain and the mail domain aren't always the same one.

Find one confirmed address inside the company with the operators from method 2, then read the rule off it. One address gives you the format for everyone else in the building. A support alias like hello@company.com tells you nothing, so keep looking until you find a human name.

Once you have the format, apply it to your person. When you couldn't find a confirmed address in step 3, paste the name and domain into the generator at the top of this page and start with the highlighted pattern. Our free email finder runs the same lookup on its own page when you'd rather bookmark it.

A guessed address is a guess until something checks it. Never send to a pattern you generated and never verified. The next section covers the three checks that you can run without paying anyone, and they don't take long.
Verification splits into three questions, and free tools answer the first two. The third one nobody answers for free, and the vendors who imply otherwise are selling you certainty they don't have.

Syntax first. The address needs one at sign, a domain with a dot, and no spaces. Every free checker runs this one, and typos are all it catches. A syntactically perfect address can still belong to nobody.

The domain check asks whether the domain accepts mail at all, and it's what catches dead companies and misspelled ones. The mailbox check goes further and asks the receiving server whether that specific box exists.

Plenty of servers refuse to answer. A catch-all domain accepts every address you throw at it and sorts the problem out later, so a checker reports it as valid, and you've learned nothing. No free checker proves a person will read your message. It proves the door opens.

Bounces don't cost you one prospect, they cost you the domain you send from. Google publishes a hard ceiling for bulk senders: keep the spam complaint rate below 0.3 percent, measured in Postmaster Tools. Cross it, and your mail lands in spam for everyone, including the people who'd have wanted to hear from you.

Which is why a list of forty verified addresses beats four hundred guesses. Fewer sends also means you'll write better ones, and the email subject line generator helps with the line that decides whether anyone opens the message.
One address at a time works for ten prospects. At three hundred it doesn't, and the job changes shape.

Before you touch a single address, build the list of companies and people. Bulk enrichment on a bad list produces bad contacts faster, and that's the whole failure mode. Filter by industry, size and geography until the list looks like the customers you already closed.

Upload a CSV of names and domains, and the tool returns addresses. Most finders charge a credit per address found, and the free tiers in the table above cap you somewhere between fifty and a few hundred a month, depending on which one you're using.

Bulk verification runs cheaper than bulk finding, often a fraction of a cent per address, so there's no reason to skip it. Run it on everything, including the addresses a finder marked as valid, because contact data doesn't sit still while you work on it. HubSpot puts B2B database decay at 2.1 percent a month, which works out near a quarter of your list a year.

Stack every free plan in the table, and you'll get somewhere between two and three hundred addresses a month, spread across seven logins and seven separate exports. Past that you either pay or you stop. Most teams of two to ten hit that wall in the second month, once the first list runs dry and nobody wants to rebuild it by hand.

The wall looks like a volume problem, and underneath it's a targeting problem. Three hundred addresses you picked badly perform worse than forty you picked well, and our guide to email outreach automation covers what changes when you put the sending on rails.

Short version: finding a published business address is legal nearly everywhere, and sending to it comes with conditions that differ by continent. You'll meet both of them below. Treat this as general information rather than legal advice, and ask a lawyer before you build a process on it.

European law draws the line at whether the address identifies a person. A generic contact@company.com identifies a company, so it falls outside GDPR. A named address like anna.mueller@company.com identifies Anna, so GDPR applies even though she's reading it at work.

GDPR still lets you email her without asking first, under the legitimate interest basis. That basis carries obligations, though: you tell her where you got the address, you explain why you're writing, and you stop the moment she asks. Legitimate interest gives you a reason to send, never a reason to keep sending.

In the United States, the FTC's CAN-SPAM guide is blunt about scope: the law makes no exception for business-to-business email. Accurate headers, a subject line that matches the message, a physical postal address and a working opt-out that you honor within ten business days.

Gojiberry runs on infrastructure built and hosted in the European Union, which matters when your legal team asks where the contact data sits. If you'd rather start from a message than a rulebook, our cold email templates show the shape these constraints produce.

We don't sell an email finder, and we'd rather say that here than let you find out later. Gojiberry is an AI-powered multichannel prospecting platform. It tracks more than 30 buying signals across socials and the web, surfaces the leads searching for what you sell right now, and triggers personalized outreach across several channels.

You just read that the free route caps out around two hundred addresses a month. The cap that hurts isn't the number of addresses, it's the number of them that deserved one. A rep who finds four hundred addresses and writes to all four hundred spends the month emailing people with no reason to answer, and burns the sending domain doing it.

So we start one step earlier. The platform reads your website to work out who's buying from you, watches for the signals that mean a company entered the market this week, scores each account against that profile, then pulls the contact and drafts the first message from whatever triggered it. Finding the address is the last step, and the easy one. Our breakdown of 13 intent signals covers the signals themselves in detail.

Pro runs $99 a month with two agents and up to 1,800 prospects contacted a month, including email waterfall enrichment across 15+ data providers. That's a flat team price rather than a per-seat one, which matters when there are three of you. If you look up a handful of addresses a month, the free finder above is enough and everything here is overhead you'd be paying for.
GTE Localize moved off static email outbound and onto intent-based outreach, and generated more than 100 meetings across two months.

Yes, and the ceiling arrives faster than most pages admit. The six methods above cost nothing at all, and the free tiers in the table give you roughly two to three hundred addresses a month, provided you're willing to stack all seven.
Past that, whichever route you take, it asks for a card. A team of three prospecting seriously passes that line in the second month.

It depends on whether you want volume or no friction. GetProspect gives the most usable free monthly allowance at 50 valid emails plus 100 verifications, and it only charges you when it finds something.

For a single lookup with no account at all, our free email finder returns the likely patterns in four seconds and asks nothing of you. It doesn't verify, so pair it with a free verifier before you send.
Confirm the person and the company domain first, then find one confirmed address inside the company and read the format off it. Apply that format to your person and verify the result.
When no confirmed address turns up, the generator at the top of this page builds the six patterns that cover most B2B domains.

The company's own website carries more named addresses than most people expect: the privacy policy, the legal notice, the press page and the team page. Google operators reach the rest, and filetype:pdf "@company.com" pulls addresses out of decks and reports.
Public sources cover the last gap. GitHub, conference speaker pages and podcast show notes all carry addresses that people published on purpose.
Yes. A domain search returns the addresses a tool already knows there, along with the pattern it's detected. Hunter, GetProspect and Skrapp all run one on their free tiers.
The site:company.com "@company.com" query does a rougher version of the same job for nothing, using whatever Google indexed.

Run three checks, because they answer different questions. Syntax catches typos, the domain check confirms the company accepts mail, and the mailbox check asks the receiving server whether that box exists.
Catch-all domains accept everything and tell you nothing, so a valid result on a catch-all stays a guess. No free checker proves a person will read the message.

In Europe, GDPR allows it under legitimate interest for named business addresses, provided you say where you got the address, explain why you're writing and stop when asked. In the United States, CAN-SPAM requires accurate headers, a postal address and an opt-out honored within ten business days.
This is general information rather than legal advice. Check your own jurisdiction and the rules of the market you're writing into.

What should you automate first?
No email required.

A three-person team decides to get serious about outbound. Somebody buys a sending tool in week one. By week three that tool pushes four hundred emails a month at a list pulled from a database filter nobody argued about. The sequence runs perfectly and the pipeline doesn't move. Nothing broke. The team automated real work in the wrong order.
Automation multiplies whatever you feed it. Send a good sequence to the wrong list and you'll reach the wrong people faster, with better follow-up.

So this page gives you two things. The first is an order: five steps to automate, starting with the one that costs nothing and breaks nothing. The second is a line: four parts of selling you keep doing by hand, and what goes wrong the day you stop. Every tool below carries the price we read on its own pricing page in August 2026, the billing period, and whether there's a free plan that covers the job.
See which accounts moved into buying mode this week
Table of contents

B2B sales automation hands the repetitive parts of a sales motion to software so a rep stops doing them by hand. It covers the mechanical work: capturing activity, sending, scheduling, reminding, updating records. It doesn't cover judgment. Software decides when something happens and you decide what it says.

In a real week for three sellers, that comes down to five jobs. You find the accounts that deserve a message. You draft a first message. You chase the people who went quiet. You get a time on the calendar. You keep the record straight afterward. Every product category with a name on it does one of those five, whatever the website calls it.

Most guides on this topic spend a third of the page right here. You already know what the category is, so we'll spend the rest of the page on the sequence that changes your week and the four jobs that stay with you.

The order runs from cheapest and safest to most consequential. Each step assumes the one above it works, and each one names what it removes from your week, which tools do it, what they cost, and how long you'll spend on setup with nobody running operations for you.

Start here because it costs nothing and breaks nothing. You connect a calendar and an inbox to a CRM, and every meeting and every thread lands on the right record without anybody typing. What it removes from your week is the Friday hour three reps spend reconstructing what they did on Tuesday. No prospect sees any of this, so a mistake here costs you a tidy-up and it won't burn an account.
Setup takes an afternoon. Connect the mailbox, connect the calendar, import whatever spreadsheet holds your deals today, and stop there. You don't need workflows yet.

A shared link ends the four-message exchange about Tuesday at three. That's the fastest payback on this list, and it pays again every week. A rep who books six meetings a month saves roughly an hour of scheduling and loses fewer slots to people who cooled off while the emails bounced around.
Setup takes twenty minutes. Pick one meeting type, set the hours you'll defend, and put the link in your signature.

Most deals die from silence, not rejection. A three-step sequence recovers more conversations than any new channel you could add this quarter, and it's the first automation a prospect will notice, so the quality bar goes up. Write them yourself and let the tool handle the timing. If you want a starting structure, our follow-up email generator drafts the second and third touches for you.

Setup takes a day of technical work and then two weeks of waiting, and you can't skip the waiting. Buy a sending domain you keep away from your main one, set your SPF, DKIM and DMARC records, and warm the mailbox before a single prospect hears from you.

This step decides whether the three above earn anything. Instead of a static list you exported in March, you're watching signals: a funding round, a job change, a hiring page that suddenly wants five sellers. US median tenure in a job runs 3.9 years, and 22% of workers have been with their employer under a year, so a list you built two quarters ago is already wrong about a chunk of it.

Setup takes half a day to describe your ICP and pick your signals. We wrote a longer piece on choosing an AI tool for sales prospecting, plus a breakdown of the 13 intent signals worth watching if you'd rather set the criteria before you shop.

The obvious question is why this sits fourth rather than first. Better targeting only pays once you can act on it. A team that can't follow up reliably gains nothing from a perfect list, because the leads it finds leak out through the same hole as the last ones did. Steps one to three build the container. Step four fills it.

A draft comes last because it's only worth automating once the four steps above run. Use the AI writer inside whichever sender you already bought rather than paying for a fifth subscription. Hunter bundles an AI Writing Assistant on every paid plan, and Lemlist and Instantly both ship one, so you're rarely paying extra for this step.

Treat the output as a first pass. The tool gets you a structure and a subject line, and you supply the one sentence that proves you've read something about the company. Our free email subject line generator handles the bit people rewrite eight times. Setup takes an hour, and most of that hour goes on the prompt that describes how your team sounds.
Most teams automate the sending and guess at the list
Gojiberry reads the intent signals your market leaves across the socials and the web, then hands you the ones worth a message this week. Flat $99 a month, whatever your headcount.
Everything above removes work from your side of the conversation. These four sit on the prospect's side, and handing them to software costs you the deal rather than the hour.

Someone answered. That's the whole event you were paying for. Write back yourself, from your own mailbox, within the day. An automated response to a human reply reads as a machine that never noticed, and the second message in a thread is where trust either forms or dies.

A prospect who tells you the price is too high or the timing is wrong just handed you their real position. An automated answer treats a specific concern as a category, and it lands as a brush-off. The conversation ends there, politely, which is why almost nobody notices it's happening.

Never let a tool quote on your behalf. A number sent by software becomes the anchor for everything after it, and you lose the two things that make a quote work: the context you'd have asked about first, and the room to move.

Automating outreach before you qualify the list scales the mistake rather than the result. The legal side compounds it: the FTC's CAN-SPAM compliance guide doesn't carve out an exception for business-to-business email, and each violating message carries penalties of up to $53,088. Volume turns a sloppy list into an expensive one.

It's an old marketing adage: a buyer needs around seven contacts with you before they act. The number comes from mid-century advertising lore rather than from research, and no study pins seven down. Treat it as folklore with a useful shape.

The useful version reads differently. Most sellers stop after the first or second message, so persistence separates the people who book meetings from those who conclude that outbound doesn't work. The chasing does the work, and consistency beats the exact count. Three touches you send every time will beat seven you send when you remember.

The count also has a ceiling. A seventh message to someone who never opened the first six won't read as persistence. It reads as a complaint waiting to happen, so set the sequence at three or four, then stop and put the account back in the pool. If you want the shape of each touch, our cold email templates cover the openers and our follow-up generator covers what comes after.

Gojiberry sits at number one because it's ours, and pretending otherwise would waste your time. Everything below it follows the five steps in order, because a booking link and an enrichment platform never compete for the same budget line. Every price here comes from the vendor's own page in August 2026. Scroll the table sideways on a phone.
How we put this list together

We opened every vendor pricing page in this article ourselves during August 2026 and wrote down the plan name, the entry price and the billing period, because roughly half the numbers circulating on review sites still quote tiers that changed earlier this year. Clay retired Starter, Explorer and Pro in March 2026 and Lemlist moved its Email plan from a per-seat charge to a per-workspace one, so anything published before the summer describes a product nobody can buy today. We tried the self-serve products on their free tiers where those exist, and we read the public reviews for the tiers we didn't buy.

One thing you won't find here: a scorecard of measured reply rates across thirteen tools. We haven't run a controlled test on an identical list across all of them, and an invented percentage would be worth less than this sentence admitting it. When we run it, the numbers land on this page. We pay for every plan ourselves, no vendor read a word of this before publication, and Gojiberry is our own product.

Two patterns show up once you line them all up. The first two steps cost almost nothing, and three people can cover both for zero with Attio and Cal.com. Steps three and four carry the real money, and they charge for it differently: senders bill by the workspace while data tools bill by the head or by the credit. That difference decides your invoice far more than the headline price does.
Here's a plan you can run without buying anything beyond what it names. Three sellers, no operations person, four weeks.
Week one
Put the record straight

Open Attio on the free plan, which covers exactly three seats, and connect each mailbox and calendar. HubSpot's free tier is the better known option and it stops free at 2 users, so a third seller pushes you to $7 a seat before you've automated anything. Import your deals from whatever spreadsheet holds them today.
Cost this week: zero.
Week two
Kill the scheduling thread
Each rep opens a free Cal.com account, sets one 30-minute meeting type, and drops the link into their signature and their email templates. Don't buy the Teams plan until somebody needs round-robin.
Still zero.
Week three
Buy one sender and start warming

Smartlead Base at $39 gives you 6,000 sends and unlimited mailboxes. Register a sending domain you keep away from your main one, connect two mailboxes on it, switch warmup on, and don't touch a prospect for fourteen days. Write your three-step sequence while you wait.
You're at $39 now, plus roughly $12 a year for the domain.
Week four
Fix the list before the sequence goes live

This is where we come in, and it's usually the week the numbers move: Gojiberry at $99 flat reads those signals for you and hands three reps the accounts in market now, with no charge per head as the team grows. Point the sequence you wrote last week at that list rather than at an export.

Run the math for a team of three. Attio at zero, plus Cal.com at zero, plus Smartlead at $39, plus Gojiberry at $99 comes to $138 a month. That's $46 a seller. Buy the same four jobs by the head, with Pipedrive Growth at $39, Calendly Standard at $10, Lemlist Multichannel at $109 and Apollo Basic at $49, and you're at $621 for the same three people. Both stacks send email. Only one of them still costs $138 the day you hire a fourth rep.
Teams that run this order tend to feel the change in week four rather than week one, because that's the week the targeting arrives on top of plumbing that already works.

A brand new domain that fires 200 emails on day one lands in spam and stays there. Google asks bulk senders to keep spam complaints under 0.3%, a threshold that has applied since February 2024, and a cold domain trips it fast. Two weeks of warmup on a domain of its own costs you nothing but patience, and it protects the mailbox you run the company from.

Bounces do double damage: they waste the send, and they tell the mailbox provider that you don't know who you're writing to. Run the list through a verifier first. Hunter's free tier covers 50 credits each month, which is enough to check a small batch before you commit a paid plan to it.

A sender that can't write back to the CRM turns your reps into copy-paste operators, which is the job you were removing. Check two things before you pay: whether the plan in front of you includes the CRM integration, and whether it's gated a tier higher. Smartlead holds the CRM and the API back on Base, and Clay kept CRM sync above its entry tier for years.

If your three reps each follow up on their own rhythm, you'll end up with three different machines and no way to tell which one worked. Write the sequence on one page first: how many touches, how many days apart, what happens on a reply, what happens on silence. An hour with a document saves you a quarter of confused reporting.
Why we built this in the first place

Before Gojiberry, Roman spent his days prospecting on the socials for Coco.ai, our previous company. The job was manual and the pattern got obvious after a few months: the accounts that replied were the ones showing some signal that week, a funding round, a new hire, a comment on the right post. He was hunting for intent by hand, one tab at a time, and the good weeks were the ones where he'd happened to look in the right place.

Coco.ai turned into the place we learned what a small team can and cannot sustain. Nobody with three sellers has an operations person to maintain a scoring model, and nobody's got the hours to check two hundred profiles a week. So we built the part Roman was doing by hand, kept the price flat so headcount stops mattering, and left the reply to a human.

It's the marketing adage that a buyer needs roughly seven contacts with you before they act. The number comes from advertising lore and no study pins it down, so take the shape and leave the count. The part that holds up: most sellers quit after one or two follow-ups, and a consistent three-touch sequence beats an inconsistent seven-touch one.

A B2B sales platform bundles several of the five steps into one subscription, usually a contact database, a sequencer and some reporting. Apollo is the common example at $49 per seat, billed annually. You're trading depth for convenience: a bundle covers everything at a passing grade, and a small team often gets more from a free CRM plus one tool that does the hard step properly.

For three people with no budget, Attio's free plan covers three seats and syncs mail and calendar, which is the whole job at this stage. HubSpot's free tools are richer but the tier tops out at two seats. Pipedrive costs $14 a seat when you pay for the year, and it earns that once your pipeline has enough stages for reporting to matter.

Logging. Connect your calendar and inbox to a CRM so activity records itself. It costs nothing, no prospect sees it, and it builds the history every later step reads from. Booking links come second for the same reason: high payback, no risk.

Partly. Logging and booking run at zero on the Attio and Cal.com plans, and Hunter gives you 50 verification credits every month. Sending is where free stops, because deliverability needs a separate domain and a warmup period, and every credible sender charges for that. Budget $39 a month as the floor.

Automation on its own doesn't. Volume on an unverified list does. Google holds bulk senders to a spam complaint rate under 0.3%, and bounces plus complaints are what push you past it. Send from a separate dedicated domain, warm it for two weeks, verify the list, and keep daily volume per mailbox low.

It replaces the parts of the job nobody wanted: data entry, scheduling messages, remembering to follow up on day four. It doesn't answer a reply, handle an objection or quote a price, and those three are where deals turn. Three sellers who automate well stay three sellers, and they spend more of the week talking to people.

Your competitors may already be attracting attention from prospects you want to reach. Much of the buyer research process can happen before prospects speak directly with sales. Buyers may compare vendors, read reviews, engage with competitor content, or research alternatives while narrowing their options. By the time a prospect reaches out directly, competing vendors may already have influenced how they think about features, pricing, and evaluation criteria.

Intent data and signal-based prospecting can help sales teams identify some of this activity earlier. Rather than proving that a company is actively evaluating a competitor, behavioral and company signals can indicate stronger relevance or better timing for outreach.

Platforms like Gojiberry AI combine ICP targeting with signals such as competitor engagement, social activity, job changes, hiring activity, and other company events to help teams prioritize prospects with a stronger reason to engage now.

Buyer intent data uses observable behavioral and company signals to infer when an account may be researching a category, comparing options, or entering a potential buying window.

Depending on the source, signals may include activity such as visiting tracked pages, researching products on review platforms, engaging with relevant content, comparing vendors, or showing company-level changes that create a reason for outreach.

These signals do not guarantee that someone is ready to buy. Their value is in helping sales teams decide who deserves attention now, rather than treating every ICP-matched account as equally ready for outreach.
Buyer intent data tracks behavioral or company signals that may indicate increased interest in a market, product category, or business problem.

The important distinction is that these signals provide context, not certainty. A prospect interacting with competitor content may be researching the market, learning about a category, or simply engaging with relevant content. It should not automatically be treated as confirmed purchase intent.
Intent and account-scoring data can help sales teams prioritize their limited prospecting capacity.

That does not mean every account displaying an intent signal will convert faster. Instead, it shows why sales teams increasingly combine ICP fit with behavioral context rather than treating every account on a prospecting list equally.

Without this additional context, sales teams may spend substantial time reaching accounts with no obvious reason to engage while prospects showing stronger buying or competitor-related signals receive the same priority as everyone else.
Traditional list-based outbound starts with a static ICP and asks:
Who could buy from us?
Signal-based prospecting adds a second question:
Who fits our ICP and has a relevant reason for us to reach out now?
That reason might be competitor engagement, hiring growth, a job change, funding, relevant social activity, or another behavioral or company signal.
This shifts prospecting away from contacting every ICP-matched account with the same urgency. Instead, teams can prioritize prospects where timing and context make outreach more relevant.

The outbound sales environment continues to change as teams adopt AI, automation, and more precise targeting strategies. These statistics show how prospecting and sales execution are evolving.

MarketIntelo estimates that the outbound sales automation AI market could grow from $4.2 billion in 2025 to $16.8 billion by 2034. The report attributes this growth to factors including greater AI adoption, demand for sales efficiency, and increased investment in automation.

Business Research Insights estimates the global outbound telemarketing market at $11.86 billion in 2026, showing that outbound calling remains a sizable commercial activity even as digital channels continue to expand.
AI is becoming increasingly common across sales organizations, affecting prospecting, lead scoring, forecasting, and outreach workflows.
Salesforce's 2024 State of Sales research found that 83% of sales teams using AI reported revenue growth, compared with 66% of teams not using AI.
The 17-percentage-point difference does not prove that AI caused the revenue growth, but it shows a strong association between AI adoption and higher-growth sales organizations in that dataset.

Gartner found that AI tools save sellers an average of 4.8 hours per week, showing that AI is already delivering measurable efficiency gains across sales organizations. However, Gartner also found that 72% of sales organizations report low reinvestment of those time savings into higher-value sales activities.
Cold outreach remains viable, but generic high-volume prospecting faces a tougher environment. Better targeting, deliverability, relevance, and timing increasingly shape campaign performance.
Gradient Works reported an 8% LinkedIn response rate in its Q1 2024 outbound benchmark, compared with 2.5% for email in the same dataset.
While this is not a current 2026 benchmark, it illustrates why LinkedIn remains an important channel to test for B2B audiences that are active on the platform.
Gradient Works reported a 5% cold-call connect rate in its Q1 2024 benchmark.

Because connect-rates can vary widely by ICP, timing, list quality, and industry, sales teams can use behavioral and company signals as additional context when deciding which prospects to prioritize and when to reach out.

Email remains a core outbound channel, but current benchmarks show that winning replies at scale is difficult. Targeting, segmentation, deliverability, messaging, and follow-up execution all influence performance.

Gartner found that 73% of B2B buyers actively avoid suppliers that send irrelevant outreach. The finding comes from a survey of 632 B2B buyers conducted in August and September 2024 and highlights how poorly targeted prospecting can reduce buyer engagement rather than create it.
In Gradient Works' Q1 2024 dataset, email converted initial outreach to sales-qualified leads at 1.2%, compared with 1.5% for calls and 2.8% for LinkedIn.
Although these figures are not current 2026 benchmarks, they support testing multiple outbound channels rather than depending entirely on email.
LinkedIn's B2B buyer research found that 78% of B2B buyers strongly agree that outreach should be personalized.

That makes personalization an important part of outbound outreach, not just message volume. Gojiberry's subject line generator can help teams generate and refine subject-line ideas so outbound emails feel more relevant and personal to the prospects receiving them.

Signal-based prospecting adds another layer to traditional ICP targeting. Instead of deciding who to contact based only on static firmographic or demographic criteria, teams can use behavioral and company signals to add context around relevance and timing.
Signals do not guarantee that someone is ready to buy, but they can help sales teams decide which prospects may be more relevant to prioritize.
SalesHive cites a 2025 benchmark of roughly 2–3% of cold-call dials resulting in a booked meeting or qualified lead.
Behavioral and company signals can provide additional context for deciding which prospects deserve priority before reps start dialing.
In Gradient Works' Q1 2024 dataset, LinkedIn outreach converted to sales-qualified leads at 2.8%, compared with 1.2% for email.
For teams whose buyers are active on LinkedIn, this benchmark supports testing LinkedIn alongside email rather than relying on a single channel.
Gradient Works' Q1 2024 benchmark put call-to-SQL conversion at 1.5%, between email at 1.2% and LinkedIn at 2.8%.
These differences support testing coordinated multichannel sequences rather than depending on one outreach channel alone.

AI is becoming increasingly common across sales workflows, including prospect research, prioritization, personalization, and outreach automation.
McKinsey's B2B Pulse research found that B2B customers regularly use 10 or more channels to interact with suppliers, up from about five in 2016.
McKinsey research found that companies that effectively sell across multiple channels can achieve more than 40% higher sales ROI than companies relying on a single-channel sales model.
The typical outbound-sourced deal requires 62 days from first contact to close. Engaging the right stakeholders earlier can help teams move opportunities through the sales process more efficiently.
Strategic lead generation fuels the outbound engine. Quality targeting upfront determines downstream conversion rates.

Sales teams that actively engage three or more stakeholders in the buying group see 30% faster close rates. Multi-threading deals can reduce reliance on a single contact and keep opportunities moving when priorities or stakeholders change.
About 70% of booked meetings actually occur. That means roughly three in ten scheduled meetings may still result in no-shows.
When reps follow up within 24 hours of booking, show rates increase to 85%. Timely confirmations and reminder sequences can help reduce preventable no-shows.

North America accounted for 42.8% of revenue share in the outbound sales automation AI market in 2025. The report attributes the region's position partly to early AI adoption and a large enterprise technology base.

The benchmarks increasingly favor more targeted, contextual outbound over undifferentiated high-volume outreach. Static lists and heavily manual workflows can make it harder to prioritize timely opportunities and execute outreach efficiently as volume grows.

Mindflow is an AI automation platform helping enterprise teams orchestrate workflows across thousands of APIs. Their customers include large organizations such as Auchan, and their sales process targets cybersecurity leaders like CISOs and SecOps teams.But generating qualified pipeline for enterprise cybersecurity software is difficult, and traditional outbound methods simply weren't enough.

Before using Gojiberry, Mindflow relied on traditional outbound built on ICP lists: building prospect lists, sending cold outreach campaigns, and manually personalizing messages. But this created a fundamental problem — most prospects had no buying intent.As Nathan Amram, Growth Automation Manager at Mindflow, puts it: "Cold outbound felt too cold. We were reaching out to people without knowing if they were actually interested." To improve results, the team experimented with technical workarounds — tracking followers of competitors, monitoring engagement on cybersecurity influencers, and searching socials manually for niche keywords.But these signals were difficult to monitor and impossible to scale. Mindflow needed a way to systematically detect buying signals.

Mindflow integrated Gojiberry's intent data directly into their internal automation agents. Instead of relying on manual prospecting, the company built an automated intent-driven pipeline that runs daily and automatically identifies new prospects showing relevant signals.
•  Engagement on competitor posts
•  Reactions to cybersecurity influencers
•  Posts mentioning niche keywords — SOAR, security automation, workflow automation, agentic AI
•  Explicit pain signals such as discussions around "alert fatigue"
These signals indicate that a prospect may already be exploring automation solutions.
Mindflow connected the Gojiberry API to its internal growth automation system. The pipeline operates in three steps.
Every day, Mindflow's internal agent pulls fresh leads directly from the Gojiberry API. These leads already contain intent signals indicating potential interest.
The automation system filters leads by company type, job titles (CISO, SecOps, DataOps), geography, and company size. Only high-quality matches enter the pipeline.
A second agent scrapes profiles, generates personalized outreach sequences, and launches campaigns — each sequence automatically adapted based on the intent signal detected.
Nathan describes the system as "a fully automated engine that feeds our outbound with fresh, intent-driven leads every day."
Nathan Amram, Growth Automation Manager at Mindflow

Using Gojiberry signals, Mindflow dramatically improved the performance of their outbound campaigns: a 31–35% reply rate, with 21% of replies converting into MQLs. Even with deliverability limitations restricting sending volume, the system consistently generates qualified conversations.

The business impact is significant. Mindflow sells enterprise software with a ~€25,000 average contract value and a ~18-month sales cycle — which means a single deal generated from intent signals can pay for Gojiberry for years.
For Mindflow, the difference is simple. Instead of contacting random ICP lists, they reach out to prospects already discussing relevant topics:
•  Security teams discussing automation challenges
•  Engineers complaining about alert fatigue
•  Professionals engaging with competitor content
This lets the team start conversations at the moment interest already exists. As Nathan summarizes: "Intent signals change outbound completely. You're no longer guessing who might be interested."

Reliability was essential too. Nathan highlights two key strengths of Gojiberry — a robust API and clear documentation. Once the integration was completed, the system required very little manual intervention: "The API and documentation are excellent. Once everything was connected, it just worked."

Mindflow plans to continue expanding their intent-driven acquisition model, with future initiatives including tracking additional cybersecurity signals, improving signal scoring, and scaling their automated growth agents.Their long-term vision is to build a fully autonomous pipeline generation system powered by AI.The takeaway: enterprise sales teams often struggle with outbound efficiency, and Mindflow solved this by combining AI automation agents with Gojiberry's intent data — a system that continuously identifies high-potential prospects and feeds their outbound engine with qualified leads.As Nathan concludes: "Intent-based lead generation is the future of outbound."

GTE Localize helps global companies scale their localization programs across content, products and international markets.

With approximately $2.5M ARR and a growing presence in North America, the company relies heavily on relationship-building through its community and podcast, Local Reset, led by VP North America Matt Grotenstein.
But like many B2B companies, GTE Localize faced a growing challenge: traditional acquisition channels were becoming less effective.
Email deliverability continued to decline, paid acquisition produced diminishing returns, and manual social outreach was difficult to scale.
The team needed a more predictable way to identify and engage high-intent prospects.
Before Gojiberry, growth primarily came from:
• Referrals and word-of-mouth
• SEO and PPC campaigns
• Cold outbound email
• Manual prospecting through Sales Navigator
Historically, these channels had performed well.
But over time, things changed.

Email response rates dropped significantly due to deliverability issues and changing buyer behavior. Prospects became harder to reach through traditional channels, while socials increasingly became the platforms where business conversations actually happened.
At the same time, manual social prospecting created new challenges:
• Prospect discovery was time-consuming
• Outreach execution was inconsistent
• Sales Navigator workflows required significant manual effort
• Community engagement and podcast visibility were difficult to translate into pipeline
As Matt, the CEO explains:
"Business conversations moved to socials. Email became noisy and less effective."
The team needed a way to identify buying intent before reaching out.
GTE Localize implemented Gojiberry to build an intent-based acquisition system.
Instead of targeting large static prospect lists, the team focused on buying signals.
Specialized agents continuously identify prospects who are:
• Engaging with competitors
• Following industry influencers
• Participating in relevant conversations
• Matching their ideal customer profile
These prospects are automatically routed into multi-step campaigns combining:
• Connection requests
• Personalized messages
• Follow-ups
• Voice notes and video messages
• Email touches when relevant
A key feature prevents overlap between automation and sales reps:
Exit on reply.
As soon as a prospect responds, automation stops and the conversation becomes human.
The team uses Gojiberry to identify prospects who:
• Engage with competitors

• Interact with localization-related content
• Match specific ICP criteria
• Show activity relevant to international growth initiatives
Rather than searching manually inside Sales Navigator, prospects are continuously surfaced through automated intent agents.

The moment a prospect responds, automation immediately stops and the conversation becomes human.
This prevents collisions between sales reps and automation while preserving authentic conversations.
He describes the process as: "Automate everything you would normally do manually on socials."

• More predictable pipeline generation

As Matt summarizes: "Sniper beats shotgun."

Traditional outbound starts with a list.
Intent-driven outbound starts with a signal.
Instead of contacting thousands of prospects with no indication of interest, the team engages professionals who are already demonstrating relevant behavior.

• Scale outreach without increasing headcount

The objective isn't to push prospects into a sales conversation.

Build a repeatable growth engine where intent signals, social outreach and community engagement work together to generate pipeline consistently.

growth depended largely on Todd’s personal network

understand which outreach stages performed best
identify the most engaged prospects
prioritize conversations based on real signals

ChargeMate is an early-stage technology company co-founded by Brad Crist, building an AI operating platform for physical energy infrastructure.

The company started with EV charging, where a major reliability gap exists: even when roughly 98% of charging assets appear online, around one in four charging attempts can still fail. ChargeMate helps charging networks and charge point operators close that gap by improving reliability, recovering revenue, retaining drivers and commercial properties, and reducing operating costs with AI.
Today, ChargeMate has nine B2B customers and is beginning to expand internationally.
But with Brad personally responsible for almost all founder-led sales, the company faced a familiar challenge: how do you scale outbound without turning thoughtful outreach into generic automation?
Before Gojiberry, ChargeMate’s outbound motion was fragmented and highly manual.
Brad used Apollo to find and enrich contacts, experimented with tools like PhantomBuster and Waalaxy for LinkedIn, and personally wrote messages to high-value prospects.
The most personalized outreach worked best — but it was also the hardest to scale.

LinkedIn and email lived in separate workflows. Contacts had to be manually tracked. Sequences often felt formulaic. And maintaining consistent outreach required Brad to repeatedly block time in his calendar for prospecting and follow-ups.
As Brad explains:
“Most of what was successful for us in getting a reply or initiating a meeting was very thoughtful manual outreach, which obviously is great, but doesn't scale.”
The goal wasn't to automate everything.
It was to automate the repetitive work while preserving the human element that made the outreach effective.
ChargeMate implemented Gojiberry to shift from traditional list-based prospecting to signal-based outbound.

Instead of building a static ICP list and contacting everyone on it, Gojiberry continuously identifies prospects based on signals that suggest there may be a relevant reason to start a conversation now.
New leads are surfaced for Brad to review. He decides who is worth contacting, adjusts the messaging when necessary, and lets Gojiberry handle the connections, sequence timing and follow-ups.
As Brad describes it:
“I might spend 15, 20 minutes reviewing some leads. And then I know that those are going to be sent off at the right time. And it kind of works almost on autopilot for me.”
The result is a workflow that scales outbound without removing Brad from the parts where his judgment matters.
For ChargeMate, the biggest change wasn't simply automating more outreach.
It was improving when that outreach happened.
Brad uses several types of signals to identify potential opportunities:
engagement with influential people in the EV and energy ecosystem
competitor engagement
company and executive followers
fundraising
job changes
hiring activity
layoffs
warm lookalike prospects
Some of the strongest results have come from tracking engagement around prominent executives, customers and companies in ChargeMate's industry.
One more unexpected signal has also proved useful: layoffs.
Changes in federal subsidies have put pressure on parts of the EV charging industry. Some operators need to manage growing infrastructure without proportionally increasing headcount.
For ChargeMate, that creates a natural moment to discuss how AI can help teams manage more assets with fewer operational resources.
Rather than reaching out simply because someone matches the ICP, ChargeMate can reach out when there is context behind the conversation.
ChargeMate combines automation with human review throughout the acquisition process:
Signal detection
Gojiberry identifies relevant prospects
Brad reviews and approves leads
AI-assisted personalization
LinkedIn + email sequences
Prospect replies
Brad takes over the conversation
The repetitive execution is automated, while messaging and conversations can remain human-controlled.
“We're automating the things that are time consuming, but still putting a human in the loop [for] the things that deserve a human touch.”

That balance is particularly important for ChargeMate because it sells into a specialized B2B market where relationships matter and burning through a limited ICP with generic messages would be costly.
Brad has taken the workflow a step further by connecting Claude with Gojiberry through MCP.
He created custom Claude skills that understand the type of sequence, copy and tone he wants.
He can take batches of five or ten LinkedIn profiles, use Claude to create contextual messaging, and push those updates into Gojiberry through MCP.
His messaging philosophy is deliberately simple: lead with curiosity rather than immediately entering sales mode.
If a prospect's company has rapidly increased the number of assets it manages, for example, the message can start by asking how the team is handling that additional operational volume.
The goal isn't to make AI write a more elaborate sales pitch.
It's to use available context to open a conversation that feels relevant and natural.
The most significant improvement has been reply rates.
Brad reports seeing 5–8x higher reply rates compared with what he previously experienced using Apollo and more traditional outbound methods.
ChargeMate has also been able to compare signal-based outreach directly against static lists.

Brad uploaded existing Apollo and Unify prospects into sequences. These contacts could still match the ICP well, but because there was no timely signal behind the outreach, they generated a lower hit rate.
“When it's driven by a signal and it's timely, the response rate is quite a bit higher.”
That comparison reinforced the core idea behind ChargeMate's outbound strategy: fit tells you who to target; signals help tell you when to target them.
Gojiberry also saves Brad approximately five hours per week.
Previously, keeping outbound moving meant manually finding prospects, sending messages, managing connections and checking who had responded.
Now he can spend roughly 15–20 minutes reviewing a batch of leads and let the sequences continue running in the background.
For a founder managing product, fundraising, customers and sales simultaneously, the consistency matters as much as the raw time saved.
Outbound no longer depends on Brad remembering to block another prospecting session in his calendar.
Within less than a month of using Gojiberry, ChargeMate had already started conversations with potential customers and partners around the world.
Among the relevant prospects who had replied or expressed interest, Brad estimated that roughly half had progressed to the meeting stage.
Instead of forcing prospects directly toward a demo, the process can start with a relevant message, continue with one or two human exchanges, and naturally progress toward a meeting.
ChargeMate's experience highlights a simple distinction between static prospecting and signal-based outbound:
Matching the ICP doesn't mean it's the right time to reach out.
A static list tells you that someone could be a customer.
A signal gives you context for why a conversation might make sense today.
That signal might be a fundraising event, a hiring change, a layoff, engagement with an industry thought leader or interaction with a relevant company.
Brad saw the difference directly: prospects discovered through timely signals consistently generated stronger response rates than similar contacts coming from static Apollo or Unify lists.
For a company operating in a relatively focused market, that also means ChargeMate can avoid repeatedly cold-messaging the same limited pool of prospects.
ChargeMate plans to continue testing different types of signals rather than relying on a single prospecting strategy.
One agent can focus on competitor and industry influencer engagement, while another tracks company-level buying events such as fundraising, hiring or other organizational changes.
The goal is to compare not just which signals generate replies, but which ultimately generate the most meetings and customers.
Brad also wants to push personalization further, with workflows that gradually learn from the way he edits messages and handles conversations.
The ideal system isn't one that removes the founder from sales.
It's one that handles more of the repetitive work around him so he can focus on the conversations where a human actually makes the difference.
ChargeMate didn't need more prospects.
It needed a better way to identify when those prospects were worth contacting.

By combining signal-based discovery, AI-assisted personalization, multi-channel sequences and human review, ChargeMate has built a founder-led outbound engine that is both more scalable and more relevant.
The early results:
5–8x higher reply rates.
5+ hours saved every week.
~50% of relevant positive conversations progressing to meetings.
For founder-led sales teams, that points to a different way of thinking about outbound:
Don't just find the right person. Find the right reason  and the right moment — to start the conversation.

A business doesn’t fail because the product is bad. Most of the time, it fails because it is offered to the wrong people. You can invest heavily in marketing and spend months building strategies, but if you are knocking on the wrong doors, growth will remain out of reach.

This is where the Ideal Customer Profile, or ICP, comes into play. An ICP is a detailed description of the companies most likely to buy your product or service, get the most value from it, and stay loyal over time. Defining it clearly is one of the most important steps in building a scalable B2B business.

A customer profile tells you broadly who your audience is. It looks at things like demographics, location, and behavior. An ICP goes deeper. It helps you identify the exact type of company you should focus on, based on size, industry, geography, revenue level, pain points, and even cultural fit. In B2B, this means narrowing down to the right accounts, not just the right people.

When your ICP is clear, everything else gets easier. Conversion rates increase, sales cycles shorten, and prospects feel more excitement about your product. It also reduces wasted marketing spend, lowers customer acquisition costs, and decreases churn, because you are serving the right people from the very beginning.

Building your ICP starts with looking at your best customers. Who are the ones that generate the most revenue, churn the least, and show the highest satisfaction? By analyzing what they have in common -industry, company size, location, goals, you begin to see patterns. Adding feedback from those customers makes the picture even clearer. Understanding the steps of their buying journey, the obstacles they face, and the triggers that make them purchase gives you insight into how to find more people like them.

It’s important to start narrow. At the beginning, the smaller and more specific your ICP is, the better. Almost comically specific. Once you prove that you can deliver value consistently to this initial group, you can gradually expand to broader segments. This focus is what transforms random outreach into predictable growth.

Many confuse ICP with buyer persona. The ICP describes the company: its size, budget, industry, and stage of growth. The buyer persona describes the decision-maker inside the company: their job title, goals, and motivations. Both are necessary, but the ICP comes first. Once you know which companies to target, it becomes easier to define the individuals within them.

At GojiberryAI, we built our system around this very idea. We believe finding the right ICP should not take weeks of manual research or endless spreadsheets. By analyzing your offer and identifying high-intent signals in real time, GojiberryAI helps you see exactly which companies fit your ICP and which people inside them are ready for a conversation. Instead of guessing who might be interested, you get a clear direction on who to target and when to reach out.
Your ICP is the foundation of your growth engine. Without it, you risk chasing the wrong leads and stretching your resources thin. With it, you gain clarity, focus, and momentum.

If you are ready to stop guessing and start targeting the right accounts, try the Free ICP Generator by GojiberryAI. Just enter your website and what you sell, and you’ll instantly receive a clear breakdown of your ideal customer profiles.

Moving from a traditional Buyer Persona to an Ideal Customer Profile (ICP) fundamentally shifts your strategy from a descriptive approach to an operational one.

A Buyer Persona often focuses on individual characteristics and storytelling, while an ICP is built to drive execution especially across SEO, paid acquisition, and outbound sales. This transition allows you to align marketing and sales efforts around profiles that are not only relevant, but also actionable and revenue-driven. 💪

With an ICP Generator like Gojiberry, the objective is not just to define who your audience is, but to identify segments that have a real buying potential, clear intent signals, and a strong fit with your offer.It enables you to craft more precise targeting strategies, refine your messaging, and deploy the right calls-to-action to attract and convert these profiles efficiently.

For example, generating multiple ICPs for a SaaS business provides immediate clarity on where to focus your efforts. You can quickly identify high-value segments, understand their specific challenges, and position your solution as a direct answer to their needs.This makes it easier to structure your outbound campaigns, prioritize your acquisition channels, and build a consistent go-to-market strategy.

Once your ICP is clearly defined, the next step is turning it into a repeatable prospecting system on LinkedIn. Instead of searching randomly, you can directly translate your ICP into precise filters such as job title, industry, company size, and geography to surface highly relevant prospects.

From there, refine your search using keywords aligned with your ICP’s pain points and responsibilities.This allows you to identify not just any leads, but decision-makers who actually match your ideal buying profile. The more accurate your ICP, the higher your response rates and conversion potential.

To go further, you can automate this entire process and enrich your targeting with intent signals using tools like Gojiberry.ai.This enables you to move from static ICPs to dynamic lead generation, where your best-fit prospects are continuously identified and ready to engage.

One of the most frequent mistakes is creating an ICP that is too broad. When your targeting lacks precision, your messaging becomes generic, which directly impacts your conversion rates. A strong ICP should be specific enough to clearly identify who you want to target not just “SaaS companies,” but for example “Head of Growth in Series A SaaS with 10–50 employees.”

Another common issue is relying only on assumptions instead of real data. Many teams build ICPs based on intuition rather than analyzing their best existing customers.Without grounding your ICP in actual performance data, you risk targeting segments that look relevant but don’t convert.

It’s also a mistake to treat your ICP as static. Markets evolve, products change, and your best customers today might not be the same tomorrow. Your ICP should be continuously refined based on feedback, campaign performance, and new opportunities.

Finally, many overlook the operational side of an ICP. An ICP is not just a document it should be directly usable for prospecting, especially on platforms like LinkedIn.If you can’t translate your ICP into clear search queries, targeting filters, and outreach angles, it won’t drive real results.

Our mission is to help B2B teams grow smarter by identifying high-intent leads in real time and turning them into conversations that drive revenue. LinkedIn Sales Navigator is one of the most powerful prospecting tools available today, but most users only scratch the surface of what its search filters can do.
Used correctly, these filters save hours of manual searching, sharpen your ICP targeting, and dramatically increase the quality of your pipeline.
In this article, you’ll learn how to master Sales Navigator’s filters, discover proven targeting strategies, and see how Gojiberry AI can help you automate and scale your outreach.
Sales Navigator makes it easy to filter LinkedIn’s vast database down to only those who match your ideal customer profile. You can mix and match filters in categories such as:
Company: headcount, industry, type, location
Role: function, job titles, seniority, years in company
Personal: name, profile language, geography, groups, education
Posted Content: keywords, hashtags, recent activity
Buyer Intent: people who viewed your profile, follow your page, or showed signals of interest
Best Path In: degrees of connection, shared experiences, past colleagues
Recent Updates: job changes, content posted, mentioned in news
Workflow: saved lists, CRM sync, people you’ve engaged with
The result: highly focused searches that surface exactly the decision-makers you want to reach.
Sales Navigator isn’t just about people. It also offers Account Filters to target organizations by attributes like:
Annual revenue
Workforce size and growth
Department growth
Headquarters location
Fortune 500 status
Industry and technologies used
With these filters, you can build Account Lists that mirror your ICP, then switch back to Lead Filters to identify the right decision-makers within those companies.
To truly master Sales Navigator, go beyond the basics. Here are six strategies that consistently deliver results:
Refine your search: Layer filters to match both your ICP and buyer persona.
Create smart saved searches: Automate monitoring of new leads fitting your criteria.
Fine-tune with exclusions: Remove competitors, partners, or irrelevant accounts.
Use Boolean search: Combine keywords with AND, OR, NOT for precision.
Upload CSVs: With Advanced plans, enrich your lists with company data.
Elevate with Gojiberry AI: Export filtered leads into Gojiberry AI to launch automated, personalized outreach sequences.
Filters help you find leads. Gojiberry AI helps you turn those leads into meetings.
Track real-time intent signals
Automate LinkedIn connection requests, follow-ups, and messaging
Build campaigns combining LinkedIn and email touchpoints
Hyper-personalize outreach with AI-powered icebreakers and dynamic variables
Manage multiple inboxes, monitor analytics, and respond to leads without leaving Gojiberry AI
By combining Sales Navigator’s filters with Gojiberry AI’s automation, you create a seamless lead generation engine that runs while you focus on closing deals.

Sales Navigator is worth the investment if you know how to fully leverage its filters.From targeting the right accounts to isolating active, high-intent leads, these features are the backbone of any serious LinkedIn prospecting strategy.
Pair it with Gojiberry AI, and you can scale outreach in a way that feels personal, efficient, and effective.
